67443.q: What was disputed in the early Church about the Letter of James and the Letter of Jude?
a: Whether they belong in the New Testament
Whether they were written in Greek
67443.e: Eusebius of Caesarea distinguished generally accepted writings from disputed ones, the antilegomena. Among the disputed ones he counted the letters of James and Jude.
67443.m: Some writings of the New Testament were disputed for a long time.

67444.q: Which letter did Martin Luther call “a right strawy epistle” in the preface to his New Testament of 1522?
67444.e: Luther missed in James the message of justification by faith alone. He placed it, together with Hebrews, Jude and Revelation, at the end of his New Testament.
67444.m: Luther called the Letter of James a strawy epistle.

a: A Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
A Latin translation of the New Testament
An Aramaic interpretation of the Torah
A Syriac translation of the Gospels
67445.e: The Septuagint was produced from the 3rd century BC for Greek-speaking Jews. The early Christians adopted it as their Old Testament.
67445.m: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.

67446.q: What does the abbreviation LXX for the Septuagint stand for?
a: The number one hundred and twenty
67446.e: “Septuaginta” is Latin for seventy. LXX is the Roman numeral for it and recalls the legend of about seventy translators.
67446.m: The abbreviation LXX stands for the number seventy.

67447.q: According to the Letter of Aristeas, how many translators worked on the Greek translation of the Torah?
67447.e: The Letter of Aristeas tells of six scholars from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. They are said to have completed the translation in 72 days.
67447.m: According to legend, 72 scholars translated the Torah into Greek.

67448.q: According to tradition, in which city was the Septuagint produced?
67448.e: A large Greek-speaking Jewish community lived in Alexandria in Egypt. The Torah was translated into Greek for them.
67448.m: The Septuagint was produced in Alexandria.

67449.q: In which kingdom was the Septuagint produced in Alexandria?
a: In the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt
67449.e: After Alexander the Great, the Ptolemies ruled Egypt. The Letter of Aristeas links the translation, legendarily, with Ptolemy II and his library.
67449.m: The Septuagint was produced in the Greek-influenced Egypt of the Ptolemies.

67450.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible was translated into Greek first?
a: The Torah (the five books of Moses)
67450.e: The Pentateuch was translated first, in the 3rd century BC. The other books followed over roughly the next two centuries.
67450.m: The Septuagint began with the translation of the Torah.

67451.q: Why was the Septuagint so important for the early Christians?
a: It was their Old Testament in Greek
It contained the letters of Paul
It was the first Latin Bible
67451.e: Most early Christians spoke Greek. The authors of the New Testament often quoted the Old Testament from the Septuagint.
67451.m: The early Christians read the Old Testament in Greek in the Septuagint.

a: One of the oldest almost complete Bible manuscripts
67452.e: The 4th-century codex contains large parts of the Septuagint and the whole New Testament. Constantin von Tischendorf found it in St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai.
67452.m: The Codex Sinaiticus is one of the oldest Bible manuscripts.

67453.q: Which Church Father produced the Latin Bible translation known as the Vulgate?
67453.e: Jerome began with the Gospels around 382 on behalf of Pope Damasus I. Later, in Bethlehem, he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew.

67454.q: With which slogan did Jerome justify translating the Old Testament from Hebrew and not just from the Septuagint?
67454.e: Jerome spoke of the “Hebrew truth”. For him, the original Hebrew text carried more weight than the Greek translation.
67454.m: Jerome translated according to the principle of Hebraica veritas.

67455.q: In which town did Jerome live while translating large parts of the Old Testament?
67455.e: Jerome moved to Bethlehem in 386 and lived there in a monastery. There he was also able to study Hebrew with Jewish scholars.

67456.q: What does the Latin name “Vulgata” mean?
67456.e: “Vulgata” comes from “vulgare”, to spread or make common. It means the commonly used Latin version of the Bible.
67456.m: Vulgate means the commonly used version.

67457.q: How did the Catholic Church describe the Vulgate in 1546 for use in the Church?
67457.e: In 1546 a council declared the Vulgate authentic for teaching, preaching and disputation. It thus became the authoritative Latin text of the Catholic Church.
67457.m: In 1546 the Catholic Church declared the Vulgate authentic.

67458.q: Which Latin Bible was published by Pope John Paul II in 1979 as the new official edition?
67458.e: The Nova Vulgata is a revision of the Vulgate based on the original Hebrew and Greek texts. It was prepared after the Second Vatican Council.
67458.m: Since 1979 the Nova Vulgata has been the official Latin Bible.

67459.q: Which Bible text did Johannes Gutenberg print in his famous 42-line Bible?
67459.e: The Gutenberg Bible was made around 1454 in Mainz. It reproduces the Latin Vulgate text that the Church used at the time.

67460.q: Why does Michelangelo's statue of Moses have horns on its head?
a: Because of the translation “cornuta” in the Vulgate
Because of a custom of shepherds in Egypt
Because horns meant wisdom in the Middle Ages
67460.e: In Exodus 34:29 the Hebrew has a word that means “to shine” but is related to “horn”. The Vulgate says Moses's face was “cornuta”, meaning horned.
67460.m: The horned images of Moses go back to a translation in the Vulgate.

67461.q: What does the Greek word “apocryphal” literally mean?
67461.e: Apocryphal means hidden. Originally it referred to writings that were not read publicly in worship.

67462.q: What does the Catholic Church call books such as Tobit, Judith and Sirach, which are called Apocrypha in the Protestant tradition?
67462.e: For the Catholic Church these books belong to the canon, but as a “second” part of it. That is why they are called deuterocanonical.
67462.m: Catholics call the Old Testament Apocrypha deuterocanonical.

67463.q: How did Martin Luther judge the Old Testament Apocrypha in his Bible of 1534?
a: Not equal to Scripture, but useful to read
67463.e: Luther placed them between the Old and New Testaments. He called them books that are not held equal to Holy Scripture, yet are useful and good to read.
67463.m: For Luther the Apocrypha were useful but not equal to Scripture.

67464.q: Near which place in Egypt was the Coptic Gospel of Thomas found in 1945?
67464.e: Near Nag Hammadi, farmers found a jar of papyrus codices in 1945. It held the only complete version of the Gospel of Thomas.
67464.m: The Gospel of Thomas was found near Nag Hammadi in 1945.

67465.q: What does the Gospel of Thomas consist of?
a: Visions of the end of the world
67465.e: The Gospel of Thomas contains no narrative of Jesus's life, death and resurrection. It lists 114 sayings (logia) of Jesus one after another.
67465.m: The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings of Jesus.

67466.q: Where do the names Joachim and Anne for Mary's parents come from?
67466.e: The Protoevangelium of James from the 2nd century tells of Mary's birth and childhood. The names of her parents are not in the New Testament.
67466.m: The names of Mary's parents come from an apocryphal writing.

67467.q: In which church does the Book of Enoch belong to the biblical canon?
67467.e: The Book of Enoch has only survived complete in the old Ethiopian language Ge'ez. In the Ethiopian church it is part of the Bible.
67467.m: The Book of Enoch is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian church.

67468.q: What does it show that the Letter of Jude in the New Testament quotes the Book of Enoch?
a: Early Christians knew and valued the Book of Enoch
The Book of Enoch was only written in the Middle Ages
The letter is by Judas Iscariot
The Book of Enoch is one of the Gospels
67468.e: Jude 14 to 15 quotes a prophecy from the First Book of Enoch. So the book was read in early Christianity, even if it later mostly did not make it into the Bible.
67468.m: The Letter of Jude quotes the Book of Enoch.

67469.q: Which verses of the Gospel of John form the Prologue of John?
67469.e: The Prologue covers the first 18 verses of the first chapter. It serves as a hymn-like introduction to the whole Gospel.
67469.m: The Prologue of John covers John 1:1 to 18.

67470.q: Which image lies behind the Greek verb with which John 1:14 says the Word “dwelt among us”?
67470.e: The verb “eskēnōsen” comes from “skēnē”, tent. It recalls Israel's tent of meeting in the wilderness.
67470.m: According to John 1:14, the Word pitched its tent among people.

67471.q: Which book of the Bible do the first words of the Prologue of John, “In the beginning”, recall?
67471.e: Genesis 1:1 also begins with “In the beginning”. In this way John places the Logos at the start of creation.
67471.m: The Prologue of John links back to the beginning of Genesis.

67472.q: Which theological term is linked with the verse “And the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14)?
67472.e: Incarnation means becoming flesh. The verse says that the divine Logos became human.
67472.m: John 1:14 is the key verse of the Incarnation.

67473.q: In Goethe's Faust, wrestling with the start of John's Gospel, how does Faust finally translate “In the beginning was the ...”?
67473.e: Faust rejects “word”, “meaning” and “power” one after another. In the end he writes “In the beginning was the deed”.
67473.m: In the end, Goethe's Faust translates Logos as deed.

67474.q: Which Greek word stands for the divine “Word” in the Prologue of John?
67474.e: Logos means word, speech or reason. Greek philosophers and the Jewish thinker Philo of Alexandria had already used the term.
67474.m: In the Prologue of John, the divine Word is called Logos in Greek.

67475.q: Which Presocratic philosopher made the Logos, as an ordering law of the world, a basic concept of philosophy?
67475.e: Heraclitus of Ephesus saw in the Logos the rational law that orders all becoming. The term was later taken up by the Stoics.
67475.m: Heraclitus made the Logos a basic concept of philosophy.

67476.q: Which person is mentioned in the middle of the Prologue of John as a witness to the light?
67476.e: Verses 6 to 8 name a man called John, sent by God. He is not the light himself but is to bear witness to it.
67476.m: In the Prologue, John the Baptist bears witness to the light.

67477.q: Why did Paul write the letter to the congregation in Rome?
a: He wanted to prepare them for his visit
He had founded the congregation himself
He wanted to punish them for a quarrel
67477.e: Paul did not yet know the congregation in Rome personally. He presented his teaching to them because he wanted to visit them and travel on from there to Spain.
67477.m: With the Letter to the Romans, Paul prepared his visit to Rome.

67478.q: Which theme is at the centre of the Letter to the Romans?
a: The righteousness of God through faith
The rules of the Temple cult
The history of the people of Israel in Egypt
The miracles of Jesus in Galilee
67478.e: Paul explains that God makes people righteous through faith and not by keeping the law. This idea later shaped the Reformation.
67478.m: The Letter to the Romans is about the righteousness of God through faith.

67480.q: Which biblical figure does Paul use in Romans 4 as an example of God counting faith as righteousness?
67480.e: Paul quotes Genesis 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. That happened before circumcision and before the law.
67480.m: In the Letter to the Romans, Abraham is the model of faith.

67481.q: Which Church Father was converted after the call “Take up and read” while reading a passage from the Letter to the Romans?
67481.e: In his “Confessions”, Augustine describes how he read Romans 13:13 to 14 in Milan in 386. Afterwards he decided to lead a Christian life.
67481.m: Augustine was converted while reading the Letter to the Romans.

67482.q: Which Swiss theologian helped found dialectical theology with his commentary “The Epistle to the Romans” (1919)?
67482.e: Karl Barth wrote the work as a pastor in Safenwil in Aargau. In it he stressed the infinite distance between God and humans.
67482.m: Karl Barth's Epistle to the Romans helped found dialectical theology.

67483.q: How were letters of Paul such as the Letter to the Romans often written?
a: Paul dictated them to a scribe
The congregations wrote them down later
67483.e: In Romans 16:22, the scribe Tertius, who wrote down the letter, sends his own greetings. Dictation was usual in ancient times.
67483.m: Paul often dictated his letters to a scribe.

67484.q: What does the long list of greetings in Romans 16 show about the first Christian congregations?
a: Only men were allowed to help
67484.e: Paul greets many women, for example the deacon Phoebe or Prisca. They led house churches or delivered letters.
67484.m: In the first congregations, women also had important roles.

67485.q: Which theologian, doctor and organist published the history of research “From Reimarus to Wrede” in 1906?
67485.e: Albert Schweitzer showed that many images of Jesus in the 19th century reflected the ideals of their authors. The work is known in English as “The Quest of the Historical Jesus”.
67485.m: Albert Schweitzer wrote the history of research on the life of Jesus.

67486.q: Who published the religion-critical fragments of Hermann Samuel Reimarus between 1774 and 1778?
67486.e: As librarian in Wolfenbüttel, Lessing published them as fragments by an unnamed author. This began the critical question about the historical Jesus.
67486.m: Lessing published the fragments of Reimarus.

67487.q: The appointment of which theologian to the University of Zurich triggered the Züriputsch (Zurich coup) in 1839?
67487.e: In 1835 Strauss had published “The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined” and interpreted many Gospel accounts as myths. The resistance to him led to the fall of Zurich's liberal government.
67487.m: The appointment of David Friedrich Strauss led to the Züriputsch in 1839.

67488.q: Who wrote the book “Vie de Jésus” (Life of Jesus) in 1863, which was very successful in France?
67488.e: Ernest Renan portrayed Jesus as a human, gentle teacher without miracles. The book sparked fierce debates in France.
67488.m: Ernest Renan wrote “Vie de Jésus” in 1863.

67489.q: Which Gospel is regarded by scholars as the oldest?
67489.e: The Gospel of Mark was probably written around AD 70. Matthew and Luke used it as a model.
67489.m: The Gospel of Mark is regarded as the oldest Gospel.

67490.q: What is meant in theology by the “historical Jesus”?
a: Jesus as historical research reconstructs him
Christ as the creed names him
Jesus as old paintings show him
67490.e: Research uses historical methods to ask what Jesus actually said and did. It distinguishes this from the Christ in whom the Church believes.
67490.m: The historical Jesus is the Jesus reconstructed by historical research.

67491.q: What does the “Third Quest” of Jesus research, so called since the 1980s, particularly stress?
a: Jesus as a pure figure of myth
67491.e: The Third Quest uses archaeological and social-historical findings. It consistently understands Jesus as a Jew in 1st-century Galilee.
67491.m: The Third Quest sees Jesus as a Jew of his time.

67492.q: Which 1st-century Jewish historian mentions Jesus outside the Bible?
67492.e: Josephus mentions Jesus in his “Jewish Antiquities” around 93. Later, Roman authors such as Tacitus follow.
67492.m: Flavius Josephus mentions Jesus outside the Bible.

67493.q: According to most scholars, which language did Jesus speak in everyday life?
67493.e: In 1st-century Galilee most people spoke Aramaic. Some Aramaic words of Jesus have been preserved in the Gospels, for example “Abba”.
67493.m: Jesus spoke Aramaic in everyday life.

67494.q: In which city was Erasmus's “Novum Instrumentum omne” published in 1516?
67494.e: The work was printed in Basel. At that time the city was a leading centre of printing and humanism.
67494.m: The Novum Instrumentum was published in Basel in 1516.

67495.q: Which printer published Erasmus's New Testament of 1516?
67495.e: Johann Froben printed many works by Erasmus. Erasmus lived in his house for a time.
67495.m: Johann Froben printed Erasmus's New Testament.

67496.q: Why is the Novum Instrumentum of 1516 so important in the history of the Bible?
a: It was the first published printed Greek New Testament
It was the first complete German Bible
It was the first printed Hebrew Bible
It was the first Bible with pictures
67496.e: The Complutensian Polyglot had already been printed in 1514 but was only distributed years later. Erasmus's edition was the first on the market.
67496.m: In 1516 Erasmus was the first to publish a printed Greek New Testament.

67497.q: What did Erasmus print alongside the Greek text in the Novum Instrumentum?
67497.e: Erasmus placed his own improved Latin version next to the Greek text. Detailed notes were added as well.
67497.m: Erasmus added his own Latin translation to the Greek text.

67498.q: From which language did Luther translate the New Testament at the Wartburg?
67498.e: Luther relied on the Greek text that Erasmus had published. His translation appeared in 1522 as the so-called September Testament.
67498.m: Luther translated from Erasmus's Greek text.

67499.q: Which movement, to which Erasmus belonged, called for a return to the sources (“ad fontes”)?
67499.e: The humanists wanted to read ancient texts in the original language. That is why Erasmus published the New Testament in Greek.
67499.m: “Ad fontes” was the motto of the humanists.

67500.q: How did Erasmus deal with the last verses of Revelation, which were missing from his only manuscript?
a: He translated them back into Greek from the Vulgate
He took them from the Codex Sinaiticus
He wrote them from memory from the Hebrew
67500.e: His manuscript of Revelation lacked verses 22:16 to 21. Erasmus translated them from Latin into Greek, which created new readings.
67500.m: Erasmus translated the end of Revelation back from Latin.

67501.q: What is the Greek text of the New Testament called that is based on Erasmus's editions and was dominant until the 19th century?
67501.e: The name comes from the preface of an Elzevir edition of 1633. It means “the text received by all”.
67501.m: The Textus receptus goes back to Erasmus's editions.

67502.q: In which city did Erasmus die in 1536, where he is buried in the Minster?
67502.e: Erasmus was born around 1466 in Rotterdam but lived in Basel for a long time. There he worked closely with printers and was buried in the Minster.
67502.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam is buried in Basel Minster.

67503.q: What did the Council of Nicaea in 325 state about Jesus Christ?
a: He is of one substance with God the Father
He is a creature of God
67503.e: The council declared the Son to be “homoousios”, that is, of one substance with the Father. In doing so it rejected the teaching of Arius.
67503.m: According to Nicaea, the Son is of one substance with the Father.

67504.q: The Council of Nicaea in 325 was mainly directed against the teaching of which Alexandrian presbyter?
67504.e: Arius taught that the Son was a creature and not eternal like the Father. The Council of Nicaea condemned this teaching.
67504.m: Arianism saw the Son as a creature of God.

67505.q: Which council in 381 confirmed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit?
67505.e: The First Council of Constantinople expanded the Nicene Creed with statements about the Holy Spirit. This produced the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.
67505.m: In 381 the divinity of the Holy Spirit was confirmed in Constantinople.

67506.q: What does the Latin addition “filioque” in the Western creed mean?
67506.e: According to Western teaching, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father “and from the Son”. The Eastern Church rejects this addition; it strained relations up to the Schism of 1054.
67506.m: The filioque dispute still divides the Western and Eastern Churches today.

67507.q: Which early Christian teaching saw Father, Son and Spirit merely as three modes of appearance of a single God?
67507.e: Modalism (also Sabellianism) understood the three as forms appearing one after another. The Church rejected it because it removes the distinction between the persons.
67507.m: Modalism dissolves the three divine persons into mere roles.

67508.q: Which formula sums up the Christian doctrine of the Trinity?
a: One God with three names one after another
67508.e: According to Christian teaching, Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three persons but one single God. Theologians of the 4th century clarified this formula.
67508.m: The Trinity means: one God in three persons.

67509.q: What does the Latin word “trinitas” mean?
67509.e: “Trinitas” comes from “tres”, three. Tertullian introduced the term into Latin theology around 200.

67510.q: Which Sunday in the church year is especially dedicated to the Trinity?
67510.e: On the Sunday after Pentecost many churches celebrate Trinity Sunday. It completes the feasts about Father, Son and Spirit.

67511.q: With which image is St Patrick said to have explained the Trinity to the Irish?
67511.e: According to legend, Patrick showed a three-leaved shamrock: three leaves, one plant. The shamrock became the symbol of Ireland.
67511.m: The shamrock is a well-known image for the Trinity.

67512.q: In which year did the Council of Chalcedon meet?
67512.e: The council took place in autumn 451. It is regarded as the fourth ecumenical council.
67512.m: The Council of Chalcedon met in 451.

67513.q: Where was the ancient city of Chalcedon?
67513.e: Chalcedon lay on the Asian shore of the Bosporus opposite Constantinople. Today the site is the Istanbul district of Kadıköy.
67513.m: Chalcedon is today the Kadıköy district of Istanbul.

67514.q: What does the Council of Chalcedon teach about Jesus Christ?
a: He is true God and true man
He is only God in human form
He is an angel created by God
67514.e: According to Chalcedon, Christ has two natures, a divine and a human one, in one person. They are neither mixed nor separated from each other.
67514.m: According to Chalcedon, Christ has two natures in one person.

67515.q: Which teaching, according to which Christ has only one single nature, did the Council of Chalcedon reject?
67515.e: Monophysitism saw Christ's human nature as absorbed into the divine one. Chalcedon, by contrast, held on to two complete natures.
67515.m: Monophysitism gives Christ only one nature.

67516.q: Which pope, known for his meeting with Attila the Hun, shaped the teaching of Chalcedon?
67516.e: In 452 Leo I is said to have persuaded Attila to withdraw from Italy. A year earlier his doctrinal letter on the two natures of Christ had shaped the Council of Chalcedon.
67516.m: Pope Leo the Great shaped the Christology of Chalcedon.

67517.q: In late antiquity, who called the great councils such as the one at Chalcedon?
67517.e: Since Constantine at Nicaea in 325, the emperors called the councils of the empire. Chalcedon was called by Emperor Marcian in 451.
67517.m: The early councils were called by the emperor.

67518.q: Which city was given a rank of honour right after Rome at the Council of Chalcedon?
67518.e: Canon 28 gave the bishop of Constantinople, as bishop of the “new Rome”, privileges right after Rome. Pope Leo I rejected this canon.
67518.m: Canon 28 strengthened Constantinople's position in the imperial Church.

67519.q: Which of these churches still does not recognise the Council of Chalcedon today?
67519.e: The Coptic, Armenian, Syriac and Ethiopian churches form the Oriental Orthodox churches. They separated from the imperial Church after the council.
67519.m: The Oriental Orthodox churches reject Chalcedon.

67520.q: In which present-day country was Hippo Regius, Augustine's episcopal city?
67520.e: Hippo Regius is today's Annaba in north-eastern Algeria. Augustine was bishop there from 395/396 until his death in 430.
67520.m: Augustine was a bishop in North Africa.

67521.q: Against which monk, who stressed people's ability to do good by their own strength, did Augustine write many works?
67521.e: Pelagius denied that Adam's sin had corrupted the nature of all people. Augustine countered this with his doctrine of original sin.
67521.m: Augustine fought Pelagianism with his doctrine of original sin.

67522.q: What did the followers of Pelagius, whose teaching was condemned in the 5th century, deny?
a: That Adam's sin corrupted all people
That there is only one God
That the Bible is God's word
67522.e: The Pelagians believed that people could live good lives by their own strength. In 418 a synod in Carthage condemned this teaching and confirmed Augustine's doctrine of original sin.
67522.m: Augustine's doctrine of original sin won out against Pelagius.

67523.q: In which New Testament letter did Augustine find the most important passage for his doctrine of original sin?
a: In the Letter to the Romans
In the Letter to the Hebrews
67523.e: In Romans 5:12, Augustine read in Latin that all had sinned in Adam. The Greek text, however, is ambiguous at this point.
67523.m: The Letter to the Romans is the basis of Augustine's doctrine of original sin.

67524.q: According to Augustine, what can save people from being entangled in original sin?
a: Good works by their own strength
67524.e: For Augustine, humanity since Adam is a “condemned mass” (massa damnata). Only God's undeserved grace saves people from it.
67524.m: For Augustine, only God's grace saves people from sin.

67525.q: What is the Latin technical term for original sin?
67525.e: Peccatum originale means “sin of origin”. It is distinguished from personal sins committed, the peccata actualia.
67525.m: Original sin is called peccatum originale in Latin.

67526.q: According to Catholic teaching, which sacrament removes original sin?
67526.e: In 1546 the Council of Trent declared that baptism takes away the guilt of original sin. It also confirmed the baptism of small children.
67526.m: According to Catholic teaching, baptism removes original sin.

67527.q: What is the name of Augustine's main autobiographical work?
67527.e: In the “Confessions”, Augustine describes his path up to his conversion in Milan in 386. The work is written as a prayer to God.
67527.m: The Confessiones are regarded as the first great autobiography of the West.

67528.q: Which event led Augustine to write “De civitate Dei” (The City of God)?
a: the division of the empire in 395
67528.e: After Rome was sacked by the Visigoths, pagans blamed the Christians. Augustine replied with his teaching of the two cities.
67528.m: The City of God was written as an answer to the sack of Rome.

67529.q: Which principle of the Reformation says that people are saved by grace alone?
67529.e: Sola gratia stresses that salvation is an undeserved gift from God. It is one of the “solas” of the Reformation.
67529.m: Sola gratia means that people cannot earn salvation.

67530.q: Whose doctrine of grace did the Synod of Orange confirm in its main features in 529?
67530.e: The synod taught that even the beginning of faith is a work of grace. It thereby rejected the view that people could come to faith by their own strength.
67530.m: The Synod of Orange confirmed Augustine's doctrine of grace.

67531.q: Which reformer taught double predestination in Geneva?
67531.e: Calvin taught that God had predestined some to salvation and others to damnation. His teaching shaped Reformed churches worldwide.
67531.m: Calvin taught the doctrine of double predestination in Geneva.

67532.q: Which 17th-century movement centred on the abbey of Port-Royal held a strict Augustinian doctrine of grace?
67532.e: Jansenism goes back to Cornelius Jansen's work “Augustinus” of 1640. Blaise Pascal was also close to it.
67532.m: Jansenism stressed the power of grace and human weakness.

67533.q: Which two things did the Jesuit Luis de Molina want to reconcile in the dispute over grace?
67533.e: For this, Molina developed the doctrine of God's middle knowledge. The Dominicans around Báñez fiercely opposed him.
67533.m: Molina wanted to combine God's foreknowledge and human freedom.

67534.q: Which famous mathematician and philosopher defended the followers of Port-Royal against the Jesuits in the dispute over grace?
67534.e: Pascal sharply attacked the Jesuits in his “Provincial Letters”. He was close to the Jansenists of Port-Royal, whose teaching the pope had condemned in 1653.
67534.m: Blaise Pascal was on the side of Port-Royal.

67535.q: In Catholic teaching, what is the lasting grace called that sanctifies a person inwardly?
67535.e: Sanctifying grace (gratia habitualis) is a lasting state of the soul. Helping grace, by contrast, works in individual actions.
67535.m: Sanctifying grace is a lasting state of the soul.

67536.q: Which synod in 1618/19 confirmed the Calvinist doctrine of grace against the Remonstrants?
67536.e: The Remonstrants followed Jacobus Arminius and rejected unconditional election. The Synod of Dort condemned their teaching.

67537.e: It means that bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ in their substance. The Fourth Lateran Council made the term binding in 1215.

67538.q: At which meeting in 1529 did Luther and Zwingli argue in vain about the Lord's Supper?
67538.e: Landgrave Philip of Hesse invited the reformers to Marburg. They agreed on many points, but not on the question of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper.
67538.m: In Marburg in 1529, agreement between Luther and Zwingli failed.

67539.q: According to the doctrine of transubstantiation, what remains unchanged in the bread and wine?
a: Only the weight of the wine
67539.e: The substance of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ. The outer properties, the accidents, remain.
67539.m: In the consecration, the substance changes, not the outer form.

67540.q: Which term is often used for Luther's teaching on the Lord's Supper, although he hardly used it himself?
67540.e: Luther taught that Christ is really present “in, with and under” the bread and wine. Bread and wine remain.
67540.m: Luther held on to the real presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper.

67541.q: Which Zurich reformer understood the words of institution in the sense of “This signifies my body”?
67541.e: Zwingli interpreted the Lord's Supper as a memorial meal. For him, bread and wine are signs and not the body of Christ itself.
67541.m: Zwingli understood the Lord's Supper symbolically as a memorial meal.

67542.q: Which two Reformed cities reached agreement on the Lord's Supper in the Consensus Tigurinus of 1549?
67542.e: Heinrich Bullinger from Zurich and John Calvin from Geneva drew up the consensus. It linked the two centres of the Reformed church.
67542.m: The Consensus Tigurinus linked Zurich and Geneva in 1549.

67543.q: Which Catholic feast especially celebrates the lasting presence of Christ in the Eucharist?
67543.e: Pope Urban IV introduced Corpus Christi for the whole Church in 1264. In the Catholic cantons of Switzerland, processions are held for it.
67543.m: Corpus Christi is the feast of the Eucharist.

67544.q: What is the part of the Mass called in which, according to Catholic teaching, the change takes place?
67544.e: During the Eucharistic Prayer the priest speaks Jesus's words of institution. At this moment, according to Catholic teaching, the bread and wine are changed.
67544.m: The change happens at the consecration in the Eucharistic Prayer.

67545.q: What does the term “eschatology” literally mean?
67545.e: The Greek word “eschatos” means “the last”. Eschatology deals with death, judgement, resurrection and the completion of the world.
67545.m: Eschatology asks about the end and goal of history.

67546.q: What is the expected return of Christ at the end of time called?
67546.e: Parousia is Greek for “arrival” or “presence”. The creed says that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead.
67546.m: The Parousia is the expected return of Christ.

67547.q: According to Catholic teaching, what is the state of purification after death called?
67547.e: Purgatory was taught at the councils of Florence and Trent, among others. The reformers rejected it.
67547.m: Purgatory is regarded as a place of cleansing before seeing God.

67548.q: Which teaching expects a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth?
67548.e: Chiliasm appeals to Revelation 20. The Greek word “chilioi” means thousand.
67548.m: Chiliasm hopes for a thousand-year kingdom of peace.

67549.q: What does the doctrine of universal reconciliation (apokatastasis) mean?
a: In the end all creatures return to God
The dead are reborn as animals
67549.e: The Church Father Origen hoped that in the end all creatures would be reconciled with God. This teaching was condemned in the 6th century.
67549.m: Apokatastasis is the hope for the restoration of all things.

67550.q: What does the Latin term “visio beatifica” mean in Christian teaching?
a: A vision of the end of the world
67550.e: Visio means vision, beatus means blessed. It means that the blessed see God face to face.
67550.m: The visio beatifica is the blessed vision of God.

67551.q: What is the medieval sequence about the Last Judgement called that begins with the words “Day of wrath”?
67551.e: The “Dies irae” is attributed to Thomas of Celano. For a long time it was part of the Requiem Mass and was often set to music, for example by Mozart and Verdi.
67551.m: The Dies irae describes the day of the Last Judgement.

67552.q: Which theologian, who later worked as a doctor in Lambaréné, held the view of “thoroughgoing eschatology”?
67552.e: Albert Schweitzer believed that Jesus had expected the end of the world soon. His interpretation shaped research in the 20th century.
67552.m: Albert Schweitzer stressed Jesus's expectation of an imminent end.

67553.q: Which Basel theologian wrote in 1922 that a Christianity that is not wholly eschatology has nothing to do with Christ?
67553.e: Karl Barth wrote the sentence in the second edition of his commentary on one of Paul's letters. In it he stressed faith's orientation towards what is to come; from 1935 he taught in Basel.
67553.m: Karl Barth put eschatology at the centre of faith.

67554.q: What does the word “theodicy” literally mean?
67554.e: The word is made up of Greek “theos” (God) and “dike” (justice). It asks how God can be just in the face of suffering.
67554.m: Theodicy asks about God's justice in suffering.

67555.q: Which philosopher wrote the essay “On the Failure of All Philosophical Attempts at Theodicy” in 1791?
67555.e: The essay appeared in 1791 in the “Berlinische Monatsschrift”. Kant thought it impossible to prove God's wisdom in the course of the world with theoretical reason.
67555.m: Kant considered philosophical theodicies to have failed.

67556.q: What did Leibniz claim about our world?
a: It is the best of all possible worlds.
It is the only conceivable world.
It is the work of an evil god.
It is a mere illusion of the senses.
67556.e: In his “Essays on Theodicy” of 1710, Leibniz argues that an all-wise and all-good God created the best of all possible worlds. Even evil has its meaning in it.
67556.m: Leibniz considered our world the best of all possible worlds.

67557.q: Which disaster of 1755 particularly shook the optimism of the Enlightenment?
67557.e: The earthquake, with a tsunami and fires, destroyed Lisbon on All Saints' Day 1755. Many thinkers then asked anew how God could allow such suffering.
67557.m: The Lisbon earthquake set off a major debate on theodicy.

67558.q: In which novel does Voltaire mock Leibniz-style optimism?
67558.e: The character Pangloss claims, despite all misfortunes, that all is for the best. Voltaire published the novel in 1759.
67558.m: In Candide, Voltaire mocked philosophical optimism.

67559.q: To which ancient philosopher is the argument attributed that God cannot be both good and all-powerful if evil exists?
67559.e: The Christian writer Lactantius passes this argument down as Epicurus's idea. Whether it really comes from Epicurus is disputed.
67559.m: The argument attributed to Epicurus poses the question of theodicy sharply.

67560.q: With which term did Augustine interpret evil as the absence of good?
67560.e: For Augustine, evil has no being of its own. It is a lack of something good, just as illness is a lack of health.
67560.m: For Augustine, evil is a lack of good.

67561.q: Which book of the Old Testament puts the question of the suffering of a righteous man at its centre?
67561.e: Job loses his possessions, children and health, although he is righteous. His friends and God himself wrestle with him for an answer.
67561.m: The Book of Job is the basic biblical text on the question of suffering.

67562.q: How does the so-called “Free Will Defence” explain that evil exists despite a good God?
a: By the freedom of humans, who can also do evil
By the chance of nature alone
By saying that evil does not exist at all
67562.e: A world with truly free creatures could be more valuable, even if they do evil. The US philosopher Alvin Plantinga made the argument well known.
67562.m: The Free Will Defence explains evil by human freedom.

67563.q: Which work by Thomas Aquinas sets out the faith mainly with rational arguments for non-Christians?
67563.e: The Summa contra gentiles was written around 1259 to 1265. It argues largely from reason, because non-Christians do not accept the Bible as an authority.
67563.m: The Summa contra gentiles relies on reasons rather than Bible quotations.

67564.q: How many ways of proving God's existence does Thomas Aquinas present in the Summa theologiae?
67564.e: Thomas calls them the “quinque viae”. They reason from observations in the world to God as the cause.
67564.m: Thomas presented five ways of proving God's existence.

67565.q: From which phenomenon does the first of Thomas's proofs of God start?
67565.e: Everything that moves is moved by something else. Since this cannot go on forever, Thomas concludes that there is a first unmoved mover.
67565.m: Thomas's first way leads to the unmoved mover.

67566.q: Which order did Thomas Aquinas belong to?
67566.e: Against his family's wishes, Thomas joined the Dominican Order of Preachers. He taught in Paris, among other places.

67567.q: After a profound experience in December 1273, what did Thomas Aquinas compare all his work to?
67567.e: According to tradition, Thomas said that everything he had written seemed to him like straw. After that he wrote no more.
67567.m: In the end, Thomas considered his work straw compared to what he had seen.

67568.q: According to Thomas Aquinas, how can people speak meaningfully about God?
67568.e: Terms like “good” apply to God neither in exactly the same way (univocally) nor in a completely different way (equivocally) as to creatures. They apply in a similar, analogous sense.
67568.m: According to Thomas, we speak about God in analogies.

67569.q: Which ancient philosopher did Thomas Aquinas combine with the Christian faith?
67569.e: Thomas adopted many of Aristotle's concepts and ways of thinking. He wanted to show that reason and faith do not contradict each other.
67569.m: Thomas combined Aristotle's thought with Christianity.

67570.q: What is the main work of Thomas Aquinas called?
67570.e: The Summa theologiae is a large, systematic account of theology. Thomas was unable to finish it before his death in 1274.
67570.m: Thomas's main work is the Summa theologiae.

67571.q: Which principle describes the relationship between grace and nature in Thomas?
67571.e: In Latin the sentence is “gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit”. So faith builds on reason and does not abolish it.
67571.m: For Thomas, grace does not abolish nature but perfects it.

67572.q: What did scholasticism want to achieve in the Middle Ages?
a: To think through faith with reason and logic
To study only the natural sciences
67572.e: Scholastics set arguments and counter-arguments against each other and resolved contradictions with reason. Abelard shaped this method with his work “Sic et non”.

a: At the new universities such as Paris and Oxford
At the courts of the caliphs
67573.e: From the 12th and 13th centuries, universities arose in Europe. There, scholastic theology was the most important subject.
67573.m: Scholasticism flourished at the medieval universities.

67574.q: Which position in the dispute over universals regards general concepts as mere names?
67574.e: For nominalism, only individual things exist. Concepts like “human” are signs for many individuals but have no reality of their own.
67574.m: Nominalism regards general concepts as names without being of their own.

67575.q: Which English Franciscan gave his name to the principle of parsimony “Ockham's razor”?
67575.e: The principle demands that you make no more assumptions than necessary. Today it is also applied in the natural sciences.
67575.m: Ockham's razor calls for the simplest possible explanations.

67576.q: Which mendicant order, founded by Francis of Assisi, produced important scholastics such as Duns Scotus?
67576.e: Alongside the Dominicans, the Franciscans shaped scholasticism. They included Bonaventure, Duns Scotus and William of Ockham.

67577.q: Which Dominican is regarded as the most important theologian of scholasticism?
67577.e: In the 13th century, Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle's philosophy with the Christian faith. His main work is the Summa theologiae.
67577.m: Thomas Aquinas is the most important thinker of scholasticism.

67578.q: Which subject was regarded in scholasticism as the “handmaid of theology” (ancilla theologiae)?
67578.e: Philosophy was to serve theology with rational concepts and arguments. This order of rank was later called into question by the Enlightenment.

67579.q: Through whom did the scholastics get to know many works of Aristotle?
a: Through Arab scholars and their translations
67579.e: Many of Aristotle's writings had been lost in the West. Arab scholars such as Averroes of Córdoba had preserved and commented on them, and through translations they reached the universities.
67579.m: Arab scholars passed on Aristotle to scholasticism.

67580.q: Which order did Meister Eckhart belong to?
67580.e: Eckhart joined the Dominican order in Erfurt and later taught in Paris. Some of his statements were condemned as heresy in 1329, after his death.

67581.q: Which theme is at the centre of many of Meister Eckhart's German sermons?
a: the birth of God in the soul
the crusade to the Holy Land
67581.e: Eckhart preached that God gives birth to his Son in the ground of the soul. For this, a person must let go of everything.
67581.m: The birth of God in the soul is a core theme of Eckhart.

67582.q: Which term of Eckhart's refers to inner freedom from everything created?
67582.e: Eckhart valued detachment more highly than many other virtues. It means letting go of all ties so that God can work.
67582.m: According to Eckhart, detachment frees the soul for God.

67583.q: With which image does Meister Eckhart describe the innermost core of the soul?
67583.e: For Eckhart, the little spark is the uncreated part of the soul in which it touches God. He also calls it the ground of the soul.
67583.m: According to Eckhart, the soul touches God in the little spark of the soul.

67584.q: In which language did Meister Eckhart give his well-known sermons?
67584.e: Eckhart wrote scholarly works in Latin but preached to nuns and lay people in the vernacular. In doing so he coined many new German words.
67584.m: Eckhart enriched the German language with many philosophical terms.

67585.q: Which well-known 14th-century German mystic was in contact with nuns at Töss convent near Winterthur?
67585.e: Henry Suso was a pupil of Meister Eckhart. The Dominican nun Elsbeth Stagel from Töss recorded his letters and conversations.
67585.m: Henry Suso links German mysticism with Winterthur.

67586.q: Which hermit in the Ranft in Obwalden is regarded as Switzerland's best-known mystic?
67586.e: Nicholas of Flüe lived as a hermit in the Ranft from 1467. He was canonised in 1947 and is regarded as the patron saint of Switzerland.
67586.m: Brother Klaus is Switzerland's best-known mystic.

67587.q: Which woman mystic wrote “The Flowing Light of the Godhead”?
67587.e: Mechthild lived as a Beguine in Magdeburg and later in Helfta convent. Her work is one of the earliest mystical writings in German.
67587.m: Mechthild of Magdeburg wrote early mystical texts in German.

67588.q: In which work did Anselm of Canterbury formulate the ontological proof of God?
67588.e: Anselm wrote the Proslogion around 1077/78 in the abbey of Bec in Normandy. In it he looks for a single argument for God's existence.
67588.m: Anselm's proof of God is in the Proslogion.

67589.q: How does Anselm define God in his ontological argument?
a: as that than which nothing greater can be thought
as the first cause of all motion
as the necessary being behind everything contingent
as the designer of purposeful nature
67589.e: In Latin the formula is “id quo maius cogitari non potest”. If this being existed only in thought, one could think of a greater one that also really exists.
67589.m: For Anselm, God is the greatest that can be thought.

67590.q: Which monk criticised Anselm with the example of a perfect lost island?
67590.e: Gaunilo argued that, by Anselm's logic, an imagined most perfect island would also have to exist. Anselm replied that his argument applied only to God.
67590.m: Gaunilo's island example is the oldest objection to Anselm.

67591.q: Which philosopher criticised the argument with the sentence “Being is obviously not a real predicate”?
67591.e: In the “Critique of Pure Reason”, Kant argues that existence adds no property to a concept. A hundred real thalers contain no more than a hundred possible ones.
67591.m: Kant denied that existence is a property.

67592.q: Which modern philosopher included the ontological argument in his “Meditations”?
67592.e: In the fifth Meditation, Descartes concludes from the concept of the perfect being that it exists. Just as the sum of its angles belongs to a triangle, existence belongs to God.
67592.m: Descartes revived the ontological argument in the modern era.

67593.q: In which town near the Swiss border was Anselm of Canterbury born?
67593.e: Anselm was born in Aosta around 1033. He became a monk in Normandy and later Archbishop of Canterbury.
67593.m: Anselm of Canterbury came from Aosta.

67594.q: Which logician formulated a modal-logic version of the ontological proof of God in the 20th century?
67594.e: Gödel worked out his proof with concepts of modal logic. It was only published in 1987, nine years after Gödel's death.
67594.m: Kurt Gödel carried the ontological proof of God over into modal logic.

67595.q: What is meant by apostolic succession in the narrower sense?
a: the unbroken line of consecration of bishops since the apostles
the order of the books in the New Testament
the election of popes by the cardinals
the sequence of the ecumenical councils
67595.e: Bishops are consecrated by other bishops through the laying on of hands. This is meant to form a chain reaching back to the apostles.
67595.m: Apostolic succession links the bishops with the apostles.

67596.q: How did the early Church argue against the Gnostics that it had the true teaching?
a: With lists of bishops going back to the apostles
With the size of its churches
67596.e: In “Against Heresies”, Irenaeus of Lyon names the bishops of Rome since the apostles. The true teaching, he says, is secured by this succession.
67596.m: Irenaeus based orthodoxy on the succession of bishops.

67597.q: With which act is apostolic succession passed on at the consecration of a bishop?
a: With the laying on of hands
With the handing over of a key
67597.e: At the consecration of a bishop, bishops lay their hands on the new bishop and pray. This is meant to pass on authority in a chain since the apostles.
67597.m: A bishop is consecrated by the laying on of hands.

67598.q: How did Pope Leo XIII judge the ordinations of the Anglican Church in 1896?
67598.e: In the bull Apostolicae curae, Leo XIII based his judgement on flaws in the ordinations under Edward VI. The Anglican Church rejected the judgement.
67598.m: In 1896 Rome declared Anglican ordinations invalid.

67599.q: Why, since the Council of Nicaea, do several bishops usually take part in the consecration of a bishop?
a: The consecration should be supported by the whole Church
A single bishop is not allowed to travel
The emperor demanded witnesses for tax purposes
It is the only way to elect the pope
67599.e: Canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea required the participation of as many bishops of the province as possible, but at least three. This shows that the new bishop is received into the community of bishops.
67599.m: A bishop is usually consecrated by three bishops.

67600.q: In which union did Old Catholic churches with episcopal succession, including the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland, join together in 1889?
67600.e: The Union of Utrecht was founded in 1889 by bishops from the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland. The Archdiocese of Utrecht had passed on its episcopal consecrations independently since the 18th century.
67600.m: The Old Catholic churches form the Union of Utrecht.

67601.q: How do the Reformed churches mainly understand the apostolicity of the Church?
a: as faithfulness to the teaching of the apostles
as an unbroken chain of consecrations
as the succession of Peter in Rome
as owning relics of the apostles
67601.e: For Zwingli and Calvin, agreement with the Gospel counts for more than a historical line of consecrations. This is called succession in teaching.
67601.m: For the Reformed, the Church is apostolic through faithfulness to the teaching.

67602.q: What did Anglicans and Nordic Lutherans agree in the Porvoo Declaration of 1992?
a: Mutual recognition of their bishops' ministries
67602.e: In the Porvoo Declaration, the churches recognise each other's episcopal ministries. It is named after the Finnish town of Porvoo.
67602.m: The Porvoo Declaration links Anglican and Lutheran churches of Northern Europe.

67603.q: In which city did the presbyter Arius, who started the Arian controversy, work?
67603.e: Arius was a priest (presbyter) in Alexandria in Egypt. There, around 318, he came into conflict with his bishop Alexander over the nature of Christ.
67603.m: The Arian controversy began in Alexandria.

67604.q: What did Arius teach about the Son of God?
a: The Son is a creature and not eternal like the Father.
The Son had only an apparent body and did not really suffer.
The Son is only a form in which the one Father appears.
The Son was only adopted at his baptism in the Jordan.
67604.e: Arius taught that the Son was created by the Father and that there was a time when he did not exist. In doing so he questioned the full divinity of Christ.
67604.m: Arius regarded the Son as a creature of the Father.

67605.q: Which Frankish king was baptised as a Catholic, not an Arian, and so won the support of the Gallo-Roman bishops?
67605.e: Many Germanic rulers were Arian Christians, but the population of Gaul was Catholic. Clovis's Catholic baptism around 500 united Franks and Gallo-Romans.
67605.m: As king of the Franks, Clovis chose the Catholic faith.

67606.q: With which Greek term did the Council of Nicaea describe the relationship of the Son to the Father?
67606.e: The Nicene Creed states that the Son is “homoousios”, that is, of the same substance as the Father. The term was aimed directly at the Arian teaching.
67606.m: According to the Council of Nicaea, the Son is of the same substance as the Father.

67607.q: Which bishop of Alexandria was the main opponent of the Arians in the 4th century and was exiled several times for it?
67607.e: Athanasius defended the Nicene Creed all his life. Under changing emperors he was sent into exile five times.
67607.m: Athanasius was the great defender of the Nicene Creed against the Arians.

67608.q: Which council in 381 confirmed the Creed of Nicaea and largely ended the Arian controversy in the Roman Empire?
67608.e: The Council of Constantinople in 381 expanded the Creed of Nicaea, mainly with statements about the Holy Spirit. This produced the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.
67608.m: In 381 the Council of Constantinople confirmed the faith of Nicaea.

67609.q: Which bishop translated the Bible into Gothic in the 4th century and spread an Arian form of Christianity among the Goths?
67609.e: Wulfila created his own Gothic script for his Bible translation. Through his mission, many Germanic peoples first became Arian Christians.
67609.m: Wulfila translated the Bible into Gothic.

67610.q: Which emperor declared the Nicene faith binding for all inhabitants of the empire with the edict “Cunctos populos” in 380?
67610.e: Theodosius I issued the edict “Cunctos populos”, the Edict of the Three Emperors, in Thessaloniki in 380. This made the Nicene faith the binding religion of the empire.
67610.m: In 380 Theodosius I made the Nicene faith binding.

67611.q: Which Church Father produced the Latin Bible translation later called the “Vulgate”?
67611.e: In the late 4th century, Jerome made a new Latin translation of large parts of the Bible, translating the Old Testament largely from Hebrew. This translation became the authoritative Bible in the West.

67612.q: Which work did Augustine write in response to the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410?
67612.e: Pagans accused the Christians of causing Rome's fall by turning away from the old gods. Augustine replied with “De civitate Dei”, in which he contrasts the earthly city with the City of God.
67612.m: After the sack of Rome, Augustine wrote The City of God.

67613.q: Which bishop of Milan baptised the later Church Father Augustine in 387?
67613.e: In Milan, Augustine got to know the sermons of Ambrose. He was baptised by him on Easter night in 387.

67614.q: What is the field of theology called that studies the life and work of the Church Fathers?
67614.e: The term patristics comes from the Latin “pater”, father. It studies the writings of the early Christian theologians up to about the 7th or 8th century.
67614.m: Patristics studies the writings of the Church Fathers.

67615.q: Which Church Father and Patriarch of Constantinople was given the nickname “Golden Mouth” for his preaching?
67615.e: The Greek nickname “Chrysostomos” means “golden mouth”. John was Patriarch of Constantinople around 400 and was regarded as the greatest preacher of the Eastern Church.
67615.m: John Chrysostom was called Golden Mouth because of his sermons.

67616.q: Which three 4th-century theologians are called the “Cappadocian Fathers”?
a: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa
67616.e: The three came from Cappadocia in Asia Minor. They decisively shaped the doctrine of the Trinity.
67616.m: Basil and the two Gregorys are called the Cappadocian Fathers.

67617.q: Which Church Father wrote a famous account of his life in the “Confessions”?
67617.e: In the “Confessiones”, written around 400, Augustine tells of his youth, his wrong turns and his conversion. The work is regarded as the first great autobiography in world literature.
67617.m: Augustine wrote his life story in the “Confessions”.

67618.q: Who, together with Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine, makes up the four great Latin Church Fathers?
67618.e: The four Doctors of the Church of the West were given special honour by Pope Boniface VIII in 1298. The fourth is Pope Gregory I, who lived around 600.
67618.m: The Western Church honours four great Latin Church Fathers.

67619.q: What does the abbreviation “OSB” after a Benedictine monk's name stand for?
67619.e: OSB means “Order of Saint Benedict”. However, the Benedictines are not a centrally run order but a federation of largely independent monasteries.

67620.q: From which Aramaic word does the title “abbot”, who leads the monastery according to the Rule of St Benedict, come?
67620.e: “Abba” means father. According to the Rule of St Benedict, the abbot represents Christ in the monastery and should care for the monks like a father.

67621.q: Which famous monastery did Benedict of Nursia found in Italy around 529?
67621.e: Benedict founded Monte Cassino between Rome and Naples and probably wrote his Rule there. His sister Scholastica lived nearby.
67621.m: Benedict founded the monastery of Monte Cassino.

67622.q: Of what has Benedict of Nursia been the patron saint since 1964?
67622.e: In 1964 Pope Paul VI honoured Benedict's importance for the Christian culture of the West. The Benedictine monasteries had spread learning and faith all over Europe.
67622.m: Since 1964 Benedict has been the patron saint of Europe.

67623.q: What does the Rule of St Benedict call the monks' common choir prayer, to which nothing should be preferred?
67623.e: Benedict calls the Liturgy of the Hours the “Opus Dei”. Chapter 43 says that nothing should be put before the divine office.
67623.m: For Benedictines, choir prayer is the work of God.

67624.q: Which special vow of the Benedictines binds a monk permanently to his monastic community?
67624.e: Besides obedience and monastic way of life, a Benedictine promises stability. He usually stays in his monastery for life.
67624.m: A Benedictine vows stability in his community.

67625.q: In which Swiss Benedictine abbey is a famous Black Madonna venerated?
67625.e: Einsiedeln Abbey in the canton of Schwyz has been a Benedictine abbey since the 10th century. The Chapel of Grace with the Black Madonna is an important place of pilgrimage.
67625.m: Einsiedeln Abbey is a major place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.

67626.q: In which town in Umbria was Benedict born around 480?
67626.e: Benedict came from Nursia, today's Norcia in Umbria. His byname comes from it.
67626.m: Benedict came from Nursia in Umbria.

67627.q: During which period was Gregory the Great pope?
67627.e: Gregory I was elected pope in 590 during a plague epidemic. He died in Rome in 604.
67627.m: Gregory the Great was pope from 590 to 604.

67628.q: Where did Gregory the Great send the monk Augustine and companions on a mission in 596?
a: To the Saxons in northern Germany
67628.e: Augustine of Canterbury landed in Kent in 597 and baptised King Æthelberht. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.
67628.m: Gregory sent missionaries to the Anglo-Saxons.

67629.q: Which humble self-description did Gregory the Great turn into a fixed title of the popes?
67629.e: “Servus servorum Dei” means “Servant of the servants of God”. Gregory deliberately used the expression as a contrast to the honorary titles of other bishops.
67629.m: Since Gregory, the pope has called himself Servant of the servants of God.

67630.q: What role did Gregory have for several years in Constantinople before he was elected pope?
a: Papal envoy at the imperial court (apocrisiarius)
Teacher at the imperial law school
67630.e: Around 579, Pope Pelagius II sent Gregory as apocrisiarius to the emperor's court. There he got to know the politics of the Eastern Roman Empire at close quarters.
67630.m: Before his election as pope, Gregory was an envoy in Constantinople.

67631.q: What did Gregory the Great do with his wealth before he became a monk?
a: He gave it away and founded monasteries
He bought the papacy with it
He built himself a palace in Rome
67631.e: Gregory came from a noble Roman family and was prefect of the city of Rome around 573. Afterwards he gave away his wealth and founded monasteries.
67631.m: Gregory gave his wealth to monasteries before becoming a monk.

67632.q: About which founder of an order has the most important biography come down to us from Gregory the Great?
67632.e: The second book of Gregory's “Dialogues” tells of the life and miracles of Benedict. Francis, Dominic and Ignatius only lived centuries later.
67632.m: Gregory's Dialogues tell the life of Benedict.

67633.q: Which work by Gregory the Great became a handbook for bishops and pastors in the Middle Ages?
67633.e: In the “Regula pastoralis” (Pastoral Care), Gregory describes how a shepherd of the Church should live and preach. The work was translated into Old English at an early date.
67633.m: With the Regula pastoralis, Gregory wrote a book for pastors.

67634.q: Which Roman building got its present name from a legend from Gregory's time?
67634.e: During a procession praying for an end to the plague in 590, the Archangel Michael is said to have appeared above Hadrian's tomb and sheathed his sword. Since then the building has been called Castel Sant'Angelo (Castle of the Holy Angel).
67634.m: Castel Sant'Angelo owes its name to a legend about the plague of 590.

67635.q: In which year was the abbey of Cluny in Burgundy founded?
67635.e: Cluny was founded in 910 and followed the Rule of St Benedict. It was the starting point of one of the most important monastic reforms of the Middle Ages.

67636.q: What did the founder of Cluny give up in the founding charter of 910?
a: Any influence of his own over the abbey
67636.e: Duke William I of Aquitaine donated the land and renounced any influence. This made Cluny free from secular rule.
67636.m: The founder of Cluny deliberately gave up any influence.

67637.q: What made Cluny's legal position special?
a: It was directly subject to the pope.
It belonged to the French king.
It was subject to the bishop of Mâcon.
It was administered by the emperor as an imperial abbey.
67637.e: Cluny was placed under the protection of the apostle Peter and thus of the pope. This protected it from interference by nobles and local bishops.
67637.m: Cluny was free from secular rule and directly subject to the pope.

67638.q: Which abuse did the Cluny reform movement oppose under the term “simony”?
67638.e: Simony is named after Simon Magus, who according to the Acts of the Apostles wanted to buy spiritual powers. The reformers fought the trade in church offices.
67638.m: Simony means trading in church offices.

67639.q: According to which monastic rule did the monks of Cluny live?
67639.e: Cluny was a Benedictine abbey and wanted to follow the Rule of St Benedict strictly. A great monastic reform started from here.
67639.m: The monks of Cluny lived by the Rule of St Benedict.

67640.q: What was the third abbey church of Cluny (Cluny III) known for?
a: For centuries it was the largest church in Christendom.
It was the first Gothic cathedral in France.
It had the highest church tower in Europe.
It was the first church with glass windows.
67640.e: The church, built from 1088, was about 187 metres long. Only the new St Peter's Basilica in Rome surpassed it.
67640.m: For a long time, Cluny III was the largest church in Christendom.

67641.q: Which monastery in western Switzerland belonged to the Cluny network as a priory?
67641.e: Romainmôtier in the canton of Vaud was placed under Cluny in the 10th century. Its Romanesque church still survives today.
67641.m: Romainmôtier monastery belonged to the Cluny network.

67642.q: How was the Cluny network of monasteries organised?
a: The dependent priories were directly subject to the abbot of Cluny.
Each monastery freely elected its abbot and remained independent.
The monasteries were subject to the local bishops.
An annual general chapter of all abbots led the order.
67642.e: At the top stood the abbot of Cluny alone; the other houses were usually led by priors. This central order made Cluny very influential.
67642.m: In the Cluny network, the abbot of Cluny led all the priories.

67643.q: What was the Investiture Controversy essentially about?
a: About lay people appointing bishops and abbots
About whether bread and wine are changed
About the veneration of images in churches
67643.e: The king installed bishops in office with ring and staff and so bound them to himself. The reforming popes saw this as illegitimate interference by lay people.
67643.m: The Investiture Controversy was about the right to appoint bishops.

67644.q: What is the collection of 27 statements called in which Pope Gregory VII set out the pope's privileges in 1075?
67644.e: The Dictatus Papae states, among other things, that the pope may depose emperors. The document shows the claim to power of the reforming papacy.
67644.m: In 1075 the Dictatus Papae stressed the pope's privileges.

67645.q: With which punishment did Pope Gregory VII strike King Henry IV in 1076?
67645.e: At the Synod of Worms in 1076, Henry had declared the pope deposed. Gregory replied with excommunication and released Henry's subjects from their oath of loyalty.
67645.m: Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV in 1076.

67646.q: With which treaty was the Investiture Controversy settled in 1122?
67646.e: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II reached agreement in Worms in 1122. The emperor gave up investiture with ring and staff.
67646.m: The Concordat of Worms ended the Investiture Controversy in 1122.

67647.q: After the Concordat of Worms, with what did the king grant a bishop his secular rights?
67647.e: Ring and staff stood for the spiritual office and were left to the Church. For the secular lands and rights, the king invested the bishop with the sceptre.
67647.m: After the Concordat of Worms, the king invested bishops with the sceptre.

67648.q: In which year did King Henry IV go to Canossa?
67648.e: In January 1077, Henry appeared before the castle of Canossa in northern Italy, where Pope Gregory VII was staying. He wanted to have his excommunication lifted.
67648.m: Henry IV went to Canossa in 1077.

67649.q: Which noblewoman owned the castle of Canossa, where Pope Gregory VII stayed in 1077?
67649.e: Margravine Matilda of Tuscany was a loyal ally of Gregory VII. She was also related to Henry IV and mediated between the two.
67649.m: The castle of Canossa belonged to Matilda of Tuscany.

67650.q: According to the sources, how long is Henry IV said to have waited in a penitent's robe outside the castle of Canossa?
67650.e: According to tradition, Henry stood barefoot in the snow before the gate for three days. Then Gregory lifted the excommunication.
67650.m: Henry waited three days as a penitent at Canossa.

67651.q: Who said the famous sentence “We are not going to Canossa” in 1872 during the Kulturkampf?
67651.e: Imperial Chancellor Bismarck said the sentence in the Reichstag during the conflict with the Catholic Church. As a result, “going to Canossa” became an expression for a humiliating submission.
67651.m: Bismarck made Canossa a symbol of submission.

67652.e: Dominic (Domingo de Guzmán) came from Caleruega in Castile. He preached in southern France and founded his community there.
67652.m: The Castilian Dominic founded the Dominicans.

67653.q: In which century was the Dominican order founded?
67653.e: Pope Honorius III confirmed the order in 1216. Like the Franciscans, it is one of the mendicant orders of the High Middle Ages.
67653.m: The Dominican order was founded in the 13th century.

67654.q: What does the abbreviation “OP” after a Dominican's name stand for?
67654.e: The official name is Ordo Praedicatorum. Preaching and fighting false teachings through education were the order's main tasks.
67654.m: The Dominicans are officially called the Order of Preachers.

67655.q: Which important 13th-century theologian and author of the “Summa theologiae” was a Dominican?
67655.e: Thomas Aquinas joined the Dominicans against his family's wishes. He combined Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.
67655.m: Thomas Aquinas was the most famous Dominican theologian.

67656.q: Which Latin pun was made from the name of the Dominicans?
67656.e: The pun “Domini canes” presents the friars as watchdogs protecting the flock from false teachings. That is why their emblem often shows a dog with a torch.
67656.m: In a pun, the Dominicans were called the hounds of the Lord.

67657.q: What is the technical term for the mendicant orders, derived from the Latin word for “to beg”?
67657.e: The Latin “mendicare” means to beg. The mendicants lived on alms and gave up large possessions even as a community.
67657.m: Begging orders are also called mendicant orders.

67658.q: Where did the mendicant orders mainly settle in the 13th century?
67658.e: Unlike many older monasteries, the mendicant orders sought to be close to the town population. There they preached and cared for the poor and sick.
67658.m: The mendicant orders worked mainly in the towns.

67659.q: Which of the following orders is NOT a mendicant order?
67659.e: The Cistercians are a reform order following the Rule of St Benedict and lived from their own farming. The great mendicant orders include the Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites and Augustinian Hermits.
67659.m: The Cistercians were not a mendicant order.

67660.q: What is the women's branch of the Franciscans called, named after a companion of Francis of Assisi?
67660.e: Clare of Assisi joined Francis in 1212 and founded a community of sisters. These nuns are called Poor Clares after her.
67660.m: The Poor Clares are the sisters of the Franciscans.

67661.q: From which Greek word does the name “Cathars” come?
67661.e: “Katharos” means pure. The Cathars saw themselves as the true, pure Christians.
67661.m: The name Cathars means the pure ones.

67663.q: What is the Cathar world view called, according to which a good and an evil first principle stand against each other?
67663.e: The Cathars believed that the spiritual world came from God but the material world from an evil power. That is why they rejected many bodily things, such as eating meat.
67663.m: The Cathars held a strict dualism of good and evil.

67664.q: After which town in southern France were the Cathars also called “Albigensians”?
67664.e: The town of Albi in Languedoc was regarded as one of their centres. That is why the Cathars in southern France were called Albigensians.
67664.m: The Cathars in southern France were also called Albigensians after the town of Albi.

67665.q: Which pope called for a crusade against the Cathars in southern France after his legate was murdered?
67665.e: After the murder of the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau, Innocent III called for the Albigensian Crusade in 1208. The campaign began in 1209 and lasted until 1229.
67665.m: Innocent III proclaimed the Albigensian Crusade.

67666.q: In which town did crusaders carry out a great massacre in 1209 at the start of the Albigensian Crusade?
67666.e: When Béziers was captured in July 1209, a large part of the population was killed, Catholics and Cathars alike. The massacre became a symbol of the crusade's harshness.
67666.m: The Albigensian Crusade began in 1209 with the massacre of Béziers.

67667.q: Which castle in the Pyrenees was one of the last refuges of the Cathars and fell in 1244?
67667.e: After Montségur surrendered in March 1244, over 200 Cathars who refused to renounce their faith were burned. With this the Cathars lost their last major stronghold.
67667.m: With the fall of Montségur in 1244, the Cathars lost their last great castle.

67668.q: Who was the founder of the Waldensian movement?
a: A merchant from Lyon called Waldes
A bishop from Milan called Waldo
A monk from Cluny called Valdus
A knight from Savoy called Waldemar
67668.e: Peter Waldes was a rich merchant in Lyon. Around 1173 he gave up his possessions and lived in poverty as a wandering preacher.
67668.m: The Lyon merchant Waldes founded the Waldensians.

67669.q: Under which name were the early followers of Waldes also known?
67669.e: The followers of Waldes gave up their possessions and preached in pairs. After their home town they were called the Poor of Lyon.
67669.m: The early Waldensians were also called the Poor of Lyon.

67670.q: What did Waldes have translated so that lay people could understand the faith better?
a: Parts of the Bible into the vernacular
The Rule of St Benedict into Greek
67670.e: Waldes had biblical texts translated into the Romance vernacular of his region. This allowed lay people to understand and retell the Gospels themselves.
67670.m: Waldes had parts of the Bible translated into the vernacular.

67671.q: Why did the Church condemn the Waldensians as heretics in the Middle Ages?
a: Because they preached without church permission
Because they elected their own pope
67671.e: Waldes and his followers preached as lay people, although the Church had forbidden it. For this they were condemned as heretics in Verona in 1184.
67671.m: The Waldensians were condemned because they preached without permission.

67672.q: Which church practice did the medieval Waldensians reject, appealing to the Sermon on the Mount?
67672.e: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says one should not swear at all. The Waldensians took this literally and refused to take oaths.

67673.q: Which movement did the Waldensians join in 1532?
67673.e: At a synod in Piedmont in 1532, the Waldensians decided to join the Reformed movement. The reformer Guillaume Farel was present.
67673.m: In 1532 the Waldensians joined the Reformation.

67674.q: From where did the Waldensians set out in 1689 on the “Glorious Return” to their valleys in Piedmont?
67674.e: After their expulsion in 1686, many Waldensians had found refuge in Switzerland. In 1689 about 900 armed men under Henri Arnaud returned home from Lake Geneva.
67674.m: In 1689 the Waldensians returned from Switzerland to Piedmont.

67675.q: In which year did the Waldensians receive equal civil rights in the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont?
67675.e: King Charles Albert granted the Waldensians civil rights in February 1848. The Waldensians still celebrate 17 February as a day of remembrance.
67675.m: Since 1848 the Waldensians in Piedmont have had equal civil rights.

67676.q: During which period did the popes reside in Avignon?
67676.e: In 1309 Pope Clement V took up residence in Avignon. Only in 1377 did the papacy return permanently to Rome.
67676.m: The popes resided in Avignon from 1309 to 1377.

67677.q: Which pope moved his seat to Avignon in 1309?
67677.e: The Frenchman Bertrand de Got was elected as Clement V in 1305. Because of the unrest in Italy and pressure from the French king, he settled in Avignon in 1309.
67677.m: Clement V was the first pope in Avignon.

67678.q: Which French king put the papacy under heavy pressure at the beginning of the 14th century?
67678.e: Philip IV quarrelled with Pope Boniface VIII over taxes and power, and in 1303 the outrage of Anagni took place. Afterwards the papacy came under French influence.
67678.m: Philip the Fair brought the papacy under French influence.

67679.q: Which Italian poet called the popes' stay in Avignon a “Babylonian Captivity”?
67679.e: Petrarch compared Avignon with Babylon, where the people of Israel had once lived in captivity. In this way he criticised the splendour and dependence of the Curia.
67679.m: Petrarch spoke of the Babylonian Captivity of the Church.

67680.q: Where did the popes who resided in Avignon between 1309 and 1377 come from?
67680.e: From Clement V to Gregory XI, seven popes resided in Avignon. All of them came from France, which shows the French influence.
67680.m: The Avignon popes were all French.

67681.q: Which woman mystic urged Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome?
67681.e: Catherine of Siena travelled to Avignon in 1376 and personally called on Gregory XI to return. In January 1377 the pope entered Rome.
67681.m: Catherine of Siena persuaded the pope to return to Rome.

67682.q: Which order of knights was dissolved in 1312 at the Council of Vienne under Clement V?
a: The Livonian Brothers of the Sword
67682.e: Under pressure from Philip IV, Clement V dissolved the Templar order in 1312. The king had previously had the Templars arrested and hoped to get their wealth.
67682.m: The Templar order was dissolved in 1312.

67683.q: What is meant by the Western Schism?
a: Two or three popes claimed the office at the same time
The separation of the Eastern and Western Churches in 1054
The split caused by the Reformation
67683.e: From 1378 to 1417, popes in Rome and Avignon, and later also from Pisa, fought over the office. The separation of the Eastern and Western Churches in 1054, by contrast, is called the East-West Schism.
67683.m: The Western Schism lasted from 1378 to 1417.

67684.q: How did the Western Schism begin in 1378?
a: Cardinals declared a papal election invalid
The emperor installed his own pope
The pope died without a successor
67684.e: The election of Urban VI took place under pressure from a Roman crowd. Because of his harsh manner, most cardinals declared it invalid and elected a second pope.
67684.m: A disputed papal election in 1378 triggered the schism.

67685.q: Where did the antipope elected by the breakaway cardinals in 1378 reside?
67685.e: In September 1378 the cardinals elected Robert of Geneva as Clement VII. He moved to Avignon, so there were now two popes.
67685.m: During the schism, a second pope resided in Avignon.

67686.q: What effect did the Council of Pisa in 1409 have on the schism?
a: Afterwards there were three popes instead of two.
It ended the schism for good.
It moved the papal seat to Pisa.
67686.e: The council deposed both popes and elected Alexander V. Since the other two did not step down, there were now three popes.
67686.m: After the Council of Pisa there were three popes at the same time.

67687.q: How did Benedict XIII, the pope of the Avignon line, react to his deposition?
a: He never accepted it until his death
He was made a cardinal for it
67687.e: Benedict XIII, Pedro de Luna, never accepted his deposition. He lived until his death in the castle of Peñíscola on the coast of Valencia.
67687.m: Benedict XIII held on to his claim to the end.

67688.q: Which council ended the Western Schism?
67688.e: The Council of Constance, from 1414 to 1418, deposed popes or accepted their resignation. In 1417 it elected Martin V as the generally recognised pope.
67688.m: The Council of Constance ended the schism in 1417.

67689.q: Which teaching, according to which a general council stands above the pope, received a great boost from the schism?
67689.e: Since the popes could not agree, many theologians saw the council as the highest authority. This teaching is called conciliarism.
67689.m: Conciliarism places the council above the pope.

67690.q: To which pope did the Kingdom of England remain loyal during the schism?
67690.e: The allegiance of countries often followed political alliances. England was fighting France in the Hundred Years' War and therefore supported the Roman pope.
67690.m: During the schism, England sided with the pope in Rome.

67691.q: Which pope was elected in Constance in 1417, thus ending the Western Schism?
67691.e: On 11 November 1417, Oddo Colonna was elected and took the name Martin V after the saint of the day. He was recognised by the whole Western Church.
67691.m: The schism ended in 1417 with the election of Martin V.

67692.q: What did the Council of Constance declare in 1415 about its relationship to the pope?
a: The council stands above the pope
The pope stands above the council
Both are independent of each other
Only the emperor stands above both
67692.e: In the decree “Haec sancta”, the council declared that its power came directly from Christ. This teaching is called conciliarism.
67692.m: In Constance the council placed itself above the pope.

67693.q: What did the Constance decree “Frequens” of 1417 lay down?
a: That general councils should be held regularly in future
That only Italians may be elected pope
That the Bible may only be read in Latin
