67693.e: “Frequens” required councils to meet at fixed intervals. In this way the Church was to be permanently overseen by councils.
67693.m: The decree “Frequens” called for regular councils.

67694.q: Which territory did the Swiss Confederates conquer in 1415 after Duke Frederick IV of Austria had helped the fleeing Pope John XXIII?
67694.e: Frederick IV had helped John XXIII flee from Constance and was outlawed. King Sigismund called on the Confederates to occupy his lands, whereupon they conquered Aargau.

67695.q: Which English theologian strongly influenced Jan Hus with his teachings?
67695.e: In the 14th century, Wycliffe criticised the wealth and power of the Church. His writings reached Prague and shaped Hus and his followers.
67695.m: Jan Hus was influenced by the teachings of John Wycliffe.

67696.q: In which Prague church did Jan Hus preach in Czech to large audiences?
67696.e: The Bethlehem Chapel had been founded especially for sermons in Czech. Hus preached there from 1402.
67696.m: Jan Hus preached in Prague's Bethlehem Chapel.

67697.q: Which event in Prague is regarded as the trigger of the Hussite Wars in 1419?
a: The fire at St Vitus Cathedral
67697.e: In July 1419, Hussites stormed the New Town Hall and threw councillors out of the window. Years of war in Bohemia followed.
67697.m: The First Defenestration of Prague in 1419 triggered the Hussite Wars.

67698.q: What happened to Jan Hus at the Council of Constance in 1415?
a: He was burned as a heretic
He was sentenced to confinement in a monastery
He managed to flee to Bohemia
67698.e: Hus had travelled to Constance with a letter of safe conduct from King Sigismund. Even so, because he did not recant his teachings, he was burned on 6 July 1415.
67698.m: Jan Hus died at the stake in Constance in 1415.

67699.q: Which object became the symbol of the Hussites?
67699.e: The Hussites demanded that lay people too be allowed to drink from the chalice at Communion. That is why the chalice became their sign.
67699.m: The chalice is the symbol of the Hussites.

67700.q: What does the Reformation principle “sola scriptura” mean?
67700.e: “Sola scriptura” means “Scripture alone”. For the reformers, the Bible is the only binding guide for faith and teaching.
67700.m: According to the principle “sola scriptura”, the Bible alone is the standard for faith and teaching.

67701.q: Which authority did the Council of Trent in 1546 place on an equal footing with Holy Scripture, contradicting the principle of “sola scriptura”?
a: The decisions of the imperial diets
67701.e: In 1546 the Council of Trent declared that Scripture and unwritten traditions were to be received with equal reverence. In this way the Catholic Church deliberately set itself apart from the Reformation's principle of Scripture.
67701.m: The Council of Trent placed tradition on an equal footing with the Bible.

67702.q: In the Protestant view, what rank do confessional documents have compared with the Bible?
a: They are subordinate to the Bible and are measured against it
67702.e: The Bible is the highest standard, the “norming norm”. Confessions such as the Heidelberg Catechism are only valid in so far as they agree with Scripture.
67702.m: For Protestants, the Bible stands above all confessions.

67703.q: How did Luther justify his refusal to recant his writings before Emperor Charles V and the imperial estates in 1521?
a: He had not been refuted by Scripture and clear reasons
The emperor had no power over monks
He had never personally criticised the pope
67703.e: Luther declared he would only recant if he were refuted by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reasons. His conscience, he said, was captive to the Word of God.
67703.m: Before the emperor, Luther appealed to Scripture and his conscience.

67704.q: What was new about Zwingli's sermons at the Grossmünster from 1519?
a: He explained whole books of the Bible continuously
He now preached only in Latin
He only read out legends of saints
He preached without a Bible text
67704.e: Zwingli broke with the prescribed order of readings and began with the Gospel of Matthew, chapter by chapter. In this way he put the Bible text itself at the centre.
67704.m: Zwingli preached through the Bible chapter by chapter.

67705.q: What was the theological school set up in Zurich in 1525 called, where the Bible was interpreted together from the original languages?
67705.e: Zwingli set up the Prophezei at the Grossmünster in 1525. There, biblical texts were translated from Hebrew and Greek and explained; the Zurich Bible translation also came out of it.
67705.m: In Zurich's Prophezei, scholars interpreted the Bible from the original languages.

67706.q: Which edition did Erasmus of Rotterdam publish in Basel in 1516, making it easier for the reformers to access the original text?
67706.e: In 1516 Erasmus published the New Testament in Greek with a Latin translation at the Basel printer Johann Froben. Luther and Zwingli worked with this edition.
67706.m: In 1516 Erasmus printed the Greek New Testament in Basel.

67707.q: What does the Reformation principle “sola gratia” mean?
a: Salvation is an undeserved gift from God
Salvation is earned through good works
Salvation can be bought through indulgences
Salvation is achieved through strict asceticism
67707.e: “Sola gratia” means “by grace alone”. People cannot earn salvation; they receive it as God's free gift.
67707.m: According to the principle “sola gratia”, God gives salvation without any merit.

67708.q: To which Church Father, who defended grace against Pelagius in the 5th century, did the reformers particularly appeal?
67708.e: In his dispute with Pelagius, Augustine of Hippo stressed that people depend entirely on God's grace. Luther was also a monk in the order of Augustinian Hermits.
67708.m: The reformers based their doctrine of grace strongly on Augustine.

67709.q: With which famous humanist did Luther argue about free will in 1524 and 1525?
67709.e: Erasmus defended human free will. Luther replied with “On the Bondage of the Will” and stressed that people depend entirely on God's grace.
67709.m: Luther and Erasmus argued about free will.

67710.q: Which church practice did Luther attack in 1517 because, in his view, it made God's grace seem something you could buy?
67710.e: With his 95 Theses in 1517, Luther criticised the sale of letters of indulgence, which Johann Tetzel among others preached for. Forgiveness, he said, cannot be bought with money.
67710.m: Luther's 95 Theses were aimed at the sale of indulgences.

67711.q: What is the teaching called, firmly rejected by the reformers, according to which people can do good and gain salvation by their own strength?
67711.e: Pelagianism goes back to the monk Pelagius and stresses people's ability to live good lives by their own will. The reformers saw this as contradicting grace.
67711.m: Pelagianism credits people with achieving salvation by their own strength.

67712.q: What does Luther call the righteousness that people do not produce themselves but receive from outside through Christ?
67712.e: Luther speaks of “iustitia aliena”, alien (foreign) righteousness. It comes from Christ and is granted to people by grace.
67712.m: According to Luther, saving righteousness is the alien righteousness of Christ.

67713.q: Which word did Luther add to Romans 3:28 in his translation, which led to him being accused of falsifying the text?
67713.e: Luther translated that a person is made righteous “without the works of the law, by faith alone” (German “allein”). He defended the word in 1530 in his “Open Letter on Translating”.
67713.m: In Romans 3:28 Luther put the word “alone” before faith.

67714.q: Which New Testament letter did Luther call a “strawy epistle” because it strongly stresses works?
67714.e: The Letter of James says that faith without works is dead. Luther saw little of the gospel of justification in it and therefore disparagingly called it a “strawy epistle”.
67714.m: Luther thought little of the Letter of James because of its stress on works.

67715.q: Which Bible passage with the sentence “The righteous shall live by faith” became central to Luther's Reformation discovery?
67715.e: In Romans 1:17, Paul quotes the prophet Habakkuk. From it Luther realised that God's righteousness makes people righteous through faith.
67715.m: Romans 1:17 was the key verse for Luther's doctrine of justification.

67716.q: What is the theological term for God declaring the sinner righteous, which the principle “sola fide” is about?
67716.e: Justification means that God declares the sinner righteous. According to Reformation teaching, this happens through faith alone, not through works.
67716.m: “Sola fide” is about justification by faith alone.

67717.q: What is Luther's insight that God's righteousness is given as a gift called, named after the place in the Wittenberg monastery?
67717.e: Luther later reported that he had gained the liberating insight in a tower room of the Wittenberg monastery. The exact date is disputed among scholars.
67717.m: The tower experience stands for Luther's Reformation discovery.

67718.q: With which Latin formula does Luther describe the believer as righteous and sinful at the same time?
67718.e: “Simul iustus et peccator” means “at the same time righteous and a sinner”. Before God the believer is declared righteous but remains a sinner in himself.
67718.m: According to Luther, a Christian is righteous and a sinner at the same time.

67719.q: In which year did Luther publish “On the Freedom of a Christian”?
67719.e: In 1520 Luther wrote his three great Reformation treatises. The work on freedom appeared in German and in Latin.
67719.m: Luther's work on freedom appeared in 1520.

67720.q: What is the first thesis of Luther's work on freedom?
a: A Christian is a free lord of all and subject to none.
A Christian is subject to the emperor in all things.
A Christian is a servant of the Church and the pope.
A Christian is free from all the commandments of the Bible.
67720.e: The first thesis stresses the believer's freedom: through faith he is free before God and subject to no power. Luther deliberately sets an apparently contradictory second thesis against it.
67720.m: Luther begins his work on freedom with the Christian's freedom over all things.

67721.q: How does Luther resolve the apparent contradiction between the Christian's freedom and service?
a: The inner person is free in faith, the outer person serves in love
A Christian is free on Sundays and serves on weekdays
The clergy are free, lay people serve
The soul is only free after death and serves in life
67721.e: Luther distinguishes between the inner, spiritual person and the outer, bodily person. In faith the Christian is free; out of love he serves his neighbour.
67721.m: For Luther, faith makes us free and love makes us serve.

67722.q: To whom did Luther address a covering letter to his work on freedom?
67722.e: Luther dedicated the work to Pope Leo X with an open letter. In it he sharply attacked the Roman Curia but wanted to spare the pope personally.
67722.m: Luther sent his work on freedom to Pope Leo X with a letter.

67723.q: To which group of Luther's writings does “On the Freedom of a Christian” belong?
67723.e: In 1520 Luther wrote three fundamental programmatic works. Together they are regarded as the great Reformation treatises.
67723.m: The work on freedom is one of Luther's great Reformation treatises of 1520.

67724.q: Which image does Luther use in his work on freedom for the exchange between Christ and the believing soul?
67724.e: Luther speaks of the “joyful exchange”: as in a marriage, Christ and the soul share everything. Christ takes on the sin, the soul receives his righteousness.
67724.m: Luther describes the joyful exchange with the image of bride and bridegroom.

67725.q: What is the second thesis of Luther's work on freedom?
a: A Christian is a dutiful servant of all and subject to all.
A Christian serves the pope alone.
A Christian must earn freedom through works.
67725.e: Luther deliberately sets service against freedom. In doing so he relies on Paul, who was free and yet made himself a servant to all.
67725.m: According to Luther, a Christian is free and at the same time a servant of all.

67726.q: Who defended his teaching before the council at the First Zurich Disputation in 1523?
67726.e: For this, Zwingli presented 67 theses, the so-called Schlussreden (concluding statements). The council then allowed him to go on preaching.
67726.m: In 1523 Zwingli defended his teaching at the First Zurich Disputation.

67727.q: In which building did the First Zurich Disputation take place?
67727.e: As the governing authority, the council invited people to the council chamber, not to a church. This shows that the city took the decision about the Reformation upon itself.
67727.m: The First Zurich Disputation met in Zurich town hall.

67728.q: To which diocese did Zurich belong at the time of the First Zurich Disputation in 1523?
67728.e: At that time Zurich belonged to the large Diocese of Constance. The bishop sent his vicar general Johannes Fabri to the disputation.
67728.m: In 1523 Zurich belonged to the Diocese of Constance.

67729.q: Who decided the outcome of the First Zurich Disputation in 1523?
a: The council of the city of Zurich
The Federal Diet of the Confederation
67729.e: The council decided that Zwingli could go on preaching and that all preachers should keep to Scripture. In this way a secular authority took over the decision on matters of faith.
67729.m: In 1523 the Zurich council decided in favour of preaching according to Scripture.

67730.q: Which topics were at the centre of the Second Zurich Disputation in October 1523?
67730.e: At the Second Disputation there were arguments about the veneration of images and the Mass as a sacrifice. The changes were then carried out step by step.
67730.m: The Second Zurich Disputation dealt with images and the Mass.

67731.q: What is the demonstrative breaking of the fast in 1522 in the house of the printer Christoph Froschauer, which preceded the disputation, called?
67731.e: During Lent in 1522, Froschauer and friends ate sausages; Zwingli was present. Afterwards he defended the breach with his work “On the Choice and Freedom of Foods”.
67731.m: Zurich's Affair of the Sausages in 1522 is regarded as the start of the Zurich Reformation.

67732.q: What was introduced in Zurich at Easter 1525 instead of the Mass?
67732.e: At Easter 1525, the Lord's Supper was celebrated in the Grossmünster for the first time according to the Reformed order. Bread and wine were handed to the congregation at tables.
67732.m: Since Easter 1525 Zurich has celebrated the Lord's Supper instead of the Mass.

67733.q: Which disputation in Aargau in 1526 ended in success for the Catholic side against Johannes Oecolampadius?
67733.e: In Baden, Johannes Eck and Oecolampadius, among others, debated; Zwingli himself stayed away. The Catholic cantons regarded the result as a victory.
67733.m: The Disputation of Baden in 1526 went in favour of the old believers.

67734.q: Whose successor in Zurich did Heinrich Bullinger become?
67734.e: After Zwingli fell in the Battle of Kappel in 1531, Zurich chose the young Bullinger. He led the Zurich church for over 40 years.
67734.m: Heinrich Bullinger was Zwingli's successor in Zurich.

67735.q: In which year did Bullinger succeed Zwingli as pastor at the Grossmünster in Zurich?
67735.e: After Zwingli fell in October 1531 in the war against the Catholic cantons, Zurich chose the 27-year-old Bullinger in December. He led the Zurich church for decades.

67736.q: What title did Bullinger hold as head of the Zurich church?
67736.e: Antistes is Latin and means “one who stands at the head”. This was the title of the leading pastors of the Reformed churches in Zurich and other Swiss cities.
67736.m: The head of the Zurich church was called the Antistes.

67737.q: For roughly how long did Heinrich Bullinger lead the Zurich church?
67737.e: Bullinger became Zwingli's successor in 1531 and died in Zurich in 1575. He thus shaped the Zurich Reformation for over four decades.
67737.m: Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

67738.q: Why is Bullinger's collection of 50 doctrinal sermons called the “Decades”?
a: It appeared in five parts of ten sermons each
It was written over ten years
It was translated into ten languages
It has ten chapters about God
67738.e: Latin “decas” means a group of ten. The sermons appeared from 1549 to 1552 in five parts of ten each and were also widely read in England.
67738.m: Bullinger's Decades are five times ten sermons.

67739.q: Roughly how many letters from and to Heinrich Bullinger have survived?
67739.e: Bullinger was in contact with scholars, pastors and princes all over Europe. With over 12,000 surviving letters, his correspondence is one of the largest of the 16th century.
67739.m: Bullinger's correspondence includes over twelve thousand surviving letters.

67740.q: At which monastery school did Bullinger teach from 1523 before he was called to Zurich?
67740.e: Abbot Wolfgang Joner brought the 19-year-old Bullinger to the monastery school at Kappel as a teacher. There Bullinger introduced Reformation-style Bible interpretation.
67740.m: From 1523 Bullinger taught at the monastery school in Kappel.

67741.q: Who wrote the Confessio Helvetica posterior (Second Helvetic Confession)?
67741.e: Zwingli's successor in Zurich first wrote the confession as a personal statement of faith. It was later adopted by many Reformed churches.
67741.m: The Second Helvetic Confession is by Heinrich Bullinger.

67742.q: In which century was the Confessio Helvetica posterior written?
67742.e: Heinrich Bullinger wrote the confession around 1561/62, and it was printed in 1566. It therefore belongs to the time of the Reformation.
67742.m: The Confessio Helvetica posterior dates from the 16th century.

67743.q: For which churches did the Confessio Helvetica posterior become an important shared confession?
67743.e: The confession by Zwingli's successor Bullinger was adopted by many Reformed churches in Switzerland and in Europe. The Lutherans had their own, the Augsburg Confession.
67743.m: The Second Helvetic Confession is a Reformed confession.

67744.q: In which city was the older First Helvetic Confession (Confessio Helvetica prior) adopted in 1536?
67744.e: In 1536, theologians from several Reformed cities drew up a joint confession in Basel. The later Confessio Helvetica posterior is more detailed.
67744.m: The First Helvetic Confession was written in Basel in 1536.

67745.q: In which country outside Switzerland is the Confessio Helvetica posterior still a central confession of the Reformed today?
67745.e: The Synod of Debrecen adopted the confession in 1567. The Reformed Church in Hungary still appeals to it today.
67745.m: The Reformed in Hungary still profess the Second Helvetic Confession today.

67746.q: Which famous sentence is in the first chapter of the Confessio Helvetica posterior?
a: “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.”
“The pope is the visible head of the Church.”
67746.e: In Latin the sentence is “Praedicatio verbi Dei est verbum Dei”. When Scripture is rightly interpreted, God speaks through the sermon.
67746.m: According to the Second Helvetic Confession, the preaching of the Word of God is itself the Word of God.

67747.q: What does the Latin word “posterior” in the name of the confession mean?
67747.e: “Posterior” means “the later one”. That is why the Confessio Helvetica posterior is called the Second Helvetic Confession in English.
67747.m: The Confessio Helvetica posterior is the later, second Helvetic Confession.

67748.q: Where was the first edition of Calvin's “Institutes of the Christian Religion” published in 1536?
67748.e: At that time Calvin was living in Basel as a refugee from France. The first edition was a short textbook in six chapters.
67748.m: Calvin's Institutes first appeared in Basel in 1536.

67749.q: To which king did Calvin dedicate the “Institutes” in a famous preface?
67749.e: Calvin wanted to defend the persecuted Protestants in France against the charge of rebellion. That is why he addressed the preface to the French king.
67749.m: Calvin dedicated the Institutes to the French king Francis I.

67750.q: In which language did Calvin write the first version of the “Institutes”?
67750.e: Like most scholars of his time, Calvin first wrote in Latin. Up to the final version of 1559 he greatly expanded the work.
67750.m: Calvin first wrote the “Institutes” in Latin.

67751.q: Into which language did Calvin himself translate the “Institutes” in 1541?
67751.e: Calvin also wanted to reach readers who knew no Latin. His translation is regarded as an important work of French prose.
67751.m: In 1541 Calvin himself translated his Institutes into French.

67752.q: What does Calvin's doctrine of double predestination say?
a: From eternity God destines some to salvation and others to damnation
Every person freely chooses between salvation and damnation
In the end all people will be saved
God determines only the salvation of the baptised
67752.e: According to Calvin, God in his eternal decree has fixed both election and rejection. The reason lies in God's will alone, not in human merit.
67752.m: Double predestination teaches election and rejection by God's eternal decree.

67753.q: In which city did John Calvin, who taught the doctrine of double predestination, work?
67753.e: Calvin worked in Geneva from 1536 and then from 1541 until his death in 1564. From there, Reformed teaching spread throughout Europe.
67753.m: Calvin made Geneva a centre of the Reformation.

67754.q: Which sociologist linked the Calvinist doctrine of predestination with the spirit of modern capitalism in 1904/05?
67754.e: In “The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism”, Max Weber argued that uncertainty about election drove people to disciplined work and self-denial. The thesis is still disputed today.
67754.m: Max Weber linked the doctrine of predestination with the spirit of capitalism.

67755.q: Which synod in 1618/19 confirmed the strict doctrine of predestination against the Arminians?
67755.e: In the Netherlands, the Arminians rejected unconditional election. The Synod of Dort, with guests also from Switzerland, condemned their teaching.
67755.m: In 1619 the Synod of Dort confirmed the Calvinist doctrine of election.

67756.q: Whom did Conrad Grebel baptise in Zurich on 21 January 1525, which marked the start of the Anabaptist movement?
67756.e: In a private house in Zurich, the former priest George Blaurock asked Grebel to baptise him on his confession of faith. Blaurock then baptised the others present.
67756.m: In 1525 Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock and so helped found the Anabaptist movement.

67757.q: Which conviction led Conrad Grebel to break with Zwingli?
a: Baptism requires a personal confession of faith
The pope should remain head of the Church
67757.e: Grebel and his circle did not find infant baptism grounded in the Bible. They wanted a congregation of conscious believers, separate from the authorities.
67757.m: Grebel called for baptism only after a personal confession of faith.

67758.q: To which radical reformer did Grebel and his friends write a detailed letter in 1524?
67758.e: Grebel was looking for like-minded people and wrote to Müntzer. But he rejected Müntzer's readiness to use violence and urged non-resistance.
67758.m: In 1524 Grebel wrote to Thomas Müntzer, rejecting violence.

67759.q: Which present-day faith communities go back to the movement Grebel helped to found?
67759.e: From the Zurich Anabaptist circle came a movement that spread in Europe and later in North America. Its best-known descendants are the Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites.
67759.m: Mennonites and Amish come from the Anabaptist movement of the Reformation period.

67760.q: What happened on 21 January 1525 in the house of the Manz family in Zurich?
a: Adults were baptised on their confession of faith for the first time
67760.e: The Anabaptist circle around Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz met in the house of the Manz family. The first believers' baptisms took place there, the start of the Anabaptist movement.
67760.m: The first believers' baptism in Zurich took place in 1525 in the house of the Manz family.

67761.q: What does Felix Manz stand for in the history of the Anabaptist movement?
a: As the first Anabaptist executed by a Reformed authority
As the founder of the Mennonites
As author of the Schleitheim Articles
As the first Anabaptist preacher in America
67761.e: Manz was an early companion of Grebel in Zurich. His execution by the Reformed Zurich council made him the first Anabaptist martyr in Zurich.
67761.m: Felix Manz is regarded as the first Anabaptist executed by a Reformed authority.

67762.q: In which language was Felix Manz a particularly respected expert?
67762.e: Like Zwingli, Manz learned Hebrew from Johann Böschenstein. Later he explained Old Testament texts in small circles.
67762.m: Felix Manz was an expert in the Hebrew language.

67763.q: How was the Anabaptist Felix Manz executed in Zurich in 1527?
a: He was drowned in the Limmat
67763.e: The Zurich council had Manz drowned in the Limmat, as a mocking reference to adult baptism. Since 2004 a memorial plaque on the Schipfe has recalled it.
67763.m: Felix Manz was drowned in the Limmat in 1527.

67764.q: Which Reformation-era faith movement adopted the Schleitheim Articles in 1527?
67764.e: Anabaptists from Switzerland and southern Germany met in Schleitheim in 1527. They agreed on a common order, the “Brotherly Union”.
67764.m: The Schleitheim Articles are the confession of the Anabaptists.

67765.q: How did the authorities, including those in Zurich, treat the Anabaptists?
a: They persecuted them, sometimes with the death penalty
They made them the state church
They gave them cantons of their own
67765.e: Anabaptists were persecuted because they rejected infant baptism, oaths and military service. In Zurich Felix Manz was drowned in 1527; Michael Sattler was executed in Rottenburg the same year.
67765.m: The Anabaptists were harshly persecuted by the authorities.

67766.q: In which present-day canton is Schleitheim?
67766.e: Schleitheim lies in the Klettgau near the border with Germany. In 1527 the village was the meeting place of the Anabaptists.
67766.m: Schleitheim is in the canton of Schaffhausen.

67767.q: Which kind of baptism do the Schleitheim Articles support?
a: Only the baptism of believers, not of infants
67767.e: Only those who have repented and consciously believe should be baptised. The Anabaptists rejected infant baptism, which is where their name comes from.
67767.m: The Anabaptists only baptised people who consciously professed their faith.

67768.q: What position on oaths do the Schleitheim Articles take?
a: Christians should not swear at all
Christians may only swear in court
Christians swear only on the Bible
Christians must swear to the authorities every year
67768.e: Based on the Sermon on the Mount, the Anabaptists rejected every oath. Because the oath was then the basis of civic duties, this stance was seen as a danger to the state.

67769.q: What is meant by “separation” in the Schleitheim Articles?
a: The separation of the congregation from the world, seen as evil
The withdrawal of believers into monasteries
The separation of men and women in worship
The expulsion of all unbaptised people from the country
67769.e: The Anabaptists saw two kingdoms: Christ's congregation and the world. Believers should keep away from the services of the state churches, from taverns and from violence.
67769.m: Separation means the congregation keeping apart from the world.

67770.q: What do the Schleitheim Articles demand in the section on the sword?
a: Christians should not hold any government office that uses the sword
Christians must be ready for military service
Christians may only fight against unbelievers
Christians should overthrow the authorities by force of arms
67770.e: According to the articles, the sword belongs to God's order outside the perfection of Christ. Christians should therefore use force neither as judges nor as soldiers.
67770.m: According to Schleitheim, Christians should not wield the power of the sword.

67771.q: In which imperial city were the peasants' “Twelve Articles” written in 1525?
67771.e: The furrier Sebastian Lotzer and the preacher Christoph Schappeler drew up the demands. Within a short time they were printed in large numbers.
67771.m: The peasants' Twelve Articles were written in Memmingen in 1525.

67772.q: Which church demand did the Twelve Articles put first?
a: The congregation should choose its own pastor
The emperor should be elected by the peasants
All monasteries should belong to the peasants
67772.e: The first article demands that every congregation may choose and dismiss its pastor. He should preach the gospel purely.
67772.m: In 1525 the peasants demanded that congregations be free to choose their pastors.

67773.q: How did the Twelve Articles justify the demand to abolish serfdom?
a: Christ had redeemed all people with his blood
The emperor had already banned it
The princes no longer needed workers
67773.e: The third article argues that Christ redeemed everyone, the shepherd as well as the highest. Therefore it is not right to hold people as property.
67773.m: The peasants based their freedom on redemption through Christ.

67774.q: In which battle on 15 May 1525 was the peasant army around Thomas Müntzer crushingly defeated?
67774.e: At Frankenhausen in Thuringia, the princes' troops defeated the rebels. Müntzer was taken prisoner and executed shortly afterwards.
67774.m: Müntzer's uprising ended at Frankenhausen in 1525.

67775.q: What is Luther's 1525 work called in which he called on the princes to act harshly against the rebels?
a: “Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants”
“To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation”
67775.e: Luther saw the uprising as a misuse of the gospel. His harsh work damaged his reputation among many ordinary people.
67775.m: In 1525 Luther took a harsh stand against the rebellious peasants.

67776.q: Which league under Georg Truchsess von Waldburg crushed the peasant bands in southern Germany in 1525?
67776.e: The Swabian League was an alliance of southern German princes and cities. Its commander Georg Truchsess von Waldburg was given the nickname “Bauernjörg” (Peasant George).
67776.m: The Swabian League defeated the peasants in southern Germany.

67777.q: Roughly how many people died in the German Peasants' War?
67777.e: Estimates are around 70,000 to 75,000 dead, mainly rebels. Many survivors were also punished with penalties and levies.
67777.m: An estimated more than seventy thousand people died in the Peasants' War.

67778.q: On which date was the Peace of Augsburg concluded?
67778.e: The peace was agreed at the Imperial Diet in Augsburg. For the time being it ended the religious wars in the Holy Roman Empire.
67778.m: The Peace of Augsburg dates from 25 September 1555.

67779.q: With which Latin formula was the basic principle of the Peace of Augsburg later summed up?
67779.e: The formula means roughly “whose realm, his religion”. The ruler decided the denomination of his subjects; the formula itself only arose around 1600.
67779.m: In the Peace of Augsburg, the ruler decided the denomination of his territory.

67780.q: Which denominations did the Peace of Augsburg recognise in imperial law?
67780.e: Only the Catholic Church and the followers of the Augsburg Confession were recognised. The Reformed only gained equal status with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
67780.m: The Peace of Augsburg recognised only Catholics and Lutherans.

67781.q: Which right did subjects receive who did not share their ruler's denomination?
a: The right to their own churches
The right to freedom from taxes
67781.e: The “ius emigrandi” allowed people of a different faith to move with their property to an area of their own denomination. There was no right to practise religion freely in their own land.
67781.m: After 1555, subjects of a different faith were allowed to emigrate.

67782.q: What did the “ecclesiastical reservation” in the Peace of Augsburg regulate?
a: Church princes lost office and rule if they changed denomination
Clergy did not have to pay taxes
Only priests were allowed to interpret the Bible
Bishops would in future be appointed by the emperor
67782.e: The reservation was meant to stop dioceses and abbeys from becoming Protestant. The Protestants never accepted it, which later led to conflicts.
67782.m: The ecclesiastical reservation secured the Catholic church territories.

67783.q: Who negotiated the religious peace in Augsburg in 1555 in place of Emperor Charles V?
67783.e: Charles V was inwardly against a peace with the Protestants and left the negotiations to his brother. Ferdinand later succeeded him as emperor.
67783.m: Ferdinand I negotiated the Peace of Augsburg for the emperor.

67784.q: Which war between the emperor and Protestant princes in 1546/47 came before the Peace of Augsburg?
67784.e: In 1547 Charles V defeated the Protestant princes of the Schmalkaldic League at Mühlberg. The princes' resistance later forced him to compromise after all.
67784.m: Before the Peace of Augsburg, the emperor fought the Protestants in the Schmalkaldic War.

67785.q: Which event started the conversion of Ignatius of Loyola in 1521?
a: A serious leg wound in the defence of Pamplona
A shipwreck on the pilgrimage to Jerusalem
A plague epidemic in his home town
A debate with Luther in Worms
67785.e: As an officer, Ignatius was hit in the leg by a cannonball. On his sickbed he read a life of Christ and legends of saints and turned to a spiritual life.
67785.m: A war wound in 1521 led Ignatius to change his life.

67786.q: What is the famous work by Ignatius called, a guide to prayer and reflection over several weeks?
67786.e: The “Spiritual Exercises” guide people in prayer, contemplation and decision-making. They still shape Jesuit spirituality today.

67787.q: What is the order called that Ignatius of Loyola founded and the pope confirmed in 1540?
67787.e: Pope Paul III confirmed the Society of Jesus in 1540. In 1541 Ignatius became its first Superior General.
67787.m: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuit order.

67788.q: What is the Latin motto of the Jesuits?
67788.e: The motto means “All for the greater glory of God” and is often abbreviated to AMDG. It expresses that every activity should be directed towards God.
67788.m: The Jesuits do everything for the greater glory of God.

67789.q: Where did Ignatius and his first companions, including Francis Xavier, take shared vows in 1534?
67789.e: The group had come together while studying in Paris. On 15 August 1534 they vowed poverty and a pilgrimage to Jerusalem or service to the pope.
67789.m: The first Jesuits took their vows on Montmartre in 1534.

67790.q: In which town of the Swiss Confederation did the Jesuits first settle in 1574?
67790.e: In Lucerne, the settlement of 1574 soon grew into a college. The Jesuits thus became leaders of the Catholic reform in Central Switzerland.
67790.m: The first Jesuit house in the Confederation was founded in Lucerne in 1574.

67791.q: In which year was the ban on Jesuits in the Swiss Federal Constitution lifted by a popular vote?
67791.e: After the Sonderbund War, the Federal Constitution of 1848 included a ban on Jesuits, which was tightened in 1874. In 1973 the people and the cantons removed this special denominational article.
67791.m: Switzerland lifted its ban on Jesuits at the ballot box in 1973.

67792.q: What is the massacre of Huguenots that began in Paris in August 1572 called?
67792.e: On the night of 24 August 1572, thousands of Protestants were killed in Paris, and afterwards in other towns as well. Many survivors fled, among other places to Geneva.
67792.m: The St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 was a massacre of the Huguenots.

67793.q: Which king granted the Huguenots toleration in the Edict of Nantes in 1598?
67793.e: The king had himself once been a Protestant and had converted to Catholicism. The edict guaranteed the Huguenots freedom of conscience and limited freedom of worship.
67793.m: Henry IV granted the Huguenots toleration in 1598.

67794.q: With which edict did Louis XIV end the toleration of the Huguenots in 1685?
67794.e: This edict banned the Reformed faith in France. Despite a ban on leaving, about 200,000 Huguenots fled abroad.
67794.m: The Edict of Fontainebleau banned the Reformed faith in France in 1685.

67795.q: What was the forced quartering of soldiers in Huguenot homes to compel conversions called?
67795.e: From 1681, dragoons were quartered with Protestant families and harassed them. Many then converted to Catholicism.
67795.m: With the dragonnades, Huguenots were forced to convert.

67796.q: From which German word does a widespread explanation derive the name “Huguenots”?
67796.e: The early French form “eygenot” referred in Geneva to a party that wanted to ally with the Swiss Confederates against Savoy. However, the origin is not completely certain.
67796.m: The name Huguenots is often derived from the word Eidgenossen.

67797.q: According to estimates, how many Huguenot religious refugees passed through Switzerland on their flight after 1685?
67797.e: After the Edict of Nantes was revoked, about 150,000 Huguenots left France, about 60,000 of whom passed through Switzerland. The influx peaked in 1687, and about 20,000 stayed for good.
67797.m: About sixty thousand Huguenots passed through Switzerland on their flight.

67798.q: Which branch of industry in Geneva was particularly boosted by Huguenot religious refugees?
67798.e: Many refugees were goldsmiths and watchmakers. Because Calvin's moral code restricted jewellery, Geneva's goldsmiths turned to watches, which founded the Geneva watch industry.
67798.m: Huguenot refugees boosted watchmaking in Geneva.

67799.q: Which country invited many Huguenots to settle with the Edict of Potsdam in 1685, often reaching it via Switzerland?
67799.e: Elector Frederick William granted the refugees tax advantages and privileges. About 20,000 Huguenots settled there, many in Berlin.
67799.m: After 1685 Brandenburg-Prussia took in many Huguenots.

67800.q: Who, with his reform work “Pia Desideria” of 1675, is regarded as the founder of Lutheran Pietism?
67800.e: In “Pia Desideria” in 1675, Spener called for the renewal of the Lutheran church through personal piety and intensive Bible study. This gave the movement its programme.
67800.m: Philipp Jakob Spener is regarded as the father of Pietism.

67801.q: What did Spener call the private house groups in which believers met to read the Bible alongside the church service?
67801.e: The “collegia pietatis” were small devotional gatherings of lay people and pastors. They strengthened the priesthood of all believers.
67801.m: In the collegia pietatis, Pietists read the Bible together.

67802.q: What is the Pietist August Hermann Francke in Halle mainly known for?
a: For a large orphanage with schools
For founding a university in Rome
67802.e: From 1698, Francke built up large educational and social institutions in Halle from an orphanage, the Francke Foundations. They show the active, social side of Pietism.
67802.m: With an orphanage and schools, Francke made Halle a centre of Pietism.

67803.q: Which community grew up from 1722 on Count Zinzendorf's estate in Upper Lusatia?
67803.e: Zinzendorf took in religious refugees from Moravia, who founded the village of Herrnhut. From it grew a worldwide Moravian Church with a strong mission.
67803.m: The Herrnhut Moravian Church goes back to Count Zinzendorf.

67804.q: Which yearly collection with a Bible verse drawn by lot for each day goes back to the Herrnhut Moravians?
67804.e: The Watchwords have appeared every year since 1731; the verses from the Old Testament are drawn by lot. Today they are read in many languages.
67804.m: The Daily Watchwords give a Bible verse for each day.

67805.q: Which Protestant missionary society was founded in Basel in 1815 in a Pietist setting?
67805.e: The Evangelical Missionary Society in Basel trained missionaries and sent them to India and China, among other places. Basel thus became a centre of Pietism.
67805.m: The Basel Mission grew out of Pietism in 1815.

67806.q: Which experience of faith did Pietism put particularly at the centre?
67806.e: Pietists stressed that faith needs an experienced conversion and a renewed life. Pure doctrine and outward churchgoing were not enough for them.
67806.m: Pietism stresses faith that is lived and experienced.

67807.q: Whom did the Pilgrim Mission on St Chrischona near Basel, founded in 1840, train?
a: Priests for the Diocese of Basel
67807.e: The Basel Pietist Christian Friedrich Spittler founded the Pilgrim Mission. It trained lay preachers and missionaries and still exists today.
67807.m: Lay preachers and missionaries were trained on St Chrischona.

67808.q: Which dogma of the First Vatican Council of 1870 helped trigger the Kulturkampf in Switzerland?
a: The Assumption of Mary into heaven
67808.e: In 1870 the council declared that the pope is infallible when he solemnly decides on faith and morals. When Bishop Eugène Lachat proclaimed the dogma, most cantons of his diocese deposed him.
67808.m: The dogma of infallibility of 1870 intensified the Kulturkampf.

67809.q: Which church arose in Switzerland during the Kulturkampf from Catholics who rejected papal infallibility?
67809.e: The Christian Catholics rejected the dogma of 1870 and founded their own church in 1875. Their first bishop was Eduard Herzog.
67809.m: The Christian Catholic Church arose during the Kulturkampf.

67810.q: What step did the Federal Council take towards the pope in December 1873?
a: It broke off relations with the Holy See
It concluded a new concordat with Rome
It set up a Swiss archdiocese
It invited the pope to negotiations in Bern
67810.e: After a sharply worded papal encyclical, the Federal Council handed the nuncio his passports. This ended the pope's diplomatic representation in Switzerland for the time being.
67810.m: The Kulturkampf led to a break between Bern and Rome.

67811.q: In which year was the papal nunciature in Switzerland re-established?
67811.e: Only after the First World War did relations return to normal, and in 1920 a nuncio returned to Bern. By then the tensions of the Kulturkampf had eased.
67811.m: Since 1920 the pope has again had a nuncio in Bern.

67812.q: In which Catholic region did the canton of Bern expel around 97 priests in 1874 who remained loyal to their bishop?
67812.e: The Catholic priests in the Jura, then part of Bern, refused to accept the deposition of their bishop. In 1875 the Confederation declared the expulsion unconstitutional.
67812.m: The Jura was a flashpoint of the Kulturkampf in the canton of Bern.

67813.q: What did the diocese article of the Federal Constitution of 1874 require?
a: New dioceses needed the approval of the Confederation
Every canton had to have its own diocese
Bishops had to be elected by the people
Dioceses were not allowed to own property
67813.e: The article was meant to stop Rome from changing diocesan boundaries without state approval. It was one of the special denominational articles of the constitution.
67813.m: The diocese article made new dioceses dependent on the Confederation's approval.

67814.q: What did Switzerland introduce nationwide during the Kulturkampf with the Federal Act on Civil Status and Marriage of 1874?
67814.e: Keeping the civil registers passed from parish offices to state officials. From then on, only a marriage concluded at the civil registry office was valid.
67814.m: Since the Kulturkampf, marriage in Switzerland has been a matter for the state.

67815.q: Which political right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 deny clergy until 1999?
a: Eligibility for election to the National Council
The right to vote in referendums
67815.e: Clergy could vote, but they could not be elected to the National Council. Only the new Federal Constitution of 1999 removed this restriction.
67815.m: Until 1999 clergy could not become members of the National Council.

67816.q: In which town is the seat of the diocese that today covers the whole of Ticino?
67816.e: Until the 19th century, Ticino's parishes belonged to the Italian dioceses of Como and Milan. After the separation, a church administration of its own was set up in Lugano, since 1971 the Diocese of Lugano.
67816.m: Ticino today forms the Diocese of Lugano.

67817.q: In which constitution was the ban on the Jesuit order in Switzerland first laid down?
67817.e: After the victory of the Liberals, the very first Federal Constitution included a ban on Jesuits being admitted to Switzerland. The order was seen as the mastermind of the other side.
67817.m: The ban on Jesuits was already in the first Federal Constitution.

67818.q: How did the Federal Constitution of 1874 tighten the ban on Jesuits compared with 1848?
a: Every member of the order was banned from any activity in church and school
The property of all monasteries was seized
The order was threatened with prison sentences
67818.e: From then on, not only were Jesuit houses forbidden, but individual Jesuits were also not allowed to work as pastors or teachers. This was a result of the Kulturkampf.
67818.m: The constitution of 1874 tightened the ban on Jesuits.

67819.q: To which group of constitutional provisions did the ban on Jesuits belong?
67819.e: The special denominational articles were provisions aimed mainly at the Catholic Church. Besides the ban on Jesuits, they included the ban on monasteries and the diocese article.
67819.m: The ban on Jesuits was a special denominational article.

67821.q: What was the result of the 1973 popular vote on lifting the ban on Jesuits?
67821.e: About 55 percent of voters said yes. The rather narrow result shows that old denominational prejudices still had an effect.
67821.m: The ban on Jesuits fell in 1973 with a narrow majority.

67822.q: Which other special denominational article was lifted in the same vote as the ban on Jesuits?
67822.e: The proposal also deleted the article that prohibited founding new monasteries or restoring dissolved ones. Both articles dated from the time of denominational conflict.
67822.m: The Jesuit and monastery articles fell in the same vote.

67823.q: According to today's view, which fundamental right did the ban on Jesuits violate?
67823.e: The ban targeted a group solely because of its religious affiliation. That is why it was increasingly seen as incompatible with freedom of belief and conscience.
67823.m: The ban on Jesuits contradicted freedom of religion.

67824.q: Joining which international treaty made the ban on Jesuits seem even more problematic in the 1960s?
67824.e: Switzerland wanted to ratify the Council of Europe's convention but would have had to make reservations because of the special articles. This gave the repeal extra momentum; ratification came in 1974.
67824.m: The Convention on Human Rights helped bring about the lifting of the ban on Jesuits.

67825.q: Which Catholic canton did NOT belong to the Sonderbund?
67825.e: Solothurn was mainly Catholic but had a liberal government and sided with the Federal Diet. The Sonderbund consisted of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden and Nidwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais.
67825.m: Not all Catholic cantons joined the Sonderbund.

67826.q: Which 1841 decision by the canton of Aargau sharpened the denominational conflict before the Sonderbund War?
67826.e: The liberal Grand Council dissolved the Aargau monasteries, which Catholics saw as a breach of the Federal Treaty. The Aargau monastery dispute poisoned the atmosphere in the Confederation.
67826.m: The Aargau monastery dispute was one of the triggers of the Sonderbund War.

67827.q: Which decision by the canton of Lucerne in 1844 particularly outraged the Liberals?
a: Calling the Jesuits to run the higher schools
67827.e: For Liberals and Radicals, the Jesuits were the symbol of a policy loyal to Rome and hostile to progress. Calling them to Lucerne provoked fierce reactions.
67827.m: Calling the Jesuits to Lucerne inflamed the conflict.

67828.q: What are the armed expeditions by radical volunteers against Lucerne in 1844 and 1845 called?
67828.e: Radical volunteers tried to overthrow the conservative government of Lucerne but failed bloodily. The attacks strengthened the Catholic cantons' wish to form an alliance.
67828.m: The Free Corps expeditions were aimed at conservative Lucerne.

67829.q: Who led the Federal Diet's troops as general in the Sonderbund War?
67829.e: Dufour from Geneva led a short campaign and ordered that the wounded and prisoners be treated with care. As a result, losses remained relatively low.
67829.m: General Dufour led the federal troops in 1847.

67830.q: Which denomination did Johann Ulrich von Salis-Soglio, commander-in-chief of the Sonderbund army, belong to?
67830.e: The officer from Chur in the Grisons was Reformed but led the troops of the Catholic conservative cantons. So the conflict was not purely denominational but also political.
67830.m: The Sonderbund was led by a Reformed general.

67831.q: Roughly how long did the Sonderbund War of 1847 last?
67831.e: The war lasted from 3 to 29 November 1847; Valais was the last to surrender. Afterwards, the federal state could be founded in 1848.
67831.m: The Sonderbund War was a short civil war in November 1847.

67832.q: Which pope called the First Vatican Council?
67832.e: The pope opened the council in St Peter's Basilica in December 1869. He wanted to strengthen the Church against liberalism and rationalism.
67832.m: The First Vatican Council was called by Pius IX.

67833.q: In which years did the First Vatican Council meet?
67833.e: The council began in December 1869 and was adjourned in autumn 1870. It was the first general council since the Council of Trent.
67833.m: The First Vatican Council met in 1869 and 1870.

67834.q: Which teaching did the First Vatican Council define as dogma in 1870?
a: The Assumption of Mary into heaven
67834.e: In 1870 the constitution “Pastor aeternus” defined the infallibility and primacy of the pope. The other teachings were defined in 1854, 1950 and at the Council of Trent.
67834.m: The First Vatican Council declared papal infallibility a dogma.

67835.q: According to the dogma of 1870, under which condition is a doctrinal decision of the pope regarded as infallible?
a: When he decides ex cathedra on faith or morals
When he preaches a sermon in St Peter's
When all the cardinals have agreed
67835.e: The pope is only infallible when, as supreme teacher of the Church, he definitively proclaims a teaching on faith or morals. Ordinary statements are not included.
67835.m: Only decisions made ex cathedra are regarded as infallible.

67836.q: Why was the vote on infallibility at the First Vatican Council almost unanimous?
a: All bishops were in favour from the start
Only cardinals were allowed to vote
67836.e: Many opponents left before the final vote so as not to have to vote against the pope. So on 18 July 1870 the result was 533 votes to 2.
67836.m: Infallibility was passed almost unanimously because many opponents had left.

67837.q: Why was the First Vatican Council not formally concluded in 1870?
a: The pope died during the council
67837.e: After the French protecting troops withdrew during the Franco-Prussian War, the Kingdom of Italy occupied Rome in September 1870. The pope adjourned the council indefinitely.
67837.m: The capture of Rome in 1870 ended the First Vatican Council early.

67838.q: Which Munich theologian rejected the dogma of infallibility and was excommunicated in 1871?
67838.e: The well-known church historian considered the dogma historically unfounded. He became a leading figure of the resistance without joining a new church himself.
67838.m: Ignaz von Döllinger was the best-known opponent of infallibility.

67839.q: Which relationship did the First Vatican Council's constitution “Dei Filius” mainly deal with?
67839.e: The 1870 constitution teaches that God can be known by natural reason, but that revelation is also necessary. It was aimed at rationalism and religious scepticism.
67839.m: Dei Filius defines the relationship between faith and reason.

67840.q: Which dogma did the Catholics reject who met in Solothurn in 1871 and later founded the Christian Catholic Church?
67840.e: The participants rejected the dogma of infallibility proclaimed in 1870. This developed into the independent Christian Catholic Church.
67840.m: The Christian Catholic Church arose in protest against papal infallibility.

67841.q: Under which name are the sister churches of the Christian Catholic Church outside Switzerland mostly known?
67841.e: In Germany, Austria and the Netherlands they are called Old Catholic churches. The Swiss name “Christian Catholic” is unusual.
67841.m: Outside Switzerland, Christian Catholics are mostly called Old Catholics.

67842.q: Who elects the bishop in the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland?
67842.e: The church has a synodal structure: clergy and lay people decide together in the National Synod. This shared decision-making was a principle from the start.
67842.m: In the Christian Catholic Church, the synod elects the bishop.

67843.q: At which university have Christian Catholic theologians been trained since 1874?
67843.e: In 1874 the canton founded a Catholic theological faculty for Catholics critical of Rome. Today the Institute for Christian Catholic Theology is part of the Faculty of Theology.
67843.m: Christian Catholic theology is taught in Bern.

67844.q: After which city is the international union of Old Catholic churches named, to which the Christian Catholics also belong?
67844.e: In 1889 the Church of Utrecht and Old Catholic churches of Germany and Switzerland joined together in the Union of Utrecht. Geneva stands for Calvin, Canterbury for the Anglicans, Wittenberg for Luther.
67844.m: The Old Catholic churches are linked in the Union of Utrecht.

67845.q: Roughly how many members does the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland have (as of 2021)?
67845.e: According to its own figures, the church had about 11,200 members nationwide in 2021. Even so, it is recognised under public law in several cantons.
67845.m: The Christian Catholic Church is a small national church.

67846.q: What has distinguished the Christian Catholic Church from the Roman Catholic Church since 2000?
a: It no longer has a bishop
It no longer celebrates the Eucharist
67846.e: In 2000 Denise Wyss was ordained as the first Christian Catholic woman priest. The Roman Catholic Church does not ordain women as priests.
67846.m: Since 2000 there have been Christian Catholic women priests.

67847.q: What applies to priests in the Christian Catholic Church with regard to marriage?
a: They may only marry before ordination
67847.e: The church abolished compulsory celibacy as early as the 19th century. This clearly distinguishes it from the Roman Catholic Church.
67847.m: Christian Catholic priests are not required to be celibate.

67848.q: Which pope opened the Second Vatican Council in 1962?
67848.e: The pope had surprisingly announced the council in 1959 and opened it on 11 October 1962. He died in 1963, before it ended.
67848.m: John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council.

67849.q: Which pope brought the Second Vatican Council to a close in 1965?
67849.e: After his predecessor died in 1963, the newly elected pope continued the council. It was solemnly closed on 8 December 1965.
67849.m: Paul VI concluded the Second Vatican Council.

67850.q: With which Italian catchword is the aim of the Second Vatican Council often summed up?
67850.e: The word means roughly “bringing up to date”: the Church should translate its message into the present. “Risorgimento”, by contrast, refers to the Italian unification movement.
67850.m: Aggiornamento means opening the Church up to the present.

67851.q: Which visible change did the constitution on the liturgy “Sacrosanctum Concilium” make possible?
a: The election of bishops by the people
The removal of all fast days
67851.e: Instead of only in Latin, Mass could now largely be celebrated in the language of the faithful. The aim was the active participation of the congregation.
67851.m: Since the council, Mass has mostly been celebrated in the local language.

67852.q: Which relationship did the Second Vatican Council renew with the declaration “Nostra aetate” of 1965?
a: The relationship with Judaism and other religions
The relationship with the natural sciences
The relationship with the trade unions
The relationship with Europe's royal houses
67852.e: The declaration deals with the non-Christian religions. It rejects any collective guilt of the Jews for the death of Jesus and condemns every form of antisemitism.
67852.m: Nostra aetate renewed the Church's relationship with Judaism.

67853.q: Which right did the council recognise in the declaration “Dignitatis humanae”?
67853.e: The declaration bases religious freedom on the dignity of the human person. This was a clear break with earlier papal statements.

67854.q: What does the Second Vatican Council's pastoral constitution “Gaudium et spes” deal with?
a: The Church in the modern world
67854.e: The document begins with the words “Joy and hope” and turns to questions of work, culture, peace and politics. It stands for the Church's dialogue with the modern world.
67854.m: Gaudium et spes describes the Church in the modern world.

67855.q: Which Swiss theologian from Sursee served as an official adviser at the Second Vatican Council?
67855.e: The young professor from Tübingen was appointed a council theologian in 1962. Later he came into conflict with Rome and lost his licence to teach as a Catholic theologian in 1979.
67855.m: Hans Küng was an adviser at the Second Vatican Council.

67856.q: In which Aargau municipality was Karl Barth pastor from 1911 to 1921?
67856.e: In this working-class village, Barth stood up for the factory workers and was called “the red pastor”. His first major book was also written here.
67856.m: Karl Barth was pastor in Safenwil for ten years.

67857.q: With which commentary on one of Paul's letters did Karl Barth become well known in 1919?
67857.e: The heavily revised second edition of 1922 shook liberal theology. In it Barth stressed the infinite distance between God and humans.
67857.m: Barth's Epistle to the Romans started a theological turning point.

67858.q: To which theological school is the early Karl Barth assigned?
67858.e: This school stresses that God is “wholly other” and reveals himself only in his Word. Other representatives were Eduard Thurneysen and Friedrich Gogarten.
67858.m: Karl Barth was a leading representative of dialectical theology.

67859.q: What is Karl Barth's unfinished main work of over 9,000 pages called?
67859.e: Barth worked on it from 1932 until his death; the work comprises 13 part-volumes. It is regarded as one of the most extensive theological works of the 20th century.
67859.m: The Church Dogmatics is Karl Barth's main work.

67860.q: Why did Karl Barth lose his professorship in Bonn in 1935?
a: He refused the unconditional oath to Hitler
He refused to teach in German
67860.e: Barth would only take the civil servants' oath with the addition “as far as I can answer for it as a Protestant Christian”. He was then dismissed.
67860.m: Karl Barth refused Hitler the unconditional oath of loyalty.

67861.q: At which university did Karl Barth teach after his expulsion from Germany until 1962?
67861.e: Barth returned to the city of his birth in 1935 and taught there until his retirement. He died there in 1968.
67861.m: From 1935 Karl Barth taught in Basel.

67862.q: Against whom did Karl Barth direct his sharp polemic “No!” on natural theology in 1934?
67862.e: The Zurich theologian believed that humans have a “point of contact” for God's revelation. Barth rejected any knowledge of God outside Christ.
67862.m: Barth and Brunner argued about natural theology.

67863.q: Which composer did Karl Barth admire so much that he dedicated a work to him?
67863.e: Barth listened to his music every morning and in 1956 wrote a tribute for his 200th birthday. He saw in it a parable of the praise of good creation.
67863.m: Karl Barth loved the music of Mozart.

67864.q: In which year was the Barmen Theological Declaration adopted?
67864.e: The declaration was adopted at the end of May that year, just over a year after the Nazis seized power. It is regarded as the founding document of church resistance.
67864.m: The Barmen Theological Declaration dates from 1934.

67865.q: Which assembly adopted the Barmen Theological Declaration?
a: The first Confessing Synod of the German Evangelical Church
The General Assembly of the Lutheran World Federation
67865.e: Representatives of the confessing congregations met in the Gemarke Church. They saw themselves as the rightful Protestant church of Germany.
67865.m: The Confessing Synod of Barmen adopted the declaration.

67866.q: Against which church group, which wanted to combine Christianity and Nazism, was the Barmen Declaration directed?
67866.e: This group wanted an “Aryan” Reich Church based on the leader principle. The declaration rejected their teachings as false doctrine.
67866.m: The Barmen Declaration opposed the German Christians.

67867.q: How many theses does the Barmen Theological Declaration consist of?
67867.e: Each thesis consists of Bible quotations, a positive statement and a rejection of false doctrine. This structure still makes it easy to recognise today.
67867.m: The Barmen Declaration has six theses.

67868.q: What does the first thesis of the Barmen Declaration state?
a: Jesus Christ is the one Word of God to which the Church listens
The Church is under the protection of the state
People and race are revelations of God
The Bible must be translated anew
67868.e: Alongside Christ, the Church may not recognise any other events, powers or figures as revelation. In this way it rejected the ideology of the Nazis.
67868.m: The first Barmen thesis binds the Church to Jesus Christ alone.

67869.q: Which theologian wrote the most important draft of the Barmen Declaration?
67869.e: The Swiss theologian, then teaching in Bonn, wrote most of the text himself. Niemöller led the Pastors' Emergency League, while Althaus was critical of the declaration.
67869.m: Karl Barth was the main author of the Barmen Declaration.

67870.q: Which denominations supported the Barmen Declaration together?
67870.e: For the first time since the Reformation, Protestant Christians of different confessions made a joint confession of faith. This was important for ecumenism.
67870.m: At Barmen, Lutherans, Reformed and United made a joint confession.

67871.q: Which shortcoming of the Barmen Declaration is often criticised today?
a: It was silent about the persecution of the Jews
It rejected the Bible as its basis
67871.e: The declaration mainly defended the freedom of the Church. A word for the persecuted Jews was missing, which was later acknowledged self-critically.
67871.m: The Barmen Declaration did not mention the persecution of the Jews.

67872.q: Which Nicaraguan priest and poet became Minister of Culture in the Sandinista government in 1979?
67872.e: The liberation theologian took up a government post after the revolution. Pope John Paul II publicly rebuked him for it in 1983.
67872.m: Ernesto Cardenal combined priesthood, poetry and politics.

67873.q: Which topics did the Latin American bishops put at the centre in Medellín in 1968?
67873.e: The bishops applied the impulses of the Second Vatican Council to Latin America and spoke of “structural sin”. The conference shaped liberation theology.
67873.m: The Medellín conference of 1968 shaped liberation theology.

67874.q: Which key phrase sums up the aim of liberation theology?
67874.e: The Church should see the world from the point of view of the poor and take their side. The Latin American bishops explicitly adopted the phrase.
67874.m: Liberation theology puts the poor at the centre.

67875.q: What are the small groups called in which lay people in Latin America read the Bible together and discuss their situation?
67875.e: In these communities, often poor people without a priest interpret the Bible in the light of their everyday lives. They became the bearers of liberation theology.
67875.m: Base communities read the Bible from the everyday life of the poor.

67876.q: Which three-step method does liberation theology often use?
67876.e: First the social situation is analysed, then judged in the light of the Gospel and finally changed. The method comes from the Young Christian Workers movement.
67876.m: Liberation theology moves from seeing to judging to acting.

67877.q: On which Brazilian liberation theologian did Rome impose a period of penitential silence in 1985?
67877.e: The Franciscan had criticised the Church's power structures in a book. Later he left the order and the priesthood.
67877.m: Leonardo Boff was ordered by Rome to keep silent.

67878.q: What did the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith especially criticise in parts of liberation theology in 1984?
a: The adoption of Marxist social analysis
67878.e: Under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, the instruction warned against narrowing faith down to class struggle. The concern for the poor was not rejected in principle.
67878.m: Rome criticised Marxist elements of liberation theology.

67879.q: In which country were six Jesuits of the Central American University murdered by soldiers in 1989?
67879.e: In November 1989, soldiers in San Salvador killed six Jesuits as well as a housekeeper and her daughter. Among the victims was the liberation theologian Ignacio Ellacuría.
67879.m: Six Jesuits were murdered in El Salvador's civil war in 1989.

67880.q: Where is the Ecumenical Institute of the World Council of Churches?
a: In the Château de Bossey on Lake Geneva
67880.e: Since 1946 the institute in Vaud has trained students from all over the world in ecumenical theology. It is close to the Council's headquarters in Geneva.
67880.m: The Ecumenical Institute of the World Council of Churches is in Bossey.

67882.q: Which large church is not a member of the World Council of Churches but works together with it?
67882.e: The Roman Catholic Church is not a member but works fully in some commissions. Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches belong to the Council.
67882.m: The Catholic Church is not a member of the World Council of Churches.

67883.q: Roughly how many member churches does the World Council of Churches have (as of the 2020s)?
67883.e: Over 350 churches from more than 120 countries belong to the Council, representing over 580 million Christians according to its own figures. They are Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant and Old Catholic churches.
67883.m: About 350 churches are united in the World Council of Churches.

67884.q: In which city did the 11th Assembly of the World Council of Churches take place in 2022?
67884.e: It was the Council's first assembly in Germany. Busan in South Korea hosted the previous assembly in 2013.

67885.q: Which conference of 1910 is regarded as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement?
a: The World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh
67885.e: Missionaries from different churches realised that their divisions hindered mission. This gave rise to movements that later flowed into the World Council of Churches.
67885.m: Modern ecumenism began in Edinburgh in 1910.

67886.q: What did the word “ecumenical” originally mean?
a: Relating to the whole inhabited earth
Relating only to one's own congregation
67886.e: The word comes from the Greek “oikoumene”, the inhabited world. Today ecumenism means the striving for unity among all Christians worldwide.
67886.m: Ecumenical means relating to the whole inhabited world.

67887.q: Against which injustice was the programme directed that the World Council of Churches launched in 1969, which particularly concerned southern Africa?
67887.e: Among other things, the programme gave humanitarian support to liberation movements in southern Africa. It was fiercely disputed in some member churches.
67887.m: The World Council of Churches campaigned against apartheid.

67889.q: In which year did the International Congress on World Evangelization take place in Lausanne?
67889.e: In July 1974, over 2,500 evangelical leaders from about 150 countries met. The congress gave the Lausanne Movement its name.
67889.m: The Lausanne Congress of 1974 shaped the evangelical movement.

67890.q: Which American evangelist played a key role in calling the Lausanne Congress?
67890.e: The world-famous revivalist preacher led the congress. For decades he was the face of the evangelical movement.
67890.m: Billy Graham was the defining figure of the Lausanne Congress.

67891.q: Which two concerns did the evangelicals' Lausanne Covenant of 1974 combine?
a: Loyalty to the pope and veneration of Mary
67891.e: Under the leadership of the Anglican John Stott, the text stressed that working for justice is part of proclaiming the Gospel. The Covenant is a basic document for many evangelicals.
67891.m: The Lausanne Covenant combines evangelism and social responsibility.

67892.q: In which city was the Evangelical Alliance founded in 1846 as the first international association of evangelical Christians?
67892.e: Christians from different Protestant churches wanted to pray and act together across borders. This gave rise to the World Evangelical Alliance, which still exists today.
67892.m: The Evangelical Alliance was founded in London in 1846.

67893.q: Which feature is regarded as typical of evangelical Christians?
67893.e: The historian David Bebbington names four marks: conversion, the Bible, the cross and activism. Icons are typical of Orthodoxy; the pope and the Latin Mass of Catholicism.

67894.q: What is the Protestant revival movement called that spread across French-speaking Switzerland from Geneva from about 1816?
67894.e: Inspired among others by the Scot Robert Haldane, free churches and missionary societies were founded in Geneva. “Refuge”, by contrast, refers to the taking in of the Huguenots.
67894.m: The Geneva Réveil was a 19th-century revival movement.

67895.q: What was the series of publications from 1910 to 1915 called, after which a Bible-believing current in the USA was named?
67895.e: The essays defended central doctrines against liberal Bible criticism. The term fundamentalism comes from them.
67895.m: The term fundamentalism comes from “The Fundamentals”.

67896.q: On which continent did the second Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization take place in 1989?
67896.e: The congress met in Manila in the Philippines in 1989. Over 4,000 participants from 173 countries adopted the Manila Manifesto.
67896.m: The Manila Manifesto of 1989 carried on the Lausanne Movement.

67897.q: Which umbrella organisation represents many evangelical churches and organisations in German-speaking Switzerland?
67897.e: The Alliance links Christians from national and free churches and organises, for example, the Alliance Week of Prayer. It is part of the World Evangelical Alliance.
67897.m: The Swiss Evangelical Alliance links many evangelicals.

67898.q: Who has been Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople since 1991 (as of 2026)?
67898.e: Bartholomew I was elected in 1991 and is thus the longest-serving Ecumenical Patriarch in history. He is known as the “green patriarch” because he is strongly committed to protecting the environment.
67898.m: Bartholomew I has led the Ecumenical Patriarchate since 1991.

67899.q: In which present-day city does the Ecumenical Patriarch have his seat?
67899.e: The Patriarchate is in the Phanar district on the Golden Horn. Istanbul used to be called Constantinople.
67899.m: The Ecumenical Patriarch has his seat in Istanbul.

67900.q: What became of the Hagia Sophia, formerly the patriarchs' main church, after the Ottoman conquest in 1453?
67900.e: Sultan Mehmed II had the Hagia Sophia turned into a mosque in 1453. Since 1601 St George's Cathedral in the Phanar has been the Patriarchate's main church.
67900.m: After 1453 the Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

67901.q: What did Pope Paul VI and the Ecumenical Patriarch jointly lift in 1965?
67901.e: On 7 December 1965, Rome and Constantinople declared at the same time that the excommunications of 1054 were to be erased from the memory of the Church. This was an important step in bringing East and West closer.
67901.m: In 1965 Athenagoras I and Paul VI lifted the excommunications of 1054.

67902.q: To which church did the Ecumenical Patriarchate grant autocephaly in January 2019?
67902.e: With the tomos of January 2019, the Orthodox Church of Ukraine was recognised as an independent (autocephalous) church. This led to a serious conflict within Orthodoxy.
67902.m: The Orthodox Church of Ukraine received autocephaly in 2019.

67903.q: Which council in 381 gave the bishop of Constantinople the rank of honour right after the bishop of Rome?
67903.e: Canon 3 of the council of 381 justified the rank by saying that Constantinople was the “new Rome”. The Council of Chalcedon confirmed this in 451.
67903.m: Since 381 Constantinople has ranked in honour right after Rome.

67904.e: After the conquest, Mehmed II had the scholar Gennadios Scholarios installed as patriarch. The patriarch became head of all the empire's Orthodox subjects.

67905.q: In which place near Geneva is the Orthodox Centre of the Ecumenical Patriarchate?
67905.e: The centre in Chambésy was founded in 1966 and was used, among other things, to prepare a pan-Orthodox council. It shows Geneva's importance for ecumenism.
67905.m: The Ecumenical Patriarchate has an Orthodox centre in Chambésy near Geneva.

67906.q: Which grand prince had himself and Kievan Rus baptised in 988?
67906.e: Vladimir I adopted Christianity from Byzantium and had the people of Kyiv baptised in the Dnieper. In Orthodoxy he is venerated as “equal to the apostles”.
67906.m: Under Vladimir I, Kievan Rus became Christian in 988.

67907.q: Which city saw itself as the “Third Rome” of Orthodoxy after the fall of Constantinople in 1453?
67907.e: After Rome and Constantinople, Moscow saw itself as the new centre of the true faith. In 1589 Moscow also became a patriarchate of its own.
67907.m: Moscow saw itself as the Third Rome.

67908.q: With which body did Peter the Great replace the office of patriarch in 1721?
67908.e: Peter the Great wanted to subordinate the Church to the state and had it run by a committee, the Most Holy Synod. A state official, the Chief Procurator, supervised this body.
67908.m: Peter the Great replaced the patriarch with the Holy Synod.

67909.q: How did the Soviet government treat the Russian Orthodox Church after 1917?
a: It persecuted the Church and seized its property
It made it the state church
It left the Church completely alone
It paid all priests a wage
67909.e: The communist government was atheist. Churches were closed or destroyed, and many priests were arrested or killed.
67909.m: The Soviet Union persecuted the Orthodox Church.

67910.q: Who has been Patriarch of Moscow and all Rus since 2009 (as of 2025)?
67910.e: Kirill I succeeded Alexy II in 2009. He is close to the policies of the Russian state and publicly supports the war against Ukraine.
67910.m: Kirill I has been Patriarch of Moscow since 2009.

67911.q: Which Moscow cathedral was blown up on the orders of the Soviet government in 1931 and rebuilt by 2000?
67911.e: The cathedral commemorated the victory over Napoleon and was blown up under Stalin. An open-air swimming pool was later built on its site before it was rebuilt in the 1990s.
67911.m: The Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was destroyed and rebuilt.

67912.q: What are the believers called who rejected Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms in the 17th century?
67912.e: Nikon brought books and rites into line with Greek practice, for example making the sign of the cross with three fingers instead of two. The opponents split off as Old Believers; this is called the Raskol (schism).
67912.m: The Old Believers rejected Nikon's reforms.

67913.q: What is the wall decorated with images called that separates the sanctuary in Orthodox churches?
67913.e: The iconostasis is a wall full of icons between the nave and the sanctuary. It is typical of Russian and other Orthodox churches.
67913.m: In Orthodox churches, the iconostasis separates the sanctuary.

67914.q: What is the large central door of an iconostasis called?
67914.e: The Royal Doors (also called the Holy Doors) lead straight to the altar. Only clergy may pass through them, and only at certain moments of the liturgy.
67914.m: The central door of the iconostasis is called the Royal Doors.

67915.q: Seen from the nave, which icon is always to the right of the Royal Doors?
67915.e: To the right of the Royal Doors there is always the icon of Christ, to the left the icon of the Mother of God. Next to them there are often John the Baptist and the patron saint of the church.
67915.m: The icon of Christ always hangs to the right of the Royal Doors.

67916.q: What is the row of icons called in which Mary and John the Baptist turn in intercession towards Christ enthroned?
67916.e: The Greek word deesis means “request” or “intercession”. Mary and John plead with Christ on behalf of humanity, and they are often followed by archangels and apostles.
67916.m: The Deesis shows Mary and John interceding with Christ.

67917.q: Who is usually shown on the two side doors of the iconostasis?
67917.e: The deacons pass through the side doors during the liturgy, which is why they are also called deacons’ doors. They usually show the archangels Michael and Gabriel or holy deacons such as Stephen.
67917.m: The side doors usually show archangels or deacons.

67918.q: What does the iconostasis separate in an Orthodox church?
a: The bell tower from the nave
67918.e: The iconostasis is a wall covered with icons in front of the sanctuary. It developed from a low chancel screen in Byzantine churches.
67918.m: The iconostasis separates the sanctuary from the nave.

67919.q: What is usually shown on the panels of the Royal Doors?
a: The Baptism of Jesus in the Jordan
67919.e: The Annunciation stands for the beginning of salvation, the Evangelists for the Good News. Both suit the door through which the Gospel book is carried out.
67919.m: The Royal Doors usually show the Annunciation and the four Evangelists.

67920.q: In which country did the tall iconostasis with several tiers develop from the late 14th century?
67920.e: In Russia the icon wall grew to four or five rows, for example in the Kremlin cathedrals. Theophanes the Greek and Andrei Rublev created an early tall iconostasis in the Cathedral of the Annunciation in 1405.
67920.m: The multi-tiered iconostasis developed mainly in Russia.

67921.q: How many great monasteries make up the monastic republic of Mount Athos?
67921.e: The 20 great monasteries have equal rights and share the whole peninsula. There are also many sketes, cells and hermitages that belong to these monasteries.
67921.m: There are 20 great monasteries on Mount Athos.

67922.q: What does the avaton, an old rule on Mount Athos, forbid?
a: Women may not enter the peninsula
67922.e: The avaton has applied for centuries and is laid down in the special status of Athos. By tradition it even applies to female domestic animals.
67922.m: The avaton forbids women from entering Athos.
