67923.q: Who governs the monastic republic of Mount Athos?
67923.e: The representatives of the 20 monasteries meet in Karyes. A Greek civil governor is also based there, because Athos is under Greek sovereignty.
67923.m: Athos is governed by the monasteries themselves.

67924.q: In which century was the oldest of the great Athos monasteries founded?
67924.e: The Great Lavra monastery was founded in 963 by Athanasius the Athonite. It ranks first among the 20 monasteries.
67924.m: Monastic life on Athos has flourished for over a thousand years.

67925.q: Why is Mount Athos both a cultural and a natural World Heritage Site of UNESCO?
a: Because of its monasteries and landscape
67925.e: Athos was listed as a mixed World Heritage Site in 1988. The monastery buildings and the unspoilt landscape are recognised.
67925.m: Athos is both cultural and natural heritage.

67926.q: Which church is Mount Athos spiritually subject to, even though it belongs politically to Greece?
67926.e: Athos is an autonomous region under Greek sovereignty. In church matters, however, it is directly under the Patriarch in Istanbul, not the national Church of Greece.
67926.m: Spiritually, Athos is under the Ecumenical Patriarchate.

67927.q: What does the fact that there are Serbian, Bulgarian and Russian monasteries on Athos show?
a: Athos is a centre of the whole Orthodox world
Athos used to belong to Russia
67927.e: Besides Greek monasteries there are, for example, the Serbian Hilandar, the Bulgarian Zograf and the Russian-influenced Panteleimon. Orthodox monks from many countries live there.
67927.m: Athos is a centre of the whole Orthodox world.

67928.q: What does a male pilgrim need in order to visit Mount Athos?
a: A baptism in an Athos monastery
67928.e: The permit is called a diamonitirion and only a limited number are issued each day. Non-Orthodox visitors get even fewer places than Orthodox pilgrims.
67928.m: You need a special permit to visit Athos.

67929.q: What does the Greek word “hesychia”, from which hesychasm takes its name, mean?
67929.e: Hesychasts seek inner peace and stillness in order to meet God. Outer and inner restlessness should come to rest in prayer.

67930.q: Which short prayer do hesychasts repeat without ceasing?
67930.e: The Jesus Prayer usually goes “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me”. It is often linked with breathing and counted on a prayer rope.
67930.m: In hesychasm the Jesus Prayer is prayed without ceasing.

67931.q: Which monk and Archbishop of Thessaloniki defended hesychasm theologically in the 14th century?
67931.e: Gregory Palamas was a monk on Athos and later Archbishop of Thessaloniki. His teaching was confirmed by synods in Constantinople in the 14th century.
67931.m: Gregory Palamas is the most important defender of hesychasm.

67932.q: What did critics in the 14th century accuse the hesychasts of?
a: That God cannot be seen with bodily eyes
That they honoured the Pope too much
67932.e: The scholar Barlaam of Calabria mocked the monks’ method of prayer and their claim to see divine light. The dispute ended with his condemnation.
67932.m: The critics denied that God can be seen in prayer.

67933.q: According to Gregory Palamas, how could people meet God even though God’s essence cannot be known?
a: Through God’s energies, which they can experience
Through journeys to the Holy Land
67933.e: Palamas distinguished between God’s unknowable essence and his uncreated energies. People can experience these energies, for example as divine light.
67933.m: Palamas distinguished God’s essence from his energies.

67934.q: Which light did the hesychasts believe they could see in prayer?
67934.e: This means the uncreated light that the disciples saw at the Transfiguration of Jesus on Mount Tabor. This light is seen as an action of God, not his essence.
67934.m: Hesychasts wanted to see the light of Tabor.

67935.q: What does the name of the collection of texts “Philokalia”, which spread the inner prayer of the Eastern Church, mean?
67935.e: Philos means loving, kalos beautiful. The collection was published in Venice in 1782 and spread hesychasm especially in Russia.
67935.m: The Philokalia collects texts on inner prayer.

67936.q: Who has been Pope and Patriarch of the Coptic Orthodox Church since 2012 (as of 2025)?
67936.e: Tawadros II succeeded Shenouda III in 2012. Following an old custom, he was chosen from three candidates by lot, drawn by a child.
67936.m: Tawadros II has been head of the Copts since 2012.

67937.q: Where does the name “Copts” come from?
a: From the Greek word for Egyptians
From the name of a pharaoh
From the Coptic word for cross
From the name of a martyr
67937.e: The Greek “Aigyptios” became “qibt” in Arabic. So originally “Copt” simply meant Egyptian.
67937.m: The word Copt originally meant Egyptian.

67938.q: With which event does the counting of the Coptic “Era of the Martyrs” begin?
a: The founding of Alexandria in 331 BC
67938.e: The Copts count their years from 284, the start of Emperor Diocletian’s reign. Under him, the Christians of Egypt suffered a particularly harsh persecution.
67938.m: The Coptic calendar begins with Diocletian in the year 284.

67939.q: Which language do most Copts speak in everyday life today?
67939.e: Since the Arab conquest, Arabic gradually became the everyday language of Egypt. Coptic, the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language, lives on almost only in the liturgy.
67939.m: Today Coptic is used almost only in church services.

67940.q: Which Egyptian founded the first monasteries in the 4th century where monks lived together under a rule?
67940.e: Around 320, Pachomius founded a monastery in Tabennisi in Upper Egypt for monks who lived together. His rule influenced later monasticism in East and West.
67940.m: Pachomius is regarded as the founder of communal monastic life.

67941.q: Which alphabet is the Coptic script based on?
67941.e: The Coptic script took over the Greek alphabet. For sounds that did not exist in Greek, a few signs were added from the Demotic script.
67941.m: The Coptic script is based on the Greek alphabet.

67942.q: What is the name of the find of writings in the Coptic language discovered in Upper Egypt in 1945?
67942.e: Farmers near Nag Hammadi found codices from the 4th century, including the Gospel of Thomas. The texts are important for research into Gnosticism.
67942.m: The Nag Hammadi writings are Coptic texts from late antiquity.

67943.q: In which city is St Mark’s Cathedral, the seat of the Coptic Pope?
67943.e: St Mark’s Cathedral in the Abbasiya district of Cairo was consecrated in 1968. The head of the church’s title still refers to Alexandria, however.
67943.m: The Coptic Pope resides at St Mark’s Cathedral in Cairo.

67944.q: On which date does the Ethiopian Orthodox Church usually celebrate Christmas?
67944.e: The church follows the Ethiopian calendar, which is shifted in a similar way to the old Julian calendar. That is why Christmas, called Genna in Amharic, usually falls on 7 January.
67944.m: Ethiopian Christians usually celebrate Christmas on 7 January.

67945.q: In which century did the Kingdom of Aksum in today’s Ethiopia become Christian?
67945.e: King Ezana adopted the Christian faith around the middle of the 4th century. The Syrian Frumentius, who became the first bishop of Aksum, played a part in this.
67945.m: Aksum became Christian as early as the 4th century.

67946.q: Which ancient language is used in the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church?
67946.e: Ge'ez was the language of the Kingdom of Aksum and today is only a church language. The modern languages Amharic and Tigrinya are related to it.
67946.m: The liturgical language of Ethiopia is Ge'ez.

67947.q: In which Ethiopian town were famous churches carved out of the rock in the 12th and 13th centuries?
67947.e: The rock-hewn churches are named after King Lalibela and were meant to represent a “new Jerusalem”. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978.
67947.m: Ethiopia’s famous rock-hewn churches are in Lalibela.

67948.q: According to Ethiopian tradition, which object is kept in the Church of St Mary in Aksum?
67948.e: According to the national epic Kebra Nagast, Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark to Ethiopia. Only a single monk is allowed to see it.
67948.m: The Ethiopian Church believes it has the Ark of the Covenant in Aksum.

67949.q: Until the 20th century, from which church did Ethiopia receive its bishop?
a: From the Coptic Church of Egypt
67949.e: For centuries the Coptic Church provided Ethiopia’s bishop. Only in 1959 did Ethiopia get its own patriarch, Abuna Basilios.
67949.m: Until 1959 the Ethiopian Church depended on the Coptic Church.

67950.q: Which event does the Ethiopian Orthodox Church celebrate with the great feast of Timkat in January?
67950.e: At Timkat the tabots, replicas of the tablets of the Law, are carried to the water in solemn processions. The feast is part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.
67950.m: Timkat is the Ethiopian feast of the Baptism of Jesus.

67951.q: Which book belongs to the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church but not to that of most other churches?
67951.e: The Book of Enoch survives complete only in Ge'ez and is regarded as Holy Scripture in Ethiopia. Judith, Tobit and Wisdom, on the other hand, are also in the Catholic Bible.
67951.m: The Book of Enoch belongs to the Ethiopian Bible.

67952.q: According to tradition, which country was the first state to make Christianity its state religion, around 301?
67952.e: King Tiridates III was baptised by Gregory the Illuminator and made Christianity the state religion. Some researchers date this rather to 314.
67952.m: Armenia is regarded as the first Christian state.

67953.q: Who is regarded as the missionary of Armenia and the first Catholicos of the Armenian Church?
67953.e: Gregory is said to have been imprisoned in a pit for years before he healed and converted the king. After him, the church is sometimes also called “Gregorian”.
67953.m: Gregory the Illuminator converted Armenia to Christianity.

67954.q: In which language does the Armenian Apostolic Church traditionally celebrate its liturgy?
67954.e: The liturgy is celebrated in Classical Armenian, called Grabar. Today’s spoken Armenian is clearly different from it.
67954.m: The Armenian Church prays in Classical Armenian.

67955.q: Which family of churches does the Armenian Apostolic Church belong to?
67955.e: Like the Coptic and Ethiopian Churches, the Armenian Church did not accept the Council of Chalcedon of 451. That is why it belongs to the Oriental Orthodox Churches.
67955.m: The Armenian Apostolic Church is an Oriental Orthodox church.

67956.q: Why was the Armenian alphabet created around the year 405?
67956.e: Mesrop Mashtots developed the alphabet with the support of Catholicos Sahak. Soon afterwards the Armenian translation of the Bible was made.
67956.m: The Armenian alphabet was created for translating the Bible.

67957.q: To which apostles does the Armenian Apostolic Church trace its origin?
67957.e: According to tradition, the apostles Thaddeus and Bartholomew preached in Armenia in the 1st century. That is why the church calls itself “apostolic”.
67957.m: Thaddeus and Bartholomew are regarded as the apostles of Armenia.

67958.q: On which day does the Armenian Apostolic Church celebrate Christmas outside Jerusalem?
67958.e: The Armenian Church has kept the old custom of celebrating the Birth and Baptism of Jesus together on 6 January. The Patriarchate of Jerusalem follows the Julian calendar and celebrates on 19 January.

67959.q: Which event led to the Armenian Catholicosate of Cilicia eventually moving to Lebanon?
67959.e: During the First World War, hundreds of thousands of Armenians were murdered and driven out in the Ottoman Empire. The Catholicosate of Cilicia found a new home in Antelias near Beirut in 1930.
67959.m: The Catholicosate of Cilicia is now based in Lebanon.

67960.q: In which present-day Indian state do most St Thomas Christians live?
67960.e: The St Thomas Christians live mainly on the Malabar Coast in south-west India. Their mother tongue is Malayalam.
67960.m: Most St Thomas Christians live in Kerala.

67961.q: What are the Christians in India called who trace their church back to the “doubting” apostle from the Gospel of John?
67961.e: The apostle Thomas at first doubted the resurrection of Jesus. According to tradition, he came to southern India in the year 52.
67961.m: The St Thomas Christians trace their church back to the apostle Thomas.

67962.q: Which European sea power came to India around 1500 and encountered the St Thomas Christians there?
67962.e: After Vasco da Gama’s voyage in 1498, the Portuguese set up bases in India. They tried to bring the St Thomas Christians into line with the Roman Church.
67962.m: The Portuguese met the St Thomas Christians in India around 1500.

67963.q: Which language shaped the liturgy of the St Thomas Christians for centuries?
67963.e: The St Thomas Christians were long connected with the Church of the East in Mesopotamia. That is why they celebrated the liturgy in Syriac, a form of Aramaic.
67963.m: The liturgy of the St Thomas Christians was originally Syriac.

67964.q: What did the “Latinisation” of the St Thomas Christians by the Portuguese mean?
a: Adapting them to Roman Catholic customs
Learning the Latin script for Malayalam
67964.e: At the Synod of Diamper in 1599, Syriac books were burned and Latin customs introduced. The St Thomas Christians were placed under Rome.
67964.m: The Portuguese adapted the St Thomas Christians to Roman customs.

67965.q: What was the result of many St Thomas Christians resisting the Portuguese in the 17th century?
a: A lasting split into several churches
All Portuguese being driven out of Asia
All St Thomas Christians converting to Hinduism
The founding of their own state
67965.e: In 1653, with the Coonan Cross Oath, many St Thomas Christians broke away from the Portuguese. Since then there have been several churches of St Thomas Christians.
67965.m: Resistance to the Portuguese split the St Thomas Christians.

67966.q: Which is the largest church of the St Thomas Christians today?
67966.e: The Syro-Malabar Church is in communion with Rome but has its own East Syriac rite. It has several million members.
67966.m: The Syro-Malabar Church is the largest church of the St Thomas Christians.

67967.q: How did the Belgian colonial authorities react from 1921 to the prophet Simon Kimbangu, who was followed by large crowds?
a: They arrested him and kept him prisoner until his death
They sent him to study in Rome
67967.e: The authorities feared his large following and sentenced him to death; later he was imprisoned for life. The Kimbanguist Church grew out of his movement.
67967.m: The Kimbanguist Church goes back to Simon Kimbangu.

67968.q: What are churches called that were founded by Africans independently of the European mission churches?
67968.e: These churches, abbreviated AIC, often combine Christianity with African forms of expression such as dance, healing and prophecy. Today they have many millions of members.
67968.m: African independent churches were founded by Africans themselves.

67969.q: Which Anglican clergyman and later Archbishop of Cape Town received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 for his non-violent struggle against apartheid?
67969.e: Desmond Tutu became Archbishop of Cape Town in 1986 and later led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. He died in 2021.
67969.m: As a churchman, Desmond Tutu fought apartheid without violence.

67970.q: What had Samuel Ajayi Crowther, who in 1864 became the first African bishop of the Anglican Church, experienced as a child?
a: He had been enslaved and was freed
He grew up as a king’s son in London
He lived in a monastery in Rome
He travelled with Livingstone as a cabin boy
67970.e: Crowther was enslaved as a child and freed by the British navy. He later translated the Bible into the Yoruba language.
67970.m: Samuel Ajayi Crowther was the first African Anglican bishop.

67971.q: According to estimates by church statisticians, which continent has had the most Christians since about 2018?
67971.e: Around 1900 only a few million Christians lived in Africa; today there are hundreds of millions. The centre of Christianity has thus shifted to the Global South.
67971.m: Today most of the world’s Christians live in Africa.

67972.q: In which present-day country did the well-known African martyrs die at the court of King Mwanga II between 1885 and 1887?
67972.e: Mwanga II, the Kabaka of Buganda, had young Christians at his court executed. The Uganda Martyrs were canonised in 1964.
67972.m: The Uganda Martyrs died under King Mwanga II.

67973.q: In which country is the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, one of the largest churches in the world?
67973.e: The basilica in Yamoussoukro was built on the model of St Peter’s and consecrated in 1990. President Félix Houphouët-Boigny had it built in his birthplace.
67973.m: The Basilica of Yamoussoukro is in Ivory Coast.

67974.q: In which country is the Zion Christian Church the largest African independent church?
67974.e: The Zion Christian Church was founded in 1924. At Easter, hundreds of thousands make a pilgrimage to its centre, Moria, in Limpopo province.
67974.m: The Zion Christian Church is South Africa’s largest independent church.

67975.q: To which indigenous man is the Virgin of Guadalupe said to have appeared near Mexico City in 1531?
67975.e: Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin is said to have received the image of Mary on his cloak. He was canonised in 2002, and the Basilica of Guadalupe is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in the world.
67975.m: According to tradition, Juan Diego saw the Virgin of Guadalupe.

67976.q: Which Peruvian theologian gave liberation theology its name with his book of 1971?
67976.e: Gutiérrez wrote “Teología de la liberación” and called for theology to start from the situation of the poor. He died in 2024.
67976.m: Gustavo Gutiérrez is regarded as the father of liberation theology.

67977.q: Which Archbishop of San Salvador was murdered during a Mass in 1980 and canonised in 2018?
67977.e: Óscar Romero denounced the violence of the army and the death squads. He was shot at the altar during Mass and is now one of the best-known saints of Latin America.
67977.m: Óscar Romero was murdered because he stood up for the poor.

67978.q: Who in 1671 became the first person from the Americas to be canonised?
67978.e: The Dominican tertiary from Lima lived from 1586 to 1617 and was canonised by Pope Clement X. She is the patron saint of Peru and Latin America.
67978.m: Rose of Lima was the first saint of the Americas.

67979.q: Which pope was the first from Latin America?
67979.e: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Archbishop of Buenos Aires, was elected in 2013. He died in April 2025.
67979.m: Francis was the first pope from Latin America.

67980.q: In which Latin American country was Pope Leo XIV, elected in 2025, a missionary and bishop for many years?
67980.e: Robert Francis Prevost from the USA worked for a long time in Peru as an Augustinian and was Bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He also holds Peruvian citizenship.
67980.m: Leo XIV was a bishop in Peru for a long time.

67981.q: Which country has the most Catholics in the world?
67981.e: Well over 100 million Catholics live in Brazil. Their share of the population is falling, however, because many are moving to evangelical and Pentecostal churches.
67981.m: Brazil is the country with the most Catholics.

67982.q: Which phrase shaped the assembly of Latin American bishops in Puebla in 1979?
67982.e: The bishops of Latin America called for the church to stand first and foremost at the side of the poor. The phrase still shapes the church on the continent today.
67982.m: The church in Latin America is committed to the preferential option for the poor.

67983.q: What is special about the beginnings of the Catholic Church in Korea in the 18th century?
a: It was founded by lay people without missionaries
It was founded by Japanese monks
It was introduced by the king himself
It arose through a Portuguese fleet
67983.e: Korean scholars learned about the faith from books from China. Yi Seung-hun was baptised in Beijing in 1784 and then baptised others in Korea himself.
67983.m: The Catholic Church in Korea was founded by lay people.

67984.q: What was special about Pope John Paul II’s canonisation of the Korean martyrs in 1984?
a: It took place in Seoul, not in Rome
It was led by a Korean pope
It was the first canonisation ever
67984.e: The 103 martyrs died in the persecutions of the 18th and 19th centuries. Contrary to tradition, the ceremony took place not in Rome but in Seoul.
67984.m: In 1984, 103 Korean martyrs were canonised in Seoul.

67985.q: What happened in 1846 to Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Catholic priest of Korea?
a: He became a cardinal in Rome
67985.e: Andrew Kim Taegon was ordained in China in 1845 and executed in Seoul in 1846. He is the patron of the Korean clergy.
67985.m: Andrew Kim Taegon was the first Catholic priest of Korea.

67986.q: Which church in Seoul is regarded as the largest single Pentecostal congregation in the world?
67986.e: David Yonggi Cho founded the congregation in a tent in 1958. It grew to hundreds of thousands of members and is divided into many house groups.
67986.m: The Yoido Full Gospel Church is a huge Pentecostal congregation in Seoul.

67987.q: From which country did the first Protestant missionaries come to Korea in 1885?
67987.e: The Americans Horace Underwood and Henry Appenzeller arrived in Korea on Easter Sunday 1885. They founded schools that became well-known universities.
67987.m: American missionaries began the Protestant mission in Korea in 1885.

67988.q: According to the South Korean census of 2015, which religious group was the largest?
67988.e: About 20 per cent of the population described themselves as Protestant, about 16 per cent as Buddhist and 8 per cent as Catholic. More than half said they had no religion.
67988.m: According to the 2015 census, Protestants were the largest religious group in South Korea.

67989.q: What is the cathedral of the Catholic Archdiocese of Seoul called?
67989.e: The neo-Gothic cathedral was consecrated in 1898. In the 1970s and 1980s it was a place of refuge for the democracy movement.
67989.m: Myeongdong Cathedral is the cathedral of Seoul.

67990.q: Who defended the rights of the indigenous peoples against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda in the Valladolid debate of 1550?
67990.e: Las Casas was himself a settler at first and then became a Dominican. He denounced the violence of the conquistadors and denied that indigenous people could be converted by force.
67990.m: Bartolomé de Las Casas stood up for the rights of indigenous peoples.

67991.q: What was the Spanish colonial system called in which settlers were given indigenous people as workers and were supposed to Christianise them in return?
67991.e: The encomienda was meant to combine protection and mission, but led to forced labour and exploitation. The New Laws of 1542 tried to restrict it.
67991.m: The encomienda combined mission with forced labour.

67992.q: For which people did the Jesuits set up the reductions in the area of present-day Paraguay in the 17th and 18th centuries?
67992.e: In the reductions the Guaraní lived in their own villages and were protected from slave hunters. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767/68, the reductions fell apart.
67992.m: The Jesuit reductions were villages of the Guaraní.

67994.q: To which West African region did the Basel Mission send missionaries from 1828?
67994.e: The Basel Mission worked in what is now Ghana, where the Presbyterian Church of Ghana grew out of it. Many of the first missionaries died of tropical diseases.
67994.m: The Basel Mission worked on the Gold Coast from 1828.

67995.q: Which Christian king of the Kingdom of Kongo spread Christianity in his realm from 1506?
67995.e: Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba) maintained close relations with Portugal and sent letters to the Portuguese king. In them he also complained about the Portuguese slave trade.
67995.m: Afonso I made the Kingdom of Kongo a Christian kingdom.

67996.q: With which three key words did the missionary David Livingstone sum up his programme for Africa?
67996.e: Livingstone hoped that legal trade would push out the slave trade. His programme shows how closely mission and colonial interests were linked at the time.
67996.m: Livingstone combined mission with commerce and civilisation.

67997.q: What was the Spanish text of 1513 called that was read out to indigenous people, calling on them to submit to the Crown and the Church?
67997.e: The Requerimiento was often read out in Spanish without translation. War against anyone who did not submit was considered justified.
67997.m: The Requerimiento called on indigenous people to submit.

67998.q: According to Article 72 of the Federal Constitution, which level of government is responsible for regulating the relationship between church and state?
67998.e: Article 72 paragraph 1 of the Federal Constitution leaves the regulation of church and state to the cantons. That is why Switzerland has 26 different solutions.
67998.m: In Switzerland, each canton regulates its own relationship with the churches.

67999.q: Which three Christian churches are officially recognised under public law as national churches in many cantons?
a: Reformed, Roman Catholic and Christ Catholic
67999.e: The Evangelical Reformed, the Roman Catholic and in many places the Christ Catholic Church are the classic national churches. They enjoy a special status under public law.
67999.m: Switzerland’s classic national churches are the Reformed, Roman Catholic and Christ Catholic churches.

68000.q: What is meant by the “dual system” of the Catholic Church in Switzerland?
a: Alongside diocese and parish there are democratically organised bodies under state law
Church and state each elect half of the bishops
Each canton has two bishops with equal rights
All services are held in two national languages
68000.e: Alongside the church structure of diocese and parish, there are parish communities and cantonal bodies under state law. They mainly manage finances and staff matters democratically.
68000.m: The dual system combines the church hierarchy with democratic bodies under state law.

68001.q: Which non-Christian community is officially recognised under public law in the canton of Zurich?
68001.e: In the canton of Zurich, besides the Christian national churches, the Israelitische Cultusgemeinde and the Liberal Jewish Community are recognised. This was the first time Jewish communities received this status in the canton.
68001.m: In the canton of Zurich, two Jewish communities are also recognised under public law.

68002.q: What changed in the canton of Bern with the National Churches Act that came into force in 2020?
a: Ministers are employed by the national churches instead of the canton
Church tax for private individuals was abolished
The national churches lost their recognition
All parishes were merged into one
68002.e: Until the end of 2019, the ministers of the national churches in the canton of Bern were employees of the canton. Since 2020 the national churches themselves have been the employers.
68002.m: Since 2020, the national churches in the canton of Bern have employed their ministers themselves.

68003.q: What right do members of a parish recognised under public law typically have?
a: They vote on the parish budget and tax rate
They elect members of the National Council
They are exempt from federal tax
They may bring cantonal laws into force
68003.e: Recognised parishes are democratically organised. Members elect their officials and decide on finances and the tax rate at meetings or at the ballot box.
68003.m: Parishes are democratic, and their members decide on the finances.

68004.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution guarantees that nobody can be forced to belong to a religious community?
68004.e: Article 15 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of religion and conscience. This includes the right to leave a church.
68004.m: Thanks to freedom of religion and conscience, anyone may leave a church.

68005.q: What legal form do national churches recognised under public law have in most cantons?
68005.e: Recognised national churches and parishes are independent public-law corporations with their own legal personality. They are, however, not part of the administration.
68005.m: A recognised national church is a public-law corporation.

68006.q: Which canton provides in its constitution for a so-called “small” cantonal recognition, which the Alevi community, for example, has received?
68006.e: Besides recognition under public law, Basel-Stadt has a cantonal recognition for communities organised under private law. It brings mainly symbolic rights but no power to levy taxes.
68006.m: Basel-Stadt has an additional, weaker form of recognition for smaller religious communities.

68008.q: On what grounds does the Federal Supreme Court consider church tax for legal entities to be constitutional?
a: Legal entities cannot claim freedom of religion
Companies are usually founded by churches
Church tax is a federal tax
Companies have voting rights in parishes
68008.e: According to established case law, for example a ruling from 1976 (BGE 102 Ia 468), companies cannot invoke freedom of religion and conscience. Many legal scholars criticise this view.
68008.m: According to the Federal Supreme Court, companies have no freedom of religion and must therefore pay church tax.

68009.q: How can a private individual stop having to pay church tax?
a: By applying to the Federal Council
68009.e: Because of freedom of religion and conscience, nobody can be forced to pay taxes to a church they do not belong to. In many cantons this does not apply to companies.
68009.m: Anyone who leaves the church no longer pays church tax.

68010.q: How did Zurich voters decide in 2014 on the initiative to abolish church tax for companies?
68010.e: Only about 28 per cent voted yes on 18 May 2014. So companies in Zurich still pay church tax.
68010.m: In 2014, Zurich voters clearly kept church tax for companies.

68011.q: Which youth party launched the Zurich initiative against church tax for companies that was rejected in 2014?
68011.e: The Young Liberals argued that companies cannot have a faith and should therefore not have to pay. The initiative clearly failed.
68011.m: In 2014, the Young Liberals wanted to abolish church tax for Zurich companies.

68012.q: What may church taxes paid by legal entities in the canton of Zurich not be used for?
a: For religious purposes such as services
For social work and youth work
For cultural heritage such as church buildings
68012.e: Zurich’s church law has a so-called negative earmarking. Money from companies is meant to fund services for society as a whole, not worship.
68012.m: In Zurich, church taxes from companies may not be used for services.

68013.q: In which canton is church tax voluntary for both individuals and legal entities?
68013.e: In Neuchâtel church tax is levied, but paying it is voluntary. The loss of large company payers therefore hits the churches hard.
68013.m: In Neuchâtel, individuals and companies decide for themselves whether to pay church tax.

68014.q: How are the national churches in the canton of Vaud financed?
68014.e: Vaud has no church tax of its own. The recognised churches receive contributions from the general state budget.
68014.m: In the canton of Vaud, the state pays the churches from general taxes.

68015.q: Who usually receives church taxes in Switzerland?
68015.e: The cantons usually recognise the Reformed, the Roman Catholic and often the Christ Catholic Church as national churches. In some cantons Jewish communities are also recognised.
68015.m: Church taxes go to the churches recognised under public law.

68016.q: How do the churches justify companies also paying church tax?
a: With their social services for everyone
With the faith of the company bosses
With companies’ voting rights in the church
68016.e: The churches point to their work in pastoral care, social work, youth work and culture, which benefits everyone. In the Grisons too, voters clearly rejected abolishing it in 2014.
68016.m: Church tax on companies is justified by the churches’ social services.

68017.q: Which two cantons have a far-reaching separation of church and state?
68017.e: Geneva separated church and state in 1907, Neuchâtel in 1941. There is no compulsory church tax in these cantons.
68017.m: Geneva and Neuchâtel largely separate church and state.

68018.q: Despite the separation, how do the churches in Geneva receive contributions from their members?
a: The tax office collects a voluntary contribution
All taxpayers pay a compulsory tax
The Confederation pays a lump sum every year
The municipalities pay the ministers’ salaries
68018.e: With your tax return you can make a voluntary contribution to a church, which the canton collects. Because many do not pay, the Geneva churches are short of money.
68018.m: In Geneva the church contribution is voluntary but is collected by the canton.

68019.q: Which law did Geneva voters accept on 10 February 2019?
a: A law on the secularism of the state
A law to bring back the state church
A law on a compulsory church tax
A law on a Diocese of Geneva
68019.e: The “Loi sur la laïcité de l'État” puts into practice the secularism laid down in the Geneva constitution. Among other things, it regulates religious symbols and religious events in public spaces.
68019.m: In 2019 Geneva set out its secularism in a law of its own.

68020.q: Which religious item of clothing was particularly in focus in the debate about the Geneva secularism law?
68020.e: The law requires state employees who deal with the public to show religious restraint. Critics saw it above all as a headscarf ban.
68020.m: In Geneva in 2019, the dispute was mainly about the headscarf.

68021.q: What does the Geneva secularism law require of state employees who deal with the public?
a: They do without visible religious symbols
They belong to a recognised church
They attend a church service every year
They pay a higher church tax
68021.e: Article 3 of the law obliges state employees who deal with the public to show religious restraint. Critics saw it above all as a ban on the headscarf.
68021.m: Geneva state employees who deal with the public should not wear religious symbols.

68022.q: Since the Geneva secularism law of 2019, who can receive the voluntary contribution via tax?
a: In principle, other religious communities too
68022.e: The contribution is now called “contribution religieuse volontaire”. It is no longer open only to the three traditional churches.
68022.m: The voluntary contribution in Geneva is now also open to other religious communities.

68023.q: How does Neuchâtel treat the churches despite the separation of church and state?
a: It recognises them as institutions of public interest
It collects a compulsory church tax
68023.e: A concordat of 2001 recognises the Reformed, the Roman Catholic and the Christ Catholic Church. There is, however, no state church.
68023.m: Despite the separation, Neuchâtel recognises churches as institutions of public interest.

68024.q: What was the result of the federal popular initiative for the separation of church and state in 1980?
68024.e: The initiative failed with 78.9 per cent voting no and was rejected by all cantons. The relationship between church and state remained a matter for the cantons.
68024.m: In 1980 Switzerland clearly rejected a nationwide separation of church and state.

68025.q: In which canton did voters reject a separation of church and state in 1977 and 1995?
68025.e: In the canton of Zurich, separation was clearly rejected in both 1977 and 1995. The national churches remained recognised.
68025.m: The canton of Zurich has twice decided against separating church and state.

68026.q: What was the Protestant Church in Switzerland (EKS) called until the end of 2019?
68026.e: The Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches (SEK) was renamed EKS on 1 January 2020. Legally it remained the same organisation with a new constitution.
68026.m: The EKS is the former Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches.

68027.q: In which year was the Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches founded?
68027.e: On 7 September 1920, 15 Reformed churches and two diaspora associations joined together. Before that there was only a loose church conference.
68027.m: The Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches was founded in 1920.

68028.q: Why was the Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches founded in Olten of all places in 1920?
a: As a transport hub, Olten was easy to reach
The Federal Council met in Olten at the time
Olten was the largest Reformed town
68028.e: The founding assembly took place in Olten town hall. Thanks to its position at a railway junction, Olten was easy to reach for delegates from all parts of the country.
68028.m: The Reformed church federation was founded in the transport hub of Olten.

68029.q: Who was elected in 2020 as the first woman president of the Council of the EKS?
68029.e: Rita Famos from the canton of Zurich is the first woman to lead the Swiss Reformed Church. Her predecessor Gottfried Locher had resigned in May 2020.
68029.m: Rita Famos is the first woman president of the Protestant Church in Switzerland.

68030.q: What is the parliament of the EKS called, which meets twice a year?
68030.e: The Synod, with about 80 members from the member churches, is the highest body. Until 2019 it was called the Assembly of Delegates.
68030.m: The parliament of the EKS is called the Synod.

68031.q: Which churches are the main members of the Protestant Church in Switzerland (EKS)?
a: The free churches of French-speaking Switzerland
68031.e: The members are 24 cantonal Reformed churches and the Evangelical Methodist Church. The EKS is their national union.
68031.m: The EKS unites the cantonal Reformed churches of Switzerland.

68032.q: Which aid organisation did the Federation of Protestant Churches found in 1946?
68032.e: The aid organisation of the Protestant churches of Switzerland (HEKS) was founded after the Second World War. Caritas and Fastenaktion are Catholic organisations.
68032.m: HEKS is the aid organisation of Switzerland’s Reformed churches.

68033.q: What did the Federation of Protestant Churches, the Bishops’ Conference and the Christ Catholic Church declare together in 1973?
a: The merger of their aid organisations
68033.e: The declaration of 1973 was an important ecumenical step. Anyone baptised in one of the three churches is not baptised again if they change church.
68033.m: Since 1973, Reformed, Catholics and Christ Catholics in Switzerland have recognised each other’s baptism.

68034.q: How many members does the Council, the executive of the EKS, have?
68034.e: The Council has seven members; until 2010 there were nine. It runs the day-to-day business of the EKS.
68034.m: The executive of the EKS is a seven-member council.

68035.q: What is the task of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference?
a: It coordinates the joint work of the Catholic bishops
68035.e: The bishops discuss shared questions of faith, pastoral care and society there. The conference has existed since 1863 and is regarded as the oldest in the world.
68035.m: The Swiss bishops work together in the Bishops’ Conference.

68036.q: What is special about the Swiss Bishops’ Conference compared with others around the world?
a: It is regarded as the first bishops’ conference in the world
It has the most members in the world
It is based in the Vatican
68036.e: The Swiss Bishops’ Conference is regarded as the oldest bishops’ conference of all. Such bodies were set up in other countries only later.
68036.m: The Swiss Bishops’ Conference is the oldest bishops’ conference in the world.

68037.q: Which monastery in the canton of Schwyz, with its Black Madonna, is the most important place of pilgrimage in Switzerland?
68037.e: The Benedictine monastery of Einsiedeln is a territorial abbey. That is why its abbot is a member of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference.
68037.m: Einsiedeln is the best-known place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.

68038.q: How many Roman Catholic dioceses are there in Switzerland?
68038.e: The dioceses are Basel, Chur, St Gallen, Lausanne-Geneva-Fribourg, Sion and Lugano. Their bishops form the Bishops’ Conference.

68039.q: Why is the Diocese of Basel based in Solothurn today?
a: The bishop had to leave Basel after the Reformation
Basel is too close to the border
The Pope banned the city of Basel
Solothurn is the largest town in the diocese
68039.e: Basel became Reformed in 1529 and the bishop moved away, among other places to Porrentruy. Solothurn has been the bishop’s seat since 1828.
68039.m: The Bishop of Basel has resided in Solothurn since 1828.

68040.q: Which Swiss diocese covers Italian-speaking Switzerland?
68040.e: The Diocese of Lugano covers the canton of Ticino. Like all Swiss diocesan bishops, its bishop is a member of the Bishops’ Conference.
68040.m: The Diocese of Lugano covers Ticino.

68041.q: Which abbey in Valais is regarded as the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in the Western world?
68041.e: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice was founded in 515. As a territorial abbot, its abbot is a member of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference.
68041.m: Saint-Maurice in Valais has existed for over 1500 years.

68042.q: How are the Catholic and Reformed churches mainly financed in most cantons?
68042.e: In most cantons, members of recognised national churches pay church taxes. The RKZ distributes part of this money for tasks across all of Switzerland.
68042.m: The national churches are financed mainly through church taxes.

68043.q: Whom does the Roman Catholic Central Conference of Switzerland (RKZ) bring together?
68043.e: Its members are the cantonal bodies under state church law, plus the dioceses of Lugano and Sion. The bishops are organised in a different body.
68043.m: The Catholic cantonal churches are joined together in the RKZ.

68044.q: Who decides on the finances in the Catholic cantonal churches of Switzerland?
a: Democratically elected bodies of church members
68044.e: Cantonal churches and parishes are democratically organised. Their elected bodies decide on the budget and tax rate, while the bishops are responsible for faith and pastoral care.
68044.m: In Switzerland, democratic bodies decide on church finances.

68045.q: In the dual system, the RKZ sees itself as the counterpart to which body?
68045.e: The RKZ represents the side governed by state church law, the Bishops’ Conference the pastoral side. The two work together institutionally.
68045.m: Together, the RKZ and the Bishops’ Conference form the two pillars of the Catholic Church in Switzerland.

68046.q: In many cantons, who else pays church taxes besides church members?
68046.e: In many cantons, legal entities, in other words companies, also pay church taxes. This money is often earmarked for social and cultural tasks.
68046.m: In many cantons, companies also pay church taxes.

68047.q: In Switzerland, who is responsible for recognising churches as national churches?
68047.e: Under the Federal Constitution, the cantons regulate the relationship between church and state. That is why it differs from canton to canton.
68047.m: In Switzerland, the relationship between church and state is a matter for the cantons.

68048.q: Why can a woman also become president of the RKZ, even though women cannot become priests in the Catholic Church?
a: The RKZ is an organisation of lay people, not of the ordained
The RKZ belongs to the Reformed Church
The Pope has made an exception for Switzerland
The RKZ is a federal department
68048.e: The RKZ represents the cantonal churches under state church law, in which lay people have a say. In 2019 Renata Asal-Steger from Lucerne became president.
68048.m: In the RKZ, women can also hold leading positions as lay people.

68049.q: What main task does the RKZ carry out for the Catholic Church in Switzerland?
a: It helps finance church tasks across Switzerland
68049.e: The RKZ collects contributions from the cantonal churches and uses them to support nationwide tasks, for example those of the Bishops’ Conference. Pastoral decisions are up to the bishops.
68049.m: The RKZ ensures the financing of nationwide church tasks.

68050.q: Which small church split from Rome after the First Vatican Council and is today recognised as a national church in several cantons?
68050.e: The Christ Catholics rejected papal infallibility, proclaimed in 1870. Alongside the Reformed and the Roman Catholic Church, it is recognised in several cantons.
68050.m: The Christ Catholic Church is a national church independent of Rome.

68051.q: What did the so-called diocese article of the Federal Constitution lay down?
a: Dioceses could only be set up with the approval of the Confederation
Each canton had to have its own diocese
Bishops had to be elected by the people
Dioceses were not allowed to levy taxes
68051.e: The article read: “Dioceses may only be established with the approval of the Confederation.” It served to give the state control over the Catholic Church.
68051.m: Under the diocese article, every new diocese needed federal approval.

68052.q: What did the diocese article, which was in the Federal Constitution until 2001, require?
a: New dioceses needed the Confederation’s approval
Bishops had to be elected by the people
Each canton had to have its own diocese
Dioceses could not levy church tax
68052.e: Without the consent of the Confederation, no diocese could be set up in Switzerland. The people and the cantons removed the article in 2001.
68052.m: The diocese article required federal approval for new dioceses.

68053.q: Who had to agree in 2001 for the diocese article to be removed from the Federal Constitution?
a: The Pope and the Federal Council
68053.e: Every change to the Federal Constitution needs a double majority of the people and the cantons. In 2001 about 64 per cent of voters and all cantons said yes.
68053.m: A constitutional amendment needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

68054.q: With which revision of the Federal Constitution was the diocese article introduced?
a: With the founding of the federal state in 1848
With the Act of Mediation of 1803
68054.e: The total revision of 1874 brought several exceptional articles aimed at the Catholic Church. In the new constitution of 1999 the article was still there as Article 72 paragraph 3.
68054.m: The diocese article entered the Federal Constitution in 1874.

68055.q: The diocese article is regarded as a relic of which conflict?
68055.e: In the Kulturkampf, liberal states and the Catholic Church fought over influence in schools and society. The federal state wanted to control how the church was organised.
68055.m: The diocese article dates from the time of the Kulturkampf.

68056.q: Which attempt by the Vatican did Switzerland respond to with the diocese article?
a: The attempt to set up a diocese in Geneva
The attempt to disband the Swiss Guard
The attempt to make Zurich an archdiocese
The attempt to nationalise the monasteries
68056.e: The Vatican wanted to create a separate diocese in Geneva, which caused great resistance in Switzerland. The Confederation then secured itself a right of approval.
68056.m: The trigger for the diocese article was a planned diocese in Geneva.

68057.q: Which Swiss church came into being after 1870 in protest against the dogma of infallibility and received its own diocese in 1876?
68057.e: Catholics who rejected the dogma of 1870 founded the Christ Catholic Church. In 1876 it obtained federal approval for its diocese, the only time the diocese article was ever applied.
68057.m: The diocese article was only applied to the Christ Catholic diocese.

68058.q: Which provision has stood since 2009 in Article 72 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, where the diocese article used to be?
a: The ban on the Jesuit order
The duty to pay church tax
The protection of the Day of Prayer
68058.e: After the minaret initiative was accepted in 2009 with about 57 per cent voting yes, the paragraph was given new content. It reads: “The construction of minarets is prohibited.”
68058.m: The former paragraph of the diocese article now contains the minaret ban.

68059.q: Which special provision against a denomination was already removed from the Federal Constitution in 1973?
68059.e: On 20 May 1973 the people and the cantons lifted the ban on Jesuits and monasteries. The diocese article remained for almost three more decades.
68059.m: The ban on the Jesuits was lifted in 1973, long before the diocese article.

68060.q: In which city does the Swiss Bishops’ Conference have its General Secretariat?
68060.e: The General Secretariat of the Bishops’ Conference is in Fribourg. The bilingual city is also home to a Faculty of Theology.
68060.m: The General Secretariat of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference is in Fribourg.

68061.q: In which city is the Protestant Church in Switzerland based?
68061.e: The EKS is organised as an association and is based in the federal city of Bern. Its Synod also meets there each November.
68061.m: The Protestant Church in Switzerland is based in Bern.

68062.q: In which year did the canton of Geneva decide to separate church and state?
68062.e: Geneva voters accepted the separation in 1907. Since then there has been no national church recognised under public law in Geneva.
68062.m: Geneva separated church and state in 1907.

68063.q: What is the principle of Catholic social teaching called which says that the goods of the earth are meant for all people?
68063.e: According to social teaching, private property is allowed but serves everyone. Nobody should be excluded from the bare necessities.
68063.m: According to social teaching, the goods of the earth are meant for all people.

a: A circular letter from the Pope
A prayer book of the church
A treaty between the Pope and a state
68064.e: With encyclicals the Pope addresses the bishops and the faithful. Catholic social teaching is mainly set out in such letters, for example in Populorum progressio of 1967.
68064.m: An encyclical is a papal circular letter.

68065.q: What do the Latin opening words “Rerum novarum” mean?
68065.e: Encyclicals are named after their first words. “Rerum novarum” literally means “of new things” and refers to the upheavals of industrialisation.
68065.m: The title Rerum novarum means “of new things”.

68066.q: What was the new name “army chaplaincy” instead of “field preacher” in the Swiss Army meant to emphasise?
a: Support through conversation rather than preaching
The duty to attend church services
68066.e: The name was changed in 2004 with the Army XXI reform. The new name emphasises pastoral care rather than preaching.
68066.m: Since Army XXI in 2004, the term army chaplaincy has been used.

68067.q: Who usually works as a hospital chaplain in Swiss hospitals?
68067.e: Hospital chaplains have usually studied theology and done additional training. They work together with doctors and nursing staff.
68067.m: Hospital chaplaincy is provided by trained theologians.

68068.q: What were the army chaplains of the Swiss Army called in the past?
68068.e: The former field preachers were responsible for all soldiers, whatever their denomination. Today the term army chaplaincy is used.
68068.m: Army chaplains used to be called field preachers.

68069.q: To which non-Christian religious communities did the Swiss army chaplaincy open up in the early 2020s?
68069.e: For almost 140 years the national churches alone provided the army chaplaincy. Then free churches as well as Jewish and Muslim chaplains joined.
68069.m: Today there are also Jewish and Muslim chaplains in the Swiss Army.

68070.q: What military rank do army chaplains hold in the Swiss Army?
68070.e: Army chaplains have the rank of captain. However, they stand outside the normal chain of command so that trust is possible.
68070.m: Army chaplains hold the rank of captain in the Swiss Army.

68071.q: Who is the army chaplaincy responsible for?
a: All members of the army, whatever their religion or beliefs
Only members of the national churches
68071.e: The army chaplaincy sees itself as a service for everyone, from the recruit to the commander. Conversations are confidential.
68071.m: The army chaplaincy is open to all members of the army.

68072.q: What applies to conversations between army members and the army chaplaincy?
a: They are reported to the commander
They are entered in the service record book
68072.e: Army chaplains are bound by confidentiality. That is why army members can talk openly about their worries without their superiors finding out.
68072.m: Conversations with the army chaplaincy remain confidential.

68073.q: What is meant by “spiritual care” in healthcare?
a: Caring for the spiritual needs of sick people through chaplaincy and health professions
A health insurance run by the churches
68073.e: Spiritual care takes into account patients’ questions about meaning, their fears and questions of faith. Chaplains work together with doctors and nursing staff.
68073.m: Spiritual care looks after the spiritual needs of sick people.

68074.q: At which university was a professorship in spiritual care created in 2015?
68074.e: The professorship at the Faculty of Theology was set up on 1 October 2015. It was the first of its kind in Switzerland.
68074.m: The University of Zurich has had a professorship in spiritual care since 2015.

68075.q: When is the hospital chaplaincy typically called?
a: When patients or relatives in a crisis would like support
68075.e: Chaplains offer support in times of fear, serious diagnoses or when someone is dying. They are there for everyone, whatever their religion.
68075.m: Hospital chaplaincy supports people in crises.

68076.q: How is the hospital chaplaincy of the national churches organised in many Swiss hospitals?
a: Ecumenically and open to all patients
Only for church members, for a fee
68076.e: Reformed and Catholic chaplains often work in a joint team. They visit people of every background, including those with no religion.
68076.m: Hospital chaplaincy is usually ecumenical and open to all patients.

68077.q: Which legal duty protects conversations with clergy, for example in hospital chaplaincy?
a: Professional confidentiality under Article 321 of the Criminal Code
The duty to report under the Civil Code
The duty to report under the Code of Obligations
The duty to provide information under tax law
68077.e: Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code lists clergy among the professions bound by confidentiality. Anyone who betrays a secret entrusted to them can be punished.
68077.m: In Switzerland, clergy are bound by professional confidentiality protected by criminal law.

68078.q: On which day is the Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer celebrated in most cantons?
a: On the third Sunday in September
On the first Sunday in October
On the last Sunday in August
On the second Sunday in November
68078.e: In almost all of Switzerland the Day of Prayer falls on the third Sunday in September. It is a state holiday, not a purely church one.
68078.m: The Federal Day of Prayer is on the third Sunday in September.

68079.q: Which body set the date of the Day of Prayer in 1832 that still applies today?
68079.e: In 1832 the Diet chose the third Sunday in September. The federal state and the Federal Council did not exist yet.
68079.m: In 1832 the Diet set the common date of the Day of Prayer.

68080.q: What is different about the Geneva Day of Prayer, the Jeûne genevois, compared with the Federal Day of Prayer?
a: It only takes place every four years
68080.e: The Jeûne genevois falls on the Thursday after the first Sunday in September. The Federal Day of Prayer, on the other hand, is a Sunday.
68080.m: Geneva celebrates its Day of Prayer on a Thursday in early September.

68081.q: In which canton is the Monday after the Day of Prayer a public holiday?
68081.e: The Lundi du Jeûne is a statutory day off in Vaud. In Neuchâtel and parts of the Bernese Jura it is also a day off, but not laid down in the same way.
68081.m: In Vaud the Monday after the Day of Prayer is also a holiday.

68082.q: What is a Day of Prayer mandate (Bettagsmandat)?
a: A public appeal by the authorities for the Day of Prayer
A law on taxes for churches
68082.e: With the mandate, the authorities ordered the day and explained its current meaning. From the late 19th century, church texts increasingly took their place.
68082.m: A Day of Prayer mandate is an appeal by the authorities for the Day of Prayer.

68083.q: Which writer wrote Day of Prayer mandates as Zurich’s state secretary?
68083.e: Gottfried Keller was First State Secretary of the canton of Zurich from 1861 to 1876. His duties included the Day of Prayer mandates.
68083.m: As state secretary, Gottfried Keller wrote Zurich’s Day of Prayer mandates.

68084.q: What was different about the Day of Prayer in the past?
a: Catholics and Reformed celebrated it on different days
It was only a holiday in Geneva
It was a holiday of the army
68084.e: For a long time the denominations celebrated the Day of Prayer on different dates. At the end of the 18th century they marked it together for the first time, and in 1832 the Diet set the third Sunday in September.
68084.m: Today Catholics and Reformed celebrate the Day of Prayer on the same day.

68085.q: Which state issued the first nationwide Day of Prayer mandate for the whole of Switzerland in 1798?
68085.e: The central government of the Helvetic Republic issued a mandate for the whole country in 1798. Before that, the Day of Prayer was a matter for the individual cantons.
68085.m: The Helvetic Republic issued the first Day of Prayer mandate for all of Switzerland in 1798.

68086.q: Since which event in church history has the Day of Prayer been celebrated ecumenically in many places?
68086.e: After the Second Vatican Council (1962 to 1965) the Catholic Church opened up to ecumenism. Today the Council of Christian Churches is especially involved.
68086.m: Since the Second Vatican Council, the Day of Prayer has often been an ecumenical holiday.

68087.q: Which pope published the encyclical Rerum novarum?
68087.e: With this encyclical Leo XIII is regarded as the founder of modern Catholic social teaching. It was the first great social encyclical.
68087.m: Rerum novarum was written by Pope Leo XIII.

68088.q: In which year was the encyclical Rerum novarum published?
68088.e: Rerum novarum was published on 15 May 1891. Later social encyclicals were often published on round anniversaries of this date.

68089.q: Which social problem did Rerum novarum mainly deal with?
a: The situation of workers during industrialisation
68089.e: The encyclical responded to the social question, in other words poverty and the exploitation of workers. It called for fair wages and allowed workers’ associations.
68089.m: Rerum novarum is the church’s answer to the social question of industrialisation.

68090.q: What position did Rerum novarum take on private property?
a: It defended it as a natural right
It allowed it only for the nobility
It left it entirely to the state
68090.e: Leo XIII opposed socialism, which wanted to abolish private property. At the same time he criticised unlimited capitalism.
68090.m: Rerum novarum defends private property and at the same time criticises exploitation.

68091.q: What did the encyclical Rerum novarum demand for workers?
a: Fair wages and the right to workers’ associations
The expropriation of all business owners
A ban on strikes in all countries
68091.e: Leo XIII called for a wage a family can live on and allowed workers’ associations. Preparatory work also came from the Fribourg Union.
68091.m: Rerum novarum called for fair wages and workers’ associations.

68092.q: With which encyclical did Pope Leo XIII found modern Catholic social teaching in 1891?
68092.e: Rerum novarum took a position on the social question of industrialisation. Leo XIII called for fair wages and allowed workers to join together.
68092.m: Rerum novarum of 1891 is regarded as the first social encyclical.

68093.q: What does the principle of subsidiarity in Catholic social teaching say?
a: What smaller communities can do should not be taken over by larger ones
The state should carry out all tasks centrally
Only the church may carry out social tasks
Everyone must look after themselves alone
68093.e: The higher level should only help when the lower level cannot cope. This way of thinking fits well with Switzerland’s federal structure.
68093.m: Subsidiarity means that the smaller unit has priority and the larger one only supports it.

68094.q: Which pope published the social encyclical Centesimus annus in 1991?
68094.e: With it John Paul II marked the 100th anniversary of the first social encyclical. He also commented on the end of communism in Eastern Europe.
68094.m: Centesimus annus by John Paul II appeared a hundred years after the first social encyclical.

68095.q: Among other reasons, why did Pope Leo XIV choose his papal name in 2025?
a: He sees artificial intelligence as a new industrial revolution
He wanted to recall the Kulturkampf
He comes from the same city as Leo XIII
He wanted to continue the First Vatican Council
68095.e: Leo XIV explained that his predecessor Leo XIII had responded to the first industrial revolution. Today, he said, artificial intelligence confronts the church with similar social questions.
68095.m: With his name, Leo XIV links up with the social teaching of his predecessor.

68096.q: Which encyclical by Pope Francis from 2015 deals with the environment and climate protection?
68096.e: In Laudato si' Francis calls for care for our “common home”, the earth. In it he links environmental protection with justice for the poor.
68096.m: Laudato si' is Pope Francis’s encyclical on the environment.

68097.q: Which work has systematically summarised Catholic social teaching since 2004?
a: The Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church
68097.e: The Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace published the Compendium in 2004. It arranges the statements of the social encyclicals by topic.
68097.m: The Compendium of 2004 brings Catholic social teaching together in one volume.

68098.q: Which painter created the painted panels of the Isenheim Altarpiece?
68098.e: Matthias Grünewald painted the panels of the Isenheim Altarpiece between about 1512 and 1516. They are regarded as his masterpiece.
68098.m: The Isenheim Altarpiece is Matthias Grünewald’s masterpiece.

68099.q: In which town is the Isenheim Altarpiece on display today?
68099.e: The altarpiece is now in the Musée Unterlinden in Colmar in Alsace. It was brought there from Isenheim at the time of the French Revolution.
68099.m: The Isenheim Altarpiece is now in the Musée Unterlinden in Colmar.

68100.q: For which order was the Isenheim Altarpiece originally made?
68100.e: The altarpiece was made for the monastery of the Antonines in Isenheim. This order mainly cared for the sick.
68100.m: The Isenheim Altarpiece was made for the Antonines in Isenheim.

68101.q: Which disease did the Antonines in Isenheim treat, which shapes the depiction of the suffering Christ on the altarpiece?
a: St Anthony’s fire caused by ergot
68101.e: St Anthony’s fire (ergotism) is caused by ergot in grain and leads to gangrene and disfigurement of the limbs. The sick were meant to recognise themselves in the tortured body of Christ.
68101.m: The Antonines cared for people suffering from St Anthony’s fire.

68102.q: What type of construction does the Isenheim Altarpiece have, so that it shows different pictures depending on the church year?
a: A rood screen with a pulpit
68102.e: The Isenheim Altarpiece is a transforming altarpiece with two pairs of wings. By opening and closing them, three different views are created.
68102.m: A transforming altarpiece shows different pictures depending on the position of its wings.

68103.q: On the Isenheim Altarpiece, which figure points at the crucified Christ with an extra-long index finger?
68103.e: John the Baptist stands next to the cross and points at Christ with an oversized finger. He was already dead at the time of the crucifixion and appears here as a theological witness.
68103.m: On the Isenheim Altarpiece, John the Baptist points at the crucified Christ.

68104.q: Which animal stands at the feet of John the Baptist on the Isenheim Altarpiece?
68104.e: The lamb with the cross staff is the Lamb of God. It points to Christ’s sacrificial death; blood flows from its breast into a chalice.
68104.m: The lamb at the Baptist’s feet stands for Christ as the Lamb of God.

68105.q: Which scene on the second view of the Isenheim Altarpiece is famous for its glowing figure of Christ made of light?
68105.e: On the second view, Christ rises from the tomb in a brightly coloured, glowing aura. The guards fall to the ground, dazzled.
68105.m: The Resurrection on the Isenheim Altarpiece shows Christ as a radiant figure of light.

68106.q: In which city was Albrecht Dürer born in 1471?
68106.e: Dürer was born in Nuremberg in 1471 and died there in 1528. At the time the city was a centre of trade and printing.
68106.m: Albrecht Dürer lived and worked mainly in Nuremberg.

68107.q: With which series of woodcuts on the Revelation of John did Dürer become famous in 1498?
68107.e: The “Apocalypse” of 1498 consists of 15 large woodcuts, including the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. Dürer published it himself as a book.
68107.m: Dürer’s “Apocalypse” made him known throughout Europe in 1498.

68108.q: Why is Dürer’s self-portrait in a fur coat from 1500 considered unusual?
a: He shows himself from the front, looking like Christ
He shows himself as an old man on his deathbed
He paints himself as a farmer working in the fields
He shows himself only from behind in a mirror
68108.e: Dürer shows himself strictly from the front, symmetrical and with long hair, the way Christ was usually shown. In this way he stressed the dignity of the artist as a creator.
68108.m: In the self-portrait of 1500, Dürer shows himself in a similar way to Christ.

68109.q: What was Dürer’s well-known drawing “Praying Hands” originally made for?
a: As a study for an altarpiece
As the title page of a Bible
As a design for a tomb
As a model for a church window
68109.e: The brush drawing of 1508 was a preparatory study for the Heller Altarpiece in Frankfurt. It shows the hands of an apostle.
68109.m: The “Praying Hands” were a preparatory study for an altarpiece.

68110.q: Which engraving by Dürer from 1513 shows a rider steadily passing two sinister figures?
68110.e: The engraving “Knight, Death and the Devil” is often interpreted as an image of the steadfast Christian knight. It is one of Dürer’s three master engravings.
68110.m: “Knight, Death and the Devil” shows a rider who is not put off by Death and the Devil.

68111.q: Which Church Father does Dürer’s master engraving of 1514 show working in a quiet study?
68111.e: “Saint Jerome in His Study” shows the Bible translator peacefully at his writing desk, with a lion and a dog. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).
68111.m: Dürer’s “Saint Jerome in His Study” shows the Bible translator at work.

68112.q: Which work did Dürer give to the Nuremberg city council in 1526, probably also as a statement of support for the Reformation?
68112.e: The two panels “The Four Apostles” bear Bible quotations in Luther’s translation. Today they hang in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich.
68112.m: With “The Four Apostles”, Dürer took a stand during the Reformation.

68113.q: In which present-day Swiss city did Dürer work for printers during his travels around 1492?
68113.e: During his journeyman years, Dürer stayed in Basel from 1492 to 1493, a centre of printing. Several woodcuts for books there are attributed to him.
68113.m: The young Dürer worked for printers in Basel around 1492.

68114.q: With which technique did Dürer create his three so-called master engravings?
68114.e: The master engravings of 1513 and 1514 are copper engravings, in which lines are cut into a copper plate with a burin. Linocut and lithography did not yet exist in Dürer’s time.
68114.m: Dürer’s master engravings are fine copper engravings.

68115.q: What did the word “baroque”, from which the art style takes its name, originally stand for?
68115.e: The Portuguese word “barroco” refers to an irregularly rounded pearl. At first “baroque” was meant negatively, in the sense of “overblown” or “strange”.
68115.m: The name baroque comes from an irregular pearl.

68116.q: Which church movement particularly encouraged the building of magnificent baroque churches?
68116.e: After the Council of Trent, the Catholic Church wanted to inspire the faithful with overwhelming splendour. The baroque church thus became a tool of the Counter-Reformation.
68116.m: Many baroque churches are an expression of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

68117.q: Which order built Il Gesù in Rome, a church that became a model for many baroque churches?
68117.e: Il Gesù is the mother church of the Jesuit order and was built from 1568. Its single-nave plan with a dome shaped church building during the Counter-Reformation.
68117.m: The Roman church of Il Gesù was a model for baroque church building.

68118.q: From which present-day Swiss canton did the Roman baroque architect Francesco Borromini come?
68118.e: Borromini was born in 1599 in Bissone on Lake Lugano. In Rome he built, among other things, the church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.
68118.m: The great baroque architect Borromini came from Ticino.

68119.q: Which artist created the great bronze canopy (baldacchino) over the papal altar in St Peter’s Basilica?
68119.e: Bernini created the baldacchino from 1624 to 1633. Later he also designed the colonnades of St Peter’s Square.
68119.m: Gian Lorenzo Bernini shaped St Peter’s with the baldacchino and the colonnades.

68120.q: In which canton is the baroque abbey church of Einsiedeln?
68120.e: The abbey church of Einsiedeln was built from 1719 to plans by the lay brother Kaspar Moosbrugger and consecrated in 1735. The Asam brothers decorated the interior.
68120.m: The abbey church of Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz is a masterpiece of the baroque.

68121.q: Which Swiss group of buildings with a late baroque cathedral has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983?
68121.e: The Abbey of St Gall with its cathedral and abbey library became a World Heritage Site in 1983. The abbey church was built from 1755 to 1766.
68121.m: The Abbey of St Gall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

68122.q: What is the painting technique on baroque ceilings called that fakes an open sky or a dome?
68122.e: With trompe-l'oeil (“deceiving the eye”), perspective makes a flat ceiling look three-dimensional. A famous example is Andrea Pozzo’s painted false dome in Sant'Ignazio in Rome.
68122.m: Trompe-l'oeil tricks the eye into seeing real space.

68123.q: Which Bavarian pilgrimage church by Dominikus Zimmermann is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
68123.e: The Wieskirche near Steingaden was built from 1745 and is regarded as a masterpiece of rococo. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1983.
68123.m: The Wieskirche is a famous rococo work by Dominikus Zimmermann.

68124.q: In which town was Le Corbusier born in 1887 as Charles-Édouard Jeanneret?
68124.e: Le Corbusier was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Neuchâtel Jura. Later he took French citizenship.
68124.m: Le Corbusier came from La Chaux-de-Fonds.

68125.q: In which country is Le Corbusier’s pilgrimage chapel Notre-Dame-du-Haut?
68125.e: The chapel stands on a hill above Ronchamp in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region. It was consecrated in 1955.
68125.m: Le Corbusier’s chapel in Ronchamp is in France.

68126.q: In which year was the chapel of Ronchamp consecrated?
68126.e: The chapel was built from 1953 to 1955 and consecrated on 25 June 1955. It replaced a chapel destroyed in the Second World War.
68126.m: The chapel of Ronchamp was consecrated in 1955.

68127.q: What is the most striking feature of the roof of the chapel of Ronchamp?
a: It is curved like a shell
It is a flat grass roof
It is made of golden tiles
68127.e: The massive, curved concrete roof is reminiscent of a shell or a ship’s hull. Le Corbusier is said to have been inspired by a crab shell.
68127.m: The roof of Ronchamp is heavy and curved like a shell.

68128.q: How does light come through the thick south wall of the chapel of Ronchamp?
68128.e: The south wall is pierced by many openings of different sizes that widen towards the inside. Partly coloured glass creates an atmospheric light.
68128.m: In Ronchamp, Le Corbusier shapes the space mainly with light.

68129.q: What is there on the east side of the chapel of Ronchamp for large groups of pilgrims?
a: A second chapel made of wood
A bell tower with a viewing platform
68129.e: For pilgrimages with many people there is an outdoor altar with a pulpit, sheltered by the overhanging roof. The faithful gather on the meadow in front of it.
68129.m: In Ronchamp, services can also be held in the open air.

68130.q: Since when has the chapel of Ronchamp, together with other buildings by Le Corbusier, been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
68130.e: In 2016, 17 buildings by Le Corbusier in seven countries were added to the World Heritage list together. They include the Villa Le Lac in Corseaux and the Immeuble Clarté in Geneva.
68130.m: The chapel of Ronchamp has been part of the World Heritage since 2016.

68131.q: On which Swiss banknote of the 8th series was Le Corbusier shown?
68131.e: The 10-franc note of the 8th series (from 1997) showed Le Corbusier. It was later replaced by the 9th series.
68131.m: Le Corbusier was on the former 10-franc note.

68132.q: Which post did Johann Sebastian Bach hold in Leipzig from 1723, for which he wrote many church cantatas?
68132.e: As Thomaskantor, Bach was responsible for the music of Leipzig’s main churches. A cantata was needed for almost every Sunday.
68132.m: As Thomaskantor in Leipzig, Bach composed many cantatas.

68133.q: Which part comes at the end of many of Bach’s church cantatas, so that the congregation recognises the melody?
68133.e: Bach ended many cantatas with a four-part chorale based on a well-known hymn. In this way the sermon was summed up in music.
68133.m: Many Bach cantatas end with a four-part chorale.

68134.q: What determined the themes of Bach’s church cantatas?
a: The church year and the Sunday readings
The order of the books of the Bible
68134.e: Each church cantata belongs to a particular Sunday or feast day. Its text takes up the Gospel of that day.
68134.m: Bach’s church cantatas follow the course of the church year.

68135.q: What does the abbreviation BWV stand for in Bach’s works, such as “BWV 140”?
68135.e: BWV stands for Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis, the catalogue of Bach’s works, published by Wolfgang Schmieder in 1950. The cantatas come at the beginning.
68135.m: Bach’s works are identified by numbers from the Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis.

68136.q: From which Bach cantata does the famous chorale movement “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring” come?
a: Heart and Mouth and Deed and Life
A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
68136.e: The movement belongs to the cantata “Heart and Mouth and Deed and Life”, BWV 147. It is known worldwide in many arrangements.
68136.m: “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring” comes from the cantata BWV 147.

68137.q: Which secular cantata by Bach is a humorous story about a father and his coffee-mad daughter?
68137.e: The Coffee Cantata “Schweigt stille, plaudert nicht”, BWV 211, was probably performed in Zimmermann’s coffee house in Leipzig. It shows that Bach did not only write sacred cantatas.
68137.m: The Coffee Cantata is a cheerful secular cantata by Bach.

68138.q: With which letters did Bach often sign his scores to dedicate his work to God?
68138.e: SDG stands for “Soli Deo Gloria”, meaning “to God alone the glory”. AMDG, on the other hand, is the motto of the Jesuits.
68138.m: Bach wrote SDG for “Soli Deo Gloria” under many works.

68139.q: In which Appenzell village does the J. S. Bach Foundation under Rudolf Lutz regularly perform Bach’s cantatas?
68139.e: The J. S. Bach Foundation from St Gallen has set itself the goal of performing all of Bach’s vocal works. The concerts mostly take place in the church in Trogen.
68139.m: Bach’s cantatas are regularly performed in Trogen by the J. S. Bach Foundation.

68140.q: In which year was Mozart working on his Requiem, which remained unfinished because of his death?
68140.e: Mozart died in Vienna on 5 December 1791 while he was writing the Requiem. It is listed in the Köchel catalogue as K. 626.
68140.m: Mozart died in 1791 while working on his Requiem.

68141.e: Count Franz von Walsegg had the commission given secretly through a messenger. He probably wanted to pass the work off as his own composition.

68142.q: Which of Mozart’s pupils completed the Requiem in its best-known version?
68142.e: Mozart’s widow Constanze had the work completed in order to receive the fee. After an attempt by Joseph Eybler, Süssmayr completed the Requiem.

68143.q: In which key is Mozart’s Requiem?
68143.e: The Requiem is in D minor, a key Mozart often used for serious and dark music. Parts of “Don Giovanni” are also in D minor.
68143.m: Mozart’s Requiem is in the serious key of D minor.

68144.q: What did Mozart leave of the Requiem when he died in 1791?
a: Only parts, much of it in sketches
68144.e: Mozart was only able to fully work out the beginning; for many movements there were only the vocal parts and the bass. His pupil Süssmayr completed the work.
68144.m: Mozart’s Requiem remained unfinished and was completed by others.

68145.q: With which Latin words does a Requiem begin?
68145.e: “Requiem aeternam dona eis” means “eternal rest grant them”. The Mass for the dead takes its name from the first word.
68145.m: The Requiem is named after its first words, “Requiem aeternam”.

68146.q: What is the medieval sequence “Dies irae” in the Requiem about?
68146.e: “Dies irae” means “day of wrath” and describes the Last Judgement. It is usually attributed to Thomas of Celano.
68146.m: The “Dies irae” describes the day of the Last Judgement.

68147.q: What kind of church service is set to music in a Requiem?
68147.e: The Requiem is the Catholic Mass for the dead, in Latin “Missa pro defunctis”. The name comes from the first words “Requiem aeternam”, “eternal rest”.
68147.m: A Requiem is a Mass for the dead.

68148.q: Into which three parts is Dante’s Divine Comedy divided?
68148.e: The three parts are called Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. Dante describes a journey through the afterlife from the deepest pit of hell to the vision of God.
68148.m: Dante’s Divine Comedy leads through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.

68149.q: How many cantos does the Divine Comedy have in total?
68149.e: Hell has 34 cantos (including an introductory canto), Purgatory and Paradise have 33 each. 34 plus 33 plus 33 makes 100.
68149.m: The Divine Comedy consists of exactly 100 cantos.

68150.q: Which Roman poet guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory?
68150.e: Virgil, the poet of the “Aeneid”, stands for human reason. As a pagan he may not go with Dante into Paradise.
68150.m: Virgil is Dante’s guide through Hell and Purgatory.

68151.q: Which woman then guides Dante through Paradise?
68151.e: Beatrice was the girl Dante adored in his youth in Florence, who died young. In the Comedy she embodies divine grace and theology.
