68152.q: Which verse form with the rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc did Dante use?
68152.e: Terza rima consists of three-line stanzas in which the middle line sets the rhyme of the next stanza. The number three also points to the Trinity.
68152.m: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in linked terza rima.

68153.q: Where is Lucifer in Dante’s Hell?
a: Frozen in ice at the lowest point
On a throne of fire at the entrance
In a burning tower in the middle
On an island in the river Styx
68153.e: In the lowest circle, Lucifer is stuck in the ice of Cocytus. With three mouths he chews Judas, Brutus and Cassius.
68153.m: In Dante, Lucifer is stuck in the ice at the bottom of Hell.

68154.q: From which city was Dante banished in 1302?
68154.e: Dante was banished from Florence during political struggles and never returned. He wrote the Comedy in exile and died in Ravenna in 1321.
68154.m: Dante wrote his Divine Comedy in exile far from Florence.

68155.q: Why was it unusual around 1300 that Dante wrote his great work in Italian?
a: Learned works were written in Latin
Italian was banned at the time
There was no Italian script yet
68155.e: Serious literature was written in Latin at the time. Dante wrote in the Tuscan vernacular and so shaped written Italian.
68155.m: Dante is regarded as the father of the Italian literary language.

68156.q: With which word do all three parts of the Divine Comedy end?
68156.e: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso each end with the word “stelle”. In this way the gaze is always directed upwards to the stars.
68156.m: Each part of the Divine Comedy ends with the word “stelle”.

68157.e: The English poet John Milton published the work in 1667. It is regarded as the greatest epic in the English language.
68157.m: “Paradise Lost” is the great epic by John Milton.

68158.q: Which Bible story is at the centre of Milton’s “Paradise Lost”?
a: The Fall of Adam and Eve
68158.e: Milton tells of Satan’s rebellion and the temptation of Adam and Eve. In the end both have to leave Paradise.
68158.m: Milton’s epic tells the story of the Fall of Adam and Eve.

68159.q: Under what limitation did Milton dictate his epic?
68159.e: Milton had gone completely blind by around 1652. He dictated the verses to helpers and family members.
68159.m: John Milton dictated “Paradise Lost” as a blind poet.

68160.q: What declared aim does Milton state at the beginning of his epic?
a: To justify the ways of God to men
To glorify the King of England
To tell the history of Rome
68160.e: Milton wants to “justify the ways of God to men”. The work is thus also a theodicy, a defence of God in the face of evil.
68160.m: With his epic, Milton wanted to justify God’s actions to humankind.

68161.q: Which word for a place full of chaos and noise goes back to Milton’s name for the capital of Hell?
68161.e: Milton formed “Pandaemonium” from Greek words for “all demons”. Today it generally means a wild uproar.
68161.m: The word pandemonium comes from Milton’s “Paradise Lost”.

68162.q: Which Zurich scholar translated Milton’s “Paradise Lost” into German in 1732?
68162.e: Bodmer published a prose translation in 1732. He defended Milton against Gottsched and thereby influenced German literature.
68162.m: Johann Jakob Bodmer made Milton known in the German-speaking world.

68163.q: In which verse form is Milton’s “Paradise Lost” written?
68163.e: Milton used blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter. He deliberately defended doing without rhyme.
68163.m: “Paradise Lost” is written in unrhymed blank verse.

68164.q: What is Milton’s sequel “Paradise Regained” of 1671 about?
a: The temptation of Jesus in the desert
68164.e: In “Paradise Regained”, Jesus resists Satan’s temptations. In this way the lost Paradise is, as it were, won back.
68164.m: In “Paradise Regained”, Jesus resists the tempter.

68165.q: What did Dostoevsky experience in 1849 before he was exiled to Siberia?
68165.e: As a member of the Petrashevsky Circle he was sentenced to death and only pardoned at the place of execution. He then had to do four years of forced labour in Omsk.
68165.m: Dostoevsky survived a mock execution in 1849.

68166.q: Which book was Dostoevsky’s most important reading during his imprisonment in a Siberian camp?
68166.e: Wives of exiled Decembrists gave him a New Testament. He read it for years and kept it until his death.
68166.m: In the prison camp, Dostoevsky mainly read the New Testament.

68167.q: Which story does Ivan tell in “The Brothers Karamazov”, in which Christ is arrested in Seville?
68167.e: In “The Grand Inquisitor” a cardinal accuses the returned Christ of having expected too much freedom of people. Christ answers only with a kiss.
68167.m: The legend of the Grand Inquisitor asks about freedom and faith.

68168.q: What is the name of the wise monk and spiritual teacher of Alyosha in “The Brothers Karamazov”?
68168.e: Zosima is a starets, a spiritual adviser in the Orthodox tradition. He teaches love and responsibility for everyone.
68168.m: In “The Brothers Karamazov”, Elder Zosima embodies active love.

68169.q: Which Bible story does Sonya read to the murderer Raskolnikov in “Crime and Punishment”?
a: The feeding of the five thousand
68169.e: Sonya reads from the Gospel of John about Lazarus, who is called out of the tomb. The scene hints at Raskolnikov’s possible inner renewal.
68169.m: In “Crime and Punishment”, the Lazarus story stands for hope of new life.

68170.q: Which painting in the Kunstmuseum Basel shook Dostoevsky so much in 1867 that it appears in “The Idiot”?
a: Holbein’s “The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb”
68170.e: Hans Holbein the Younger painted the dead Christ in 1521/22 with unsparing realism. In the novel it is said that this picture could make you lose your faith.
68170.m: Holbein’s dead Christ in Basel deeply moved Dostoevsky.

68171.q: Which of Dostoevsky’s characters is conceived as a “perfectly beautiful person” and a Christ figure?
68171.e: Prince Myshkin in “The Idiot” is kind, innocent and forgiving. Dostoevsky wanted to portray a “positively beautiful person”.
68171.m: Prince Myshkin is Dostoevsky’s attempt to show a completely good person.

68172.q: Which Christian denomination did Dostoevsky belong to?
68172.e: Dostoevsky was deeply rooted in Russian Orthodox piety. His novels often defend it against Western rationalism.
68172.m: Dostoevsky’s faith was shaped by Russian Orthodoxy.

68173.q: What was Jeremias Gotthelf’s real name?
68173.e: Albert Bitzius chose the name of the main character of his first novel as his pen name. He lived from 1797 to 1854.
68173.m: Jeremias Gotthelf’s real name was Albert Bitzius.

68174.q: In which Emmental municipality was Gotthelf the minister from 1832?
68174.e: Bitzius worked as the minister in Lützelflüh until his death in 1854. The Gotthelf Centre is there today.
68174.m: Gotthelf was the minister in Lützelflüh in the Emmental.

68175.q: What is the title of Gotthelf’s first novel of 1837, whose first-person narrator gave him his name?
68175.e: In “Der Bauernspiegel” the foster boy Jeremias Gotthelf tells of his hard life. Bitzius took the name as his pen name.
68175.m: Gotthelf’s career as a writer began with “Der Bauernspiegel”.

68176.q: In which of Gotthelf’s novellas do villagers make a pact with the Devil, who appears as the Green Huntsman?
68176.e: In “The Black Spider” (1842) the pact brings disaster in the form of a deadly spider. The frame story is set at a christening party.
68176.m: “The Black Spider” tells of the consequences of a pact with the Devil.

68177.q: How is the spider in Gotthelf’s novella finally trapped?
a: It is shut inside a window post
It is burnt in the fire
It is thrown into the river
It is buried under a bell
68177.e: The spider is locked into a hole in the window post and sealed with a wooden plug. As long as the plug holds, the village is safe.
68177.m: In “The Black Spider”, evil stays trapped in a wooden post.

68178.q: Which of Gotthelf’s novels tells how a young farmhand finds an orderly life through hard work and faith?
68178.e: “Uli the Farmhand” (1841) shows a farmhand who improves under the influence of his master. Later came “Uli the Tenant”.
68178.m: “Uli the Farmhand” is a novel of education by Gotthelf.

68179.q: Which social concern did Gotthelf pursue particularly as a minister and writer?
a: The misery of the poor and of foster children forced to work
68179.e: Gotthelf denounced poverty and the fate of “Verdingkinder”, children placed with farmers as cheap labour. He also campaigned for schools and education for the poor.
68179.m: With his books, Gotthelf fought against poverty and child labour in foster placements.

68180.q: Which natural event in the Emmental in 1837 did Gotthelf describe in a story of its own?
68180.e: In “Die Wassernot im Emmental” (The Flood in the Emmental, 1838) he describes the devastating flood of the river Emme. He also interprets it as a warning from God.
68180.m: Gotthelf described the Emme flood of 1837 in “Die Wassernot im Emmental”.

68181.q: In which town was Albert Bitzius born in 1797 as the son of a minister?
68181.e: Bitzius was born in Murten, where his father was the minister. Later he grew up in Utzenstorf.
68181.m: Jeremias Gotthelf was born in Murten.

68182.q: What task does Jesus give his listeners in the Sermon on the Mount with the images of salt and light?
a: To do visible good in the world
To withdraw completely from the world
To renew the Temple in Jerusalem
To collect wealth for the community
68182.e: In Matthew 5:13 to 16, Jesus calls the disciples “the salt of the earth” and “the light of the world”. Their good deeds should shine so that people praise God.
68182.m: According to the Sermon on the Mount, the disciples should be the salt of the earth and the light of the world.

68183.q: What are the sentences at the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount called that begin with “Blessed are”?
68183.e: The Beatitudes promise salvation to the poor, those who mourn and the peacemakers. They are in Matthew 5:3 to 12.
68183.m: The Sermon on the Mount begins with the Beatitudes.

68184.q: What promise do the peacemakers receive in the Sermon on the Mount?
a: They will be called children of God
68184.e: Matthew 5:9 says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” The other promises belong to other Beatitudes.
68184.m: In the Sermon on the Mount, peacemakers are called children of God.

68185.q: What is the form “You have heard that it was said ... But I say to you” called, with which Jesus makes commandments stricter?
68185.e: In the six antitheses in Matthew 5, Jesus sets his own interpretation against traditional commandments. He aims at a person’s inner attitude.
68185.m: In the antitheses, Jesus radically reinterprets the commandments.

68186.q: Which rule from the Sermon on the Mount says: “Do to others whatever you would have them do to you”?
68186.e: The Golden Rule is in Matthew 7:12. Similar rules exist in many religions and cultures.
68186.m: The Golden Rule asks you to treat others as you would like to be treated.

68187.q: Which prayer does Jesus teach in the Sermon on the Mount?
68187.e: The Lord’s Prayer is in Matthew 6:9 to 13. It is the most important prayer shared by all Christian denominations.
68187.m: The Lord’s Prayer comes from the Sermon on the Mount.

68188.q: With which image does the Sermon on the Mount end, to show how important it is to put the words into practice?
a: A house built on rock or sand
A shepherd with a hundred sheep
A mustard seed that becomes a tree
68188.e: Whoever hears the words and acts on them is like a wise man who builds on rock. Whoever only hears them builds on sand, and his house collapses.
68188.m: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the image of the house on the rock.

68189.q: Which book about the Sermon on the Mount did Dietrich Bonhoeffer publish in 1937?
68189.e: In “The Cost of Discipleship” (German “Nachfolge”) Bonhoeffer criticises “cheap grace” and calls for a life according to the Sermon on the Mount. “Letters and Papers from Prison” was only published after his death.
68189.m: Bonhoeffer’s “The Cost of Discipleship” is an interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount.

68190.q: Which commandment on how to treat enemies does Jesus give in Matthew 5:44?
a: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
Avoid your enemies and stay silent
68190.e: Jesus says: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” In this he goes beyond love of one’s neighbour.
68190.m: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus asks us to love even our enemies.

68191.q: Which Old Testament rule does Jesus refer to when he says you should also turn the other cheek?
a: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth
68191.e: The principle of retaliation, “an eye for an eye”, originally limited revenge. Jesus sets against it giving up retaliation (Matthew 5:38 to 39).
68191.m: Jesus contrasts the principle of “an eye for an eye” with giving up retaliation.

68192.q: According to the Gospel of Luke, what words does Jesus speak on the cross about those tormenting him?
a: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing
My God, why have you forsaken me
68192.e: The plea for forgiveness is in Luke 23:34. It is seen as an example of love for one’s enemies put into practice.
68192.m: On the cross, Jesus asks for forgiveness for those tormenting him.

68193.q: According to the Acts of the Apostles, which first Christian martyr prayed for his murderers as he was dying?
68193.e: Stephen was stoned and cried out: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them!” (Acts 7:60). He is regarded as the first martyr.
68193.m: Stephen followed Jesus’s example and forgave his murderers.

68194.q: Which confession of the Swiss Anabaptists from 1527 rejected violence and the use of the sword by Christians?
68194.e: The Schleitheim Articles were agreed in 1527 in Schleitheim in the canton of Schaffhausen, largely by Michael Sattler. Among other things, they called for non-violence.
68194.m: The Schleitheim Confession is an early statement of Christian non-violence.

68195.q: Which groups are counted among the historic peace churches?
68195.e: Mennonites, Quakers and the Church of the Brethren traditionally refuse military service. The Mennonites go back to the Anabaptist movement.
68195.m: The historic peace churches refuse military service for reasons of faith.

68196.q: Which Church Father developed the doctrine of just war, which stands in contrast to strict pacifism?
68196.e: Augustine asked under what conditions war could be allowed, for example to fend off injustice. Thomas Aquinas later developed the doctrine further.
68196.m: The doctrine of just war goes back to Augustine.

68197.q: In which year did Swiss voters accept civilian service as an alternative for those refusing military service?
68197.e: On 17 May 1992 an alternative civilian service was laid down in the constitution. The Civilian Service Act came into force in 1996.
68197.m: Switzerland has had civilian service since the vote of 1992.

68198.q: According to Islamic tradition, with which command did the first revelation to Muhammad begin?
68198.e: According to tradition, the revelation began with the word “iqra”, the beginning of Surah 96. The name Quran (qur'an) means “reading” or “recitation”.
68198.m: The first revelation began with the word “Read!” from Surah 96.

68199.q: According to Surah 97, in which night did the sending down of the Quran begin?
a: In the Night of the Heavenly Journey
In the Night of the Hijra
In the night before the Festival of Sacrifice
68199.e: Surah 97 calls it “Laylat al-Qadr” and says it is better than a thousand months. It is sought in the last nights of Ramadan.
68199.m: The Night of Power falls during Ramadan.

68200.q: According to Islamic teaching, through which angel was the Quran passed on?
68200.e: According to Islamic teaching, the angel Jibril brought God’s revelation to Muhammad. He is also called “the trustworthy spirit”.
68200.m: In Islam, the angel Gabriel is called Jibril.

68201.q: According to tradition, over what period of time did the revelation of the Quran take place?
68201.e: The revelation came gradually from about 610 until Muhammad’s death in 632. That makes about 23 years.
68201.m: The Quran was revealed over about 23 years.

68202.q: According to tradition, under which caliph was the binding standard version of the Quran produced?
68202.e: Around 650, Caliph Uthman had a uniform version produced and sent to the major cities. Copies that differed were to be destroyed.
68202.m: The standard version of the Quran goes back to Caliph Uthman.

68203.q: What role did Zayd ibn Thabit, who according to tradition collected the text of the Quran, have with Muhammad?
a: He was one of his scribes
He was his opponent in Mecca
68203.e: Zayd ibn Thabit wrote down revelations for Muhammad. According to tradition, he later collected them in a codex.
68203.m: Zayd ibn Thabit is regarded as the collector of the Quran text.

68204.q: Which printed edition of 1924 became the standard text of the Quran used worldwide?
68204.e: The edition published in Egypt in 1924 under King Fuad follows the Hafs reading from Asim. It still shapes almost all printed Qurans today.
68204.m: The Cairo edition of 1924 is today’s standard printed Quran.

68205.q: What did the radiocarbon dating of the Birmingham Quran manuscript (2015) show?
68205.e: The dating by the University of Oxford gave, with high probability, a period from 568 to 645. This makes it one of the oldest known Quran fragments.
68205.m: The Birmingham manuscript is one of the oldest Quran fragments.

68206.q: What is special about letters such as “Alif Lam Mim” at the beginning of some surahs?
a: Their meaning is still unexplained today
They give the number of verses
They name the scribe of the surah
They mark the year of the revelation
68206.e: These single letters are called muqatta'at and appear at the beginning of 29 surahs. Scholars have suggested many interpretations, but none is certain.
68206.m: The meaning of the mysterious letters at the start of some surahs is unknown.

68207.q: According to the traditional division, where do most surahs of the Quran come from?
a: From the time after Muhammad’s death
68207.e: The widely used standard edition assigns 86 surahs to the Meccan period and 28 to the Medinan period. Researchers disagree about where some individual surahs belong.
68207.m: According to the traditional division, most surahs come from Mecca.

68208.q: Which event separates the Meccan from the Medinan period of revelation?
68208.e: The Medinan period begins with the emigration to Medina in 622. Surahs before it are regarded as Meccan, those after it as Medinan.
68208.m: The Hijra separates the Meccan from the Medinan surahs.

68209.q: Which features are typical of early Meccan surahs?
a: Short verses about God and the Judgement
Treaties with the tribes of Medina
68209.e: Early Meccan surahs are mostly short, rhyming and urgent. They stress God’s oneness, creation and the Last Judgement.
68209.m: Early Meccan surahs are short and revolve around God and the Judgement.

68210.q: What did the German orientalist Theodor Nöldeke try to do with the surahs of the Quran in 1860?
68210.e: In his “History of the Quran”, Nöldeke distinguished early, middle and late Meccan as well as Medinan surahs. In the Quran itself they are roughly ordered by length.
68210.m: Nöldeke arranged the surahs in a historical order.

68211.q: In which surah is the famous Throne Verse (Ayat al-Kursi)?
68211.e: The Throne Verse is verse 255 of the second surah. It describes God’s almighty power and knowledge and is often recited for protection.
68211.m: The Throne Verse is one of the best-known verses of the Quran.

68212.q: By what principle are the surahs in the Quran roughly arranged?
68212.e: After the opening surah come the long surahs first and the short ones at the end. So the order does not match the order of revelation.
68212.m: The surahs are roughly ordered from long to short.

68213.q: What is the Basmala, with which almost all surahs begin?
a: The formula “In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful”
The call to prayer from the minaret
The name of the first surah
68213.e: The Basmala stands at the beginning of 113 of the 114 surahs. Only Surah 9 begins without it.
68213.m: Only Surah 9 has no Basmala at the beginning.

68214.q: What does the name of the first surah, al-Fatiha, mean?
68214.e: Al-Fatiha comes from the Arabic verb for “to open”. The surah opens the Quran.
68214.m: Al-Fatiha is the opening surah of the Quran.

68215.q: How many verses does the surah al-Fatiha have?
68215.e: Al-Fatiha has seven verses; in the counting usual today, the Basmala is the first verse. That is why it is also called “the seven oft-repeated”.
68215.m: The Fatiha consists of seven verses.

68216.q: During which act is al-Fatiha recited most often in the daily life of believing Muslims?
a: In every unit of the ritual prayer
68216.e: The Fatiha is recited in every rak'a of the obligatory prayer. With five daily prayers, it is said at least 17 times a day.
68216.m: Without the Fatiha, the ritual prayer is not complete.

68217.q: Which title of honour does al-Fatiha have, among others?
68217.e: Al-Fatiha is seen as a summary of the whole Quran and is therefore called “Mother of the Book”. “Heart of the Quran”, on the other hand, usually refers to Surah 36.
68217.m: The Fatiha is honoured as the “Mother of the Book”.

68218.q: What do those praying explicitly ask for in al-Fatiha?
68218.e: The verse “Guide us on the straight path” (as-sirat al-mustaqim) is the heart of the request. The path is then described in more detail.
68218.m: In the Fatiha, believers ask for guidance.

68219.q: With which praise does al-Fatiha begin after the Basmala?
a: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds
There is no god but God
Glory be to my Lord, the Most High
68219.e: In Arabic the verse is “al-hamdu li-llahi rabbi l-alamin”. It praises God as Lord of all the worlds.
68219.m: The Fatiha begins by praising God as Lord of the worlds.

68220.q: Which word do many Muslims say after the end of al-Fatiha?
68220.e: After the Fatiha, “Amin” is said, which means “so be it”. It is not itself part of the surah.
68220.m: After the Fatiha comes the word “Amin”.

68221.q: What does the Arabic term tafsir refer to?
68221.e: Tafsir means explanation or commentary. It refers to the scholarly interpretation of the text of the Quran.
68221.m: Tafsir is the Islamic science of interpreting the Quran.

68222.q: Which scholar wrote one of the most important early commentaries on the Quran in the 10th century, which collects many traditions?
68222.e: Al-Tabari (died 923) wrote the commentary “Jami al-bayan”. In it he collected many traditions from the early generations.
68222.m: Al-Tabari’s commentary is a foundational work of tradition-based interpretation.

68223.q: What does tradition-based interpretation of the Quran mainly rely on?
a: Statements of the Prophet and his companions
68223.e: This interpretation is called tafsir bi-l-ma'thur, interpretation based on what has been handed down. The other form relies more on one’s own reasoned judgement.
68223.m: Tradition-based interpretation is called tafsir bi-l-ma'thur.

68224.q: What does the study of “asbab al-nuzul” examine?
a: The number of words in the Quran
68224.e: Asbab al-nuzul means “occasions of revelation”. They explain in what situation a verse is said to have been revealed and help with its interpretation.
68224.m: The occasions of revelation help to understand verses in their context.

68225.q: What does the doctrine of abrogation in Quranic studies examine?
a: Whether a later verse replaces the rule of an earlier one
How to pronounce the Quran correctly
How many words a surah has
68225.e: Abrogation is called naskh in Arabic. How far it applies is disputed among scholars.
68225.m: The doctrine of abrogation examines which verses cancel others.

68226.q: What does the name of the widely used Quran commentary “Tafsir al-Jalalayn” mean?
68226.e: Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli began the commentary and Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti completed it in the 15th century.
68226.m: The commentary of the “two Jalals” is short and widely used.

68227.q: Which two kinds of verses does the Quran distinguish in Surah 3, verse 7?
68227.e: Clear verses are called muhkam, ambiguous ones mutashabih. The clear ones are described as the foundation of the Book.
68227.m: Clear verses are called muhkam, ambiguous ones mutashabih.

68228.q: What did Fakhr al-Din al-Razi combine in his “Great Commentary” on the Quran?
a: Quran interpretation with theology and philosophy
68228.e: Al-Razi (died 1209) wrote one of the most extensive Quran commentaries. In it he discussed many theological and philosophical questions.
68228.m: Al-Razi’s commentary combines Quran interpretation with theology.

68229.q: What is the isnad of a hadith?
68229.e: The isnad names who heard the report from whom, all the way back to the Prophet. It serves as evidence of authenticity.
68229.m: The isnad is the chain of transmitters of a hadith.

68230.q: What is the actual text of a hadith called, as opposed to the chain of transmitters?
68230.e: A hadith consists of isnad and matn. The matn contains the statement or action that has been handed down.
68230.m: The matn is the content of a hadith.

68231.q: In hadith criticism, what rating does a hadith with an unbroken chain of reliable transmitters receive?
68231.e: A hadith is regarded as sahih if the chain is unbroken and all transmitters are reliable and accurate. It must also have no hidden flaws.
68231.m: A sound hadith is called sahih.

68232.q: Which two collections are regarded in Sunni Islam as the most reliable hadith works?
a: Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan al-Nasa'i
68232.e: The collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim are together called “the two Sahihs”. They are among the six canonical books.
68232.m: Al-Bukhari and Muslim compiled the most respected hadith collections.

68233.q: Why is a hadith that is “mutawatir” regarded as particularly certain?
a: It was handed down through very many independent chains
It is in the Quran word for word
It was confirmed by a caliph
68233.e: Mutawatir means roughly “transmitted by many”. Such reports are regarded as certain knowledge, unlike reports from single chains (ahad).
68233.m: A hadith handed down by many is called mutawatir.

68234.q: What does hadith criticism examine about the people in a chain of transmitters?
68234.e: The “science of men” (ilm al-rijal) collects information on the transmitters’ dates, teachers and trustworthiness. The assessment of an isnad is based on this.
68234.m: Criticism of transmitters examines the trustworthiness of each person in the chain.

68235.q: What did the Hungarian orientalist Ignaz Goldziher critically question in the 19th century?
a: The existence of the city of Mecca
The number of surahs in the Quran
68235.e: In his “Muslim Studies”, Goldziher showed that many hadiths reflect later developments. He shaped Western hadith research.
68235.m: Goldziher founded critical Western hadith research.

68236.q: What theory did Joseph Schacht put forward about isnads in 1950?
a: Many chains were later extended backwards
68236.e: In “The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence”, Schacht argued that many chains had later been extended back to the Prophet. His theory was later partly confirmed and partly criticised.
68236.m: Schacht believed many isnads had been extended afterwards.

68237.q: What does kalam refer to in Islam?
a: The art of reciting the Quran
68237.e: Kalam literally means “speech”. It refers to theology that defends beliefs with rational arguments.
68237.m: Kalam is the argumentative theology of Islam.

68238.q: What are the representatives of kalam called?
68238.e: Mutakallimun are the “speakers” or debaters. They discussed questions such as God’s attributes and free will.
68238.m: The theologians of kalam are called mutakallimun.

68239.q: Which theory of nature was widespread in kalam?
a: The theory of the four elements alone
The heliocentric view of the world
68239.e: Many mutakallimun saw the world as made up of the smallest particles and accidents. God, they said, creates these anew in every moment.
68239.m: Kalam often explained the world with a theory of atoms.

68240.q: Which question did early Islamic theologians argue about especially fiercely?
a: Whether the earth is a sphere
Whether Medina or Damascus is holy
68240.e: The Jabriyya (“compulsion”) taught that God determines all actions. The Qadariyya, on the other hand, held that humans have free will.
68240.m: Early theologians argued about predestination and free will.

68241.q: What did it mean that the early Murji'a movement “left it to God” to judge serious sinners?
a: People should not judge the faith of others
There was no such thing as sin
68241.e: The name comes from “irja”, to postpone. The Kharijites, on the other hand, declared serious sinners to be unbelievers.
68241.m: The Murji'a postponed judgement on sinners and left it to God.

68242.q: In which regions is the Sunni theological school of the Maturidis particularly widespread today?
a: In Turkey, Central Asia and South Asia
68242.e: Al-Maturidi worked in Samarkand in the 10th century. His school is closely linked with the Hanafi school of law and is widespread where it dominates.
68242.m: The Maturidis are one of the great Sunni theological schools.

68243.q: Which work by al-Ghazali was directed against the Islamic philosophers?
68243.e: In “Tahafut al-falasifa”, al-Ghazali attacked teachings such as the eternity of the world. Ibn Rushd later replied with “The Incoherence of the Incoherence”.
68243.m: Al-Ghazali criticised the philosophers in a famous polemical book.

68244.q: What were the Mu'tazilites known for in early Islam?
a: They based faith strongly on reason
They were an order of warriors
They lived as hermits in the desert
68244.e: The Mu'tazilites arose in Basra in the 8th century. They wanted to settle questions of faith with reasoned arguments and strongly influenced Islamic theology.
68244.m: The Mu'tazilites were a school of theologians who stressed reason.

68245.q: Where does the name “Mu'tazilites” come from?
a: From the name of a city
From the name of a caliph
68245.e: The name goes back to the Arabic verb “i'tazala”. It recalls the breakaway of Wasil ibn Ata.

68246.q: What position did the Mu'tazilites give to a serious sinner?
a: An intermediate position between believer and unbeliever
68246.e: The doctrine is called “manzila bayna al-manzilatayn”, the position between the two positions. In this way they set themselves apart from the Kharijites and the Murji'a.
68246.m: For the Mu'tazilites, a serious sinner was in an intermediate position.

68247.q: What doctrine about the Quran did the Mu'tazilites hold?
a: The Quran is eternal and uncreated
The Quran is only human words
The Quran is a part of God
68247.e: The Mu'tazilites feared that an eternal Quran alongside God would violate his oneness. That is why they held that it was created by God.
68247.m: The Mu'tazilites taught that the Quran was created.

68248.q: What was the mihna that an Abbasid caliph introduced in the 9th century?
a: A state test of faith for judges and scholars
68248.e: From 833, Caliph al-Ma'mun demanded that judges and scholars declare that the Quran was created. The test was later abolished.
68248.m: The mihna was a state test of faith in the caliphate.

68249.q: What did scholars risk who refused during the mihna to declare that the Quran was created?
68249.e: The best-known person who refused was Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Despite imprisonment and beatings he stuck to his position and became a role model for many Sunnis.
68249.m: Ibn Hanbal resisted the Mu'tazilite test of faith.

68250.q: Besides God’s oneness, which principle is one of the five basic principles of the Mu'tazilites?
68250.e: The five principles include oneness, justice, the promise and the threat, the intermediate position and commanding what is right. Human free will follows from justice.
68250.m: God’s justice was a core principle of the Mu'tazilites.

68251.q: In which branches of Islam did Mu'tazilite thought live on in particular?
a: In Shiite theology, for example among the Zaydis
In the Maliki law of North Africa
In the Hanbali law of Arabia
In the Sufism of Central Asia
68251.e: After its decline in the Sunni world, Zaydis and Twelver Shiites took over many Mu'tazilite ideas. In the 20th century some reform thinkers also referred to them.
68251.m: Mu'tazilite thought lived on mainly in Shiite theology.

68252.q: Which main branch of Islam does the Ash'arite school of theology belong to?
68252.e: Al-Ash'ari (died around 935) defended Sunni positions by means of reason. His school became the most important Sunni theology.
68252.m: The Ash'arites are the most important Sunni school of theology.

68253.q: What does the Ash'arite school mainly deal with?
68253.e: The Ash'arites belong to kalam, Islamic theology. Their founder al-Ash'ari was first a Mu'tazilite and then turned away from that school.
68253.m: The Ash'arites are a school of Islamic theology.

68254.q: How did the Ash'arites understand statements about God’s “hand” or “throne”?
a: As mere images without any content
68254.e: The formula “bila kayfa” means “without how”. The attributes are affirmed without comparing God with creatures.
68254.m: The Ash'arites affirmed God’s attributes “without how”.

68255.q: Which question did the Ash'arites want to answer with their doctrine of the “acquisition” of actions?
a: How God’s almighty power and human responsibility fit together
How to calculate prayer times exactly
How to translate the Quran correctly
68255.e: According to Ash'arite teaching, God creates all actions and humans acquire them. In this way divine almighty power was meant to be compatible with human responsibility.
68255.m: The Ash'arites spoke of humans acquiring their actions.

68256.q: How did Ash'arite teaching explain fire burning cotton?
a: God creates the burning anew each time
Fire has a power of its own
68256.e: Al-Ghazali gave the example: fire and burning only occur together out of habit. The real cause, he said, is God. This is called occasionalism.
68256.m: The Ash'arites saw God as the real cause of everything that happens.

68257.q: Which colleges contributed strongly to spreading Ash'arite teaching in the 11th century?
68257.e: The Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded madrasas in Baghdad and other cities. Ash'arite scholars such as al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali taught there.
68257.m: The Nizamiyya schools spread Ash'arite theology.

68258.q: What doctrine about the Quran did the Ash'arites hold?
a: God’s speech is eternal and uncreated
The Quran is a work of the angels
The Quran is purely human speech
68258.e: The Ash'arites saw the word of God as an eternal attribute of God. They distinguished the written and recited text from it.
68258.m: For the Ash'arites, God’s speech is eternal.

a: The oneness and uniqueness of God
68259.e: Tawhid comes from the Arabic word for “one”. It is the central principle of faith in Islam.
68259.m: Tawhid is the belief in the one God.

68260.q: In Islam, what is the most serious offence against tawhid called, associating other beings with God?
68260.e: Shirk means “association”. The Quran calls it the sin that God does not forgive if someone dies in it.
68260.m: Shirk is the opposite of tawhid.

68261.q: Which short surah is regarded as the most concise summary of tawhid?
68261.e: Surah 112 says that God is one, that he does not beget and is not begotten. Nobody is equal to him.
68261.m: The surah al-Ikhlas sums up belief in the one God.

68262.q: Which part of the declaration of faith expresses tawhid?
a: There is no god but God
Muhammad is the messenger of God
68262.e: The shahada begins with “la ilaha illa llah”. This part declares the oneness of God, the second part Muhammad’s prophethood.
68262.m: The first part of the shahada declares the oneness of God.

68263.q: Which three-part division of tawhid is particularly common in Wahhabism?
68263.e: The parts are tawhid al-rububiyya, al-uluhiyya and al-asma wa-l-sifat. The division goes back mainly to Ibn Taymiyya and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.
68263.m: In Wahhabism, tawhid is divided into three areas.

68264.q: Which Christian doctrine does the Quran explicitly reject with reference to tawhid?
68264.e: Surah 4, verse 171 warns: “Do not say three.” In Islam, Jesus is regarded as a prophet, not as the Son of God.
68264.m: The Quran sees Jesus as a prophet and rejects the Trinity.

68265.q: Which artistic feature of Islamic mosques is often linked with tawhid?
68265.e: Because God cannot be compared with anything created, he is not depicted. That is why mosques are decorated with calligraphy and ornaments.
68265.m: Mosques show calligraphy and ornaments instead of images of God.

68266.q: What did the word sharia originally mean?
68266.e: Sharia referred to the well-trodden path to a watering place. In a figurative sense it means the path shown by God.
68266.m: Sharia originally means the path to the watering place.

68267.q: What is the human science of law called that interprets the sharia?
68267.e: Fiqh means “understanding”. It is the interpretation of the divine norms worked out by scholars, which often differs between them.
68267.m: Fiqh is the human understanding of the sharia.

68268.q: Which four sources does classical Sunni legal theory name?
68268.e: The order is Quran, Sunna, ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy). It was systematised mainly by al-Shafi'i.
68268.m: Sunni law is based on four sources.

68269.q: Into how many categories does Islamic legal theory divide human actions?
68269.e: The categories are obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden. So there is more than just permitted or forbidden.
68269.m: The sharia has five ratings for human actions.

68270.q: What is the area of the sharia called that regulates prayer, fasting and pilgrimage?
68270.e: The ibadat concern the relationship between humans and God. The mu'amalat regulate matters such as trade, contracts and family.
68270.m: Prayer and fasting belong to the ibadat.

68271.q: What does the Islamic discipline “usul al-fiqh”, literally “roots of law”, examine?
a: The sources and methods of finding the law
68271.e: Usul al-fiqh asks how rules are derived from the Quran, Sunna, consensus and analogy. The specific individual rulings, on the other hand, are called furu, the “branches”.
68271.m: Usul al-fiqh are the foundations for finding the law.

68272.q: What is the scholar al-Shafi'i (died 820) mainly known for in Islamic legal history?
a: He arranged the sources of law systematically
He founded the city of Baghdad
68272.e: In his work “Risala”, al-Shafi'i arranged the sources of law and stressed the Sunna. One of the four Sunni schools of law is named after him.
68272.m: Al-Shafi'i’s Risala founded Islamic legal method.

a: The higher goals of the sharia
The names of the legal scholars
68273.e: Classically, the protection of religion, life, intellect, offspring and property are named. Al-Shatibi (died 1388) greatly developed this doctrine.
68273.m: The maqasid ask about the purpose of the norms.

68274.q: How many major Sunni schools of law exist today?
68274.e: Today there are the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools of law. Other schools, such as the Zahiri, have died out.
68274.m: In Sunni Islam there are four major schools of law.

68275.q: What is a school of law (madhhab) in Islam?
a: A tradition of how Islamic law is interpreted
68275.e: The schools of law differ in their methods. The Hanafis, for example, may depart from strict analogy by using juristic preference (istihsan).
68275.m: A school of law is a tradition of legal interpretation.

68276.q: Many Muslims in Switzerland come from the Western Balkans and Turkey. Which school of law do the Sunnis there traditionally follow?
68276.e: In the Balkans and in Turkey, the Ottoman Empire shaped the Hanafi tradition. Many immigrants bring this background with them.
68276.m: Muslims from the Balkans and Turkey are mostly shaped by the Hanafi school.

68277.q: In which present-day country did Abu Hanifa, after whom the Hanafi school is named, teach?
68277.e: Abu Hanifa (died 767) taught in Kufa in Iraq. His school gave a lot of room to one’s own reasoned judgement.
68277.m: The Hanafi school arose in Kufa in Iraq.

68278.q: In which city did Malik ibn Anas, the founder of the Maliki school, live and teach?
68278.e: Malik stressed the practice of the people of Medina, the city of the Prophet. His work al-Muwatta is one of the oldest collections of law.
68278.m: Malik ibn Anas taught in Medina.

68279.q: In which region is the Maliki school of law dominant?
68279.e: The Malikis shape Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and large parts of West Africa. In the past the school was also widespread in Islamic Spain.
68279.m: North Africa is mainly shaped by the Maliki school.

68280.q: Which school of law dominates in Indonesia, the country with the most Muslims?
68280.e: The Shafi'i school spread along trade routes to South-East Asia and East Africa. Its founder al-Shafi'i died in Egypt in 820.
68280.m: In Indonesia most Muslims follow the Shafi'i school.

68281.q: Which Sunni school of law shapes the law of Saudi Arabia?
68281.e: The Hanbali school sticks closely to the Quran and hadith. The Wahhabi movement in Arabia relied on it.
68281.m: Saudi Arabia is shaped by the Hanbali school.

68282.q: What is the school of law of the Twelver Shiites called, which is not one of the Sunni schools?
68282.e: It is named after the sixth imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq. It is widespread in Iran and Iraq, for example.
68282.m: Twelver Shiites follow the Ja'fari school of law.

a: A legal opinion by a scholar
A death sentence passed by a court
68283.e: A fatwa answers a religious or legal question. In principle it is an opinion and not a court ruling.
68283.m: A fatwa is a religious legal opinion.

68284.q: What is a scholar who issues fatwas called?
68284.e: The mufti gives opinions, the qadi passes verdicts as a judge. The imam and muezzin have tasks in prayer.
68284.m: A mufti gives fatwas, a qadi passes verdicts.

68285.q: How binding is a fatwa compared with the verdict of a qadi?
a: In principle it is not binding
It can always be enforced by the state
It applies to all Muslims worldwide
68285.e: The person asking can seek the opinion of another mufti. A court ruling, on the other hand, is binding on the parties.
68285.m: A fatwa is a recommendation, not a verdict.

68286.q: Against which writer did Ayatollah Khomeini issue a world-famous fatwa in 1989?
68286.e: The cause was the novel “The Satanic Verses”. The fatwa led to an international crisis and to attacks on translators.
68286.m: The fatwa against Salman Rushdie triggered a worldwide crisis in 1989.

68287.q: What was the highest mufti in the Ottoman Empire called?
68287.e: The Shaykh al-Islam in Istanbul was the highest religious authority. His fatwas could even legitimise decisions of the sultan.
68287.m: The Shaykh al-Islam was the highest mufti of the Ottomans.

68288.q: Which body was founded in 1997 to produce fatwas for Muslims living in Europe?
a: The European Council for Fatwa and Research
68288.e: The council was founded in London in 1997 and is based in Dublin. It deals with questions faced by Muslims as a minority.
68288.m: There is a special fatwa council for Muslims in Europe.

68289.q: Which declaration of 2004 and 2005 recognised eight schools of law and restricted the issuing of fatwas?
68289.e: Hundreds of scholars endorsed the Amman Message in 2005. Among other things, it required that only qualified scholars issue fatwas.
68289.m: The Amman Message strengthened mutual recognition of the schools of law.

68290.e: Ijtihad comes from the same root as jihad. It means the independent effort to reach a legal ruling from the sources.
68290.m: Ijtihad is a scholar’s independent legal reasoning.

68291.q: What is a scholar who is qualified for ijtihad called?
68291.e: A mujtahid must have a thorough command of Arabic, the Quran, hadith and legal method. Someone who follows him is called a muqallid.
68291.m: Someone who reasons out the law independently is called a mujtahid.

68292.q: What is the counterpart of ijtihad called, following an accepted opinion of a school?
68292.e: With taqlid you adopt the ruling of a scholar or a school of law. For lay people this is considered the normal way.
68292.m: Taqlid means following a school of law.

68293.q: What does the idea of the “closed gate of ijtihad” say?
a: That independent reasoning is no longer allowed
That non-Muslims may not enter a mosque
That the Quran may not be translated
That Mecca is closed to pilgrims
68293.e: For a long time researchers thought that from about the 10th century scholars only followed the opinions of their schools. In 1984 the historian Wael Hallaq showed that independent reasoning continued afterwards too.
68293.m: The idea of the closed gate of ijtihad is disputed today.

68294.q: Which Egyptian reformer called for a renewal of ijtihad around 1900?
68294.e: Muhammad Abduh (died 1905) was Mufti of Egypt. He wanted to link Islam with the modern world through reason and new legal reasoning.
68294.m: Muhammad Abduh called for new ijtihad.

68295.q: In which branch of Islam is ijtihad still explicitly regarded as open and important today?
68295.e: Among Twelver Shiites, believers follow a living mujtahid, a recognised highest authority. These scholars constantly practise ijtihad.
68295.m: Among Twelver Shiites, senior scholars continually practise ijtihad.

68296.q: Which sources does a scholar rely on first and foremost in ijtihad?
68296.e: Ijtihad begins where the Quran and Sunna give no clear answer. A well-known hadith about the Prophet’s companion Mu'adh ibn Jabal is regarded as evidence for this.
68296.m: Ijtihad begins where the Quran and Sunna are silent.

68297.q: What title do senior Shiite scholars who practise ijtihad hold, for example in Iran or Iraq?
68297.e: Ayatollah means “sign of God”. The highest ayatollahs are regarded as models whom believers follow in religious questions.
68297.m: Senior Shiite scholars hold the title ayatollah.

68298.q: On the site of which building was the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus built from about 705?
68298.e: Caliph al-Walid I had the mosque built on the site of a basilica of St John. It is regarded as one of the oldest surviving great mosques.
68298.m: The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus was built under al-Walid I.

68299.q: Which reform is mainly associated with the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik?
a: Arabic as the language of administration
68299.e: Abd al-Malik (685 to 705) replaced Greek and Persian in the administration with Arabic. He also had his own coins struck with Arabic inscriptions.
68299.m: Under Abd al-Malik, Arabic became the language of the empire’s administration.

68300.q: Which commander crossed over to Hispania with Muslim troops in 711?
68300.e: Tariq ibn Ziyad landed at the southern tip of Spain in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic. The name Gibraltar goes back to “Jabal Tariq”, the mountain of Tariq.
68300.m: The name Gibraltar recalls the commander Tariq ibn Ziyad.

68301.q: Who stopped the advance of an Umayyad army into the Frankish kingdom at the Battle of Tours and Poitiers in 732?
68301.e: The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeated the army of the governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi in 732. The battle roughly marks the furthest advance to the north-west.
68301.m: Charles Martel defeated an Arab army near Tours and Poitiers in 732.

68302.q: In which year were the Umayyads in Damascus overthrown by the Abbasids?
68302.e: After the defeat at the Great Zab in 750, Umayyad rule collapsed. Almost the entire ruling family was killed afterwards.
68302.m: Umayyad rule in Damascus ended in 750.

68303.q: Where did the Umayyad Abd al-Rahman I, who had fled, found his own emirate in 756?
68303.e: Abd al-Rahman I escaped the massacre by the Abbasids and fled to al-Andalus. In Córdoba he founded an emirate which became a caliphate in 929 and lasted until 1031.
68303.m: After 750 a branch of the Umayyads continued to rule in Córdoba.

68304.q: Under the Umayyads, what were non-Arab Muslims called, who were often at a disadvantage compared with Arabs?
68304.e: Mawali were non-Arabs who had converted to Islam and had to attach themselves to an Arab tribe. Their discontent contributed to the fall of the Umayyads.
68304.m: The disadvantages suffered by the mawali weakened Umayyad rule.

68305.q: In which year did the Battle of Karbala take place?
68305.e: The battle was fought on 10 Muharram in the year 61 after the Hijra, which corresponds to October 680. It deepened the split between Sunnis and Shiites.
68305.m: The Battle of Karbala took place in 680.

68306.q: Which grandson of the Prophet Muhammad was killed at the Battle of Karbala?
68306.e: Husayn, son of Ali and Fatima, was killed with many relatives and companions. For Shiites he is the third imam and the model of martyrdom.
68306.m: Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson, died as a martyr at Karbala in 680.

68307.q: Against the troops of which caliph did Husayn fight at Karbala?
68307.e: Husayn refused to swear allegiance to Yazid I, the son of Mu'awiya. An army sent by the Umayyad governor of Kufa confronted him at Karbala.
68307.m: Husayn refused to pay homage to the Umayyad Yazid I.

68308.q: In which present-day country is Karbala?
68308.e: Karbala lies about 100 kilometres south-west of Baghdad in Iraq. Husayn’s shrine is there.
68308.m: The holy city of Karbala is in present-day Iraq.

68309.q: On which day of the month of Muharram is Ashura observed?
68309.e: The word Ashura comes from the Arabic word for ten. On 10 Muharram Shiites remember the death of Husayn.
68309.m: Ashura falls on the tenth day of the month of Muharram.

68310.q: What are the Shiite passion plays called that recall Husayn’s martyrdom, especially in Iran?
68310.e: Ta'zieh are staged plays of mourning that re-enact the events of Karbala. They are performed mainly in the first ten days of Muharram.
68310.m: In ta'zieh, the drama of Karbala is performed as a passion play.

68311.q: What is the main significance of Ashura in the Sunni tradition?
a: The festival of breaking the fast
68311.e: According to hadiths, Muhammad fasted on Ashura and recommended it. A link to the rescue of Moses and the Israelites is handed down.
68311.m: Many Sunnis fast voluntarily on Ashura.

68312.q: What is the great Shiite pilgrimage to Karbala called, which takes place 40 days after Ashura?
68312.e: Arba'een means forty and ends the traditional 40-day period of mourning for Husayn. Millions of people make the pilgrimage to Karbala, often on foot.
68312.m: Arba'een is the pilgrimage to Karbala on the 40th day after Ashura.

68313.q: Why is Karbala in Iraq a particularly holy city for Shiites?
a: The tomb of Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson, is there
68313.e: Husayn was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680. Next to his shrine is also that of his half-brother and standard-bearer al-Abbas ibn Ali.
68313.m: Because of Husayn’s tomb, Karbala is a major place of pilgrimage.

68314.q: Who does the name of the Abbasids go back to?
a: Abbas I, a Shah of Persia
68314.e: The Abbasids based their claim on al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of the Prophet. Descent from his family strengthened their legitimacy.
68314.m: The Abbasids referred to al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet.

68315.q: Which dynasty did the Abbasids overthrow in 750?
68315.e: The uprising began in Khorasan in the east of the empire. In 750 the Umayyads were defeated; only one prince escaped to Andalusia.
68315.m: In 750 the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads.

68316.q: Which caliph founded the city of Baghdad in 762?
68316.e: Al-Mansur had Baghdad laid out on the Tigris as a new capital. Its location linked important trade routes between Mesopotamia and Iran.
68316.m: Baghdad was founded in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur.

68317.q: What shape did the original centre of Baghdad have?
68317.e: The “Round City” had double walls and four gates. The palace and the main mosque stood in the centre.
68317.m: Early Baghdad was laid out as the “Round City”.

68318.q: With which European ruler did Harun al-Rashid exchange embassies?
68318.e: Frankish sources report embassies around 800. As a gift, Charlemagne is said to have received an elephant called Abul-Abbas.
68318.m: Harun al-Rashid and Charlemagne exchanged envoys.

68319.q: Which city was the residence of the Abbasid caliphs instead of Baghdad from 836 to 892?
68319.e: Caliph al-Mu'tasim moved the residence to Samarra, partly because of tensions with his Turkish troops in Baghdad. The mosque with the spiral minaret there is famous.
68319.m: Samarra was the Abbasid capital for a few decades in the 9th century.

68320.q: Against which empire did the Abbasids fight at the Battle of Talas in 751?
68320.e: At the Talas in Central Asia, the Abbasids defeated an army of the Tang. According to tradition, papermaking reached the Islamic world after this.
68320.m: The Battle of Talas in 751 is linked with the spread of paper.

68321.q: What was the “House of Wisdom” in Baghdad known for under the Abbasids?
68321.e: Scholars there translated works by Aristotle, Euclid and others into Arabic. Baghdad thus became a centre of science.
68321.m: Greek works were translated in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.

68322.q: Which colour was the symbol of the Abbasids on flags and clothing?
68322.e: The Abbasids appeared with black flags, while the Umayyads were associated with white. Black remained the court colour of the Abbasids.
68322.m: Black was the dynastic colour of the Abbasids.

68323.q: Which branch of faith did the Fatimids belong to?
68323.e: The Fatimids were Ismaili imams and claimed the caliphate. This put them in competition with the Sunni Abbasids.
68323.m: The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shiite dynasty.

68324.q: Who did the Fatimids refer to with their name?
68324.e: The Fatimids traced their descent from the Prophet through Fatima and Ali. From this they derived their claim to the imamate.
68324.m: The Fatimids referred to Fatima, the Prophet’s daughter.

68325.q: In which region did the Fatimids establish their rule in 909?
68325.e: With the support of Berber tribes, Ismaili missionaries overthrew the Aghlabids. The first caliph was Abdallah al-Mahdi.
68325.m: The Fatimid caliphate arose in North Africa in 909.

68326.q: Which city did the Fatimids found after conquering Egypt in 969?
68326.e: The general Jawhar laid out the palace city of al-Qahira, “the Victorious”, next to Fustat. It became the capital of the Fatimid empire.
68326.m: Cairo was founded by the Fatimids in 969.

68327.q: Which mosque and place of learning, still existing today, did the Fatimids found in Cairo?
68327.e: The al-Azhar Mosque was built from 970 to 972 and soon became a place of learning. Today it is an important Sunni institution.
68327.m: Al-Azhar in Cairo goes back to the Fatimids.

68328.q: Which Fatimid caliph had the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem destroyed in 1009?
68328.e: Al-Hakim bi-amr Allah persecuted Christians and Jews at times. The destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre caused a great stir in Europe.
68328.m: The Fatimid al-Hakim had the Church of the Holy Sepulchre destroyed in 1009.

68329.q: Which religious community grew out of the veneration of the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim?
68329.e: Followers around Hamza ibn Ali saw al-Hakim as a divine manifestation. The Druze live mainly in Lebanon, Syria and Israel today.
68329.m: The Druze go back to the veneration of Caliph al-Hakim.

68330.q: Who ended Fatimid rule in Egypt in 1171?
68330.e: Saladin, vizier of the last Fatimid caliph, had the Friday prayer said again in the name of the Abbasid caliph. He founded the Sunni Ayyubid dynasty.
68330.m: Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171.

68331.q: Which Ismaili branch split off in 1094 after the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir?
68331.e: Some Ismailis did not recognise al-Musta'li but his brother Nizar. Under Hasan-i Sabbah, the Nizaris built up the fortress of Alamut.
68331.m: The Nizaris split from the Fatimids in 1094.

68332.q: Which battle is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the Reconquista?
a: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
68332.e: Around 722, the Asturian leader Pelayo defeated a Muslim army at Covadonga. Later this victory was seen as the starting point of the Christian reconquest.
68332.m: According to tradition, the Reconquista begins with Covadonga around 722.

68333.q: What are the small Muslim kingdoms called that arose after the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031?
68333.e: After 1031, al-Andalus broke up into many rival taifa kingdoms. Their fragmentation made Christian expansion easier.
68333.m: After 1031, al-Andalus broke up into taifa kingdoms.

68334.q: Which important city did Alfonso VI of Castile conquer in 1085?
68334.e: Toledo, the old capital of the Visigoths, fell to Castile in 1085. The city then became a centre for translating Arabic works into Latin.
68334.m: Toledo was conquered by Alfonso VI in 1085.

68335.q: Where did the Almoravids come from, who came to help the Muslims in al-Andalus after the fall of Toledo in 1085?
68335.e: The Almoravids were a Berber dynasty from present-day Morocco. Their ruler Yusuf ibn Tashfin defeated Alfonso VI at Zallaqa in 1086.
68335.m: The Almoravids intervened in al-Andalus after the fall of Toledo.

68336.q: Which dynasty was defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212?
68336.e: An alliance of Christian kings defeated the army of the Almohad caliph al-Nasir. Afterwards many large cities quickly fell to the Christian kingdoms.
68336.m: Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 broke Almohad power in Spain.

68337.q: When did Ferdinand III of Castile conquer the former caliphal city of Córdoba?
68337.e: Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville followed in 1248. After that, only the Emirate of Granada remained in Muslim hands.
68337.m: Córdoba was conquered by Castile in 1236.

68338.q: Which rulers are called the “Catholic Monarchs”, who took Granada in 1492?
a: Charles V and Isabella of Portugal
68338.e: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon united two crowns through their marriage. Pope Alexander VI gave them the title “Catholic Monarchs”.
68338.m: Isabella I and Ferdinand II conquered Granada in 1492.

68339.q: What happened in the early 17th century to the Moriscos, the forcibly baptised descendants of Muslims in Spain?
a: They were given full religious freedom
68339.e: King Philip III ordered their expulsion in 1609. About 300,000 people had to leave Spain, many of them going to North Africa.
68339.m: The Moriscos were expelled from Spain from 1609.

68340.q: Which people did the Seljuks come from?
68340.e: The Seljuks were a ruling clan of the Oghuz Turks from Central Asia. They converted to Sunni Islam and advanced westwards.
68340.m: The Seljuks were an Oghuz Turkic ruling dynasty.

68341.q: Which title did the Seljuk Tughril Beg receive from the caliph in Baghdad in 1055?
68341.e: Tughril Beg drove the Shiite Buyids out of Baghdad. The caliph remained the spiritual head, but worldly power now lay with the sultan.
68341.m: Tughril Beg was recognised as sultan in Baghdad in 1055.

68342.q: Which battle did Alp Arslan win against the Byzantine Empire in 1071?
68342.e: At Manzikert even Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was taken prisoner. Afterwards Anatolia opened up to Turkish settlers.
68342.m: The Battle of Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to the Turks.

68343.q: What did the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk found in Baghdad and other cities in the 11th century?
68343.e: Nizam al-Mulk served Alp Arslan and Malik Shah. His madrasas, the Nizamiyya, promoted Sunni learning.
68343.m: Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya madrasas.

68344.q: Which city was the capital of the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia?
68344.e: The Seljuks of Rum ruled large parts of Anatolia from Konya. The name Rum refers to the former Roman Empire.
68344.m: Konya was the capital of the Seljuks of Rum.

68345.q: Which European event was partly triggered by the advance of the Seljuks?
68345.e: After its losses in Anatolia, Byzantium asked the West for help. In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at Clermont.
68345.m: The advance of the Seljuks was one reason for the First Crusade.

68346.q: Which scholar worked on a calendar reform under Sultan Malik Shah?
68346.e: Omar Khayyam led the astronomers who created the very accurate Jalali calendar. Today he is also known for his quatrains.
68346.m: Omar Khayyam worked on the calendar of the Seljuk Malik Shah.

68347.q: Against whom did the Seljuks of Rum lose the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243?
68347.e: After the defeat at Köse Dağ, the Seljuks of Rum had to pay tribute to the Mongols. Their empire then broke up into small principalities.
68347.m: The defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243 made the Seljuks of Rum dependent on the Mongols.

68348.q: Which Mongol commander conquered Baghdad in 1258?
68348.e: Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, led the campaign to the west. After a short siege the city was taken in February 1258.
68348.m: Baghdad fell to the Mongol Hülegü in 1258.

68349.q: Which caliphal dynasty lost its rule in Baghdad with the fall of the city in 1258?
68349.e: The last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, al-Musta'sim, surrendered to the Mongols and was executed. This ended the caliphate in Baghdad after about 500 years.
68349.m: With the fall of Baghdad in 1258, the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad ended.

68350.q: According to tradition, why was the caliph killed wrapped in a carpet in 1258?
a: Royal blood was not to be spilled
He was to be buried secretly
He was to be taken to Karakorum
68350.e: According to Mongol custom, the blood of rulers was not allowed to flow onto the ground. That is why this form of execution was chosen.
68350.m: The Mongols avoided spilling the blood of rulers.

68351.q: Which empire did Hülegü found after his conquests in Iran and Iraq?
68351.e: The Ilkhanate included Iran, Iraq and parts of Anatolia. It lasted until about 1335.
68351.m: Hülegü founded the empire of the Ilkhans.

68352.q: Which religion did the Mongol rulers of the Ilkhanate adopt around 1300?
68352.e: Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295. Islam thus became the religion of the rulers of the Ilkhanate.

68353.q: Which fortress of the Nizaris (Assassins) did Hülegü’s troops destroy in 1256?
68353.e: Before attacking Baghdad, Hülegü subdued the castles of the Nizaris in Iran. The fortress of Alamut surrendered in 1256.
68353.m: Hülegü destroyed the Assassins’ fortress of Alamut in 1256.

68354.q: What happened to many books from the libraries when Baghdad was conquered in 1258?
a: They were destroyed, many ended up in the Tigris
They were carefully taken to Rome
They were given away to scholars
68354.e: According to reports, the ink of the books turned the Tigris dark. With the fall of Baghdad the Islamic world lost an important centre of learning.
68354.m: In 1258 countless books were destroyed in Baghdad.

68355.q: Which Central Asian conqueror devastated Baghdad again in 1401?
68355.e: Timur, also called Tamerlane, conquered Baghdad in 1401 and had many inhabitants killed. The city took a long time to recover.
68355.m: Timur destroyed Baghdad once more in 1401.

68356.q: What did the Arabic word “mamluk” originally mean?
a: Owned, in other words a slave
68356.e: Mamluks were purchased slaves, usually of Turkish or Circassian origin, who were trained as soldiers. They could rise to the highest offices.
68356.m: Mamluks were elite soldiers bought as slaves and trained.

68357.q: Which city was the capital of the Mamluk Sultanate?
68357.e: The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517. Cairo was its residence and one of the largest centres of the Islamic world.
68357.m: The Mamluks ruled their empire from Cairo.

68358.q: Whom did the Mamluks defeat at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
68358.e: Sultan Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in Palestine. The Mongol advance towards Egypt was stopped.
68358.m: The Mamluks stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.

68359.q: What role did the Abbasid caliph have whom Sultan Baybars installed in Cairo in 1261?
a: He gave the sultans legitimacy but did not rule
He was the real ruler of Egypt
68359.e: Baybars took in an Abbasid who had fled and made him caliph. This is called a shadow caliphate.
68359.m: Under the Mamluks there was an Abbasid shadow caliphate in Cairo.

68360.q: Which Crusader city did the Mamluks conquer in 1291 as the last great stronghold?
68360.e: With the fall of Acre in 1291, Crusader rule in the Holy Land largely came to an end. Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil led the siege.
68360.m: The fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Crusader states.

68361.q: Which empire conquered the Mamluk empire in 1517?
68361.e: The Ottoman sultan Selim I won at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and near Cairo in 1517. Egypt and Syria became Ottoman provinces.
68361.m: The Ottomans ended the Mamluk Sultanate in 1517.

68362.q: Against whom did the Mamluks fight at the Battle of the Pyramids in 1798?
68362.e: Even under Ottoman rule, the Mamluks remained powerful in Egypt. At the Pyramids their cavalry was defeated by Napoleon’s infantry.
68362.m: Napoleon defeated the Mamluks at the Pyramids in 1798.

68363.q: Who eliminated the Mamluks in Egypt in 1811 with a massacre in the Citadel of Cairo?
68363.e: The Ottoman governor Muhammad Ali invited the Mamluk leaders to a celebration and had them killed. After that he ruled Egypt almost independently.
68363.m: Muhammad Ali removed the power of the Mamluks in 1811.

68364.q: Which ruler founded the Safavid Empire in 1501?
68364.e: Ismail I conquered Tabriz in 1501 and had himself crowned Shah. At the time he was only about 14 years old.
68364.m: Ismail I founded the Safavid Empire in 1501.

68365.q: Which branch of faith did the Safavids make the state religion in Iran?
68365.e: Ismail I declared Twelver Shia the state religion and often enforced it violently. This is how Iran became a mainly Shiite country.
68365.m: Since the Safavids, Iran has been mainly Twelver Shiite.

68366.q: Where does the name of the Safavids come from?
a: From the Sufi order of Safi al-Din of Ardabil
From the city of Safawa on the Caspian Sea
From the Arabic word for pure
68366.e: Safi al-Din (died 1334) founded a Sufi order in Ardabil. His descendants turned it into a political and military movement.
68366.m: The Safavids grew out of a Sufi order in Ardabil.

68367.q: What were the Turkmen warriors of the Safavids called, after their red headgear?
68367.e: Qizilbash means “red head” in Turkish. The red cap with twelve folds referred to the twelve imams.
68367.m: The Qizilbash wore red caps as a sign of loyalty to the Safavids.

68368.q: In which battle did the Ottomans defeat the Safavids in 1514?
68368.e: At Chaldiran, Selim I used firearms and artillery. Ismail I lost, and eastern Anatolia came under Ottoman control.
68368.m: At Chaldiran in 1514 the Safavids were defeated by the Ottomans.

68369.q: Which city did Abbas I make the capital of the Safavids at the end of the 16th century?
68369.e: Abbas I moved the residence to Isfahan in 1598 and had the city splendidly developed. A Persian saying calls Isfahan “half the world”.
68369.m: Under Abbas I, Isfahan became a magnificent capital.

68370.q: What is the great square in Isfahan called, laid out under Abbas I and part of the UNESCO World Heritage?
68370.e: The square is surrounded by the Shah Mosque, the Lotfollah Mosque, the Ali Qapu Palace and the bazaar. It was added to the World Heritage list in 1979.
68370.m: Naqsh-e Jahan Square is the heart of Safavid Isfahan.

68371.q: Why did the Safavids at first bring Shiite scholars to Iran from abroad?
a: There were still too few Shiite scholars in Iran
Iranian scholars did not speak Persian
The Ottomans sent them as a gift
68371.e: At the time Iran was mainly Sunni. Scholars from the Jabal Amil region in present-day southern Lebanon helped to build up Twelver Shia as the state religion.
68371.m: Lebanese scholars helped to build up Shia Islam in Iran.

68372.q: Who founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 after the First Battle of Panipat?
68372.e: Babur defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat in 1526. He used field artillery effectively.
68372.m: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in India in 1526.

68373.q: From which conqueror was Babur descended on his father’s side?
68373.e: On his father’s side Babur was a descendant of Timur, on his mother’s side of Genghis Khan. The name “Mughal” comes from “Mongol”.
68373.m: Babur was a descendant of Timur.

68374.q: Which empire did Akbar rule in the 16th century?
68374.e: Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605, almost 50 years. Under him the Mughal Empire grew greatly and was reorganised.
68374.m: Akbar was ruler of the Mughal Empire.

68375.q: Which tax for non-Muslims did Akbar abolish in 1564?
68375.e: The jizya was a poll tax for protected non-Muslims. Abolishing it won Akbar the support of the Hindu majority.
68375.m: Akbar abolished the jizya for non-Muslims.

68376.q: What is Akbar particularly known for in the history of religion?
68376.e: In the “House of Worship”, Akbar had Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Parsis and Jesuits debate with each other. He searched for shared truths.

68377.q: What is the religious and ethical teaching created by Akbar called, which combined elements of several religions?
68377.e: Din-i Ilahi, the “divine faith”, had only a few followers at court. It combined elements from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and other teachings.
68377.m: Akbar’s Din-i Ilahi combined elements of several religions.

68378.q: Which city did Akbar have built as a new residence?
68378.e: Fatehpur Sikri was built of red sandstone from about 1571. Akbar left the city again as early as around 1585; a lack of water is usually given as the reason.
68378.m: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri as a new capital.

68379.q: Which religion did most of Akbar’s subjects belong to?
68379.e: Akbar and the Mughal rulers were Muslims but ruled over a Hindu majority. That is why Akbar sought balance, for example by abolishing the jizya.
68379.m: Akbar was a Muslim and ruled over many Hindus.

68380.q: What was the jizya, which the Mughal ruler Aurangzeb reintroduced in 1679?
68380.e: Aurangzeb followed a stricter Sunni policy than Akbar, who had abolished the tax. Reintroducing it increased tensions with Hindus.

68381.q: Who, as leader of the new Turkey, had the caliphate abolished in 1924?
68381.e: At Mustafa Kemal’s urging, the National Assembly in Ankara decided on abolition on 3 March 1924. The Ottoman dynasty had to leave the country.
68381.m: Atatürk had the caliphate abolished in 1924.

68382.q: What was abolished in Turkey as early as 1 November 1922, that is before the caliphate?
68382.e: In 1922 the National Assembly separated the sultanate from the caliphate. The caliph remained only as a spiritual office without political power.
68382.m: The sultanate ended in 1922, the caliphate only in 1924.

68383.q: Which ruling house held the title of caliph until it was abolished in 1924?
68383.e: Since the 16th century the Ottoman sultans had also held the title of caliph. The last caliph was Abdülmecid II.
68383.m: Until 1924 the Ottomans were the caliphs.

68384.q: To which country did Abdülmecid II first go into exile after he was deposed in 1924?
68384.e: In 1924 Abdülmecid II first went to Switzerland and moved on to Nice in the same year. He died in Paris in 1944.
68384.m: In 1924 the last caliph first went into exile in Switzerland.

68385.q: Which state was proclaimed in 1923 after the end of the Ottoman Empire?
68385.e: On 29 October 1923 the National Assembly in Ankara proclaimed the republic. The last sultan, Mehmed VI, had already left the country in 1922.
68385.m: The Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923.

68386.q: What was the movement in British India called that campaigned from 1919 to keep the Ottoman caliphate?
68386.e: The Khilafat Movement combined Muslim concerns with the Indian struggle against British rule. Mahatma Gandhi supported it for a time.
68386.m: The Khilafat Movement in India fought for the Ottoman caliphate.

68387.q: Who had himself proclaimed caliph in March 1924, shortly after Ankara had abolished the Ottoman caliphate?
68387.e: Sharif Husayn ibn Ali claimed the title but found little recognition. During the war against Ibn Saud he abdicated in October 1924, and by the end of 1925 the Hejaz was entirely lost to the Saudis.
68387.m: In 1924 Sharif Husayn of Mecca claimed the caliphate in vain.

68388.q: What does the Arabic word “caliph” originally mean?
68388.e: The caliph was regarded as the Prophet’s successor in leading the Muslim community. After 1924, scholars such as Ali Abd al-Raziq disputed that the office was religiously necessary.
68388.m: Caliph means successor of the Prophet.

68389.q: Which expedition in 1798 is often regarded as the beginning of modern European intervention in the Arab world?
68389.e: In 1798 Napoleon landed in Egypt with soldiers and scholars. The campaign is often seen as a turning point in relations between Europe and the Middle East.
68389.m: Napoleon’s Egyptian campaign of 1798 brought Europe directly into the Middle East.

68390.q: In which year did France conquer Algiers?
68390.e: The French invasion began in 1830 with the capture of Algiers. Algeria remained under French rule until 1962.

68391.q: Who led the resistance against the French conquest of Algeria from 1832?
68391.e: Emir Abd al-Qadir fought against France until 1847. Later, in 1860, he saved many Christians from a massacre in Damascus.
68391.m: Abd al-Qadir led the Algerian resistance against France.

68392.q: In which year did Great Britain occupy Egypt?
68392.e: After the Urabi revolt, British troops landed in Egypt in 1882. Protecting the Suez Canal was a main reason.

68393.q: Who led an uprising in Sudan in which Khartoum was captured in 1885?
68393.e: Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the Mahdi in 1881 and fought against Egyptian and British rule. The British general Gordon died when Khartoum was taken.
68393.m: The Mahdist uprising captured Khartoum in 1885.

68394.q: Which leader of the Sanusiyya fought against Italy in Libya and was executed in 1931?
68394.e: Omar al-Mukhtar led the resistance in Cyrenaica for about 20 years. The Italian colonial power had him hanged in 1931.
68394.m: Omar al-Mukhtar became a symbol of Libyan resistance.

68395.q: What is the secret agreement of 1916 called in which Great Britain and France divided up the Middle East?
68395.e: Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot set out zones of influence in the Arab territories of the Ottoman Empire. The agreement shaped the later mandate borders.
68395.m: The Sykes-Picot Agreement divided up the Middle East in 1916.

68396.q: Which territories did France receive as League of Nations mandates after the First World War?
68396.e: The League of Nations gave France the mandates for Syria and Lebanon. Great Britain received Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan.
68396.m: Syria and Lebanon became French mandate territories.

68397.q: What is the name of the twelfth imam who, according to Twelver Shia teaching, went into hiding (occultation)?
68397.e: According to Twelver Shia teaching, Muhammad al-Mahdi lives on in hiding and will return at the end of time. Hasan al-Askari was his father and the eleventh imam.
68397.m: Twelver Shiites await the return of the hidden imam Muhammad al-Mahdi.

68398.q: What is the hiddenness of the twelfth imam called in Twelver Shia?
68398.e: Ghayba means absence or hiddenness. A distinction is made between the minor occultation (874 to 941), during which deputies kept in contact, and the major occultation since 941.
68398.m: According to Shiite belief, since the major ghayba the twelfth imam has been hidden without visible deputies.

68399.q: Which dynasty made Twelver Shia the state religion in Persia from 1501?
68399.e: Shah Ismail I founded Safavid rule in 1501 and made Twelver Shia the official religion. This permanently gave Persia a Shiite character.
68399.m: With the Safavids, Persia became a Shiite country from 1501.

68400.q: After which imam is the school of law of the Twelver Shiites named?
68400.e: The Ja'fari school of law goes back to the sixth imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, who taught in Medina in the 8th century.
68400.m: Twelver Shiites follow the Ja'fari school of law.

68401.q: What is the principle of rule by the legal scholar, put forward by Ruhollah Khomeini, called?
68401.e: According to velayat-e faqih, a senior legal scholar should lead the state in the absence of the twelfth imam. This principle was laid down in the constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran in 1979.
68401.m: Velayat-e faqih gives a legal scholar the highest political power in Iran.

68402.q: What does the Shiite title “marja-e taqlid” mean?
68402.e: A marja-e taqlid is a high-ranking scholar whose legal opinions believers follow. Believers choose such a scholar as their model in legal questions.
68402.m: In legal questions, Twelver Shiite believers follow a “source of emulation”.

68403.q: Which city in Iran is the most important centre for training Shiite scholars?
68403.e: Qom has many theological colleges (hawzas). Besides Qom, Najaf in Iraq is the second great centre of Shiite learning.
68403.m: Qom is the most important city of Shiite scholarship in Iran.

68404.q: In which Iraqi city is the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the first imam of the Shiites?
68404.e: The Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf is one of the most important places of pilgrimage for Shiites. The city is also an important centre of Shiite scholars.
68404.m: Ali ibn Abi Talib is buried in Najaf in Iraq.

68405.q: What is the legal method called in which a Shiite scholar independently derives rulings from the sources?
68405.e: Among Twelver Shiites, the Usuli school has prevailed, which stresses the ijtihad of living scholars. A scholar with this authority is called a mujtahid.
68405.m: A Shiite mujtahid may make legal rulings independently through ijtihad.

68406.q: Unlike the Twelver Shiites, whom do the Ismailis recognise as the seventh imam?
68406.e: After the death of Ja'far al-Sadiq, the Shiites split. The Ismailis followed the line of his son Ismail, the Twelver Shiites that of Musa al-Kazim.
68406.m: The Ismailis are named after Ismail, the son of Ja'far al-Sadiq.

68407.q: Which Ismaili dynasty founded the city of Cairo in 969?
68407.e: The Fatimids conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo as their new capital. They also founded the Al-Azhar Mosque there.
68407.m: Cairo was founded by the Ismaili Fatimids.

68408.q: In which city was Karim Aga Khan IV, imam of the Nizaris from 1957 to 2025, born in 1936?
68408.e: Karim Aga Khan IV was born in Geneva in 1936 and grew up partly in Switzerland. He led the Nizari Ismailis for almost 68 years.
68408.m: Aga Khan IV was born in Geneva.

68409.q: Who has been the Aga Khan, and therefore imam of the Nizari Ismailis, since February 2025?
68409.e: After the death of Karim Aga Khan IV on 4 February 2025, his eldest son Rahim became the 50th imam as Aga Khan V. He was named in his father’s will.
68409.m: Since 2025, Rahim Al-Hussaini has been imam of the Nizaris as Aga Khan V.

68410.q: From which ruler did Hasan Ali Shah receive the title “Aga Khan” in the 19th century?
68410.e: The Qajar Shah Fath Ali Shah gave Hasan Ali Shah the title of honour when he appointed him governor of Qom. Hasan Ali Shah later moved to British India.
