68410.m: The title Aga Khan originally came from the Persian royal court.

68411.q: Which mountain fortress in present-day Iran was the centre of the Nizaris under Hasan-i Sabbah from 1090?
68411.e: Hasan-i Sabbah took the castle of Alamut in 1090 and built up a Nizari state from there. The Mongols captured the fortress in 1256.
68411.m: Hasan-i Sabbah made the castle of Alamut the centre of the Nizaris.

68412.q: What were many splits in Shiite Islam about, for example among the Ismailis in 1094?
68412.e: After the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir, some supported his son Nizar and others al-Musta'li. This is how the Nizaris and the Musta'lis came about.
68412.m: The succession dispute after al-Mustansir split the Ismailis in 1094.

68413.q: Which religious community, independent today, emerged from the Ismailis in the 11th century?
68413.e: The Druze arose around the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, whom they revered as a divine manifestation. Today they live mainly in Lebanon, Syria and Israel.
68413.m: The Druze have their origins in the Ismaili Fatimid period.

68414.q: In which country does the Ismaili community of the Dawoodi Bohras mainly live?
68414.e: The Dawoodi Bohras are a branch of the Musta'li Ismailis with their centre in Mumbai. Many of them are traders.
68414.m: The Dawoodi Bohras are Musta'li Ismailis from India.

68415.q: What is the multi-volume didactic poem called that is regarded as Rumi’s main work?
68415.e: The Masnavi has six books with about 25,000 couplets full of stories and mystical teachings. It is often called “the Quran in the Persian language”.
68415.m: Rumi’s main work is the Masnavi.

68416.q: In which language did Rumi write most of his works?
68416.e: Although Rumi lived in Anatolia, he wrote poetry almost only in Persian, the cultural language of his time. Only a few verses are in Arabic or Greek.

68417.q: Which wandering dervish became Rumi’s formative spiritual friend in 1244?
68417.e: Meeting Shams of Tabriz transformed Rumi from a scholar into an ecstatic poet. After Shams mysteriously disappeared, many love poems were written.
68417.m: Shams of Tabriz turned Rumi into a mystical poet.

68418.q: What is Rumi’s great collection of lyric poems called, which he dedicated to a friend?
68418.e: Thousands of ghazals are collected in the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi. In it Rumi often used the name of his friend Shams instead of his own as the poet’s name.
68418.m: Rumi’s lyric poems are collected in the Divan-e Shams.

68419.q: What does the name “Rumi” refer to?
a: The city of Rome in Italy
68419.e: “Rum” was the Islamic name for the Byzantine Empire and Anatolia. So Rumi means “the one from Rum”, because he spent most of his life there.
68419.m: The name Rumi refers to Anatolia, which was then called Rum.

68420.q: Which title of honour, meaning “our master”, do Rumi’s followers give him?
68420.e: Mawlana (Turkish Mevlana) means “our lord” or “our master”. That is why Rumi is mostly known as Mevlana in Turkey.
68420.m: Rumi is reverently called Mawlana, “our master”.

68421.q: What do Rumi’s followers call the anniversary of his death on 17 December?
68421.e: The day of remembrance is called Şeb-i Arus, the “wedding night”. Death is seen as the union of the soul with God, the Beloved.
68421.m: The anniversary of Rumi’s death is celebrated as his wedding night with God.

68422.q: With which image does Rumi’s Masnavi begin?
a: The lament of a reed flute
68422.e: The Masnavi begins with the “Song of the Reed”, which laments because it has been cut from the reed bed. It stands for the soul longing for its origin with God.
68422.m: The lamenting reed flute in the Masnavi stands for the longing of the soul.

68423.q: What is the work called in which al-Ghazali criticised Islamic philosophers such as Avicenna?
a: The Revival of the Religious Sciences
68423.e: In “Tahafut al-falasifa”, al-Ghazali accused the Aristotelian philosophers of unbelief on three points, for example because of the doctrine that the world is eternal.
68423.m: In “The Incoherence of the Philosophers”, al-Ghazali criticised the philosophers of his time.

68424.q: What is al-Ghazali’s extensive main work on religious life called?
a: The Revival of the Religious Sciences
68424.e: The “Ihya ulum al-din” deals in forty books with worship, everyday life, vices and paths to salvation. It combines law, theology and mysticism.
68424.m: Al-Ghazali’s main work is “The Revival of the Religious Sciences”.

68425.q: In which city did al-Ghazali teach at a famous college from 1091?
68425.e: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk appointed him to the Nizamiyya madrasa in Baghdad. In 1095 he gave up the post after a personal crisis.
68425.m: Al-Ghazali taught at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad.

68426.q: Which movement did al-Ghazali in particular bring together with Sunni orthodoxy?
68426.e: After his crisis al-Ghazali lived as a Sufi for years. He showed that mysticism and faithfulness to the law do not contradict each other, which anchored Sufism more firmly in Sunni Islam.
68426.m: Al-Ghazali reconciled mysticism with Sunni Islam.

68427.q: What does al-Ghazali describe in his autobiography “Deliverance from Error”?
a: His doubts and his search for certainty
His work as a court doctor
68427.e: In “al-Munqidh min al-dalal”, al-Ghazali describes his doubts and his path through theology and philosophy to mysticism.
68427.m: In “Deliverance from Error”, al-Ghazali tells of his spiritual journey.

68428.q: Which title of honour did al-Ghazali receive?
68428.e: Al-Ghazali is called “Hujjat al-Islam”, Proof of Islam. He is regarded as one of the most influential Sunni scholars.
68428.m: Al-Ghazali bears the title of honour “Proof of Islam”.

68429.q: With which example did al-Ghazali deny a necessary connection between cause and effect?
68429.e: According to al-Ghazali, cotton does not necessarily burn because fire touches it, but because God creates the burning each time. The regularity rests on God’s habit.
68429.m: For al-Ghazali, cotton burns by God’s will and not necessarily because of the fire.

68430.q: In which region was al-Ghazali born around 1058 and where did he die in 1111?
68430.e: Al-Ghazali came from Tus in Khorasan in the north-east of present-day Iran. He also died there in 1111.
68430.m: Al-Ghazali came from Tus in Khorasan.

68431.q: Under which nickname was Averroes famous in the Latin Middle Ages?
68431.e: Averroes wrote detailed commentaries on almost all of Aristotle’s works. That is why Thomas Aquinas simply called him “the Commentator”.
68431.m: In Europe Averroes was regarded as “the Commentator” on Aristotle.

68432.q: What is the work called with which Averroes replied to al-Ghazali’s criticism of the philosophers?
68432.e: In “Tahafut al-tahafut”, Ibn Rushd defended philosophy against al-Ghazali’s accusations. The title itself alludes to al-Ghazali’s work.
68432.m: Averroes defended philosophy in “The Incoherence of the Incoherence”.

68433.q: Which office did Ibn Rushd hold in Seville and Córdoba?
68433.e: Ibn Rushd was a qadi, a judge under Islamic law, and also wrote about jurisprudence. He was also personal physician at the court.
68433.m: Averroes worked as a judge and a doctor.

68434.q: In which city in al-Andalus was Averroes born in 1126?
68434.e: Ibn Rushd came from a respected family of jurists in Córdoba. Later he served the Almohad caliphs as judge and personal physician.

68435.q: What is the philosophical movement at European universities called that referred to Averroes?
68435.e: Latin Averroists such as Siger of Brabant taught in Paris in the 13th century. Their theses were condemned by the church in 1270 and 1277.
68435.m: Averroism shaped philosophy at the University of Paris.

68436.q: In which famous Renaissance fresco is Averroes shown?
68436.e: From 1510 to 1511 Raphael painted “The School of Athens” in the Vatican, with many philosophers. Averroes can be seen in it wearing a turban.
68436.m: Raphael shows Averroes in “The School of Athens”.

68437.q: What did Averroes want to show in his “Decisive Treatise”?
a: That philosophy and religion are compatible
That the world had a beginning in time
68437.e: In the “Fasl al-maqal”, Ibn Rushd argues that the Quran calls for reasoned reflection. True philosophy, he says, cannot contradict revelation.
68437.m: For Averroes, reason and revelation do not contradict each other.

68438.q: What is Ibn Khaldun’s famous introductory work from 1377 called?
68438.e: The Muqaddimah is the introduction to his world history. In it Ibn Khaldun develops a theory of society, economy and history.
68438.m: Ibn Khaldun’s best-known work is the Muqaddimah.

68439.q: Which concept did Ibn Khaldun place at the centre of his explanation of how dynasties rise?
68439.e: Asabiyya means group cohesion or solidarity. According to Ibn Khaldun, groups with strong cohesion seize power but lose it again in the prosperity of the cities.
68439.m: According to Ibn Khaldun, a dynasty’s power depends on its asabiyya.

68440.q: In which city was Ibn Khaldun born in 1332?
68440.e: Ibn Khaldun came from an Andalusian family that had emigrated to Tunis. He died in Cairo in 1406.
68440.m: Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis.

68441.q: Which conqueror did Ibn Khaldun meet outside Damascus in 1401?
68441.e: During the siege of Damascus, Ibn Khaldun had himself taken to Timur and had several conversations with him. He wrote about this in his autobiography.
68441.m: Ibn Khaldun met the conqueror Timur in 1401.

68442.q: Ibn Khaldun is regarded in particular as a forerunner of which modern science?
68442.e: Ibn Khaldun systematically studied how human society, tribes and cities work. That is why he is regarded as an early pioneer of sociology.
68442.m: Ibn Khaldun is regarded as a forerunner of sociology.

68443.q: According to Ibn Khaldun, how many generations does the heyday of a dynasty typically last?
68443.e: Ibn Khaldun thought a dynasty usually lasted no more than three generations, about 120 years. The founders are tough, while their descendants grow soft in luxury.
68443.m: According to Ibn Khaldun, a dynasty usually declines after about three generations.

68444.q: Which office did Ibn Khaldun hold several times in Cairo?
68444.e: The Mamluk sultan appointed Ibn Khaldun several times as the highest judge of the Maliki school of law. He also taught at colleges in Cairo.
68444.m: In Cairo, Ibn Khaldun was chief Maliki judge.

68445.q: What is the Muqaddimah the introduction to?
68445.e: The Muqaddimah introduces Ibn Khaldun’s world history “Kitab al-Ibar”, which deals especially with the history of the Arabs and Berbers.
68445.m: The Muqaddimah is the introduction to the world history “Kitab al-Ibar”.

68446.q: What does the term “salaf” in the word Salafism refer to?
a: The pious forebears of the first generations
The legal scholars of the Ottoman Empire
The mystics of the Middle Ages
The caliphs of the Abbasid era
68446.e: “Al-salaf al-salih” means the first three generations of Muslims. Salafists want to model their faith and life strictly on their example.
68446.m: Salafists refer to the pious forebears among the early Muslims.

68447.q: Which scholar of the 13th and 14th centuries do Salafists refer to particularly often?
68447.e: Ibn Taymiyya (1263 to 1328) fought against innovations and the veneration of saints. His writings are fundamental for Salafists and Wahhabis.
68447.m: Ibn Taymiyya is an important authority for Salafism.

68448.q: Which three main branches of Salafism do researchers often distinguish?
68448.e: Quietists withdraw from politics, political Salafists want to change society and jihadists support violence. This division goes back to Quintan Wiktorowicz.
68448.m: Researchers distinguish quietist, political and jihadist Salafists.

68449.e: Bid'a refers to practices that did not exist in the Prophet’s time, such as certain festivals or the veneration of saints. Salafists reject them as un-Islamic.
68449.m: Salafists reject religious innovations, called bid'a.

68450.q: What did the influential Salafist scholar al-Albani mainly deal with in the 20th century?
68450.e: Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani (1914 to 1999) re-examined thousands of reports about the Prophet. He is regarded as an important figure of quietist Salafism.
68450.m: Al-Albani shaped Salafism through his criticism of hadiths.

68451.q: What is the typical attitude of Salafists towards being bound to one of the traditional schools of law?
a: They follow only the Hanafi school
They follow all four at once
68451.e: Salafists criticise taqlid, following a school of law without question. They want to rely directly on the Quran and Sunna.
68451.m: Salafists reject taqlid towards the schools of law.

68452.q: Which principle of faith do Salafists stress particularly strongly?
a: Imamate, the leadership of the imams
Wahdat al-wujud, the unity of being
68452.e: For Salafists, tawhid is central. They see the veneration of saints and tombs as a violation of this oneness.
68452.m: Tawhid is at the heart of Salafist teaching.

68453.q: What is the 19th-century reform movement called, from which today’s Salafism clearly differs?
68453.e: The reformist Salafiyya wanted to combine Islam with reason and modern science. Today’s Salafism, by contrast, is mostly strictly literal.
68453.m: The reformist Salafiyya was more modern than today’s Salafism.

68454.q: Who founded the teaching of Wahhabism in the 18th century?
68454.e: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703 to 1792) preached a strict return to original Islam on the Arabian Peninsula. The movement is named after him.
68454.m: Wahhabism goes back to Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.

68455.q: With which ruler did Ibn Abd al-Wahhab form a far-reaching alliance in 1744?
68455.e: The alliance of Diriyah linked religious teaching with political power. The first Saudi state grew out of it.
68455.m: Since 1744 the Saud family and Wahhabism have been closely linked.

68456.q: What do the followers of Wahhabism call themselves?
68456.e: The name “Wahhabis” was given to them by others. They call themselves muwahhidun, those who profess the oneness of God.

68457.q: Which Sunni school of law is Wahhabism based on?
68457.e: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab came from the Hanbali tradition, which is regarded as the strictest of the four Sunni schools.
68457.m: Wahhabism is rooted in the Hanbali school of law.

68458.q: In which region of the Arabian Peninsula did Wahhabism arise?
68458.e: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab came from Uyayna in Najd, the highlands of central Arabia. Diriyah near Riyadh is also there.
68458.m: Wahhabism comes from Najd in central Arabia.

68459.q: Who destroyed the first Saudi Wahhabi state in 1818?
a: Egyptian troops acting for the Ottomans
68459.e: On behalf of the Ottoman sultan, Ibrahim Pasha, son of the Egyptian governor Muhammad Ali, conquered Diriyah in 1818.
68459.m: The first Saudi state was ended by Egyptian troops in 1818.

68460.q: In which present-day state is Wahhabism closely linked with the ruling family?
68460.e: Since the 18th century the House of Saud has based its rule on the Wahhabi scholars. The teaching is also widespread in Qatar.
68460.m: In Saudi Arabia, Wahhabism is the dominant state doctrine.

68461.q: Which practice did the Wahhabis particularly fight against, for example by destroying tomb buildings?
a: The veneration of saints and tombs
68461.e: Wahhabis saw the veneration of saints and tombs as polytheism. That is why many tomb domes in Mecca and Medina, for example, were demolished.
68461.m: Wahhabis strictly reject the veneration of saints’ tombs.

68462.q: Which high office did Muhammad Abduh hold in Egypt from 1899?
68462.e: As Grand Mufti of Egypt, Abduh wrote legal opinions and campaigned for reforms in education and law. He held the office until his death in 1905.
68462.m: From 1899 Muhammad Abduh was Grand Mufti of Egypt.

68463.q: Who was Muhammad Abduh’s most important teacher and fellow campaigner?
68463.e: Al-Afghani taught in Cairo and called for the unity and renewal of Muslims against colonialism. Abduh became his best-known pupil.
68463.m: Al-Afghani was Abduh’s teacher and companion.

68464.q: What did the journal that al-Afghani and Abduh published in exile in Paris in 1884 call for?
68464.e: The journal “The Firmest Bond” appeared for only a few months. It was nevertheless read throughout the Islamic world.
68464.m: Abduh and al-Afghani published the journal “The Firmest Bond” in Paris.

68465.q: How were Muhammad Abduh’s ideas mainly spread around 1900?
68465.e: His pupil Rashid Rida founded al-Manar (The Lighthouse) in Cairo in 1898. The journal was read throughout the Islamic world.
68465.m: Rashid Rida spread Abduh’s ideas in the journal al-Manar.

68466.q: What happened to Muhammad Abduh after he supported an Egyptian uprising against the British in 1882 that failed?
68466.e: Abduh supported the national movement around Ahmed Urabi. After its defeat he lived in exile in Beirut and Paris.
68466.m: Abduh went into exile after the Urabi revolt.

68467.q: What did Muhammad Abduh call for instead of simply imitating earlier scholars?
68467.e: Abduh criticised taqlid, simply following older authorities. Muslims should understand the sources anew with reason and so reconcile them with the modern world.
68467.m: Abduh wanted to link Islam with the modern world through independent thinking.

68468.q: Which college did Abduh particularly want to reform?
68468.e: Abduh campaigned for modern subjects and new teaching methods to be introduced at Al-Azhar. Many of his plans met with resistance.

68469.q: How did Muhammad Abduh explain faith in his “Treatise on the Oneness of God”?
68469.e: In the “Risalat al-tawhid”, Abduh explains Islamic doctrine with rational arguments. The book has been translated into many languages.
68469.m: Abduh wrote the “Treatise on the Oneness of God”.

68470.q: What does the term “Islamism” mean in academic research?
a: A political ideology that wants to reshape state and society according to Islamic norms
The teaching of the Islamic schools of law
68470.e: Islamism means political movements that want to impose what they understand as an Islamic order. It must be distinguished from Islam as a religion.
68470.m: Islamism is a political ideology and not the same as Islam.

68471.q: Who founded the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt in 1928?
68471.e: The teacher Hasan al-Banna founded the movement in Ismailia. It became the most influential Islamist organisation in the Arab world.
68471.m: Hasan al-Banna founded the Muslim Brotherhood in 1928.

68472.q: Which Egyptian Islamist thinker wrote the book “Milestones” and was executed in 1966?
68472.e: Sayyid Qutb wrote “Milestones” in prison. He declared existing societies to be un-Islamic, which strongly influenced radical groups.
68472.m: Sayyid Qutb shaped radical Islamism with his book “Milestones”.

68473.q: In which countries is the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami mainly active today?
68473.e: Abul A'la Maududi founded Jamaat-e-Islami in Lahore in 1941. After the partition of India it became active mainly in Pakistan and Bangladesh.

68474.q: What do Islamists such as Maududi and Qutb mean by the “sovereignty of God”?
a: Only God may make laws, not humans
Religion and state must be separate
68474.e: The concept is called hakimiyya. From it Islamists derived their rejection of man-made laws and of democracy.
68474.m: By hakimiyya, Islamists mean the sole sovereignty of God.

68475.q: What does the term “jahiliyya” originally refer to in Islam?
68475.e: Sayyid Qutb applied the term to the present day. In doing so he also denied the legitimacy of states shaped by Islam.
68475.m: Qutb called societies he considered un-Islamic jahiliyya.

68476.q: What do researchers call Islamists who pursue their goals through elections and parties?
68476.e: Legalist Islamists use political institutions, for example the Ennahda party in Tunisia. Jihadists, by contrast, rely on violence.
68476.m: Legalist Islamists take part in elections.

68477.q: Which movement did the Palestinian Hamas grow out of in 1987?
68477.e: Hamas arose at the beginning of the First Intifada from the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood.
68477.m: Hamas is an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood.

68478.q: Which Tunisian party under Rached Ghannouchi was long regarded as an example of moderate political Islam?
68478.e: Ennahda won the first free elections after the Arab Spring in 2011. In 2016 it declared that it wanted to separate religious mission from politics.
68478.m: After 2011, Ennahda stood in elections as a party in Tunisia.

68479.q: What did the American theologian Amina Wadud do in New York in 2005 that caused a worldwide stir?
a: She led a Friday prayer for women and men
She opened the first mosque in the USA
She translated the Quran into English
68479.e: Amina Wadud reread the Quran from women’s point of view, for example in her book “Qur'an and Woman” of 1992. A woman leading men in prayer is highly controversial among Muslims.

68480.q: What did the Moroccan sociologist Fatima Mernissi critically examine?
a: Hadiths hostile to women and how they were handed down
The grammar of the Berber languages
68480.e: In “The Veil and the Male Elite”, Fatima Mernissi examined how hadiths hostile to women had been handed down. She showed that women played an active role in the early days of Islam.
68480.m: Fatima Mernissi studied the position of women in early Islam.

68481.q: What does the Musawah movement, founded in 2009, campaign for?
a: Equal rights in Muslim family law
68481.e: Musawah means “equality” in Arabic. The movement campaigns for fair family laws based on Islamic sources.
68481.m: Musawah fights for equality in Muslim family law.

68482.q: What is typical of groups such as “Sisters in Islam”?
a: They base women’s rights on Islamic sources
They call for more rights for men
68482.e: Sisters in Islam was founded in Malaysia at the end of the 1980s. The group campaigns for women’s rights within an Islamic framework.
68482.m: Sisters in Islam is a Malaysian women’s rights organisation.

68483.q: What did the Egyptian women’s rights campaigner Huda Sha'arawi do publicly at Cairo railway station in 1923?
a: She became the first woman minister
She was the first woman to drive a car
She called for a boycott of British goods
68483.e: Huda Sha'arawi founded the Egyptian Feminist Union in 1923. Her removing the veil became a symbol of the women’s movement.
68483.m: Huda Sha'arawi was a pioneer of the women’s movement in Egypt.

68484.q: What did the Egyptian author Qasim Amin call for in 1899 in his book “The Liberation of Women”?
68484.e: Qasim Amin called for better education for women and criticised veiling. The book sparked heated debates in the Arab world.
68484.m: As early as 1899, Qasim Amin called for the liberation of women.

68485.q: Which method do Islamic feminists mainly use?
a: A gender-just reinterpretation of the Quran
Rejecting any interpretation of the Quran
68485.e: Islamic feminists argue from within Islam. They distinguish between the Quran and the patriarchal interpretations of later scholars.
68485.m: Islamic feminism reinterprets the Quran in a gender-just way.

68486.q: What is special about the liberal Ibn Rushd-Goethe Mosque in Berlin?
a: Women and men pray together, and women may lead prayers
It is open only to men
Sermons are given only in Arabic
It is on the roof of a church
68486.e: Seyran Ateş founded the mosque in 2017. The names Ibn Rushd and Goethe stand for reason and dialogue between cultures.
68486.m: The liberal mosque in Berlin bears the names of Ibn Rushd and Goethe.

68487.q: Which 13th-century saint is particularly important for the Alevis?
68487.e: Hacı Bektaş Veli is regarded as the man after whom the Bektashi order is named. His tomb in the central Anatolian town of Hacıbektaş is an important Alevi place of pilgrimage.
68487.m: Hacı Bektaş Veli is a central figure for the Alevis.

68488.q: In which city did many Alevi artists and intellectuals die in an arson attack on a hotel in 1993?
68488.e: On 2 July 1993 an angry mob set fire to the Madımak Hotel in Sivas, where an Alevi cultural festival was taking place. At least 35 people died.
68488.m: For Alevis, the Sivas attack of 1993 is a day of mourning.

68489.q: Which string instrument accompanies the Alevi religious service?
68489.e: Among the Alevis the saz is regarded as a sacred instrument. Folk poets such as Pir Sultan Abdal handed down their teachings in songs played on the saz.
68489.m: The saz is played in the Alevi religious service.

68490.q: What is the Alevi system of teaching called that describes the path to perfection?
a: Seven stages and three wise men
68490.e: The four gates are called sharia, tariqa, marifa and haqiqa. At each level there are ten stages, so forty in total.
68490.m: Alevis strive for perfection through four gates and forty stages.

68491.q: Which person do the Alevis particularly revere?
68491.e: Alevis revere Ali and the twelve imams from his family. In this they are close to the Shia.
68491.m: For the Alevis, Ali is particularly important.

68492.q: What were followers of Alevi beliefs often called in the Ottoman Empire?
68492.e: Kızılbaş means “red head” and referred to the red headgear of the Safavids’ followers. The term was later also used in a derogatory way.
68492.m: In the Ottoman Empire, the ancestors of many Alevis were called Kızılbaş.

68493.q: Which Turkish authority has so far not recognised the Alevi cemevis as places of worship?
68493.e: The Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) is Sunni in character and funds mosques but not cemevis. The European Court of Human Rights criticised this in 2014.
68493.m: Many Alevis call on the Diyanet to recognise their cemevis.

68494.q: What are the spiritual leaders of Alevi communities called?
68494.e: Dedes lead the cem service and advise the community. Traditionally they come from families that trace their descent back to the Prophet.
68494.m: A dede leads the Alevi community.

68495.q: What is the ritual round dance called that women and men dance together in the Alevi religious service?
68495.e: The semah is one of the twelve services of the cem and is danced to saz music. It is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
68495.m: The semah is the sacred round dance of the Alevis.

68496.q: What does a federal popular initiative like the minaret initiative of 2009 need in order to be accepted?
a: A majority of the people and of the cantons
Only a majority of the people
The approval of the Federal Council
68496.e: The minaret initiative received 57.5 per cent yes and 19½ to 3½ cantons. It thus became part of the Federal Constitution.
68496.m: To change the constitution, a popular initiative needs a majority of the people and of the cantons.

68497.q: In which part of the country did several cantons reject the minaret initiative in 2009?
68497.e: Geneva, Vaud and Neuchâtel as well as the half-canton of Basel-Stadt rejected it. All other cantons voted in favour.
68497.m: French-speaking Switzerland mostly rejected the minaret ban.

68498.q: In which year did Swiss voters accept the minaret initiative?
68498.e: The initiative was launched in 2007 and accepted on 29 November 2009 with 57.5 per cent voting yes. Since then no new minarets may be built.
68498.m: The minaret initiative was accepted in 2009.

68499.q: How many valid signatures does a federal popular initiative like the minaret initiative need?
68499.e: The signatures must be collected within 18 months. In 2008 the minaret initiative handed in about 113,500 valid signatures.
68499.m: A popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures.

68500.q: What was surprising about the vote on the minaret initiative in 2009?
a: Polls predicted a no, but it was accepted
The result was an exact tie
The vote had to be repeated
68500.e: The SRG poll by gfs.bern in October showed 53 per cent against. On voting day, however, 57.5 per cent said yes.
68500.m: Polls before votes are snapshots, not reliable forecasts.

68501.q: What did the Federal Council and Parliament recommend to voters on the minaret initiative?
68501.e: The National Council recommended rejecting the initiative by 132 votes to 51, the Council of States by 39 to 3. The people accepted it nevertheless.
68501.m: Parliament can recommend rejecting a popular initiative, but the people have the last word.

68502.q: Which fundamental right does the minaret ban mainly violate, in the view of the Federal Council and legal scholars?
68502.e: The European Convention on Human Rights protects freedom of religion in Article 9 and forbids discrimination in Article 14. A building ban only for minarets specifically targets one religion.
68502.m: The minaret ban conflicts with freedom of religion.

68503.q: How did the European Court of Human Rights deal with the complaints against the Swiss minaret ban in 2011?
a: It did not admit them, as nobody was directly affected
It found a violation of freedom of religion
It ordered Switzerland to pay compensation
It referred the cases to the UN
68503.e: The applicants had no specific minaret project and were therefore not considered victims within the meaning of the Convention. So the Court did not decide on the content of the ban.
68503.m: At the European Court of Human Rights you must be personally and specifically affected by a measure.

68504.q: Which international organisation criticised the Swiss minaret ban as discrimination?
68504.e: The UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion, Asma Jahangir, and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights criticised the result.
68504.m: The minaret ban was strongly criticised internationally.

68505.q: What was the result of the vote on the initiative “Yes to a ban on face coverings” on 7 March 2021?
68505.e: 51.2 per cent voted yes, and a majority of the cantons was also reached. Turnout was 51.4 per cent.
68505.m: The ban on face coverings was only narrowly accepted in 2021.

68506.q: Where was the ban on face coverings first laid down after the vote of 2021?
68506.e: Because it was a popular initiative, the ban went into the Federal Constitution as Article 10a. A federal law has put it into practice since 2025.
68506.m: The ban on face coverings is in the Federal Constitution.

68507.q: Since when has the national law banning face coverings applied?
68507.e: Parliament passed the federal law in September 2023. It came into force on 1 January 2025.
68507.m: The national ban on face coverings has applied since 2025.

68508.q: What is the maximum fine for breaking the national ban on face coverings?
68508.e: The federal law on the ban on covering the face provides for a fine of up to 1,000 francs. It puts Article 10a of the Federal Constitution into practice.
68508.m: Anyone who ignores the ban on face coverings risks a fine of up to 1,000 francs.

68509.q: Which canton was the first to introduce a ban on face coverings, in 2016?
68509.e: Ticino voters accepted a corresponding constitutional amendment in 2013. The law putting it into practice came into force on 1 July 2016.
68509.m: Ticino had a ban on face coverings even before the Confederation.

68510.q: In which canton did voters confirm a cantonal ban on face coverings in 2018?
68510.e: The cantonal parliament had passed the ban in 2017, and voters approved it on 23 September 2018. This made it the second canton after Ticino.
68510.m: St Gallen was the second canton with a ban on face coverings.

68511.q: According to Article 10a of the Federal Constitution, in which places is covering the face explicitly not banned?
68511.e: The ban applies in public spaces and places open to the public, but places of worship such as mosques are exempt. Other exceptions concern health and safety, for example.
68511.m: The ban on face coverings does not apply in places of worship.

68512.q: Which exception to the ban on face coverings allows masks at Carnival (Fasnacht), for example?
68512.e: Article 10a of the Federal Constitution names health, safety, climatic conditions and local customs as exceptions. Carnival masks fall under local customs.
68512.m: Carnival masks remain allowed despite the ban on face coverings.

68513.q: Which country was the first in Europe to introduce a nationwide ban on face coverings, in 2011?
68513.e: The French law came into force in April 2011, and Belgium followed in the same year. Austria and Denmark followed suit in 2017 and 2018.
68513.m: In 2011 France was the first country in Europe with a nationwide ban on face coverings.

68514.q: What aim did the ECtHR accept in 2014 in the case S.A.S. v. France to justify the ban on face coverings?
a: Protecting the conditions of living together
68514.e: The Court accepted the aim of “vivre ensemble”, meaning the conditions of living together. It did not consider security arguments alone sufficient for a general ban.
68514.m: The ECtHR upheld the French ban on face coverings on the grounds of living together.

68515.q: What role does the FIDS play among Muslim organisations in Switzerland?
a: It is the largest Muslim umbrella organisation
It is a state supervisory authority
It is the college for imams
It is the representation of Turkey
68515.e: The FIDS brings together cantonal umbrella organisations and those based on origin. Through them it represents around 240 centres and associations.
68515.m: The FIDS is the largest Muslim umbrella organisation in Switzerland.

68516.q: What task does a Muslim umbrella organisation such as the FIDS take on?
a: It represents mosque associations towards the authorities and the public
It collects taxes from all Muslims
It employs imams as federal civil servants
68516.e: The FIDS is a point of contact for politicians, the media and other religious communities. Many, but not all, mosque associations belong to it through a cantonal or origin-based association.
68516.m: Not all mosque associations are organised in an umbrella organisation.

a: As an umbrella of cantonal and origin-based associations
As a federal office in the Department of Home Affairs
As a regional church under public law
As a foundation of the University of Fribourg
68517.e: The FIDS is a private association of umbrella organisations. Its members include cantonal associations as well as Albanian, Bosnian and Turkish associations.
68517.m: The FIDS is an umbrella organisation of umbrella organisations.

68518.q: Who decides in Switzerland whether a Muslim community is officially recognised under public law?
68518.e: The relationship between the state and religious communities is a matter for the cantons. Recognition is a long political process.
68518.m: The cantons decide on the recognition of religious communities.

68519.q: Why are umbrella organisations such as the FIDS useful for the authorities?
a: They are a point of contact for many associations at once
They replace the police in mosques
They decide the laws of the cantons
They pay the wages of all imams
68519.e: Instead of negotiating with hundreds of individual associations, the authorities can talk to one organisation. The FIDS is represented by an elected presidency.
68519.m: The FIDS has an elected president who represents it in public.

68520.q: Roughly what share of the Swiss population is Muslim (as of the 2020s)?
68520.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, about 6 per cent of the population aged 15 and over describe themselves as Muslim. After Christians and people without religion, they are the third largest group.
68520.m: About 6 per cent of people in Switzerland are Muslim.

68521.q: According to ETH researchers, why do Muslims in Switzerland find it hard to speak with one voice?
a: Because they are divided into ethnically based associations
Because they are not allowed to found their own associations
Because the Confederation banned their associations
Because almost all of them live in one canton
68521.e: In 2017 the researchers Fabien Merz and Darius Farman pointed to the fragmentation by origin and language. Umbrella organisations such as the FIDS try to bring this diversity together.
68521.m: The Muslim community in Switzerland is organised in very diverse ways.

68522.q: What is the Swiss Centre for Islam and Society (SZIG)?
a: A research and further education centre of the University of Fribourg
68522.e: The SZIG was founded in 2015 at the University of Fribourg. It researches Islam in Switzerland and offers further education, but it does not train imams.
68522.m: The SZIG researches the relationship between Islam and society in Switzerland.

68523.q: What status does the SZIG have at the University of Fribourg?
68523.e: The SZIG is an interfaculty institute of the Faculties of Theology, Law and Humanities. In this way it links theology, law and the social sciences.
68523.m: Three faculties of the University of Fribourg work together at the SZIG.

68524.q: Which three fields work together at the SZIG at the University of Fribourg?
68524.e: The SZIG is an institute of the Faculties of Theology, Law and Humanities. It is led by the theologian Hansjörg Schmid.
68524.m: Theology, law and social sciences work together at the SZIG.

68525.q: Which federal body funded the SZIG from its start until the end of 2024?
a: The State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation
68525.e: A working group at SERI prepared the centre from 2012 to 2014. Since 2025 it has been funded by the University of Fribourg and with project money.
68525.m: SERI funded the SZIG in its first ten years.

68526.q: Which task is explicitly not part of the SZIG’s mission?
68526.e: The centre does research, trains young academics and offers further education. Training imams is explicitly excluded because it is a matter for the religious communities.
68526.m: The SZIG does not train imams.

68527.q: Which party launched a popular initiative against the SZIG in the canton of Fribourg?
68527.e: The initiative was titled “Against the opening of a Centre for Islam and Society at the University of Fribourg”. In 2015 it gathered 8,734 valid signatures.
68527.m: The Centre for Islam and Society was politically controversial.

68528.q: How did the Grand Council of the canton of Fribourg decide on the initiative against the SZIG in 2016?
a: It accepted it without a popular vote
It sent it to the Federal Council
It postponed it by ten years
68528.e: The Council of State relied on two legal opinions and proposed declaring it invalid. The Grand Council followed it in March 2016.
68528.m: A cantonal parliament can declare unconstitutional initiatives invalid.

68529.q: Why did the Federal Supreme Court confirm that the Fribourg initiative against the SZIG was invalid?
a: It was aimed one-sidedly at a single religion
It breached the unity of form
68529.e: Four out of five judges saw discrimination on religious grounds, because the title and text targeted only Islam. This contradicts the Federal Constitution.
68529.m: Cantonal initiatives must not discriminate against any religion.

68530.q: What question does the SZIG’s doctoral programme “Islamic theological studies” explore?
a: How Islam can be understood and lived in Switzerland
How to learn Arabic as fast as possible
68530.e: From 2015 the programme was supported by the Mercator Foundation Switzerland, among other things with doctoral grants. It links Islamic theology with the Swiss context.
68530.m: The SZIG doctoral programme was made possible by a private foundation.

68531.q: What conclusion did the Federal Council reach in 2021 in its report on professionalising religious carers?
a: Imam training set up by the state is not appropriate
The Confederation should found its own imam college
Imams should only come from Saudi Arabia
Mosques should be run by the cantons
68531.e: Instead, further education should be promoted for carers who grew up in Switzerland. This includes religious teachers, chaplains and youth leaders.
68531.m: The Federal Council relies on further education rather than state imam training.

68532.q: With which instrument did the National Council instruct the Federal Council in 2017 to examine the role of imams and report on it?
68532.e: A postulate obliges the Federal Council to examine a question and report on it. This postulate concerned moderate imams as key figures against radicalisation.
68532.m: A postulate instructs the Federal Council to examine a question and report on it.

68534.q: According to the ZHAW study commissioned by the Confederation, what has a major influence on the radicalisation of young Muslims?
a: Real contacts, above all with people their own age
68534.e: According to the study, imams and mosques play a minor role and the internet tends to have a supporting effect. Personal contacts are decisive, especially among peers.
68534.m: Radicalisation often happens through personal contacts among peers.

68535.q: Is there a uniform, standardised training for imams in Switzerland?
a: Yes, at every cantonal grammar school
68535.e: A 2019 SZIG study showed that the roughly 130 regularly active imams have very different educational backgrounds. There is no standardised imam training in Switzerland.
68535.m: There is no uniform imam training in Switzerland.

68536.q: According to the 2019 SZIG study, where are the most common places of training for imams in Switzerland?
a: The Balkans, Turkey, Egypt and Saudi Arabia
68536.e: The choice of place of study depends on grants, Arabic courses and theological orientation. Meanwhile, the first imams who grew up in Switzerland are also working.
68536.m: Most imams in Switzerland were trained abroad.

68537.q: Why do many people call for more imams to be trained in Switzerland?
a: So that they know Swiss language and society well
So that they ask for lower wages
68537.e: Most imams come from abroad, and only a few receive a permit each year. Training in Switzerland should produce imams who speak the national language and know Swiss society.
68537.m: Imams trained in Switzerland know the language and society better.

68538.q: What ability does the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act require of religious carers from non-EU countries?
a: Communicating in the national language of their place of work
68538.e: Under Article 26a of the Act, they must be familiar with the social and legal values and be able to communicate in the local national language. In this way they should build bridges to society.
68538.m: Imams from non-EU countries must speak a national language.

68539.q: What do imams mainly learn in the Zurich further education course “Zurich competence”?
a: How the state, law and society work in Switzerland
68539.e: The canton of Zurich, the SZIG and VIOZ have run the short course together since 2022. It teaches about living together, the legal order and the religious landscape in Switzerland.
68539.m: “Zurich competence” is a short further education course for imams and Muslim carers.

68540.q: Where are Islamic theologians trained in Germany?
68540.e: In Germany there are chairs of Islamic theology at several state universities. In France, by contrast, imam training is in the hands of private providers.
68540.m: Germany trains Islamic theologians at several universities.

68541.q: In which language does the Islamkolleg Deutschland, founded in 2019, train imams?
68541.e: The Islamkolleg Deutschland in Osnabrück offers practical imam training in German. Imams are to be trained in the country instead of coming from abroad.
68541.m: With the Islamkolleg, Germany has its own imam training in German.

68542.q: What is the task of Muslim chaplaincy in Zurich hospitals?
a: It supports patients and relatives in difficult situations
68542.e: Chaplains listen, offer comfort and help with religious questions. In the canton of Zurich an association organises this service with support from the canton and the churches.
68542.m: The canton of Zurich has an organised Muslim chaplaincy.

68543.q: Which gap did the organised Muslim chaplaincy, which has existed in the canton of Zurich since 2017, fill?
a: Muslim patients previously had hardly any chaplaincy of their own in hospital
Muslims were not allowed to visit hospitals before
There were no mosques in the canton before
Hospitals had no chaplaincy at all before
68543.e: Christian chaplaincy has existed in hospitals for a long time. For Muslims, a comparable service was missing for a long time.
68543.m: Muslim chaplaincy in Zurich has been organised since 2017.

68544.q: Who jointly runs the Zurich association for Muslim chaplaincy?
68544.e: It is run by the Zurich Directorate of Justice and Home Affairs and the Association of Islamic Organisations in Zurich. The regional churches also support the service.
68544.m: The canton and Muslim organisations jointly run the Zurich chaplaincy.

68545.q: In 2018, what did extending Muslim chaplaincy from the federal asylum centre in Zurich to other centres depend on?
a: On a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court
68545.e: The pilot project in Zurich was rated positively by asylum seekers, staff and Christian chaplains. For an extension, however, the Confederation required clarified funding and better training for the chaplains.
68545.m: Muslim chaplaincy in asylum centres was first tested in Zurich.

68546.q: What was new in 2022 in the training of Swiss Army chaplains?
a: For the first time Jewish and Muslim chaplains were trained too
For the first time women were admitted
Only pastors were allowed to take part
68546.e: Until then army chaplains came from the Christian regional churches. Since 2022 Jewish and Muslim chaplains have also been included.
68546.m: Army chaplaincy is now open to members of all religions.

68547.q: How can Muslims reach the Muslim chaplaincy in Zurich outside hospital too?
68547.e: Since 2020 there has been a telephone and online chaplaincy. Volunteers are available there around the clock.
68547.m: Muslim chaplaincy is also available by phone.

68548.q: In which three Zurich institutions was a permanent Muslim chaplaincy service tested in 2023 and 2024?
a: University Hospital, Winterthur Cantonal Hospital and Psychiatric University Hospital
Airport, main station and city hospital
Cantonal grammar school, university and ETH
Pöschwies prison, police and fire brigade
68548.e: A team of six chaplains worked there. The SZIG evaluated the project, after which the service was continued.
68548.m: Large Zurich hospitals have permanent Muslim chaplaincy.

68549.q: Who should fund Muslim chaplaincy in Zurich in the long term?
68549.e: So far the canton and the Reformed and Catholic churches have contributed. In the long term the Muslim community should support the service itself.
68549.m: The canton and the churches support Muslim chaplaincy in Zurich.

68550.q: According to the Federal Council, what may public institutions require of Muslim chaplains?
a: Training and further education as well as a security check
68550.e: The Federal Council recommends giving religious communities organised under private law access to paid chaplaincy. In return, quality requirements can be set.
68550.m: Chaplaincy in hospitals and prisons requires training and trust.

68551.q: What is special about the chaplaincy training programme the University of Bern has offered since 2021?
a: Chaplains of different religions learn together
68551.e: The Institute of Practical Theology trains chaplains of different religions together. According to SRF, the programme is unique in Europe.
68551.m: The University of Bern trains chaplains of different religions together.

68552.q: What was the case Osmanoğlu and Kocabaş v. Switzerland, decided by the ECtHR in 2017, about?
a: Muslim girls and mixed swimming lessons
68552.e: Parents had not sent their daughters to compulsory mixed swimming lessons. The Court found no violation of human rights.
68552.m: In January 2017 the ECtHR ruled on swimming lessons in Switzerland.

68553.q: Which canton did the case on mixed swimming lessons decided by the ECtHR in 2017 come from?
68553.e: In 2008 the parents had not sent their daughters to compulsory mixed swimming lessons. The school authority then fined them.
68553.m: The swimming lessons case started at a school in Basel.

68554.q: What consequence did it have for the Basel parents that their daughters did not take part in swimming lessons?
a: The school closed its indoor pool
68554.e: The school authority fined the parents a total of 1,400 francs. The ECtHR did not consider this fine disproportionate.
68554.m: Anyone who keeps children away from compulsory lessons can be fined.

68555.q: Which right under the ECHR did the parents invoke in the swimming lessons case?
a: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
68555.e: The parents relied on Article 9 of the ECHR. The Court recognised an interference but considered it justified.
68555.m: Article 9 of the ECHR protects freedom of religion.

68556.q: What was the ECtHR’s ruling in the 2017 swimming lessons case?
a: Unanimously no violation of the Convention
A narrow finding of a violation of the Convention
Unanimously a violation of the Convention
No ruling, the case was withdrawn
68556.e: All the judges concluded that Switzerland had not violated freedom of religion. They stressed the states’ margin of appreciation.
68556.m: The ECtHR unanimously ruled in favour of Switzerland in the swimming lessons case.

68557.q: What was the ECtHR’s main argument for giving swimming lessons priority?
a: They promote integration and prevent exclusion
They are needed to pass the Matura
They are compulsory throughout the EU
68557.e: Swimming together with the class is important for social integration, even if children learn to swim privately. The interest in a complete school education outweighed the wish for an exemption.
68557.m: School also has the task of including children in the community.

68558.q: What concession did the school offer the Muslim girls in swimming lessons?
a: A burkini and separate changing rooms
An exemption until the age of 18
Lessons only with female teachers in full-body suits
68558.e: The girls were allowed to swim in a burkini and to change and shower separately. For the ECtHR this lessened the interference with freedom of religion.
68558.m: With a burkini, Muslim girls can take part in swimming lessons.

68559.q: Which court confirmed the fine in the Basel swimming lessons case in 2012, before the ECtHR ruled?
68559.e: The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 7 March 2012. The family then turned to the Court in Strasbourg.
68559.m: Before going to Strasbourg, you must use up all legal remedies in your own country.

68560.q: How had the Federal Supreme Court ruled in an earlier swimming lessons case in 1993?
a: It granted a Muslim girl an exemption
It banned swimming lessons for everyone
68560.e: In 1993 it placed freedom of religion above compulsory schooling in swimming. From 2008 it gave more weight to integration and changed its practice.
68560.m: Courts can change their case law over time.

68561.q: According to the FSO, how large was the share of Muslim communities in the Swiss population in 2023?
68561.e: According to the FSO, in 2023 about 6 per cent of the population belonged to Muslim communities or communities that emerged from Islam. In 2000 the figure was considerably lower.
68561.m: About 6 in 100 people in Switzerland belong to a Muslim community.

68562.q: According to the FSO, how large was the share of Muslims in the Swiss population in 1970?
68562.e: In 1970 only about 16,000 Muslims lived in Switzerland. Only with immigration from the 1970s did their number rise sharply.
68562.m: In 1970 there were very few Muslims in Switzerland.

68563.q: Roughly what share of the Swiss population were Muslims according to the 2000 census?
68563.e: In 2000 more than 300,000 Muslims were counted. Since then their share has continued to rise.
68563.m: The share of Muslims has risen considerably since 2000.

68564.q: According to a 2025 statement by the canton of Zurich, roughly how many Muslims live in the canton of Zurich?
68564.e: As the most populous canton, Zurich also has the most Muslims. That is why hospital chaplaincy, for example, is particularly in demand there.
68564.m: About 100,000 Muslims live in the canton of Zurich.

68565.q: In 2023, what rank did Muslim communities hold among the religious communities of Switzerland?
a: First, ahead of all Christian churches
68565.e: In 2023 about 31 per cent were Catholic and 19 per cent Protestant. The Muslim communities follow with about 6 per cent.
68565.m: After the two main churches, Muslims are the largest religious community.

68566.q: According to the 2024 FSO survey, how common is belief in one single God among Muslims in Switzerland compared with Catholics?
68566.e: About 91 per cent of Muslims believe in one single God, compared with 51 per cent of Catholics and 40 per cent of Protestants.
68566.m: Almost all Muslims in Switzerland believe in one God.

68567.q: According to the 2024 FSO survey, how often do Muslims in Switzerland pray?
a: Very differently: just over a third daily, about 30 per cent never
Almost all five times a day
68567.e: The survey on language, religion and culture asked about the previous twelve months. Religious practice is very varied.
68567.m: The religious practice of Muslims in Switzerland varies greatly.

68568.q: According to the 2024 FSO survey, what share of Muslims in Switzerland attended a religious service or event at least once a week?
68568.e: About a fifth attend every week, while about 46 per cent never attend a service. So religious practice varies greatly.
68568.m: Only a minority of Muslims go to the mosque every week.

68569.q: Which Muslim community opened the Mahmud Mosque in Zurich in 1963, regarded as the first mosque in Switzerland?
68569.e: The Ahmadiyya is small in Switzerland, with a few hundred members. Its Mahmud Mosque in Zurich has a small minaret.
68569.m: The Ahmadiyya is a small Muslim community in Switzerland.

68570.q: Which nationality does the largest group of Muslims in Switzerland have today?
68570.e: About 37 per cent of Muslims in Switzerland held a Swiss passport in 2019 to 2023. Many received it through naturalisation.
68570.m: More than a third of Muslims in Switzerland are Swiss citizens.

68571.q: How did many Muslims in Switzerland obtain a Swiss passport?
a: Simply by being born in Switzerland
By buying a piece of land
68571.e: In Switzerland, being born in the country does not on its own make anyone Swiss. In 2000 only 11 per cent of Muslims had a Swiss passport; today it is considerably more.
68571.m: The share of naturalised Muslims has risen sharply since 2000.

68572.q: Apart from Turkey, which region do many Muslims in Switzerland come from?
68572.e: Many come from Kosovo, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina or Albania. In 2019 to 2023 about 31 per cent held the nationality of a Balkan state.
68572.m: Many Muslims in Switzerland come from the Balkans.

68573.q: Why did many Muslims from the former Yugoslavia come to Switzerland in the 1990s?
a: Because of the wars during the break-up of Yugoslavia
Because of a great drought in the Balkans
Because of an earthquake in Serbia
Because of the introduction of the euro
68573.e: Many fled the wars in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Kosovo, while others came through family reunification. In 2000, 58 per cent of Muslims in Switzerland came from the former Yugoslavia.
68573.m: In 2000 more than half of Muslims came from the former Yugoslavia.

68574.q: In 2000, which country was the most important country of origin of Muslims in Switzerland after the former Yugoslavia?
68574.e: In 2000, 21 per cent of Muslims came from Turkey. Many Turkish families have lived in Switzerland for several generations.
68574.m: In 2000 about a fifth of Muslims came from Turkey.

68575.q: What is true about the origins of Muslims in Switzerland?
a: They come from very many different countries
Almost all come from Saudi Arabia
All speak Arabic as their mother tongue
68575.e: According to the 2000 census, Muslims in Switzerland came from 105 countries. Besides the Balkans and Turkey, many come from North Africa, the Middle East and Asia.
68575.m: Switzerland’s Muslims come from very many countries.

68576.q: Which two groups does the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland name as the main share of Muslims from the former Yugoslavia?
68576.e: This means above all Albanians from Kosovo and Macedonia and Bosniaks from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They shape many mosque associations in German-speaking Switzerland.
68576.m: Many Muslims in Switzerland have Albanian or Bosnian roots.

68577.q: From which decade did the Swiss economy increasingly recruit workers from Turkey?
68577.e: During the economic boom Switzerland looked for workers abroad, including in Turkey. Later many families followed.
68577.m: Turkish immigration began with guest workers in the 1960s.

68578.q: What has been offered at state schools in Kreuzlingen since 2010?
a: A ban on praying in the playground
68578.e: The lessons started in 2010 as a pilot project. They are seen as a model for Islamic education in German-speaking Switzerland.
68578.m: Since 2010 Kreuzlingen has offered Islamic religious education at school.

68579.q: Which mosque communities jointly founded the association for Islamic education in Kreuzlingen?
a: The Albanian and the Turkish mosque
The Bosnian and the Arab mosque
The Iranian and the Pakistani mosque
The Somali and the Eritrean mosque
68579.e: The two mosques together form the sponsoring association VIUK. In this way children of different origins learn together.
68579.m: In Kreuzlingen’s Islamic lessons, children of different origins learn together.

68580.q: In which language is Islamic religious education taught in Kreuzlingen?
68580.e: The lessons are deliberately in German so that all children can take part. Many children also attend mosque classes in their language of origin.
68580.m: Islamic lessons at school are taught in German.

68581.q: Which school years is Islamic religious education in Kreuzlingen intended for?
68581.e: The lessons are aimed at the middle level of primary school. They take place for one lesson a week.
68581.m: Kreuzlingen offers Islamic lessons at middle primary level.

68582.q: Where did the curriculum originally used for Islamic lessons in Kreuzlingen come from?
a: From the curriculum of Cairo University
68582.e: The subject curriculum had been approved in Bavaria in 2004 and 2006. Teaching materials include the book “Saphir 5/6”.
68582.m: Islamic lessons in Kreuzlingen are based on German models.

68583.q: Who pays for Islamic religious education in Kreuzlingen after the pilot phase?
a: The parents and the mosque communities
68583.e: There is no mosque tax. In the pilot phase parents, mosques and sponsors each paid a third; afterwards parents and the two mosques shared the costs.
68583.m: Islamic lessons at school are often privately funded.

68584.q: What is the prayer leader of a mosque called, who in Kreuzlingen also teaches religious education?
68584.e: The imam leads prayers and often also teaches. The muezzin calls people to prayer, and a mufti issues legal opinions.
68584.m: As imam, Rehan Neziri shapes Islamic education in Kreuzlingen.

68585.q: Who drew up the Thurgau curriculum for Islamic religious education that SRF reported on in 2024?
a: The Interreligious Working Group in the canton of Thurgau
68585.e: The religious education office of the Catholic Church of Thurgau also took part in the project. The Confederation funded it through fedpol as part of the National Action Plan against radicalisation and extremism.
68585.m: In Thurgau the Islamic curriculum was created on an interreligious basis.

68586.q: How widespread was Islamic religious education at state schools in Thurgau in 2024?
68586.e: The aim is to offer lessons at all schools with more than 20 per cent Muslim children. In 2024 only a handful of places in Thurgau offered such lessons.
68586.m: Islamic religious education at schools is still rare in Switzerland.

68587.q: What is the name of the FSO survey that regularly measures attitudes such as hostility towards Muslims in Switzerland?
68587.e: According to this survey, 14 per cent were hostile towards Muslims in 2016. Towards Jews the figure was 8 per cent.
68587.m: Hostility towards Muslims is measurably widespread in Switzerland.

68588.q: According to the 2016 FSO survey, what was more widespread in Switzerland?
a: Distrust of Islam as a religion
68588.e: 33 per cent distrusted Islam as a religion, while 14 per cent were hostile towards Muslims. The survey distinguishes between the two.
68588.m: Studies measure hostility towards Islam and hostility towards Muslims separately.

68589.q: According to the FSO, how did negative prejudices about Muslims in Switzerland change between 2018 and 2020?
68589.e: In 2018, 14 per cent agreed with negative prejudices; in 2020 it was 20 per cent.

68590.q: How many respondents in the ETH study “Security 2017” considered Islam a threat to Switzerland’s security?
68590.e: 46 per cent saw Islam as a threat. The ETH Zurich study surveys attitudes to security every year.
68590.m: Many people link Islam with fears about security.

68591.q: According to the 2019 FSO survey, how many Muslim respondents experienced discrimination because of their religion within twelve months?
68591.e: About 35 per cent reported it, most often at work, at school or in training and in public spaces.
68591.m: About a third of Muslims experience discrimination in everyday life.

68592.q: Which federal commission published a dossier on anti-Muslim racism in 2023?
a: The Federal Commission for Women’s Issues
68592.e: In it, the FCR distinguishes between hostility towards Muslims as people and hostility towards the religion. Legitimate criticism of religion remains allowed.
68592.m: The FCR works against racism towards Muslims.

68593.q: Which provision of the Swiss Criminal Code can be applied to public incitement against Muslims?
68593.e: The anti-racism provision (Article 261bis of the Criminal Code) has applied since 1995. It also prohibits incitement because of religion, for example in comments on social media.
68593.m: Racist incitement against Muslims can be a criminal offence.

68594.q: According to a large EU study from 2024, how many Muslims in the EU experienced racial discrimination?
68594.e: According to the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA), it was 47 per cent. In the 2016 survey it had been 39 per cent.
68594.m: Almost one in two Muslims in the EU experiences discrimination.

68595.q: In 2024 the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights studied discrimination against Muslims in Europe. Why is Switzerland missing from this study?
a: It is not a member of the EU
It rejected the study in a popular vote
68595.e: The study covered only EU states. Muslims reported the most discrimination in Austria, Germany and Finland.
68595.m: Hostility towards Muslims is a Europe-wide problem.

a: The first written collection of the oral Torah
68596.e: The Mishnah records in writing the teachings on religious law that had been passed down orally. It forms the basis of the Talmud.
68596.m: The Mishnah is the written version of the oral Torah.

68597.q: Around what time was the Mishnah completed?
68597.e: After the destruction of the Temple in AD 70, the oral teachings were collected. Around AD 200 the Mishnah received its final form.
68597.m: The Mishnah was completed around AD 200.

68598.q: Which great work of Judaism builds on the Mishnah and comments on it?
68598.e: The Talmud consists of the Mishnah and its interpretation, the Gemara. After the Bible it is the most important work of Judaism.
68598.m: The Talmud builds on the Mishnah.

68599.q: Which tractate of the Mishnah contains ethical sayings and is called “Sayings of the Fathers”?
68599.e: Pirkei Avot collects the rabbis' wisdom for life, for example Hillel's “If I am not for myself, who will be for me?”. The tractate is traditionally read on summer Sabbaths.
68599.m: In Hebrew the “Sayings of the Fathers” are called Pirkei Avot.

68600.q: In which language is the Mishnah written?
68600.e: The Mishnah is written in a later form of Hebrew, known as Mishnaic Hebrew. The Gemara of the Talmud, by contrast, is mostly in Aramaic.
68600.m: The Mishnah is written in Hebrew.

68601.q: Which older text does the Gemara explain and discuss?
68601.e: The Gemara was written from about AD 200 to 500 in Palestine and Babylonia. In it scholars discussed the laws of the Mishnah.

68602.q: Which two parts together make up the Talmud?
68602.e: The Mishnah contains the laws passed down orally. The Gemara adds discussions and explanations.
68602.m: The Talmud consists of the Mishnah and the Gemara.

68603.q: In which period was the Babylonian Talmud essentially completed?
68603.e: The Gemara of the Babylonian academies grew over centuries. Its final editing dates to about the 6th century.
68603.m: The Babylonian Talmud was completed around the 6th century.

68605.q: In which city was Maimonides born in the 12th century?
68605.e: Moses ben Maimon was born in 1135 or 1138 in Córdoba in Muslim Spain. Because of persecution by the Almohads, the family later fled to Morocco and Egypt.
68605.m: Maimonides came from Córdoba in Spain.

68606.q: In which period did Maimonides live?
68606.e: Maimonides lived from about 1138 to 1204. He is considered the most important Jewish scholar of the Middle Ages.

68607.q: In which language did Maimonides write the “Guide for the Perplexed”?
68607.e: His main philosophical work was written in Arabic, using Hebrew letters. Later it was translated into Hebrew and Latin.
68607.m: Maimonides wrote the “Guide for the Perplexed” in Arabic.

68608.q: How many principles of faith did Maimonides formulate?
68608.e: In his commentary on the Mishnah he set out 13 principles, such as the unity of God and belief in the Messiah. They were later added to the liturgy as the hymn “Yigdal”.
68608.m: Maimonides summed up the Jewish faith in 13 principles.

68609.q: Which profession did Maimonides practise in Egypt alongside his work as a scholar?
68609.e: Maimonides was personal physician at the court of the Ayyubids in Cairo at the time of Saladin. He also wrote medical treatises.
68609.m: Maimonides worked in Cairo as a court physician.

68610.q: By which Hebrew acronym is Maimonides known?
68610.e: Rambam stands for “Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon”. Ramban, on the other hand, is Nachmanides.
68610.m: Maimonides is known by the abbreviation Rambam.

68611.q: With the teaching of which Greek philosopher did Maimonides want to reconcile the Jewish faith?
68611.e: Maimonides knew Aristotle through Arab philosophers such as Avicenna and Averroes. He wanted to show that reason and revelation do not contradict each other.
68611.m: Maimonides combined Jewish faith with the philosophy of Aristotle.

68612.q: Which famous sultan ruled Egypt when Maimonides worked as a doctor in Cairo?
68612.e: Maimonides was personal physician at the court of the Ayyubids, Saladin's dynasty. Saladin is known from the Crusades.
68612.m: Maimonides worked in Cairo at the time of Saladin.

68613.q: What does the Hebrew word “Kabbalah” literally mean?
68613.e: Kabbalah comes from the verb “kibbel”, to receive. It means a received, handed-down teaching about the hidden side of God.

68614.e: The Kabbalah asks about the hidden side of God and of creation. It arose in the Middle Ages, mainly in southern France and Spain.

68615.q: What is the best-known book of the Kabbalah, written in Spain in the 13th century, called?
68615.e: The Zohar, the “Book of Splendour”, interprets the Torah mystically. It became the most important work of the Kabbalah.
68615.m: The main work of the Kabbalah is called the Zohar.

68616.q: Which event of 1492 brought many Jewish scholars, including Kabbalists, to the Ottoman Empire?
a: The expulsion of the Jews from Spain
68616.e: After the expulsion from Spain, many Jews settled in the Ottoman Empire. Safed in Galilee thus became a centre of the Kabbalah.
68616.m: The expulsion from Spain in 1492 brought the Kabbalah to the east.

68617.q: What does the Jewish expression “Tikkun Olam”, which comes from the Kabbalah, mean?
68617.e: In the Kabbalah of Isaac Luria, tikkun means the restoration of the world. Today the expression often stands for social commitment.
68617.m: Tikkun Olam means improving the world.

68618.q: What does the Hebrew book title “Zohar” mean?
68618.e: The title refers to a verse in the Book of Daniel in which the wise shine like the splendour of the sky. The Zohar is the main work of the Kabbalah.

68619.q: According to modern research, when and where was the Zohar written?
68619.e: Moses de León spread the Zohar in Castile from about 1280 and was probably also its main author. The text, however, presents itself as much older.
68619.m: The Zohar was written in Spain in the 13th century.

68620.q: Why do many devout Jews consider the Zohar to be ancient?
a: It presents itself as the teaching of a rabbi from the 2nd century
It was found in the caves of Qumran
It belongs to the Hebrew Bible canon
According to tradition it was written by Moses
68620.e: In the Zohar, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai from the 2nd century appears as a teacher with his pupils. That is why many devout Jews consider him the author.
68620.m: Traditionally a rabbi from the 2nd century is regarded as the author of the Zohar.

68621.q: What was the real name of the Baal Shem Tov?
68621.e: Israel ben Eliezer lived from about 1700 to 1760. His followers gave him the honorary name Baal Shem Tov.
68621.m: The Baal Shem Tov's real name was Israel ben Eliezer.

68622.q: What does the honorary name “Baal Shem Tov” mean?
68622.e: A “Baal Shem” was a miracle worker who healed using the name of God. The word “tov” means “good”.
68622.m: Baal Shem Tov means Master of the Good Name.

68623.q: In which present-day country did the Baal Shem Tov work?
68623.e: He last lived in Medzhybizh in Podolia, which is now part of Ukraine. From there Hasidism spread across Eastern Europe.
68623.m: The Baal Shem Tov worked in present-day Ukraine.

68624.q: In which century did the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidism, live?
68624.e: The Baal Shem Tov lived from about 1700 to 1760. His teachings were passed on by pupils such as Dov Ber of Mezeritch.
68624.m: The Baal Shem Tov lived in the 18th century.

68625.q: What is the spiritual leader of a Hasidic community called?
68625.e: The Rebbe or Tzaddik is seen as a mediator between God and the followers. Many Hasidic groups have dynasties of Rebbes.
68625.m: A Hasidic community follows its Rebbe.

a: Joy, prayer and closeness to God in everyday life
68626.e: Hasidism relies on enthusiasm, singing and prayer. Its opponents, the Mitnagdim, by contrast stressed learned study of the Talmud.

68627.q: What did Lithuanian scholars accuse the Hasidim of in the 18th century?
a: Neglecting Talmud study and revering their Rebbes too much
68627.e: Led by the Vilna Gaon, the opponents even pronounced bans against the Hasidim. Lithuania became a centre of this opposition.
68627.m: The opponents of the Hasidim stressed the study of the Talmud.

68628.q: Which Hasidic movement goes back to Schneur Zalman of Liadi and today runs centres all over the world?
68628.e: Schneur Zalman wrote the basic work “Tanya”. Today Chabad is known for its community centres around the world, including in Switzerland.
68628.m: Chabad-Lubavitch was founded by Schneur Zalman of Liadi.

68629.q: Which intellectual movement of the 18th century did Moses Mendelssohn belong to?
68629.e: Mendelssohn was an important philosopher of the Enlightenment and a friend of Lessing. He is regarded as the father of the Jewish Enlightenment (Haskalah).
68629.m: Moses Mendelssohn was a philosopher of the Enlightenment.

68630.q: For which of Lessing's stage characters is Moses Mendelssohn considered the model?
68630.e: Lessing and Mendelssohn were close friends. The wise and tolerant Nathan has features of Mendelssohn.
68630.m: Lessing's Nathan has features of Moses Mendelssohn.

68631.q: Which text did Mendelssohn translate into German and have printed in Hebrew letters?
68631.e: The translation appeared from 1780 with a Hebrew commentary. This is how many Jews learnt standard German.
68631.m: Mendelssohn translated the Torah into German.

68632.q: What did Moses Mendelssohn argue for in his work “Jerusalem” of 1783?
68632.e: The full title is “Jerusalem, or on Religious Power and Judaism”. In it Mendelssohn demanded that the state should not force anyone to believe.
68632.m: In “Jerusalem” Mendelssohn argued for freedom of religion.

68633.q: Which composer was a grandson of Moses Mendelssohn?
68633.e: Felix was the son of Abraham Mendelssohn, a son of Moses. The family had the children baptised as Christians.
68633.m: Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy was the grandson of Moses Mendelssohn.

68634.q: What does the Hebrew word “Haskalah” mean?
68634.e: Haskalah comes from “sekhel”, reason. The movement wanted to bring Jews closer to secular education and the language of the country.

68635.q: Which Berlin philosopher is considered the most important pioneer of the Jewish Enlightenment?
68635.e: Moses Mendelssohn translated the Torah into German and was a friend of Lessing. He is regarded as the father of the Haskalah.
68635.m: Moses Mendelssohn was the leading thinker of the Haskalah.

68636.q: What did the Haskalah want to bring closer to the Jews of Europe?
a: Secular education and the language of the country
The secret teaching of the Kabbalah
68636.e: Followers of the Haskalah founded modern schools and promoted science. At the same time they cultivated the Hebrew language.
68636.m: The Haskalah promoted education and openness to society.

68637.q: In which country did Reform Judaism arise at the beginning of the 19th century?
68637.e: The first Reform temples were set up in Seesen and Hamburg. They introduced sermons in German and choral singing.

68638.q: In which city was the “New Israelite Temple” opened in 1818?
68638.e: The Hamburg Temple published its own Reform prayer book. It became a model for Reform congregations.
68638.m: The Hamburg Temple of 1818 was an early centre of Reform.

68639.q: Which instrument did many Reform congregations introduce into the service in the 19th century?
68639.e: The organ was meant to make the service more solemn. Traditional Jews rejected it because no instrument should be played on the Sabbath.

68640.q: What is a basic idea of Reform Judaism, as opposed to Orthodox Judaism?
a: Religious commandments may be adapted to modern times
All commandments apply unchanged as they did 2,000 years ago
The Torah is no longer read as holy scripture
Services only take place in Israel
68640.e: Reform Judaism arose in Germany in the 19th century. It sees Judaism as a religion that develops further and adapts many customs to the present.
68640.m: Reform Judaism adapts religious commandments to modern times.

68641.q: In which country is Reform Judaism the largest Jewish movement today?
68641.e: Reform Judaism arose in Germany but grew strongly above all in the USA. There it is the largest Jewish movement today, whereas in Israel it is a small minority.
68641.m: Reform Judaism is strongest in the USA today.

68642.q: What has been possible in Reform Judaism since the 20th century, but not in Orthodox Judaism?
a: No service is held on the Sabbath
The Torah is no longer read aloud
68642.e: In Reform Judaism women and men have equal rights. The first female rabbi, Regina Jonas, was ordained in Germany in 1935.
68642.m: In Reform Judaism women can become rabbis.

68643.q: Which innovation did Reform congregations introduce into the service in the 19th century?
a: Prayers and sermons in the language of the country as well
68643.e: Reform congregations in Germany also prayed and preached in German and often introduced organ and choir. This was so that worshippers could understand the service better.
68643.m: Reform congregations introduced prayers in the language of the country.

68644.q: Between which two branches of Judaism does Conservative Judaism stand?
68644.e: Conservative Judaism holds on to tradition and religious law but allows careful adaptations. It arose in Germany in the 19th century.
68644.m: Conservative Judaism lies between Orthodoxy and Reform.

68645.q: In which country does Conservative Judaism have the most followers today?
68645.e: Conservative Judaism is widespread mainly in North America. In Israel it is known as the Masorti movement, but it is much smaller.
68645.m: Conservative Judaism is widespread mainly in the USA.

68646.q: Under which name is Conservative Judaism known outside North America, for example in Israel?
68646.e: Masorti means “traditional”. The movement holds on to halakhah but interprets it historically.
68646.m: In Israel Conservative Judaism is called Masorti.

68647.q: Which language remains at the centre of Conservative Jewish services, unlike in early Reform congregations?
68647.e: Early Reform congregations partly replaced Hebrew with the language of the country. Conservative Judaism holds on to Hebrew as the language of prayer.
68647.m: In Conservative Judaism prayers are mainly in Hebrew.

68648.q: What is Conservative Judaism's position on the Jewish dietary laws (kashrut)?
68648.e: Conservative Judaism sees halakhah, and therefore also the dietary laws, as binding. Individual rules can, however, be reinterpreted.
68648.m: For Conservative Judaism the dietary laws still apply.

68649.q: How does Conservative Judaism understand halakhah?
a: As binding, but able to develop over history
68649.e: Conservative Judaism regards religious law as binding. But it allows adaptations if they are well justified.
68649.m: For Conservative Judaism halakhah applies, but it can develop.

68650.q: Since when has Conservative Judaism also ordained women as rabbis?
a: Not at all up to now
68650.e: In 1985 Amy Eilberg was ordained as the first Conservative female rabbi at the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York. Reform Judaism had gone ahead in 1972.
68650.m: There have been female rabbis in Conservative Judaism since 1985.

68651.q: In which city was Theodor Herzl born in 1860?
68651.e: Herzl was born in Pest, which is now part of Budapest. Later the family moved to Vienna.
68651.m: Theodor Herzl was born in Pest, today's Budapest.

68652.q: Which trial, which Herzl experienced as a journalist in Paris, strengthened his idea of a Jewish state?
68652.e: The Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus was wrongly convicted of treason in 1894. Herzl witnessed open antisemitism and concluded that Jews needed their own state.
68652.m: The Dreyfus affair shaped Herzl's Zionism.

68653.q: Which novel by Herzl from 1902 has the motto “If you will it, it is no fairy tale”?
68653.e: In Altneuland (Old New Land) Herzl describes a modern Jewish society in Palestine. Its Hebrew title “Tel Aviv” later became the name of a city.
68653.m: Herzl's novel Altneuland has the motto “If you will it, it is no fairy tale”.

68654.q: Which sentence did Herzl write in his diary after the First Zionist Congress?
a: “At Basel I founded the Jewish State.”
68654.e: Herzl added that everyone would laugh at this, but in 50 years they would see it. A little over 50 years later, in 1948, Israel was founded.
68654.m: Herzl saw the Basel congress as the founding of the Jewish state.

68655.q: On which days did the First Zionist Congress take place in Basel?
68655.e: About 200 delegates from many countries met in Basel at the end of August 1897. They elected Herzl president of the new organisation.
68655.m: The First Zionist Congress met in Basel at the end of August 1897.

68656.q: Which organisation was founded at the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897?
