68656.e: At the congress in Basel's Stadtcasino, the Zionist Organisation was founded, later called the World Zionist Organization. Theodor Herzl became its first president.
68656.m: The World Zionist Organization was founded at the First Zionist Congress.

68657.q: In which city was the First Zionist Congress originally supposed to take place?
68657.e: The Jewish community and the association of rabbis in Germany opposed a congress in Munich. So it was moved to Basel instead.
68657.m: The Zionist Congress was moved from Munich to Basel.

68658.q: What did the Basel Programme of 1897 demand?
a: A publicly and legally secured home in Palestine
A Jewish state in East Africa
Equal civil rights only in Europe
68658.e: The Basel Programme became the founding text of the World Zionist Organization. The word “home” was deliberately more cautious than “state”.
68658.m: The Basel Programme called for a secured home in Palestine.

68659.q: In which city has the Zionist Congress met since 1951?
68659.e: Until 1946 the congress often took place in Basel, ten times in all. Since 1951 it has met in Jerusalem; in 2022 Basel celebrated the 125th anniversary.
68659.m: Since 1951 the Zionist Congress has met in Jerusalem.

68660.q: What is the Israeli day of remembrance for the victims of the Shoah called?
68660.e: On Yom HaShoah sirens sound across Israel and traffic stops for two minutes. The day is in spring, close to the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.
68660.m: Israel remembers the victims of the Shoah on Yom HaShoah.

68661.q: With which cover term did the Nazis refer to the plan to murder the Jews of Europe?
68661.e: The term disguised the systematic mass murder. Aktion T4, on the other hand, referred to the murders of sick and disabled people.
68661.m: “Final Solution” was the cover term for the murder of the Jews.

68662.q: Which lawyer coined the term “genocide” in 1944?
68662.e: The Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin then campaigned for the UN Genocide Convention of 1948. Many of his relatives were murdered in the Holocaust.
68662.m: Raphael Lemkin created the term genocide.

68663.q: Which Nazi organiser of the deportations was put on trial in Jerusalem in 1961?
68663.e: Eichmann was captured in Argentina in 1960 by the Israeli secret service. He was convicted and executed in 1962.
68663.m: Adolf Eichmann was tried in Jerusalem in 1961.

68664.q: Which philosopher coined the phrase “the banality of evil” in her report on the Eichmann trial?
68664.e: Hannah Arendt reported from Jerusalem for the magazine “The New Yorker”. She described Eichmann as a thoughtless bureaucrat.
68664.m: Hannah Arendt spoke of “the banality of evil”.

68665.q: Which ghetto in Bohemia did the SS stage as a showcase camp for a visit by the ICRC in 1944?
68665.e: The camp was made to look nicer for the visit in order to deceive the world. Afterwards a Swiss ICRC delegate wrote a report that made things look better than they were.
68665.m: In 1944 Theresienstadt was shown to the ICRC as a deception.

68666.q: Which woman living in Bern became known as the “mother of refugees” because she spoke up for Jewish refugees to the Federal Council in 1942?
68666.e: Gertrud Kurz led the refugee aid of the Crusaders, later the Christian Peace Service. In August 1942 she pleaded with Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger against closing the border.
68666.m: As the “mother of refugees”, Gertrud Kurz helped Jewish refugees.

68667.q: With which slogan is Swiss refugee policy of 1942 often summed up?
68667.e: In 1942 Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a crowded lifeboat. This became the well-known slogan.
68667.m: “The boat is full” stands for the harsh refugee policy of 1942.

68668.q: In which year did Swiss Jews gain freedom of settlement through a popular vote?
68668.e: In 1866 the people and the cantons removed the restriction to Christians. Full freedom of belief and worship only came with the constitution of 1874.
68668.m: In 1866 freedom of settlement was extended to Jews.

68669.q: What was the result of the 1866 popular vote on freedom of settlement for Jews?
68669.e: With about 53 per cent voting yes, the result was close. Some cantons such as Geneva and Neuchâtel approved very clearly, while others rejected it.
68669.m: In 1866 equal rights of settlement were only narrowly approved.

68670.q: What was special about the constitutional vote of January 1866?
a: Only freedom of settlement for Jews was approved
The people were not allowed to vote at all
68670.e: Of nine proposals, only freedom of settlement for non-Christians won a majority. That is why people speak of the “only yes of 1866”.
68670.m: In 1866, of several proposals, only freedom of settlement was approved.

68671.q: Which treaty of 1864 made equal treatment of Swiss Jews in matters of settlement urgent?
68671.e: The treaty allowed French Jews to settle freely in Switzerland. Otherwise Swiss Jews would have been worse off than foreign ones.
68671.m: The treaty with France of 1864 sped up equal rights for Jews.

68672.q: To whom did the Federal Constitution of 1848 grant freedom of settlement throughout Switzerland?
a: Only to Swiss of Christian denomination
Only to men who owned land
68672.e: The constitution of 1848 excluded Jews from freedom of settlement. In 1866 this restriction was removed.
68672.m: The constitution of 1848 disadvantaged Jews in matters of settlement.

68673.q: In which year did Jews in Switzerland receive full freedom of belief and worship?
68673.e: Only the fully revised Federal Constitution of 1874 guaranteed general freedom of belief and worship. In 1866 it was only about settlement and equality before the law.
68673.m: Full religious freedom for Jews came with the constitution of 1874.

68674.q: How did other countries contribute to equal rights for Swiss Jews in the 1860s?
a: States such as France and the Netherlands applied pressure through treaties
The Pope demanded it in a letter
68674.e: Countries such as France, the Netherlands and the USA did not want treaties that disadvantaged their Jewish citizens. This pressure sped up equal rights.
68674.m: Pressure from abroad helped to bring equal rights for Swiss Jews.

68675.q: In which year did the Swiss people approve the ban on kosher slaughter, the first popular initiative ever to be accepted?
68675.e: The popular initiative has existed since 1891. The ban on slaughter without stunning in 1893 was the first initiative to be approved, and it was also supported for antisemitic reasons.
68675.m: The ban on kosher slaughter of 1893 was the first popular initiative to be approved.

68676.q: Who submitted the popular initiative for the ban on kosher slaughter?
68676.e: The animal protection societies of German-speaking Switzerland demanded that animals be stunned before bleeding. Historians also see antisemitic motives among many supporters.
68676.m: The animal protection societies launched the initiative against kosher slaughter.

68677.q: Which canton supported the ban on kosher slaughter most strongly in 1893, with over 90 per cent?
68677.e: In Aargau, where many Jews lived in the Surb valley, 90.1 per cent voted yes. French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino clearly rejected the ban.
68677.m: Aargau supported the ban on kosher slaughter most clearly.

68678.q: What exactly did the ban of 1893 forbid?
a: Slaughtering animals without stunning them first
68678.e: In ritual slaughter the animal is killed with a single cut without stunning and the blood drains out. The ban mainly affected the Jewish community.
68678.m: The ban forbids slaughter without stunning.

68679.q: Into which law was the ban on slaughter without stunning moved in 1978?
68679.e: The Animal Protection Act of 1978 took over the ban in Article 20. As a result it was no longer in the constitution.
68679.m: Since 1978 the Animal Protection Act has contained the ban on slaughter without stunning.

68680.q: How do Jewish and Muslim communities in Switzerland obtain kosher or halal meat despite the ban on slaughter without stunning?
a: Through special permits from the cantons
68680.e: Slaughtering mammals without stunning is banned in Switzerland, but importing the meat is allowed. The SIG received an import licence for this from the authorities.
68680.m: Kosher meat is imported into Switzerland.

68681.q: In the view of its opponents, which fundamental right did the ban on kosher slaughter violate?
68681.e: Opponents such as former Federal Councillor Numa Droz warned that the ban interfered with the religious practice of a minority. The Federal Council and parliament also rejected the initiative.
68681.m: Opponents saw the ban on kosher slaughter as an attack on freedom of religion.

68682.q: What is the Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities (SIG)?
a: The umbrella organisation of Jewish communities in Switzerland
68682.e: The SIG was founded in 1904 and represents the Jewish communities towards the authorities and the public. It is not a religious office and does not represent the State of Israel.
68682.m: The SIG is the umbrella organisation of Jewish communities in Switzerland.

68683.q: In the old Swiss Confederation, in which canton were Jews allowed to live almost exclusively until the 19th century?
68683.e: Until the 19th century Jews in the Confederation were allowed to settle almost only in Endingen and Lengnau in the Surb valley. That is why Aargau is especially important for the Jewish history of Switzerland.
68683.m: Endingen and Lengnau in Aargau were for a long time the only Jewish villages in Switzerland.

68684.q: Since when have Jews had full freedom of settlement throughout Switzerland?
68684.e: The Federal Constitution of 1848 granted freedom of settlement only to Christians. Only a popular vote in 1866 extended it to Jews.
68684.m: Since 1866 Jews have been allowed to settle anywhere in Switzerland.

68685.q: Roughly how many Jewish people live in Switzerland today?
68685.e: About 18,000 Jewish people live in Switzerland, around 0.2 per cent of the population. The largest communities are in Zurich, Geneva and Basel.
68685.m: About 18,000 Jewish people live in Switzerland.

68686.q: How did Switzerland behave towards many Jewish refugees in the Second World War?
a: It turned many away at the border
It took everyone in without conditions
It sent everyone on to America
It only let in families with passports
68686.e: From 1942 Switzerland closed the border to people persecuted only on grounds of race. Thousands were turned away. The SIG largely had to pay for the Jewish refugees who were taken in itself.
68686.m: In the Second World War Switzerland turned away many Jewish refugees.

68687.q: What is the Jewish refugee and social welfare organisation closely linked with the SIG called?
68687.e: At the beginning of 1945 the Association of Swiss Jewish Welfare Organisations looked after about 23,000 refugees. Today it is the social department of the SIG.
68687.m: The VSJF is the Jewish aid organisation of Switzerland.

68688.q: Against what did the SIG set up its own information office at the end of 1936?
a: Against the missionary work of the national churches
68688.e: The Jewish news agency JUNA collected information about antisemitic groups and disproved their propaganda. In the 1930s Frontists were active in Switzerland too.
68688.m: In 1936 the SIG fought back against antisemitic propaganda with an information office.

68689.q: In which city was Martin Buber born in 1878?
68689.e: Buber was born in Vienna and then grew up with his grandfather in Lemberg. There he came to know Hasidism.
68689.m: Martin Buber was born in Vienna.

68690.q: What is the title of Buber's main work of 1923 on dialogical relationships?
68690.e: Buber distinguishes the I-Thou relationship of real encounter from the I-It relationship to things. The book shaped philosophy, theology and education.
68690.m: In “I and Thou” Buber describes real encounter.

68691.q: Which great work did Martin Buber translate into German together with Franz Rosenzweig?
68691.e: The German translation of the Scriptures began in 1925. After Rosenzweig's death, Buber only completed it in 1961.
68691.m: Buber and Rosenzweig translated the Bible together.

68692.q: Which collection of Hasidic stories did Buber publish in 1949?
68692.e: Buber made the legends of the Hasidic masters known to a wide public. He saw in them a living form of Jewish piety.
68692.m: Buber collected the Tales of the Hasidim.

68693.q: At which university did Buber teach after emigrating in 1938?
68693.e: Buber left Nazi Germany and taught social philosophy in Jerusalem. He died in Jerusalem in 1965.
68693.m: From 1938 Buber taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

68694.q: Which prize did Martin Buber receive in Frankfurt am Main in 1953?
a: Peace Prize of the German Book Trade
68694.e: Buber accepted the prize as a sign of understanding, which was controversial in Israel. In his speech he talked about real dialogue between peoples.
68694.m: In 1953 Buber received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade.

68695.q: Which political solution did Buber support for Palestine?
a: A binational state for Jews and Arabs
68695.e: Buber was active in groups such as Ihud for living together with equal rights. He understood Zionism as a cultural and ethical renewal.
68695.m: Buber supported a shared state for Jews and Arabs.

68696.q: Roughly what does the Sanskrit word “Upanishad” literally mean?
68696.e: The word is made up of upa (near), ni (down) and shad (sit). It refers to pupils who sit down close to their teacher for lessons.
68696.m: Upanishad means sitting down close to the teacher to learn.

68697.q: Why are the Upanishads also called “Vedanta”?
a: They form the end of the Vedas
68697.e: Vedanta literally means “end of the Veda”. As the youngest layer, the Upanishads come at the end of Vedic literature.
68697.m: As Vedanta, the Upanishads are the crowning conclusion of the Vedas.

68698.q: What does the famous phrase “Tat tvam asi” (“That you are”) from the Upanishads express?
a: The inner self is one with the ground of the world
The king is lord of the world
68698.e: In the conversation between Uddalaka and his son Shvetaketu, the phrase shows the unity of Atman and Brahman. It is one of the most important sayings of Vedanta.
68698.m: “Tat tvam asi” teaches the unity of the self with the ground of the world.

68699.q: In the Katha Upanishad, what does the boy Nachiketa ask Yama, the god of death?
a: What remains of a person after death
How to become rich and powerful
Who will be the next king
68699.e: Yama offers Nachiketa wealth and a long life, but he insists on his question. Yama then teaches him about the immortal self.
68699.m: Nachiketa asks Death about the immortal self.

68700.q: Which formula from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad describes the Absolute only by negation?
68700.e: “Neti neti” means “not this, not this”. Every description is rejected because the Absolute goes beyond all concepts.
68700.m: With “neti neti” you say that the Absolute cannot be put into words.

68701.q: What does India's motto “Satyameva Jayate”, which comes from the Mundaka Upanishad, mean?
68701.e: The phrase appears beneath India's state emblem. It shows how the Upanishads still shape Indian culture today.

68702.q: Which sacred syllable do the Upanishads interpret as the sound of the Absolute?
68702.e: The short Mandukya Upanishad explains Om through the states of waking, dreaming and deep sleep and a fourth state. Om is still spoken at the start of prayers today.
68702.m: Om is regarded as the sacred sound of the Absolute.

68703.q: Which 19th-century German philosopher called the Upanishads the consolation of his life?
68703.e: Schopenhauer read the Upanishads in a Latin translation of a Persian version. Indian thought strongly shaped his philosophy.

68704.q: What does “Brahman” mean in the Upanishads?
a: The creator god with four heads
68704.e: Brahman is the impersonal source of all things. It must not be confused with the god Brahma or the caste of Brahmins.
68704.m: Brahman is the highest reality and not the god Brahma.

a: Rebirth in the form of an animal
The law of cause and effect
68705.e: Atman is the unchanging self behind body, thoughts and feelings. It is often translated as “soul”, but it means the pure core of consciousness.
68705.m: Atman is the unchanging inner self of every being.

68706.q: According to the teaching of the Upanishads, how is Atman related to Brahman?
a: At its core it is one with Brahman
It is a servant of Brahman
It has nothing to do with Brahman
68706.e: The Upanishads teach that the innermost self (Atman) is one with the highest reality (Brahman). Whoever realises this is freed from the cycle of rebirths.
68706.m: According to the Upanishads, Atman and Brahman are one.

68707.q: With which set of three is Brahman often described?
68707.e: The Sanskrit Sat-Chit-Ananda means being, consciousness and bliss. The formula describes the Absolute without limiting it.
68707.m: Brahman is described as Sat-Chit-Ananda, that is being, consciousness and bliss.

68708.q: What is the difference between Brahman and Brahma in Hinduism?
a: Brahman is the impersonal highest reality, Brahma a creator god
Both names mean exactly the same
Brahman is a god, Brahma a priestly caste
Brahma is the soul, Brahman the body
68708.e: Brahman is the source of all things, often thought of as without any qualities (Nirguna). Brahma, on the other hand, is a god with four heads who creates the world.
68708.m: Brahman is the highest reality, Brahma a creator god.

68709.q: Which sentence from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is considered a “great saying” about the unity of the self?
68709.e: “Aham brahmasmi” means “I am Brahman”. It is one of the four Mahavakyas, the great sayings of the Upanishads.

68710.q: According to Hindu teaching, what binds the Atman to the cycle of rebirths?
a: The position of the stars alone
68710.e: Deeds leave effects that determine a new birth. As long as karma and ignorance remain, the self stays in samsara.
68710.m: Karma keeps a person in the cycle of rebirths.

68711.q: In which epic is the Bhagavad Gita embedded?
68711.e: The Gita is in the sixth book (Bhishma Parva) of the Mahabharata. So it is part of the great epic about the war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas.
68711.m: The Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata.

68712.q: Between whom does the conversation of the Bhagavad Gita take place?
68712.e: The warrior Arjuna is full of doubt before the battle, and his charioteer Krishna teaches him. In doing so, Krishna reveals himself as God.
68712.m: In the Gita, Krishna teaches the doubting warrior Arjuna.

68713.q: On which battlefield is the Bhagavad Gita set?
68713.e: The Gita begins with a sentence about the “field of dharma, Kurukshetra”. There the related armies of the Pandavas and Kauravas face each other.
68713.m: The Gita is set before the battle on the field of Kurukshetra.

68714.q: How many chapters does the Bhagavad Gita have?
68714.e: The Gita has 18 songs with about 700 verses. The number 18 also plays a big role in the Mahabharata, which has 18 books.
68714.m: The Bhagavad Gita has 18 chapters with about 700 verses.

68715.q: What does the Gita ask for with the ideal of “Nishkama Karma”?
a: Acting without craving for the result
Acting only for your own benefit
Acting only on the orders of priests
68715.e: Krishna advises Arjuna to do his duty without clinging to the fruits of his actions. In this way no binding karma arises.
68715.m: Nishkama Karma means doing your duty without craving success.

68716.q: Which three paths to liberation does the Bhagavad Gita present?
68716.e: The Gita describes the path of selfless action, the path of knowledge and the path of loving devotion. All three lead to God.
68716.m: The Gita knows the paths of action, knowledge and devotion.

68717.q: Which verse of the Gita did Robert Oppenheimer quote after the first atomic bomb test?
a: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds
68717.e: Oppenheimer remembered a verse from chapter 11, in which Krishna shows his all-embracing form. He later told this in an interview.
68717.m: Oppenheimer linked the atomic test with a verse from the eleventh chapter of the Gita.

68718.q: Why does Arjuna hesitate to go into battle at the start of the Bhagavad Gita?
a: He would have to fight relatives and teachers
68718.e: On the other side are Arjuna's cousins, uncles and teachers. Krishna persuades him to do his duty as a warrior.
68718.m: Arjuna hesitates because he would have to fight his own family.

68719.e: A-dvaita literally means “not two”. The school teaches that in the end there is only one reality, namely Brahman.

68720.q: How does Advaita Vedanta explain the variety of the visible world?
a: As the work of many equal gods
68720.e: The variety is seen as an appearance that arises through ignorance (avidya). Only Brahman is real.
68720.m: For Advaita, the variety of the world is maya.

68721.q: Which comparison does Advaita often use to explain illusion?
a: A rope that is mistaken for a snake
A river flowing into the sea
68721.e: In the twilight you mistake a rope for a snake. As soon as you look closely, the snake disappears and only the rope remains, just like Brahman behind the world.
68721.m: The rope mistaken for a snake shows the illusion of maya.

68722.q: Which sacred scriptures is Vedanta mainly based on?
68722.e: Vedanta means “end of the Veda”. This refers to the Upanishads, which form the conclusion of the Vedic scriptures. The Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras are also important.
68722.m: Vedanta is based mainly on the Upanishads.

68723.q: In Advaita Vedanta, what is Brahman?
68723.e: For Advaita Vedanta, in the end there is only Brahman. Even a person's innermost self, Atman, is identical with Brahman.
68723.m: In Advaita Vedanta, Brahman is the only reality.

68724.q: Which teaching did the Indian philosopher Shankara hold?
a: The inner self and the Absolute are ultimately one
There is no God and no soul
The world consists of two eternal gods
Only sacrifice in the temple leads to salvation
68724.e: Shankara founded the school of Advaita Vedanta, “non-duality”. For him Atman, the self, and Brahman, the ground of the world, are at heart the same.
68724.m: Shankara taught the unity of Atman and Brahman.

68725.q: According to tradition, what way of life did Shankara lead?
a: He wandered through India as an ascetic
He ruled as king in Delhi
He lived as a trader on the coast
He served as a warrior at court
68725.e: Shankara is said to have renounced the world as a young man. As a wandering monk he held debates with scholars all over India.
68725.m: Shankara lived as a wandering ascetic.

68726.q: According to tradition, which institutions did Shankara found in the four corners of India?
68726.e: Mathas in Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Jyotirmath are named. They are still led by Shankaracharyas today.
68726.m: Shankara is said to have founded four monasteries in the four corners of India.

68727.q: On which three basic texts did Shankara write commentaries (Prasthanatraya)?
68727.e: The three starting points of Vedanta are called Prasthanatraya. Anyone who wanted to found their own school of Vedanta had to comment on them.
68727.m: Shankara commented on the three basic texts of Vedanta.

68728.e: Bhakti is the personal, heartfelt worship of a deity such as Krishna, Rama or Shiva. It is open to everyone, regardless of caste or education.
68728.m: Bhakti is loving devotion to a deity.

68729.q: Which religion arose in the 15th and 16th centuries, partly under the influence of the Bhakti movement?
68729.e: Guru Nanak shared with the Bhakti movement a deep love of God and rejection of caste barriers. The Guru Granth Sahib also contains verses by Bhakti poets.
68729.m: Sikhism was shaped by the Bhakti movement.

68730.q: Which god is praised as a beloved herdsman in many Bhakti songs?
68730.e: According to legend, Krishna grew up among cowherds. Poets such as Mirabai worshipped him as beloved and lord.

68731.q: Why was it important that Bhakti poets wrote in everyday languages instead of Sanskrit?
a: This way ordinary people could understand the religious texts too
Sanskrit was banned at the time
Only this way were women allowed to read the texts
68731.e: Sanskrit was understood mainly by learned Brahmins. Tulsidas, for example, told the story of Rama in Awadhi in the 16th century and so made it accessible to everyone.
68731.m: Bhakti poets made religion accessible to everyone in everyday languages.

68732.q: Which 15th-century Bhakti poet is honoured equally by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs?
68732.e: Kabir criticised outward show in both religions and stressed inner love of God. Some of his verses are in the Sikhs' Guru Granth Sahib.
68732.m: Kabir's verses connect Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.

68733.q: What is typical of worship in the Hare Krishna movement?
68733.e: This singing is called kirtan. It was spread in the 16th century by the Bengali saint Chaitanya, to whom the movement refers.
68733.m: Hare Krishna followers sing Krishna's names together.

68734.q: In which city was the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON) founded in 1966?
68734.e: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada founded ISKCON in New York in 1966. The movement became known worldwide as “Hare Krishna”.
68734.m: The Hare Krishna movement ISKCON was founded in New York in 1966.

68735.q: Why was the Bhakti movement considered socially important?
a: It opened the way to God for all castes and for women
It abolished the caste system by law
It only allowed Brahmins to pray
68735.e: Many Bhakti saints came from low castes or were women. They taught that true devotion matters more than origin and rituals.
68735.m: Bhakti made love of God more important than caste and origin.

68736.q: What does moksha mean in Hinduism?
a: Liberation from the cycle of rebirths
The duty to obey your parents
A festival in honour of Shiva
68736.e: Moksha is the highest goal of many Hindu teachings. Whoever reaches it is not reborn again.
68736.m: Moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirths.

68737.q: Which city on the Ganges do many Hindus consider a place where dying grants moksha?
68737.e: Varanasi, also called Kashi, is the holy city of Shiva. Many Hindus are cremated there at the ghats on the Ganges.
68737.m: Varanasi is regarded as a city where death grants liberation.

68738.q: Which Buddhist term comes closest to the Hindu moksha?
68738.e: Both terms mean the end of the cycle of rebirths. Samsara, by contrast, refers to that very cycle.
68738.m: Moksha in Hinduism roughly corresponds to nirvana in Buddhism.

68739.q: According to Advaita Vedanta, what is the decisive means of liberation?
a: Realising the unity of Atman and Brahman
As many animal sacrifices as possible
68739.e: According to Shankara, bondage arises from ignorance. That is why only the knowledge (jnana) that the self is Brahman sets you free.
68739.m: Advaita sees knowledge as the path to liberation.

68740.q: How do many Bhakti schools describe the state of liberation?
a: As eternal loving communion with God
As a return to earthly life
68740.e: For Ramanuja and other Bhakti teachers, the soul remains distinct from God even in liberation. It enjoys closeness to him.
68740.m: For Bhakti, liberation is eternal closeness to God.

68741.q: Which stage of life in the traditional order is devoted entirely to striving for moksha?
a: Brahmacharya, the time as a student
68741.e: The sannyasin gives up possessions and family. He devotes himself only to liberation.
68741.m: In sannyasa a person devotes themselves entirely to liberation.

68742.q: Which translation best captures the term “dharma”?
68742.e: Dharma refers to the cosmic order and the duties of human beings that follow from it. No single English word fully captures the term.
68742.m: Dharma means order, law and duty all at once.

68743.q: What do many Hindus call their own religion?
68743.e: Sanatana Dharma means “eternal order”. The term “Hinduism”, on the other hand, was coined from outside.
68743.m: Many Hindus call their religion Sanatana Dharma, the eternal order.

68744.e: Svadharma is the duty that results from a person's position and stage of life. The Gita says your own duty is better than someone else's, even if you fulfil it imperfectly.
68744.m: Svadharma is a person's own duty.

68745.q: What is the best-known law book of the Dharmashastra literature called?
68745.e: The Manusmriti regulates the duties of the social classes and stages of life. It was controversial early on because it fixes the caste order in writing.
68745.m: The Manusmriti is the best-known dharma law book.

68746.q: What does the term “varnashrama dharma” sum up?
a: Duties according to social class and stage of life
68746.e: Varna means the four social classes, ashrama the four stages of life. Together they determine a person's traditional duties.
68746.m: Varnashrama dharma sets duties according to class and stage of life.

68747.q: How many stages of life (ashramas) does traditional Hindu teaching recognise?
68747.e: The four stages are student, householder, forest hermit (vanaprastha) and renunciant. They divide life into learning, family, withdrawal and letting go.
68747.m: Hindu teaching recognises four stages of life.

68748.q: In traditional Hindu teaching, which stage of life follows the time as a student?
68748.e: After the student years comes the stage of the householder (grihastha). He starts a family, works and supports society and ascetics.
68748.m: The student years are followed by the stage of family and work.

68749.q: How many goals of life (purusharthas) does classical Hindu teaching recognise?
68749.e: The four goals are dharma, artha, kama and moksha. In earlier times people often spoke only of the first three.
68749.m: Hinduism recognises four goals of life.

68750.q: Which of the four goals of life means prosperity and material success?
68750.e: Artha covers possessions, work and political success. It is considered legitimate if it is in harmony with dharma.
68750.m: Artha is the life goal of prosperity.

68751.q: Which of the four goals of life means joy, pleasure and a sense of beauty, for example in art and music?
68751.e: Kama refers to wishes and joy in pleasant things. This goal too is meant to be limited by dharma.
68751.m: Kama is the life goal of joy and pleasure.

68752.q: According to classical teaching, which goal of life is meant to order and limit the other goals?
68752.e: Prosperity and pleasure are only good if they agree with the right order. That is why dharma forms the framework.
68752.m: Dharma orders the life goals of artha and kama.

68753.q: Which goal of life is considered the highest because it leads beyond worldly life?
68753.e: The first three goals concern life in the world. Moksha aims at liberation from the cycle of births.
68753.m: Moksha is regarded as the highest of the four goals of life.

68754.q: Which ancient Indian textbook on statecraft and economics belongs to the life goal of artha?
68754.e: The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), an adviser to the Maurya king Chandragupta. It deals with administration, taxes and diplomacy.
68754.m: The Arthashastra is a textbook on statecraft.

68755.q: Why does the teaching of the purusharthas not reject wealth and pleasure in principle?
a: They are considered legitimate goals within the framework of dharma
They are considered the only goals of life
They are only allowed to priests
68755.e: Hinduism sees different phases of life with different tasks. Worldly goals have their place as long as they respect the order.
68755.m: Within the framework of dharma, wealth and pleasure are permitted goals.

68756.e: Vivekananda, then called Narendranath Datta, met Ramakrishna in Calcutta and became his most important pupil. He spread his teaching around the world.

68757.q: At which event in 1893 did Vivekananda make Hinduism known in the West?
a: At the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago
At the World Exhibition in Paris
At the League of Nations Assembly in Geneva
68757.e: He began his speech with “Sisters and Brothers of America” and received great applause. Afterwards he gave many lectures in the USA and Europe.
68757.m: Vivekananda became famous at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893.

68758.q: Which organisation did Vivekananda found in 1897?
68758.e: The Ramakrishna Mission combines spirituality with education, hospitals and help in emergencies. Its headquarters are in Belur near Calcutta.
68758.m: Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

68759.q: What was Swami Vivekananda's birth name?
68759.e: Narendranath Datta was born in Calcutta in 1863. He took the monastic name Vivekananda later.
68759.m: Vivekananda was originally called Narendranath Datta.

68760.q: What does India celebrate every year on Swami Vivekananda's birthday?
68760.e: Since 1985, 12 January has been National Youth Day. Vivekananda is seen as a role model for young people in India.
68760.m: Vivekananda's birthday is India's National Youth Day.

68761.q: Which school of Vedanta did Vivekananda put especially in the foreground in his lectures?
68761.e: Vivekananda interpreted Advaita as a basis for tolerance and service to people. He saw the divine in every person.
68761.m: Vivekananda made Advaita Vedanta known in the West.

68762.q: Which book by Vivekananda from 1896 explained Patanjali's Yoga Sutras to the West?
68762.e: “Raja Yoga” was based on lectures in New York. It did much to make yoga known in the West.
68762.m: Vivekananda's book “Raja Yoga” explained the Yoga Sutras to the West.

68763.q: Which writer, who lived in Villeneuve on Lake Geneva, wrote biographies of Ramakrishna and Vivekananda around 1930?
68763.e: The French Nobel Prize winner Romain Rolland lived for a long time in Villeneuve in the canton of Vaud. He made the two Indian mystics known in Europe.
68763.m: Romain Rolland wrote about Ramakrishna and Vivekananda in Switzerland.

68764.q: In which classical text does ahimsa come first among the five yamas (ethical rules)?
68764.e: Patanjali names as yamas ahimsa, truthfulness, not stealing, moderation and non-possessiveness. Ahimsa comes first.
68764.m: In the Yoga Sutras, ahimsa is the first of the ethical rules.

68765.q: In which religion is ahimsa practised so strictly that monks often sweep the path in front of them?
68765.e: Jain monks take care not to kill even small insects. Ahimsa is the first of their vows.
68765.m: In Jainism ahimsa is lived especially strictly.

68766.q: What did Gandhi call his method of non-violent resistance?
68766.e: Satyagraha means roughly “holding firmly to the truth”. Gandhi developed the method in South Africa against discriminatory laws.
68766.m: Gandhi's non-violent resistance is called satyagraha.

68767.q: What was Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 directed against?
a: The British salt monopoly and the salt tax
68767.e: Gandhi walked about 385 kilometres to the sea at Dandi and made salt there himself. Thousands followed his example and so broke the British law.
68767.m: With the Salt March in 1930 Gandhi protested against the British salt tax.

68768.q: In which country did Gandhi develop his method of non-violent resistance as a young lawyer?
68768.e: Gandhi lived in South Africa for about twenty years and fought against laws there that disadvantaged Indians. In 1915 he returned to India.
68768.m: Gandhi developed non-violent resistance in South Africa.

68769.q: For Gandhi, which symbol stood for economic self-reliance (swadeshi)?
68769.e: Gandhi called on people to spin cloth themselves instead of buying British textiles. The spinning wheel (charkha) became the symbol of the independence movement.
68769.m: The spinning wheel was Gandhi's symbol of self-reliance.

68770.q: Which of the five precepts (Pancasila) for Buddhist lay people comes closest to the commandment of ahimsa?
68770.e: The first of the five precepts asks you to refrain from killing living beings. In this way Buddhism shares the Indian ideal of non-violence.
68770.m: In Buddhism too, the first rule is not to kill living beings.

68771.q: What is the title of Gandhi's autobiography?
a: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
68771.e: Gandhi wrote the work in Gujarati in the 1920s. In it he describes his life as a search for truth.
68771.m: Gandhi's autobiography is about his experiments with truth.

68772.e: Godse accused Gandhi of making too many concessions to Muslims and Pakistan. Gandhi died in Delhi on his way to prayers.
68772.m: In 1948 Gandhi was shot by the Hindu nationalist Nathuram Godse.

68773.q: Which population group did B. R. Ambedkar belong to by birth?
68773.e: Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a Mahar family, who were regarded as “untouchable”. He himself experienced severe discrimination at school.
68773.m: Ambedkar came from a Dalit family.

68774.q: What role did Ambedkar have in the founding of independent India?
a: He chaired the committee that drafted the constitution
68774.e: Ambedkar was chairman of the Drafting Committee and India's first law minister. The constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
68774.m: Ambedkar is regarded as the father of the Indian constitution.

68775.q: What does the Indian constitution of 1950 expressly forbid?
68775.e: Article 17 bans untouchability in any form, and practising it is a criminal offence. Ambedkar chaired the committee that drafted the constitution.

68776.q: What is Ambedkar's famous work against the caste system from 1936 called?
68776.e: The speech was meant for a conference, but it was cancelled there. Ambedkar published it himself and called for the abolition of castes.
68776.m: In “Annihilation of Caste” Ambedkar called for the abolition of castes.

68777.q: Which religion did Ambedkar convert to in 1956 together with very many followers?
68777.e: On 14 October 1956 he converted in Nagpur together with hundreds of thousands of Dalits. He saw Buddhism as a religion without a caste order.
68777.m: In 1956 Ambedkar converted to Buddhism with many Dalits.

68778.q: Which law book did Ambedkar publicly burn in protest in 1927?
68778.e: Ambedkar saw the Manusmriti as the justification for untouchability. The burning on 25 December 1927 was a symbolic act.
68778.m: In 1927 Ambedkar burned the Manusmriti in protest.

68779.q: What was the Poona Pact of 1932 between Ambedkar and Gandhi about?
a: The political representation of the Dalits
68779.e: Ambedkar wanted separate electorates for Dalits; Gandhi rejected this and fasted. They agreed on reserved seats in joint electorates.
68779.m: The Poona Pact settled the political representation of the Dalits.

68780.q: Why is Ambedkar still a role model for many Dalits today?
a: Despite discrimination he became one of India's most highly educated politicians
He was the richest man in India
He came from a Brahmin family
He led India into a war
68780.e: Ambedkar earned a doctorate at Columbia University and studied at the London School of Economics. As a Dalit he fought against the caste system all his life.
68780.m: For Dalits, Ambedkar is a role model for education and equal rights.

68781.q: Which politician, Prime Minister of India since 2014, is closely associated with the Hindutva movement?
68781.e: Narendra Modi was active early on in the Hindutva organisation RSS. He leads the BJP party in government.
68781.m: Narendra Modi stands for India's Hindutva-oriented politics.

68782.q: What does “Hindutva” mean as a political idea?
a: A Hindu nationalism that sees India as a Hindu nation
68782.e: Hindutva sees Hindu culture as the basis of the Indian nation. Critics see it as disadvantaging religious minorities.
68782.m: Hindutva is the ideology of Hindu nationalism.

68783.q: Which organisation was founded in Nagpur in 1925 and is regarded as the core of the Hindutva movement?
68783.e: The RSS was founded by K. B. Hedgewar and is a volunteer organisation. Several parties and associations grew out of its circles.
68783.m: The RSS was founded in Nagpur in 1925.

68784.q: Which party, founded in 1980, is politically close to the Hindutva idea?
68784.e: The BJP grew out of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh. Since 2014 it has provided the prime minister, Narendra Modi (as of 2025).
68784.m: The BJP is the party close to the Hindutva idea.

68785.q: What happened in Ayodhya on 6 December 1992?
a: The Babri Mosque was destroyed by Hindu activists
A new Ram temple was consecrated
68785.e: The activists believed the mosque stood on the birthplace of the god Rama. Afterwards there were severe riots with many deaths.
68785.m: The Babri Mosque in Ayodhya was destroyed in 1992.

68786.q: When was the new Ram temple in Ayodhya consecrated?
68786.e: After a ruling by the Supreme Court in 2019, the temple was allowed to be built. The consecration took place on 22 January 2024.
68786.m: The Ram temple in Ayodhya was consecrated in January 2024.

68787.q: How did Savarkar define a Hindu in his work on Hindutva?
a: Someone who regards India as fatherland and holy land
Someone who recites the Vedas every day
Someone born into a Brahmin family
68787.e: Savarkar called India Pitribhumi (land of the ancestors) and Punyabhumi (holy land). For him this also included Jains, Buddhists and Sikhs.
68787.m: For Savarkar a Hindu was someone who saw India as fatherland and holy land.

a: A Hindu pilgrimage festival with ritual bathing in holy rivers
A harvest festival in the temple
A festival of lights in autumn
A festival of colours in spring
68788.e: Millions of pilgrims bathe on the festival days to cleanse themselves of sins. The Kumbh Mela is regarded as the largest religious gathering in the world.
68788.m: The Kumbh Mela is a huge pilgrimage festival with ritual bathing.

68789.q: How often is the great Kumbh Mela celebrated in the same place?
68789.e: The Kumbh Mela moves between four places on holy rivers, including Prayagraj and Haridwar. At each place it takes place about every twelve years.
68789.m: The Kumbh Mela takes place in the same place about every twelve years.

68790.q: What does “Kumbh” mean in Kumbh Mela?
68790.e: The myth tells of a pot of the nectar of immortality (amrita). In the fight over it, drops are said to have fallen to earth at the four festival sites.
68790.m: Kumbh means pot and recalls the pot of nectar.

68791.q: Which rivers meet at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj?
a: The Ganges, the Yamuna and the mythical Sarasvati
The Indus, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra
The Godavari, the Krishna and the Kaveri
The Narmada, the Tapti and the Yamuna
68791.e: The Ganges and the Yamuna visibly flow together there. The Sarasvati is regarded as an invisible third river.
68791.m: At the Triveni Sangam the Ganges, the Yamuna and the mythical Sarasvati meet.

68792.q: How many visits did the authorities report for the Maha Kumbh Mela 2025 in Prayagraj?
68792.e: The festival lasted from 13 January to 26 February 2025. The government of Uttar Pradesh reported over 660 million pilgrim visits (66 crore), counting repeated baths too.
68792.m: According to official figures, the Maha Kumbh Mela 2025 had about 660 million visits.

68793.q: Onto which UNESCO list was the Kumbh Mela added in 2017?
68793.e: UNESCO honoured the festival as a living tradition. It is passed on mainly orally and by taking part.
68793.m: Since 2017 the Kumbh Mela has been part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage.

68794.q: Who are the sadhus, who can be seen in large numbers at the Kumbh Mela?
a: Hindu ascetics who give up possessions
Pilgrim guides of the Indian government
68794.e: Sadhus live without possessions and devote themselves entirely to religion. Some wander about almost naked and covered in ash and lead the processions to the holy bath.

68795.q: What determines the timing of the Kumbh Mela?
a: The positions of Jupiter, the Sun and the Moon
The will of the Prime Minister
The Gregorian calendar, every ten years
68795.e: Astrological calculations fix the place and time. Jupiter matters most; it takes about twelve years to orbit the Sun.
68795.m: The Kumbh Mela follows the positions of Jupiter, the Sun and the Moon.

68796.q: By which name, meaning ‘Three Baskets’, is the Pali Canon also known?
68796.e: The Pali Canon is divided into three collections, figuratively called ‘baskets’ (pitaka). That is why it is called Tipitaka, or Tripitaka in Sanskrit.
68796.m: The Pali Canon is also called the Tipitaka, the Three Baskets.

68797.q: Which ‘basket’ of the Pali Canon contains the rules for monks and nuns?
68797.e: The Vinaya Pitaka collects the rules of monastic life together with the stories of how they came about. It is the basis of monastic discipline.
68797.m: The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of the Buddhist monastic community.

68798.q: How was the Pali Canon passed on before it was written down?
a: Orally, by learning it by heart
68798.e: Monks learnt the texts by heart and recited them together. They were only written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BC.
68798.m: The Pali Canon was first passed on orally.

68799.q: According to tradition, where was the Pali Canon first written down in the 1st century BC?
68799.e: Before that, the canon was passed on orally. According to the chronicles of Sri Lanka, monks wrote it down on palm leaves at the Aluvihara monastery.
68799.m: The Pali Canon was first written down in Sri Lanka.

68800.q: For which living main branch of Buddhism is the Pali Canon the authoritative collection of scriptures?
68800.e: Theravada, widespread in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar for example, relies on the Pali Canon. Other branches mainly use Chinese and Tibetan canons.
68800.m: Theravada Buddhism is based on the Pali Canon.

a: A well-known collection of verses on the Buddha’s teaching
A festival for the Buddha’s birthday
68801.e: The Dhammapada contains 423 short verses on ethical living and wisdom. It is one of the most widely read Buddhist texts.
68801.m: The Dhammapada is a collection of verses on the Buddha’s teaching.

68802.q: Which language group does Pali, the language of the Pali Canon, belong to?
68802.e: Pali is a Middle Indo-Aryan language, related to the Prakrit languages. Today it is used mainly as a sacred language.
68802.m: Pali is a Middle Indian language.

68803.q: What does the Sutta Pitaka, one of the three ‘baskets’ of the Pali Canon, contain?
68803.e: The Sutta Pitaka collects the discourses of the Buddha and his disciples. The monastic rules, by contrast, are in the Vinaya Pitaka.
68803.m: The Sutta Pitaka contains the Buddha’s discourses.

68804.q: Which idea from the Upanishads does the Buddhist teaching of anatta reject?
a: the law of cause and effect
68804.e: Anatta means ‘non-self’. The Buddha taught that no part of a person contains a lasting, independent self.
68804.m: Anatta denies an eternal, unchanging self.

68805.q: Which two characteristics, together with non-self, make up the three marks of existence in Buddhism?
68805.e: The three marks of existence are impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta). They describe everything that is conditioned.
68805.m: Impermanence, suffering and non-self are the three marks of existence.

68806.q: According to Buddhist teaching, how many aggregates (skandhas) make up a person?
68806.e: A person consists of form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. None of these aggregates is a lasting self.
68806.m: A person consists of five aggregates.

68807.q: According to Buddhist teaching, what is one of the five aggregates of a person?
68807.e: The five aggregates are body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. According to the anatta teaching, a lasting soul is precisely not one of them.
68807.m: Consciousness is one of the five aggregates.

68808.q: According to tradition, to whom did the Buddha give the discourse on the characteristic of non-self (Anattalakkhana Sutta)?
68808.e: The discourse is regarded as the Buddha’s second, after his first sermon in the Deer Park. After hearing it, the five ascetics are said to have attained liberation.
68808.m: The discourse on non-self was addressed to the five ascetics.

68809.q: With which comparison does the monk Nagasena explain to King Milinda that the name ‘Nagasena’ does not refer to a fixed self?
68809.e: A chariot is neither the axle nor the wheels nor the pole, but a name for them working together. In the same way, a person is just a label for the aggregates.
68809.m: The chariot simile shows that a person is just a name for parts.

68810.q: Which image does Buddhist tradition often use to explain rebirth without a travelling self?
a: a flame passed from candle to candle
a bird flying from branch to branch
68810.e: The new flame is neither the same as the old one nor completely different. So there is a causal link without anything unchanging moving on.
68810.m: Rebirth is like a flame being passed on.

68811.q: What does the Buddhist term ‘anatta’ mean?
68811.e: Anatta means non-self. The Buddha taught that a person has no lasting, independent self. Non-violence, on the other hand, is called ahimsa.

68812.q: What does the Buddhist teaching of dependent origination say?
a: Everything arises from conditions and passes away with them
Everything was created by a god
68812.e: Dependent origination (Sanskrit: pratityasamutpada) describes how nothing exists by itself. It is regarded as the core of Buddhist teaching.
68812.m: According to dependent origination, everything arises from conditions.

68813.q: According to Buddhist teaching, what follows from dependent origination for the ‘I’?
a: The ‘I’ turns to stone after death
68813.e: If everything arises from conditions, the ‘I’ cannot exist by itself either. This teaching of non-self is called anatta in Pali.
68813.m: Buddhism teaches that there is no fixed ‘I’.

68814.q: Which link comes at the start of the twelve-link chain of dependent origination?
68814.e: Ignorance of the true nature of things conditions the mental formations and so the whole chain. If it is removed, the cycle ends.
68814.m: The chain of dependent origination begins with ignorance.

68815.q: Which link comes at the end of the twelve-link chain of dependent origination?
68815.e: Birth is followed by ageing and death, along with sorrow and pain. This closes the chain, which begins again through ignorance.
68815.m: Ageing and death are the last link in the chain.

68816.q: According to Buddhist teaching, what is the cause of suffering?
68816.e: The second of the Four Noble Truths names thirst (tanha) as the cause of suffering. In the chain of dependent origination, thirst is followed by clinging.
68816.m: For Buddhism, craving is the cause of suffering.

68817.q: Which basic formula sums up dependent origination in the early discourses?
a: When this is, that is; when this arises, that arises.
All is one, and one is all.
68817.e: The formula describes conditionality in general: something exists because its conditions exist. When the conditions fall away, it passes away.
68817.m: ‘When this is, that is’ is the basic formula of conditionality.

68818.q: What does the Tibetan Wheel of Life show?
a: The history of the Dalai Lamas
68818.e: The Wheel of Life shows the three poisons of the mind at the centre, then the realms of rebirth and, on the outside, the twelve links of dependent origination. It is held by a figure of death.
68818.m: The Tibetan Wheel of Life shows the cycle of rebirths.

68819.q: What does Buddhism call the extinction of the cycle of suffering and rebirth?
68819.e: According to the teaching of dependent origination, when ignorance falls away, all the other links fall away too. This extinction is called nirvana, whereas samsara is the cycle itself.
68819.m: Nirvana is the extinction of the cycle of suffering and rebirth.

68820.q: What does the term ‘bodhisattva’ literally mean?
68820.e: Bodhi means awakening or enlightenment, sattva means being. A bodhisattva strives for buddhahood for the good of all living beings.
68820.m: A bodhisattva is an enlightenment being.

68821.q: Why does a bodhisattva put off his final entry into nirvana for the time being?
a: To help all other living beings reach liberation
Because he still has too much karma
Because the gods will not accept him
Because he is afraid of nirvana
68821.e: In Mahayana, the bodhisattva ideal is regarded as higher than that of the arhat, who only attains his own liberation. The bodhisattva acts out of compassion for all.
68821.m: A bodhisattva gives up his own extinction out of compassion.

68822.q: In which major branch of Buddhism is the bodhisattva ideal central?
68822.e: Mahayana, the ‘Great Vehicle’, puts the bodhisattva at the centre. His path begins with the resolve to attain enlightenment for the good of all beings (bodhicitta).
68822.m: The bodhisattva ideal shapes Mahayana Buddhism.

68823.q: Which virtue is one of the perfections (paramitas) of a bodhisattva?
68823.e: The classic six paramitas are generosity, moral conduct, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom. Later lists extend them to ten.
68823.m: Generosity is one of the bodhisattva’s perfections.

68824.q: Under what name is Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, worshipped in China?
68824.e: In China, Avalokiteshvara was mostly portrayed as a woman, Guanyin. In Japan the figure is called Kannon.
68824.m: In China, Avalokiteshvara is called Guanyin.

68825.q: Which bodhisattva is regarded in all major branches as the future Buddha?
68825.e: According to tradition, Maitreya waits in the Tushita heaven for his birth as the next Buddha. His name is linked to ‘friendliness’.
68825.m: Maitreya is the Buddha of the future.

68826.q: Which attitude above all marks out a bodhisattva?
68826.e: Compassion (karuna) and wisdom are the two pillars of the bodhisattva path. Texts such as Shantideva’s Bodhicaryavatara describe this path in detail.
68826.m: Compassion shapes the path of the bodhisattva.

68827.q: What does the flaming sword with which the bodhisattva Manjushri is often shown stand for?
68827.e: Manjushri embodies wisdom. His sword cuts through ignorance, and he often also holds a text of the wisdom literature.

68828.q: Which philosophical school of Mahayana goes back to Nagarjuna?
68828.e: Madhyamaka means ‘school of the middle’. It seeks a path between the extremes of being and non-being.

68829.q: In which country did the Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna live?
68829.e: Nagarjuna probably lived in southern India. His teaching later became very influential in China, Japan and Tibet.

68830.e: His dates are uncertain; usually around AD 150 to 250 is assumed. He probably lived in southern India.
68830.m: Nagarjuna lived around the 2nd century AD.

68831.q: According to Nagarjuna, what are all things ‘empty’ (shunyata) of?
68831.e: Emptiness does not mean that nothing exists. Things have no independent essence that exists by itself.
68831.m: Emptiness means being empty of inherent nature.

68832.q: Which two levels does Nagarjuna distinguish in his teaching of the two truths?
68832.e: On the conventional level we can meaningfully speak of things and persons. On the ultimate level, everything turns out to be empty.
68832.m: Nagarjuna distinguishes conventional and ultimate truth.

68833.q: What does Nagarjuna mean by the ‘Middle Way’?
a: A path between the extremes of being and non-being
A pilgrimage route through central India
The path between Hinduism and Islam
68833.e: Nagarjuna shows that neither the claim ‘everything really exists’ nor ‘nothing exists’ is true. That is why his school is called Madhyamaka, the school of the middle.
68833.m: Nagarjuna’s Middle Way lies between being and non-being.

68834.q: What does ‘dependent origination’ mean in Buddhism?
a: Everything arises from causes and conditions
Everything was created by a god
Only living beings depend on each other
Everything arises by chance and without reason
68834.e: Nothing exists by itself; everything depends on something else. For Nagarjuna, this is exactly why all things are ‘empty’.
68834.m: Dependent origination means everything arises through conditions.

68835.q: What is Nagarjuna’s central term meaning ‘emptiness’?
68835.e: Shunyata means that things have no independent essence. It does not mean that nothing exists.

68836.q: In which Buddhist tradition did Nagarjuna’s teaching later become especially authoritative?
68836.e: Madhyamaka philosophy is still a foundation of Tibetan monastic education today. Nagarjuna also had a strong influence in China and Japan.

68837.q: In which country is Amida Buddhism one of the largest Buddhist branches today?
68837.e: In Japan, the Pure Land schools are among the largest Buddhist communities. In Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, by contrast, Theravada prevails.
68837.m: Amida Buddhism is especially widespread in Japan.

68838.q: What is the paradise called in which followers of Amida Buddhism hope to be reborn?
68838.e: The Pure Land (Sanskrit Sukhavati) is the land of the Buddha Amida. There one can attain enlightenment under ideal conditions.
68838.m: Amida’s paradise is called the Pure Land.

68839.q: According to tradition, in which direction does Amitabha’s Pure Land lie?
68839.e: Amitabha is regarded as the Buddha of the West. That is why believers speak of the ‘Western Paradise’.
68839.m: Amitabha’s Pure Land lies in the west.

68840.q: What is the Japanese formula of the nembutsu?
68840.e: The nembutsu is the invocation of the Buddha Amida. In the Pure Land schools it is regarded as the central practice.
68840.m: The nembutsu is Namu Amida Butsu.

68841.q: According to the monk Honen, what should believers do above all to reach the Pure Land?
a: Call on the name of the Buddha Amida
68841.e: Honen founded the Jodo-shu in Japan in 1175. He taught that calling on Amida (nembutsu) is enough, opening the way for people of all classes.
68841.m: Honen taught calling on Amida’s name.

68842.q: What was new for Japan about Shinran’s school, Jodo Shinshu?
a: Its priests were allowed to marry and have families
68842.e: Shinran, a disciple of Honen, married himself. In Jodo Shinshu, priests may still have families today, which was unusual for Buddhist monks at the time.
68842.m: In Shinran’s Jodo Shinshu, priests may marry.

68843.q: According to tradition, what did the future Buddha Amida promise in his vows?
a: To bring all who call on him with trust to the Pure Land
To admit only monks to paradise
To found a kingdom on earth
68843.e: As the bodhisattva Dharmakara he made 48 vows. The 18th vow promises rebirth in the Pure Land to all who call on him with trust.
68843.m: Amida promised the Pure Land to all believers.

68844.q: What do followers of Jodo Shinshu rely on for their liberation?
68844.e: Jodo Shinshu calls this tariki, ‘other power’, as opposed to jiriki, ‘own power’. Liberation comes through Amida’s power alone.
68844.m: Jodo Shinshu relies on Amida’s power.

68845.q: Where did the Pure Land school develop as a branch of its own before it reached Japan?
68845.e: In China, Huiyuan founded a community devoted to Amitabha in the year 402. From there the teaching spread to Korea and Japan.
68845.m: The Pure Land school arose in China.

68846.e: Vajra means thunderbolt or diamond and stands for indestructibility. Yana means vehicle.

68847.q: What is the Tibetan yogi Milarepa still famous for today?
a: His songs about life as a hermit
68847.e: Milarepa lived in the 11th and 12th centuries and meditated in caves for years. His ‘Hundred Thousand Songs’ are very well known in Tibet.
68847.m: Milarepa is famous for his songs.

68848.q: Which ritual object is used together with the vajra in Vajrayana and stands for wisdom?
68848.e: The vajra and bell are usually held in the right and left hand. The vajra stands for method and compassion, the bell for wisdom.
68848.m: The bell complements the vajra as a symbol of wisdom.

68849.q: Who is worshipped in Tibetan Buddhism as ‘Guru Rinpoche’?
68849.e: Padmasambhava is said to have come to Tibet in the 8th century and helped build Samye Monastery. The Nyingma in particular revere him as a second Buddha.
68849.m: In Tibet, Padmasambhava is called Guru Rinpoche.

68850.q: What happens to a Tibetan sand mandala once it is finished?
a: It is destroyed and the sand scattered.
It is put under glass and exhibited.
It is buried in a monastery.
It is copied onto a thangka.
68850.e: Monks often spend days laying out the mandala. Afterwards it is swept away, and the sand often goes into a river or lake; this shows impermanence.
68850.m: Sand mandalas are dissolved to show impermanence.

68851.q: To which country did the monk Kukai bring esoteric Buddhist teachings from China in the 9th century?
68851.e: Kukai, also called Kobo Daishi, founded the Shingon school in Japan. Its centre is still Mount Koya today.
68851.m: Kukai brought esoteric Buddhism to Japan.

68852.q: Which of the four major schools of Tibetan Buddhism is regarded as the oldest?
68852.e: Nyingma means ‘the old ones’. The school traces itself back to the first spread of Buddhism in Tibet in the 8th century.
68852.m: The Nyingma are the oldest Tibetan school.

68853.q: From which country did many teachers come in the Middle Ages to bring Buddhism to Tibet?
68853.e: Scholars such as Padmasambhava and Atisha came from India to Tibet. Tibetan translators rendered many Sanskrit texts into their language.
68853.m: Tibetan Buddhism has its roots in India.

68854.q: What is a tulku in Tibetan Buddhism?
a: A teacher recognised as the rebirth of a predecessor
A festival for Tibetan New Year
68854.e: Tulkus are sought out as children and recognised as the rebirth of a deceased teacher. The first such line was that of the Karmapas, the best known that of the Dalai Lamas.
68854.m: A tulku is a reborn teacher.

68855.q: How is a new Dalai Lama traditionally found?
a: A child regarded as his rebirth is sought
The monks choose the oldest lama
The predecessor’s son inherits the office
68855.e: After a Dalai Lama dies, monks search for a child using signs and tests. The title was first granted in 1578 by the Mongol ruler Altan Khan.
68855.m: A new Dalai Lama is sought as a reborn child.

68856.q: What does the Mongolian word ‘Dalai’ in the title Dalai Lama mean?
68856.e: ‘Dalai’ is a translation of ‘Gyatso’, part of the name Sonam Gyatso. The title is often interpreted as ‘Ocean of Wisdom’.

68857.q: Which number Dalai Lama is Tenzin Gyatso, born in 1935?
68857.e: Tenzin Gyatso was recognised as a child as the rebirth of his predecessor. He belongs to the Gelug school.
68857.m: Tenzin Gyatso is the 14th Dalai Lama.

68858.q: Which Dalai Lama, called ‘the Great Fifth’, had the Potala Palace in Lhasa built from 1645?
68858.e: Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso united Tibet under the rule of the Dalai Lamas with Mongol help. The Potala became their winter palace and seat of government.
68858.m: The Great Fifth Dalai Lama had the Potala built.

68859.q: Which lottery procedure did China’s Qing dynasty introduce in 1793 to identify high-ranking reincarnations?
68859.e: The names of the candidates were placed on slips in a golden urn and drawn. Today China refers to this procedure to gain influence over the succession.
68859.m: The Qing introduced the Golden Urn in 1793.

68860.q: What happened to the boy the Dalai Lama recognised as Panchen Lama in 1995?
a: Chinese authorities detained him, and he has been missing ever since
He became the next Dalai Lama
He fled to India and lives there publicly
68860.e: Gedhun Choekyi Nyima was taken into custody shortly after his recognition. China installed another candidate as Panchen Lama.
68860.m: The Panchen Lama recognised in 1995 has been missing ever since.

68861.q: What did the Dalai Lama declare about his succession in July 2025?
a: The office will continue, and his own office will recognise the rebirth
He would be the last Dalai Lama
The people should elect the successor
68861.e: Shortly before his 90th birthday he confirmed that the institution would continue. Recognition lies solely with the Gaden Phodrang Trust, his office.
68861.m: The Dalai Lama wants his office to recognise his successor.

68862.q: Which dynasty did Emperor Ashoka belong to?
68862.e: Ashoka was a grandson of the dynasty’s founder, Chandragupta Maurya. The Maurya Empire covered large parts of the Indian subcontinent.
68862.m: Ashoka was a ruler of the Maurya dynasty.

68863.q: According to Ashoka’s own inscriptions, which bloody campaign led him to turn away from violence?
68863.e: In the 13th Rock Edict, Ashoka regrets the many dead and deported in Kalinga. After that he wanted to rule only through the dharma.
68863.m: The Kalinga War made Ashoka change his ways.

68864.q: How did Emperor Ashoka make his messages known throughout the empire?
a: With inscriptions on rocks and pillars
68864.e: Ashoka had his edicts on dharma, non-violence and tolerance carved into rocks and pillars. Most are written in the Brahmi script.
68864.m: Ashoka proclaimed his edicts on rocks and pillars.

68865.q: Which work from Ashoka’s time is today the national emblem of India?
68865.e: The capital shows four lions standing back to back. It once crowned a pillar at the place of the Buddha’s first sermon.
68865.m: The Lion Capital of Sarnath is India’s national emblem.

68866.q: How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra in the middle of the Indian flag have?
68866.e: The blue wheel comes from the Lion Capital and stands for the dharma. Its 24 spokes are often linked to the hours of the day.

68867.q: Which religion did Ashoka help to spread beyond India as far as Sri Lanka?
68867.e: Ashoka sent missionaries to other countries, according to tradition his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka. There Buddhism is still the most important religion today.
68867.m: Ashoka promoted the spread of Buddhism.

68868.q: What was the third Buddhist council under Ashoka meant to achieve?
a: Cleanse the teaching of false doctrines
Decide on a war against Kalinga
68868.e: According to Theravada tradition, the council took place in Ashoka’s capital, Pataliputra. Under Moggaliputta Tissa, the teaching was to be protected against false interpretations.
68868.m: The third council was meant to purify Buddhist teaching.

68869.q: What does an Ashoka inscription in Greek and Aramaic in present-day Afghanistan show?
a: Ashoka himself spoke no Indian language
68869.e: The bilingual rock inscription near Kandahar was found in 1958. It shows the contacts between the Maurya Empire and the Hellenistic world.
68869.m: With his inscriptions, Ashoka also addressed Greek subjects.

68870.q: Why was almost nothing known about Emperor Ashoka in India for a long time?
a: Nobody could read his old script any more
His inscriptions were all under water
He had never left anything in writing
68870.e: Only in 1837 did the Briton James Prinsep decipher the Brahmi script. This made the edicts readable again, and Ashoka was rediscovered as a historical figure.
68870.m: Ashoka was rediscovered through the deciphering of the Brahmi script.

68871.q: Which religion spread along the Silk Road from India to China in the first millennium?
68871.e: Monks and merchants brought Buddhism to China via the oasis cities of Central Asia. From there it spread further to Korea and Japan.
68871.m: Buddhism reached China via the Silk Road.

68872.q: From which language did monks translate most Buddhist scriptures into Chinese?
68872.e: Many Buddhist texts were written in Sanskrit or related Indian languages. Translators along the Silk Road rendered them into Chinese over centuries.
68872.m: Buddhist scriptures were mainly translated from Sanskrit into Chinese.

68873.q: Which classic Chinese novel was inspired by the monk Xuanzang’s journey to India (629 to 645)?
68873.e: In the 16th-century novel, the Monkey King Sun Wukong accompanies the monk. The historical Xuanzang brought hundreds of scriptures to China.
68873.m: Xuanzang’s journey inspired the novel ‘Journey to the West’.

68874.q: With which technique were Buddhist scriptures already being printed in China in the 9th century?
68874.e: In woodblock printing, a whole page is carved in mirror image into a wooden block. The Diamond Sutra of 868 from Dunhuang is regarded as the oldest dated printed book.
68874.m: China printed books with woodblocks long before Gutenberg.

68875.q: Where did the two huge Buddha statues stand that the Taliban blew up in 2001?
68875.e: The statues dated from the 6th century and were carved into a cliff. The valley lay on a trade route between India and Central Asia.
68875.m: The Buddhas of Bamiyan were destroyed in 2001.

68876.q: In which region did Hellenistic art combine with Buddhist motifs to create early images of the Buddha?
68876.e: In Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan, the Buddha is shown with flowing robes and wavy hair. Greek influences reached the region from the time of Alexander the Great.
68876.m: Gandhara art combines Greek and Buddhist forms.

68877.q: Which Indian ruler of the 3rd century BC promoted Buddhism and sent monks to other countries?
68877.e: Emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhism after a bloody war. He had edicts carved in stone and sent monks as far as Sri Lanka and Central Asia.
68877.m: Emperor Ashoka carried Buddhism beyond India.

68878.q: What are the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang on the Silk Road famous for?
a: Hundreds of caves with Buddhist paintings
The tomb of the first emperor
68878.e: Over a thousand years, cave temples were carved into the cliffs near Dunhuang and painted. Dunhuang was an important stopping place for merchants and pilgrims.
68878.m: The Mogao Caves show Buddhist art on the Silk Road.

a: A mindfulness programme for coping with stress
68879.e: Jon Kabat-Zinn developed Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction in the USA in 1979. He combined meditation from Buddhist traditions with a non-religious course.
68879.m: MBSR is a mindfulness programme for coping with stress.

68880.q: From which religion do the forms of meditation come on which many modern mindfulness programmes are based?
68880.e: Programmes such as MBSR take exercises from Buddhist traditions but offer them without a religious framework. A classic MBSR course lasts eight weeks.
68880.m: Mindfulness programmes go back to Buddhist meditation.

68881.q: Which Buddhist path does right mindfulness belong to?
68881.e: The Noble Eightfold Path shows the way out of suffering. Right mindfulness (Pali: sati) is one of its eight parts.
68881.m: Right mindfulness is part of the Noble Eightfold Path.

68882.q: In a simple mindfulness meditation, what do people often focus their attention on first?
68882.e: The breath is always there and is a good way to arrive in the moment. The Satipatthana Sutta names four foundations of mindfulness; mindfulness of breathing belongs to the first, the body.
68882.m: Mindfulness meditation often begins with the breath.

68883.q: Which MBSR exercise guides attention through the regions of the body one after another?
68883.e: In the body scan you usually lie down and notice one part of the body after another without changing anything. The exercise trains non-judgemental attention.
68883.m: The body scan guides attention through the body.

68884.q: What was Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) originally developed for?
68884.e: Segal, Williams and Teasdale combined MBSR with cognitive behavioural therapy. Studies show a benefit for people with several episodes of depression.
68884.m: MBCT aims to prevent relapses into depression.

68885.q: With which food do participants in MBSR courses often practise mindful eating for the first time?
68885.e: The raisin is looked at, felt, smelt and eaten slowly. In this way an everyday action is experienced consciously.
68885.m: The raisin exercise trains mindful eating.

68886.q: What is the well-known definition of mindfulness coined by the founder of MBSR?
a: on purpose, in the moment, non-judgementally
68886.e: Mindfulness means paying attention in a particular way: deliberately, in the present moment and without judging. This definition shapes many programmes.
68886.m: Mindfulness is deliberate, non-judgemental attention in the moment.

68887.q: Which term made the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh known worldwide?
68887.e: He called for meditation to be combined with work for peace and social justice. The term became the name of a worldwide movement.
68887.m: Thich Nhat Hanh coined engaged Buddhism.

68888.q: What is the name of the monastery Thich Nhat Hanh founded in south-west France in 1982?
68888.e: Plum Village (Village des Pruniers) lies east of Bordeaux. It became the centre of his worldwide community.
68888.m: Thich Nhat Hanh founded Plum Village monastery.

68889.q: Who nominated Thich Nhat Hanh for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967?
68889.e: King called him an ‘apostle of peace and non-violence’. The prize was not awarded that year.
68889.m: Martin Luther King nominated Thich Nhat Hanh for the Nobel Prize.

68890.q: What does Thich Nhat Hanh’s term ‘interbeing’ mean?
a: Everything is connected with everything and depends on each other
68890.e: Thich Nhat Hanh explained it with a sheet of paper: it contains the cloud, the rain, the tree and the logger. He also named his order after the term.
68890.m: Interbeing means that everything is connected.

68891.q: Which 1975 book by Thich Nhat Hanh made mindfulness in everyday tasks such as washing up known worldwide?
a: The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying
68891.e: The book began as a letter to co-workers in Vietnam. It shows how any activity can be done with awareness.
68891.m: ‘The Miracle of Mindfulness’ is a well-known book by Thich Nhat Hanh.

68892.q: In which year was Thich Nhat Hanh able to travel to Vietnam again for the first time after almost 40 years in exile?
68892.e: He had gone abroad in 1966 and was not allowed to return for a long time. In 2005 he was given permission to visit his homeland.
68892.m: Thich Nhat Hanh first returned to Vietnam in 2005.

68893.q: In which year did Thich Nhat Hanh die at his home monastery in Hue?
68893.e: He died on 22 January 2022 at the age of 95. He spent his last years at Tu Hieu Temple.

68894.q: How did Thich Nhat Hanh’s movement help during the Vietnam War?
a: Volunteers rebuilt destroyed villages, schools and clinics
It sold weapons to both sides
It took all the monks abroad
68894.e: The ‘School of Youth for Social Service’ sent young volunteers into war zones. In this way Buddhist ethics was combined with practical help.
68894.m: Thich Nhat Hanh combined meditation with help for war victims.

68895.q: What does the name ‘Akal Takht’ literally mean?
68895.e: ‘Akal’ means timeless and refers to God; ‘Takht’ means throne. The name expresses that authority is exercised here in the name of God.
68895.m: The Akal Takht is the Throne of the Timeless One.

68896.q: What did Guru Hargobind want to show by building the Akal Takht next to the Golden Temple?
a: That the Sikhs also have worldly leadership
That the Sikhs no longer need gurus
That the Sikhs were converting to Islam
That women may not enter the temple
68896.e: Guru Hargobind had the Akal Takht built in 1606. Alongside the Golden Temple as the spiritual centre, it was to make the worldly authority of the Sikhs visible.
68896.m: The Akal Takht stands for the worldly leadership of the Sikhs.

a: In the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar
Next to Parliament in New Delhi
On the banks of the Ganges in Varanasi
68897.e: The Akal Takht is in Amritsar in Punjab, directly opposite the Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple. Together they form the most important centre of Sikhism.
68897.m: The Akal Takht stands opposite the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

68898.q: Which religion does the Akal Takht belong to?
68898.e: The Akal Takht is the most important of the five thrones of authority in Sikhism. It stands in Amritsar in Punjab.
68898.m: The Akal Takht is a central place of Sikhism.

68899.q: How many takhts (thrones of authority) are there in Sikhism?
68899.e: Sikhism has five takhts, including Patna Sahib and Hazur Sahib. The Akal Takht is regarded as the most important of them.
68899.m: Among the five Sikh takhts, the Akal Takht is the most important.

68900.q: In which military operation was the Akal Takht badly damaged in June 1984?
68900.e: In June 1984 the Indian Army stormed the temple complex to drive out armed separatists. The Akal Takht was badly destroyed and later rebuilt.
68900.m: Operation Blue Star in 1984 badly damaged the Akal Takht.

68901.q: What is the role of the head (jathedar) of the Akal Takht?
a: He speaks for the Sikh community and decides religious questions
He governs the Indian state of Punjab
He translates the holy scripture into English
68901.e: The jathedar is the head of the Akal Takht. He is appointed by the Sikh body SGPC and can issue binding instructions to the Sikhs.
68901.m: The jathedar speaks for the Sikh community.

68902.q: In which city does the Akal Takht stand together with the most important Sikh shrine?
68902.e: The Akal Takht stands in Amritsar in Punjab, opposite the Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib). From here it issues binding instructions to the Sikhs.
68902.m: The Akal Takht and the Golden Temple are in Amritsar.

68903.q: What is special about the monks of the Digambara branch of Jainism?
a: They stay silent all their lives
They live married in the monastery
68903.e: ‘Digambara’ means ‘clad in the sky’ or ‘sky-clad’. The monks live naked as a sign of owning absolutely nothing.
68903.m: Digambara monks are sky-clad and wear no clothes.

68904.q: Which religion does the Digambara branch belong to?
68904.e: Jainism is divided into two major branches: the Digambara and the Shvetambara. Shvetambara monks wear white clothing.
68904.m: The Digambara are one of the two major branches of Jainism.

68905.q: What does a Digambara monk use a whisk of peacock feathers for?
a: To gently brush small creatures away
68905.e: Jains do not want to harm any living being. With the soft whisk, the monk brushes insects away before he sits down.
68905.m: The peacock-feather whisk protects small creatures.

68906.q: What does ahimsa, a basic principle of the Jains, mean?
68906.e: Ahimsa means not harming. Jains try not to hurt any living being and so live strictly vegetarian lives.

68907.e: Shvetambara monks and nuns wear simple white robes. This visibly distinguishes them from the naked Digambara monks.

68908.q: In Jainism, what are the 24 great teachers called who showed the way to liberation?
68908.e: Tirthankara means ‘ford-maker’: they show the way across the river of rebirths. Bodhisattvas belong to Buddhism, avatars to Hinduism.

68909.q: What do monks of some Shvetambara groups, such as the Sthanakvasi, wear over their mouths?
68909.e: The mouth cloth (muhpatti) is meant to stop tiny creatures from being swallowed or hurt when speaking or breathing. It is an expression of ahimsa, non-violence.
68909.m: The mouth cloth protects the tiniest creatures and stands for ahimsa.

68910.q: Who is regarded as the last of the 24 Tirthankaras and the most important teacher of Jainism?
68910.e: Mahavira lived in northern India in the 6th or 5th century BC, around the same time as the Buddha. Shvetambara and Digambara both revere him.
68910.m: Mahavira is the most important teacher of Jainism.

a: The collection of holy scriptures of Zoroastrianism
The law book of the Sikhs
68911.e: The Avesta contains prayers, hymns and purity rules of the Zoroastrians. It is written in the ancient Iranian language Avestan.
68911.m: The Avesta is the holy scripture of the Zoroastrians.

68912.q: Which part of the Avesta is regarded as the work of Zarathustra himself?
