68912.e: The Gathas are 17 hymns in archaic Old Avestan and are attributed to Zarathustra. They are embedded in the liturgy of the Yasna.

68913.q: What does the Vendidad (Videvdad) in the Avesta mainly deal with?
a: Purity laws and warding off demons
68913.e: The Vendidad, the ‘law against the demons’, regulates ritual purity, for example how to deal with the dead. It is a kind of priestly law book.
68913.m: The Vendidad contains the purity laws of Zoroastrianism.

68914.q: In which language is the Avesta written?
68914.e: Avestan is an old Iranian language related to Sanskrit. Later the Avesta was rendered into Middle Persian in a commentary, the Zand.
68914.m: The Avesta is written in the ancient Iranian language Avestan.

68915.q: According to Zoroastrian teaching, what is the bridge called that every soul must cross after death?
68915.e: For the righteous, the Chinvat Bridge becomes wide and leads to paradise; for liars it becomes as narrow as a blade. There the fate of the soul is decided.
68915.m: At the Chinvat Bridge the soul is judged after death.

68916.q: Which pair of terms describes the ethical dualism of Zoroastrianism?
68916.e: Asha stands for truth and cosmic order, Druj for lies and chaos. Every person is to choose Asha freely.
68916.m: In Zoroastrianism, the truth Asha fights against the lie Druj.

68917.q: Which Zoroastrian idea is found in a similar form in Judaism, Christianity and Islam?
a: A saviour at the end of time and a Last Judgement
Worship of the emperor as a god
68917.e: Zoroastrianism expects the saviour Saoshyant, who will raise the dead and defeat evil. The Abrahamic religions have similar ideas about the end of time.
68917.m: Zoroastrianism has a saviour at the end of time.

68918.q: What is the three-part principle of Zoroastrian ethics?
a: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds
68918.e: In Avestan it is Humata, Hukhta, Hvarshta. It sums up how a person stands on the side of good.
68918.m: Zoroastrians strive for good thoughts, good words and good deeds.

68919.e: Baha’u’llah is an Arabic title of honour meaning ‘Glory of God’. His birth name was Mirza Husayn Ali Nuri.

68920.q: In which city was Baha’u’llah born in 1817?
68920.e: Baha’u’llah was born in Tehran in 1817 into a noble family. Later he was exiled from Persia because of his faith.
68920.m: Baha’u’llah was born in Tehran in 1817.

68921.q: Who was Baha’u’llah’s forerunner, executed in Tabriz in 1850?
68921.e: The Bab announced the coming of a new messenger of God and was publicly shot in 1850. Baha’is see Baha’u’llah as the fulfilment of this announcement.
68921.m: The Bab is regarded as the forerunner of Baha’u’llah.

68922.q: What does the twelve-day Baha’i festival of Ridvan commemorate?
a: Baha’u’llah’s declaration that he was a messenger of God
68922.e: Before leaving Baghdad in 1863, Baha’u’llah spent twelve days in the Garden of Ridvan and proclaimed his mission there. Ridvan is regarded as the most important Baha’i festival.
68922.m: The festival of Ridvan commemorates Baha’u’llah’s declaration in Baghdad.

68923.q: Which basic idea is at the centre of Baha’u’llah’s teaching?
a: The oneness of God, of the religions and of humanity
The superiority of a single people
The rejection of all earlier prophets
Withdrawal from the world into monasteries
68923.e: Baha’u’llah taught that all the great religions come from the same God and that humanity is one. His laws are in the Kitab-i-Aqdas, the ‘Most Holy Book’.
68923.m: Baha’is stress the oneness of God, religions and humanity.

68924.q: In which city did Baha’u’llah spend his last exile from 1868?
68924.e: The Ottomans exiled him to the fortress city of Acre. He died in 1892 at the nearby mansion of Bahji, where his shrine is now the holiest place for Baha’is.
68924.m: Baha’u’llah spent his last years near Acre.

68925.q: Whom did Baha’u’llah appoint as his successor and interpreter of his writings?
68925.e: In his will, Baha’u’llah named his eldest son Abdu’l-Baha the centre of the covenant. Only after him did Shoghi Effendi follow as Guardian.

68926.q: Where is the Universal House of Justice, the supreme body of the Baha’is, based?
68926.e: The body, first elected in 1963, is based on Mount Carmel in Haifa. The Shrine of the Bab with its famous terraced gardens is also there.
68926.m: The Universal House of Justice is based in Haifa.

68927.q: How is the Confucian term ‘ren’ usually translated?
68927.e: Ren is the highest virtue for Confucius and means kindness and humanity towards others. The character is made up of the parts for ‘person’ and ‘two’.

68928.q: What is the Golden Rule in the Analects of Confucius?
a: What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others
68928.e: Confucius phrases the rule negatively, as a prohibition. It is regarded as the core of ren, because it reasons from one’s own feelings to those of others.
68928.m: Confucius taught not to do to others what you do not want yourself.

68929.q: Whom does Confucius mean by the ‘gentleman’ (junzi) who realises ren?
a: A person who is exemplary through character and education
A person from a noble family
A hermit living far from people
A warrior in the emperor’s service
68929.e: Junzi originally meant ‘son of a prince’. Confucius reinterpreted the term: noble is whoever stands out through virtue and education, not through birth.
68929.m: For Confucius, noble is whoever is exemplary in character.

68930.q: Which virtue does Confucius name as the root of ren, humaneness?
68930.e: The Analects of Confucius say that filial piety and respect for older siblings are the root of humaneness. In the family you learn to treat others well.
68930.m: For Confucius, humaneness begins in the family.

68931.q: What does the Confucian term ‘li’ (礼) refer to?
68931.e: Li covers rituals, forms of politeness and rules of proper behaviour. They give order to living together and to relationships.
68931.m: In Confucianism, li stands for rites and good custom.

68932.q: What does the Confucian term ‘ren’ mean?
68932.e: For Confucius, ren is the most important virtue: kindness and humanity towards others. It shows itself in proper behaviour according to the rites (li).
68932.m: For Confucius, humaneness and custom belong together.

68933.q: Which relationship is especially important in Confucianism and is regulated by rites?
a: The relationship between parents and children
The relationship between trader and customer
The relationship between humans and animals
The relationship between strangers on a journey
68933.e: Children’s reverence for their parents (filial piety) is regarded as the basis of all virtues. Rites also regulate the veneration of ancestors.
68933.m: Respect for parents is central in Confucianism.

68934.q: Which of the Confucian Five Classics collects rules and explanations about the rites?
68934.e: The Book of Rites (Liji) describes ceremonies, mourning customs and rules of propriety. Two of its chapters were later read as books in their own right.
68934.m: The Book of Rites is called the Liji in Chinese.

68935.q: In which dynasty did Zhu Xi (1130 to 1200) live?
68935.e: Zhu Xi worked during the Southern Song. He is regarded as the most important thinker of Neo-Confucianism.
68935.m: Zhu Xi lived in the Song dynasty.

68936.q: Which pair of concepts is at the centre of Zhu Xi’s philosophy?
68936.e: For Zhu Xi, everything consists of the shaping principle li and the material force qi. This li is not the same character as li for rites.
68936.m: Zhu Xi explained the world through principle and vital matter.

68937.q: Which collection of texts did Zhu Xi compile with commentaries?
68937.e: The Four Books are the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. With Zhu Xi’s commentaries they became the basic texts of education.
68937.m: Zhu Xi made the Four Books the core of education.

68938.q: Which method of gaining knowledge did Zhu Xi emphasise?
68938.e: By ‘gewu’ Zhu Xi meant examining the principle in individual things. In this way a person gains knowledge and moral clarity step by step.
68938.m: Zhu Xi taught the investigation of things as the way to knowledge.

68939.q: Which teachings did Neo-Confucianism mainly set itself against, while still taking ideas from them?
68939.e: Neo-Confucians wanted to strengthen Confucianism against the influence of Buddhism and Daoism. In doing so, they took up their metaphysical questions.
68939.m: Neo-Confucianism was a response to Buddhism and Daoism.

68940.q: What were the commentaries of the Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi used for in China for centuries?
a: As material for the civil service examinations
68940.e: Anyone who wanted to become an official had to know the classics as Zhu Xi interpreted them. The examination system was only abolished in 1905.
68940.m: Zhu Xi’s commentaries were exam material for officials.

68941.q: Which scholar is regarded as the most important representative of Neo-Confucianism?
68941.e: Zhu Xi lived in the 12th century and brought together Neo-Confucian teaching. Laozi, by contrast, is regarded as the founder of Daoism.
68941.m: Zhu Xi is the most important Neo-Confucian.

68942.q: In which country did Neo-Confucianism become the state ideology of the Joseon dynasty?
68942.e: The Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) based state and society on the teaching of Zhu Xi. Buddhism was pushed back as a result.

68943.q: Which famous parable comes from the Zhuangzi?
a: The parable of the mustard seed
68943.e: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and afterwards wondered whether a butterfly was dreaming it was Zhuangzi. The parable questions the fixed boundary between self and world.
68943.m: The butterfly dream shows how fluid the boundaries of reality are.

68944.q: Roughly in which century did the Daoist thinker Zhuangzi live?
68944.e: Zhuangzi lived from about 365 to 290 BC, in the Warring States period. This made him a contemporary of the Confucian Mencius.
68944.m: Zhuangzi lived in the 4th century BC.

68945.q: What does the parable in the Zhuangzi about the cook whose knife never goes blunt when carving an ox show?
a: Effortless mastery in harmony with nature
The value of hard, dogged work
The duty not to kill animals
The power of a good tool
68945.e: Cook Ding follows the natural joints of the animal instead of cutting against bone. The image shows effortless mastery in harmony with the Dao.
68945.m: Cook Ding cuts effortlessly because he follows the natural joints.

68946.q: What is the famous conversation in the Zhuangzi about the joy of fish about?
a: The limits of what we can know
68946.e: On a bridge, Zhuangzi’s friend Huizi asks how Zhuangzi can know that the fish are happy. The conversation is a classic on the limits of knowledge.
68946.m: Zhuangzi and Huizi argued about the joy of fish.

68947.q: According to tradition, how did Zhuangzi react to the death of his wife?
a: He drummed on a bowl and sang
68947.e: Zhuangzi explained that death is only a transformation, like the change of the seasons. Endless mourning is therefore against the natural course of things.
68947.m: Zhuangzi saw death as a natural transformation.

68948.q: What does the giant bird Peng in the first chapter of the Zhuangzi stand for?
68948.e: The fish Kun turns into the enormous bird Peng, which flies thousands of miles. The chapter is called ‘Free and Easy Wandering’.
68948.m: In Zhuangzi, Kun and Peng stand for boundless freedom.

68949.q: According to legend, how did Zhuangzi explain why he would not accept a post as minister?
a: He would rather live like a turtle in the mud
He was too old for office
He had already become a monk
He had no money for the journey
68949.e: A dead sacred turtle may be honoured in the temple, but a living one would rather drag its tail through the mud. So he preferred freedom to fame.
68949.m: Zhuangzi preferred a free life to a post of honour.

68950.q: How does the book Zhuangzi convey its teaching, unlike the terse Daodejing?
68950.e: The Daodejing consists of short, puzzling sayings. The Zhuangzi, by contrast, tells witty stories and parables, such as the butterfly dream.
68950.m: The Zhuangzi conveys its teaching with stories and parables.

68951.q: How is the Daoist term ‘wu wei’ usually translated?
68951.e: Wu wei literally means ‘without doing’. It does not mean laziness, but acting without force, following the natural course.
68951.m: Wu wei is acting without force.

68952.q: In which founding text of Daoism is wu wei a central term?
68952.e: The Daodejing is attributed to Laozi and has 81 short chapters. It recommends non-action to the sage and to the ruler.

68953.q: Which paradoxical formula from the Daodejing sums up wu wei?
a: Through not doing, nothing is left undone
Rest is the beginning of the end
68953.e: The formula ‘wu wei er wu bu wei’ appears in chapter 48, for example. It says that it is precisely unforced action that lets everything succeed.
68953.m: According to the Daodejing, through not doing nothing is left undone.

68954.q: Which image from nature does the Daodejing often use to illustrate wu wei?
68954.e: Water is soft and yielding, yet it wears away even hard stone. It flows to low places and does not compete.
68954.m: In Daoism, water is the image of gentle action.

68955.q: What does wu wei mean for a ruler in the Daodejing?
a: He interferes as little as possible in people’s lives
He leaves power to the army
68955.e: The ideal ruler governs so modestly that the people say everything happened by itself. According to Laozi, too many laws only create unrest.
68955.m: According to Laozi, a wise ruler governs with as little interference as possible.

68956.q: Which Daoist term for ‘being so of itself’ is closely linked to wu wei?
68956.e: Ziran describes the spontaneity with which things unfold naturally. Whoever practises wu wei lets ziran happen.
68956.m: Ziran is the natural ‘being so of itself’.

68957.q: Which other great Chinese thinker also praised ruling through non-action?
68957.e: In the Analects of Confucius, the mythical ruler Shun is praised for ruling without interfering. So wu wei was not only a Daoist term.
68957.m: Confucius also knew of ruling through non-action.

68958.q: According to Chinese folk belief, which god reports to the Jade Emperor about the family before New Year?
68958.e: The Kitchen God Zao Jun watches the family throughout the year. So that he gives a good report, he is given sweets before his journey.
68958.m: The Kitchen God reports to the Jade Emperor about the family.

68959.q: Who is at the top of the heavenly hierarchy in Chinese folk religion?
a: The Queen Mother of the West
68959.e: The Jade Emperor rules heaven like an emperor with his officials. The world of the gods thus mirrors the administration of ancient China.
68959.m: The Jade Emperor rules over the Chinese gods.

68960.q: Which goddess is especially worshipped by seafarers in Fujian and Taiwan?
68960.e: Mazu is said to have lived in the 10th century as a girl called Lin Moniang and to have rescued sailors. In Taiwan she is one of the most popular deities.
68960.m: Mazu is the protective goddess of seafarers.

68961.q: Which general of the Three Kingdoms is worshipped as the god of loyalty and war?
68961.e: After his death Guan Yu was deified as Guandi. He is also regarded as the patron of merchants and police officers.
68961.m: Guan Yu is worshipped as the god of loyalty.

68962.q: At which festival do Chinese people tend the graves of their ancestors in spring?
68962.e: At the Qingming Festival, around the beginning of April, families clean the graves and make offerings. That is why it is also called Tomb-Sweeping Day.
68962.m: At the Qingming Festival, families honour their ancestors at the graves.

68963.q: What do believers often burn as an offering for the dead?
68963.e: So-called hell money or spirit money is meant to benefit the ancestors in the afterlife. Today paper models of houses or cars are burnt too.
68963.m: Burnt paper money is meant to help the ancestors in the afterlife.

68964.q: In which lunar month does the Ghost Festival take place, when hungry ghosts are fed?
68964.e: In the seventh lunar month, the gates of the underworld are said to open. On the 15th day, food and offerings are set out for the wandering ghosts.
68964.m: The Ghost Festival falls in the seventh lunar month.

68965.q: According to folk belief, which local god protects a village or piece of land?
68965.e: Tudigong is the earth god of a place and often has a small shrine by the roadside. He is regarded as a lowly official of the gods, close to ordinary people.
68965.m: Tudigong is the earth god of a place.

68966.q: Which political upheaval in 1868 began the building of State Shinto in Japan?
68966.e: With the Meiji Restoration, power went back to the emperor. Shinto became the ideological support of the new state.
68966.m: State Shinto arose with the Meiji Restoration.

68967.q: Which religion was closely mixed with Shinto in Japan until 1868 and was then separated from it by the state?
68967.e: For centuries, kami were often regarded as manifestations of Buddhas. The Meiji government separated the two religions, and many Buddhist temples were damaged afterwards.
68967.m: From 1868, Shinto and Buddhism were separated in Japan.

68968.q: According to the teaching of State Shinto, from which deity was the Tenno descended?
68968.e: The sun goddess Amaterasu was regarded as the ancestor of the imperial house. Her main shrine is the Ise Shrine.
68968.m: The Tenno was regarded as a descendant of the sun goddess Amaterasu.

68969.q: How did the Meiji government get round the contradiction between State Shinto and freedom of religion?
a: It declared shrine Shinto a state cult rather than a religion
It made Buddhism the state religion
68969.e: Since shrine visits counted as a patriotic duty rather than religion, they could be demanded of everyone. Formally, the religious freedom of the 1889 constitution remained.
68969.m: State Shinto officially counted as a state cult, not a religion.

68970.q: Which document of 1890 linked loyalty to the emperor with Confucian values and was read out in all schools?
a: The Charter Oath of Five Articles
68970.e: The Rescript on Education demanded loyalty to the emperor and filial piety. It was solemnly recited in schools and revered along with portraits of the emperor.
68970.m: The 1890 Rescript on Education shaped schools in the spirit of State Shinto.

68971.q: Who abolished State Shinto in December 1945 with the Shinto Directive?
68971.e: On 15 December 1945, the occupation authority under General MacArthur banned state support for Shinto. Shrines became private religious bodies.
68971.m: The occupying power ended State Shinto in 1945.

68972.q: What did Emperor Hirohito deny in his New Year declaration of 1 January 1946?
68972.e: In the so-called Humanity Declaration, he rejected the idea that the emperor was a living god. This removed a central point of State Shinto.

68973.q: In which city is the Yasukuni Shrine?
68973.e: The shrine is in Chiyoda ward in the centre of Tokyo, near the Imperial Palace. It commemorates the people who died for Japan in war.
68973.m: The Yasukuni Shrine is in Tokyo.

68974.q: For whom was the Yasukuni Shrine originally founded?
a: For those killed in the wars around the Meiji Restoration
For the victims of a great earthquake
68974.e: Emperor Meiji had the shrine built in 1869 for those killed in the Boshin War, which secured the Meiji Restoration. Later, the dead of all Japan’s wars were added.
68974.m: The Yasukuni Shrine was founded for Japan’s war dead.

68975.q: What does the name ‘Yasukuni’ roughly mean?
68975.e: The name goes back to a classical Chinese expression and means bringing peace to the country. It was given in 1879.

68976.q: Roughly how many war dead are commemorated at the Yasukuni Shrine?
68976.e: The shrine’s register lists more than 2.46 million names. Most died in the Pacific War from 1941 to 1945.
68976.m: About 2.5 million war dead are commemorated at the Yasukuni Shrine.

68977.q: Why has the Yasukuni Shrine been especially controversial since 1978?
a: 14 Class A war criminals were enshrined there
68977.e: In 1978, 14 people accused as major war criminals were added in a secret ceremony, including Hideki Tojo. Since then, visits by politicians have sparked protests.
68977.m: The enshrinement of war criminals makes Yasukuni controversial.

68978.q: Which countries protest most when Japanese heads of government visit the Yasukuni Shrine?
68978.e: China and South Korea suffered greatly under Japanese occupation. For them, a visit is seen as playing down war crimes.
68978.m: Yasukuni visits strain Japan’s relations with China and South Korea.

68979.q: What is the war museum on the grounds of the Yasukuni Shrine called?
68979.e: The Yushukan displays weapons and mementoes of Japan’s wars. Critics accuse it of presenting a whitewashed picture.
68979.m: The Yushukan war museum belongs to the Yasukuni Shrine.

68980.q: What does the Japanese weather service use a cherry tree at the Yasukuni Shrine for?
a: As the reference tree for the start of cherry blossom in Tokyo
As a measuring point for earthquakes
As a sign of the start of typhoon season
68980.e: When enough blossoms are open on this Somei Yoshino tree, the cherry blossom in Tokyo is officially declared. Every spring this is news across the whole country.
68980.m: A cherry tree at the Yasukuni Shrine marks Tokyo’s cherry blossom.

68981.q: In which country did Caodaism arise in 1926?
68981.e: Caodaism was officially founded in southern Vietnam in 1926. At that time the area belonged to the French colony of Cochinchina.

68982.q: Which symbol stands for God in Caodaism?
68982.e: The divine eye reminds believers that God sees everything. It is often shown above a globe or in a triangle.
68982.m: The divine eye is the sign of Caodaism.

68983.q: Which French writer is venerated as a saint in Caodaism?
68983.e: Caodaists regard Victor Hugo as a spiritual intermediary with whom they made contact in seances. He is shown in a famous picture in the temple at Tay Ninh.
68983.m: Victor Hugo is venerated as a saint in Caodaism.

68984.q: Where is the Holy See of Caodaism with its great temple?
68984.e: The Holy See is in Tay Ninh, north-west of Ho Chi Minh City. The colourful temple is a well-known destination for visitors.
68984.m: The Holy See of the Caodaists is in Tay Ninh.

68985.q: Which three teachings are represented in Caodaism by the colours yellow, blue and red?
68985.e: Yellow stands for Buddhism, blue for Daoism and red for Confucianism. The robes of the dignitaries show these three branches.
68985.m: In Caodaism, yellow, blue and red stand for three teachings.

68986.q: How did the founders of Caodaism receive their messages?
68986.e: The founders held seances in which spirits and God himself are said to have spoken. Such sessions still play a role today.
68986.m: Caodaism is based on messages from spiritualist seances.

68987.q: On which church model is the hierarchy of Caodaism based?
68987.e: There is a pope, cardinals, archbishops, bishops and priests. This shows the French Catholic influence of the colonial period.
68987.m: The offices of Caodaism resemble those of the Catholic Church.

68988.q: Which group of religions does Tenrikyo belong to?
a: The new religions of Japan from the 19th century
68988.e: Tenrikyo arose in 1838 and is regarded as one of the first new religions of Japan. It has roots in Shinto but is a religion of its own.
68988.m: Tenrikyo is a new religion from Japan.

68989.q: Who founded the Japanese religion Tenrikyo?
a: A farmer’s wife who experienced a revelation
68989.e: Nakayama Miki from the Nara area experienced a revelation in 1838. Her followers lovingly call her Oyasama, ‘Parent’.
68989.m: Tenrikyo was founded by a woman.

68990.q: Which Japanese city bears the name of the religion Tenrikyo, which has its headquarters there?
68990.e: The city of Tenri near Nara was named after the religion in 1954. It is home to the place Tenrikyo venerates as the origin of humankind.
68990.m: The city of Tenri is the centre of Tenrikyo.

68991.q: What life goal do followers of Tenrikyo pursue?
68991.e: God is said to have created human beings in order to see them live a joyous life. To this end, the mind is to be freed from selfishness and greed.
68991.m: Tenrikyo strives for the joyous life.

68992.q: What does Tenrikyo teach about the human body?
a: It is a prison of the soul
68992.e: The body is regarded as ‘a thing lent’; only the mind belongs to the person. That is why the body should be used with gratitude.
68992.m: According to Tenrikyo, the body is lent by God.

68993.q: What does Tenrikyo compare bad thoughts such as greed, hatred and arrogance to?
a: Dust that has to be swept away
Poison you can never get rid of
68993.e: Tenrikyo names eight kinds of mental dust. Like dust, they gather easily but can be swept away regularly.
68993.m: For Tenrikyo, bad thoughts are like dust.

68994.q: What is the most important scripture of revelation in Tenrikyo, written by the founder?
68994.e: The Ofudesaki, ‘Tip of the Writing Brush’, contains about 1,700 verses in poetic form. There are also the Mikagura-uta and the Osashizu.
68994.m: The Ofudesaki is the main scripture of Tenrikyo.

68995.q: Which god rises to become king of the gods in the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish?
68995.e: In the epic, Marduk defeats the primeval goddess Tiamat and is made king by the gods for it. He was the city god of Babylon.
68995.m: In the Enuma Elish, Marduk becomes king of the gods.

68996.q: Which primeval goddess embodies the salty sea water in the Enuma Elish?
68996.e: Tiamat stands for salt water, her partner Apsu for fresh water. The first gods arise from the mixing of the two.
68996.m: In the Enuma Elish, Tiamat is the salty primeval sea.

68997.q: What does the primeval god Apsu stand for in the Enuma Elish?
a: The fresh water beneath the earth
68997.e: Apsu is the underground fresh water. He is killed by the god Ea, who builds his dwelling on top of him.
68997.m: In the Enuma Elish, Apsu embodies fresh water.

68998.q: Which culture does the creation epic Enuma Elish come from?
68998.e: The Enuma Elish has come down to us in Akkadian cuneiform. It celebrates Marduk, the city god of Babylon.
68998.m: The Enuma Elish is Babylon’s creation myth.

68999.q: Which Bible text is the Enuma Elish often compared with?
a: The creation story in the Book of Genesis
68999.e: Both texts tell how heaven and earth arise from the primeval waters. The biblical account, however, distances itself from the battle of the gods.
68999.m: The Enuma Elish and Genesis 1 both tell of creation.

69000.q: At which festival was the Enuma Elish recited in Babylon?
a: At the Akitu New Year festival
At the harvest festival of Sukkot
At the Wag festival of the dead
At the festival of lights, Diwali
69000.e: At the Akitu festival in spring, the epic was recited and Marduk’s rule was solemnly renewed. The festival lasted several days.
69000.m: The Enuma Elish was recited at the Akitu New Year festival.

69001.q: What are humans created for in the Enuma Elish?
a: To take the work off the gods
To give names to the animals
69001.e: Humans are made from the blood of the defeated god Kingu. They are to work for the gods so that the gods can rest.
69001.m: In the Enuma Elish, humans serve the gods.

69002.q: What does Marduk form from Tiamat’s body after his victory?
69002.e: Marduk splits Tiamat’s body in two halves. From one he makes the sky, from the other the earth.
69002.m: Marduk creates heaven and earth from Tiamat’s body.

69003.q: What was the main building material of the ziggurats of Mesopotamia?
69003.e: The core was made of sun-dried mud bricks, the outer shell often of fired bricks with bitumen as mortar. Natural stone was scarce in the land between the two rivers.
69003.m: Ziggurats were mainly built of mud bricks.

69004.q: Which people built the first ziggurats in Mesopotamia?
69004.e: The first ziggurats appeared in Sumerian cities such as Ur and Uruk. King Ur-Nammu had the Great Ziggurat of Ur built in the 21st century BC.
69004.m: The Sumerians built the first ziggurats.

69005.q: In which present-day country is the Elamite ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
69005.e: Chogha Zanbil was built in the 13th century BC by the Elamite king Untash-Napirisha. It is regarded as one of the best-preserved ziggurats.
69005.m: The ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil is in Iran.

69006.q: According to ancient accounts, what stood on the top level of a ziggurat?
a: A high temple for the deity
69006.e: Herodotus describes a temple at the top of the ziggurat of Babylon. The ziggurat was regarded as a link between heaven and earth.
69006.m: A high temple stood at the top of a ziggurat.

69007.q: What does the Egyptian goddess and idea of Maat stand for?
69007.e: Maat refers to the right order of the world, of society and of actions. The goddess Maat embodies this principle.
69007.m: Maat stands for truth, justice and order.

69008.q: Which symbol does the goddess Maat wear on her head?
69008.e: The ostrich feather is Maat’s emblem. It also serves as the hieroglyph for her name.
69008.m: The goddess Maat wears an ostrich feather.

69009.q: In the Egyptian judgement of the dead, what is weighed against the feather of Maat?
a: The heart of the dead person
The name of the dead person
69009.e: The heart was regarded as the seat of conscience. If it was no heavier than the feather, the dead person could enter the afterlife.
69009.m: In the judgement of the dead, the heart is weighed against Maat’s feather.

69010.q: According to Egyptian belief, which hybrid creature eats the heart of a guilty dead person?
69010.e: Ammit has parts of a crocodile, a lion and a hippopotamus. Whoever’s heart she devours is destroyed for ever.
69010.m: Ammit eats the hearts of the guilty.

69011.q: Which jackal-headed god operates the scales at the Egyptian judgement of the dead?
69011.e: Anubis was the god of mummification and accompanied the dead. Thoth writes down the result of the weighing.
69011.m: Anubis operates the scales at the judgement of the dead.

69012.q: What is the collection of spells called that Egyptians placed in the tomb with the dead?
69012.e: The Book of the Dead was meant to help the dead person survive the dangers of the afterlife. It also says how he declares his innocence before the judgement of the dead.
69012.m: The Egyptian Book of the Dead helped the dead in the afterlife.

69013.q: What was the pharaoh’s role with regard to Maat?
a: He had to make Maat a reality on earth
He could change Maat as he wished
He had to choose Maat anew every year
69013.e: The king was regarded as the guarantor of world order. In rituals he presented the gods with a small figure of Maat as an offering.
69013.m: The pharaoh was obliged to make Maat a reality.

69014.q: In Egyptian mythology, the goddess Maat is regarded as the daughter of which god?
69014.e: Maat was worshipped as the daughter of Ra, who set up world order at creation. It was said that Ra lived on Maat.
69014.m: The goddess Maat is regarded as the daughter of the sun god Ra.

69015.q: To which two goddesses were the Eleusinian Mysteries dedicated?
69015.e: At the centre were Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone, also called Kore. Eleusis lies north-west of Athens.
69015.m: The Eleusinian Mysteries honoured Demeter and Persephone.

69016.q: According to myth, why does Persephone have to spend part of every year in the underworld?
a: Because she had eaten pomegranate seeds there
Because she had poisoned a river
Because she had ignored an oracle
69016.e: Anyone who had eaten food of the underworld was bound to it. The myth explained the time of her absence as winter, when nothing grows.
69016.m: Because of the pomegranate seeds, Persephone returns to the underworld every year.

69017.q: Why is so little known even today about the exact course of the initiation at Eleusis?
a: The initiates were bound to strict secrecy
All texts were destroyed in an earthquake
The ceremonies only took place once
69017.e: Anyone who revealed the secrets faced the death penalty. That is why ancient authors only hinted at what happened.
69017.m: The initiates of Eleusis had to keep silent.

69018.q: What was the road called along which the procession of the Greater Mysteries went from Athens to Eleusis?
69018.e: The Sacred Way linked Athens with Eleusis, about 20 kilometres away. The participants walked the route on foot.
69018.m: The procession to Eleusis went along the Sacred Way.

69019.q: Which natural phenomenon did the myth of Demeter and Persephone explain?
69019.e: As long as Persephone is in the underworld, Demeter mourns and nothing grows. When her daughter returns, the earth blossoms again.
69019.m: The myth of Demeter and Persephone explains the seasons.

69020.q: What was the high priest of the Eleusinian Mysteries called, who showed the sacred objects?
69020.e: Hierophant means ‘the one who shows the sacred’. He traditionally came from the family of the Eumolpidae.
69020.m: The hierophant led the Eleusinian Mysteries.

69021.q: Which symbol belongs to the goddess Demeter, who was worshipped at Eleusis?
69021.e: Demeter is the goddess of grain and fertility. The trident belongs to Poseidon, the owl to Athena and the thunderbolt to Zeus.
69021.m: The ear of grain is Demeter’s symbol.

69022.q: When did the Eleusinian Mysteries end?
a: At the end of the 4th century AD
69022.e: Emperor Theodosius I banned the pagan cults, and in AD 396 the Visigoths under Alaric laid waste to the sanctuary. This ended a tradition of more than a thousand years.
69022.m: The Eleusinian Mysteries ended at the end of the 4th century AD.

69023.q: Which mythical figure is Orphism named after?
69023.e: Orpheus was regarded as a divinely gifted singer who even went down into the underworld. The sacred writings of the Orphics were attributed to him.
69023.m: Orphism is named after the singer Orpheus.

69024.q: What does the Orphic formula ‘soma sema’ say?
a: The body is a tomb of the soul
The soul dies with the body
The soul lives in the heart
69024.e: The Orphics saw the soul as locked in the body as if in a prison. Plato takes up this play on words in the dialogue ‘Cratylus’.
69024.m: For the Orphics, the body was a tomb of the soul.

69025.q: What idea about the soul did the Orphics hold?
a: A single life with no afterlife
69025.e: According to Orphic teaching, the soul travels through several bodies. Through a pure life it could free itself from this cycle.
69025.m: The Orphics believed in a cycle of rebirths.

69026.q: Which rule of life has come down to us for followers of Orphism?
a: A daily bath in the sea
69026.e: Because the soul could also live in animals, the Orphics avoided blood sacrifices and meat dishes. People spoke of the ‘Orphic life’.

69027.q: According to the Orphic myth, what do humans come from?
a: The ashes of the Titans who had killed Dionysus
69027.e: The Titans had killed the child Dionysus and were burnt by Zeus with his thunderbolt. That is why humans carry both a Titanic and a divine inheritance.
69027.m: According to Orphism, humans come from the ashes of the Titans.

69028.q: According to the Orphic gold tablets, what should the dead do in the underworld?
a: Drink from the spring of Mnemosyne
69028.e: The inscribed gold tablets from graves warn against the spring of forgetting. Instead, the dead person is to drink the water of memory.
69028.m: The gold tablets advised the dead to drink from the spring of memory.

69029.q: Which Greek philosopher took Orphic ideas such as the transmigration of souls into his works?
69029.e: In several dialogues, Plato speaks of the immortal soul and its journey through different lives. In doing so he takes up Orphic ideas.
69029.m: Plato took over Orphic ideas about the soul.

69030.q: What were the ecstatic female followers of Dionysus called?
69030.e: The maenads, or bacchantes, roamed the mountains in ecstasy. Their name comes from the Greek word for ‘to rave’.
69030.m: The female followers of Dionysus were called maenads.

69031.q: Apart from the grapevine, which plant is a typical sign of Dionysus?
69031.e: Dionysus and his followers wear wreaths and carry staffs with ivy and vine leaves. Laurel belongs to Apollo, the olive branch to Athena.
69031.m: Ivy and the grapevine are signs of Dionysus.

69032.q: Which art form arose in Athens as part of the festivals for Dionysus?
69032.e: At the Great Dionysia, tragedies were performed in competition. The Theatre of Dionysus lay on the southern slope of the Acropolis.
69032.m: Tragedy arose at the festivals for Dionysus.

69033.q: Who are the parents of Dionysus in Greek myth?
69033.e: Semele was a mortal king’s daughter from Thebes. Zeus carried the unborn child in his thigh after Semele had been burnt up.
69033.m: Dionysus is the son of Zeus and Semele.

69034.q: In which tragedy by Euripides does King Pentheus resist the cult of Dionysus?
69034.e: Euripides wrote ‘The Bacchae’ at the end of his life. Pentheus of Thebes persecutes the new cult and is cruelly punished for it.

69035.q: What did the Romans call the wild festivals in honour of Dionysus?
69035.e: To the Romans, Dionysus was Bacchus. Because the Bacchanalia were considered dangerous, the Senate strictly restricted them in 186 BC.
69035.m: The festivals for Bacchus were called Bacchanalia.

69036.q: Which hybrid creatures with horses’ tails belong to the followers of Dionysus?
69036.e: Satyrs are boisterous nature spirits with animal features. The satyr play, which followed three tragedies, is named after them.
69036.m: Satyrs belong to the followers of Dionysus.

69037.q: Which Roman was the first to be officially raised to a state god, ‘Divus’, after his death?
69037.e: In 42 BC the Senate declared Caesar Divus Iulius. A comet after his death was seen as a sign that he had been taken up among the gods.
69037.m: Caesar was the first Roman to be made a divus.

69038.q: Which title did Octavian, later Augustus, use after Caesar’s deification?
69038.e: Divi filius means ‘son of the deified one’. Octavian was Caesar’s adopted son and used this descent for political ends.
69038.m: Augustus called himself Divi filius, son of the deified one.

69039.q: By what authority was a dead emperor officially deified in Rome?
a: By a decision of the Senate
By the high priest in Alexandria
69039.e: This elevation was called consecratio. Emperors whom the Senate rejected received no deification or were even condemned.
69039.m: The Senate decided on an emperor’s deification.

69040.q: With which goddess was Augustus worshipped jointly in the eastern provinces during his lifetime?
69040.e: In the east, Augustus only allowed temples together with the goddess Roma, for example in Pergamon. In this way both Rome itself and the ruler were honoured.
69040.m: In the east, Augustus was worshipped together with Roma.

69041.q: Which present-day city was called Lugdunum in Roman times and was a centre of the imperial cult in Gaul?
69041.e: Lugdunum had a great altar to Roma and Augustus. Representatives of the Gallic tribes gathered there every year.
69041.m: The emperor was worshipped in Roman Lugdunum, today’s Lyon.

69042.q: According to Suetonius, which emperor is said to have joked on his deathbed: ‘Oh dear, I think I am becoming a god’?
69042.e: Vespasian died in AD 79 and was known for his dry humour. The remark refers to the usual deification of dead emperors.
69042.m: Vespasian joked on his deathbed about his deification.

69043.q: What did Emperor Decius demand of all the empire’s inhabitants in 249/250?
a: A sacrifice to the gods with a written certificate
The building of an imperial temple in every town
A tax for the imperial cult
69043.e: Anyone who had sacrificed received a certificate, a so-called libellus. Many Christians refused to sacrifice and were persecuted.
69043.m: Decius demanded a certified sacrifice from everyone.

69044.q: In Egyptian mythology, who is the husband of the goddess Isis?
69044.e: Isis gathered the pieces of Osiris, who had been killed by Set, and brought him back to life. Their son is Horus.
69044.m: Isis is the wife of Osiris.

69045.q: In which ancient novel is Lucius turned back from a donkey into a human by the goddess Isis?
69045.e: The ‘Metamorphoses’ is also called ‘The Golden Ass’. In the eleventh book, Lucius is initiated into the mysteries of Isis.
69045.m: In Apuleius, Isis rescues Lucius, who has been turned into a donkey.

69046.q: What was celebrated at the festival Navigium Isidis in March?
a: The opening of the sailing season
69046.e: In the Roman Empire, Isis was regarded as the protector of seafarers. At the festival a decorated ship was launched into the sea.
69046.m: The Navigium Isidis opened the sailing season.

69047.q: Which musical instrument is typical of the cult of Isis?
69047.e: The sistrum has movable metal discs on rods. It was shaken in processions and services.
69047.m: The sistrum is the instrument of Isis.

69048.q: What was the great sanctuary of Isis on the Campus Martius in Rome called?
69048.e: The Iseum Campense was splendidly rebuilt under Domitian. Several Egyptian obelisks in Rome come from there.
69048.m: The Iseum Campense was the temple of Isis on the Campus Martius.

69049.q: Which Hellenistic god was often worshipped together with Isis in the Roman Empire?
69049.e: Serapis was introduced in Egypt under Ptolemy I. He combined features of Osiris and of Greek gods.
69049.m: Serapis was often worshipped together with Isis.

69050.q: In which town near Vesuvius was a temple of Isis well preserved by the eruption of AD 79?
69050.e: The temple of Isis in Pompeii had been rebuilt after an earthquake. The ash preserved it along with its wall paintings.
69050.m: A temple of Isis survived in Pompeii.

69051.q: Which temple of Isis is regarded as the last in use and was closed under Emperor Justinian?
69051.e: On the Nile island of Philae, Isis was still worshipped into the 6th century. Because of the Aswan Dam, the temple was moved to a neighbouring island.
69051.m: The temple of Isis at Philae was the last to be closed.

69052.q: What does the Greek word ‘gnosis’ mean?
69052.e: The Gnostics believed that secret knowledge about God and the origin of the soul brings salvation. That is where the name comes from.

69053.q: What do Gnostic teachings call the lesser creator of the material world?
69053.e: In Gnosticism, the demiurge is regarded as ignorant or even evil. He is distinguished from the highest, hidden God and is sometimes called Yaldabaoth.
69053.m: In Gnosticism, the demiurge is the creator of matter.

69054.q: How do most Gnostic teachings view the material world?
a: As a prison from which the divine spark must be freed
As the perfect work of the highest God
As a meaningless mirror of the gods
As an eternal and unchanging order
69054.e: According to Gnostic teaching, there is a divine spark of light in every human. Through knowledge it is to return to the heavenly world.
69054.m: Gnosticism sees matter as the prison of the divine spark.

69055.q: Where was an important collection of Gnostic writings discovered in 1945?
a: At Qumran by the Dead Sea
69055.e: Farmers found 13 papyrus volumes in the Coptic language in a clay jar. Before that, Gnosticism was known almost only from the writings of its opponents.
69055.m: Gnostic writings were found at Nag Hammadi in 1945.

69056.q: Which gospel, with 114 sayings of Jesus, is known in full only from the Nag Hammadi find?
69056.e: The Gospel of Thomas contains no narrative but a collection of sayings. It is not part of the New Testament.
69056.m: The Gospel of Thomas is known in full from Nag Hammadi.

69057.q: How did the early Church judge the teachings of the Gnostics?
a: As the basis of the New Testament
As the teaching of the apostle Peter
69057.e: Church Fathers such as Irenaeus of Lyon wrote against the Gnostics and called their teachings heresies. For a long time Gnosticism was known almost only from these polemics.
69057.m: The early Church fought Gnosticism as heresy.

69058.q: According to Gnostic teaching, how is a person saved?
69058.e: The Gnostics believed that the divine spark in a person is freed through knowledge. This knowledge was only available to initiates.

69059.q: Who founded Manichaeism in the 3rd century?
69059.e: Mani was born in 216 in the region of Babylonia. He proclaimed his teaching in the Persian Sasanian Empire.
69059.m: Mani founded Manichaeism in the 3rd century.

69060.q: Which two primal principles are opposed in Manichaeism?
69060.e: Manichaeism teaches a strict dualism. Parts of the light are trapped in matter and are to be set free.
69060.m: In Manichaeism, light and darkness struggle with each other.

69061.q: Which three founders of religions did Mani see as his predecessors?
69061.e: Mani saw himself as the last messenger in a line of prophets. That is why he took in elements of different religions.
69061.m: Mani saw Zarathustra, Buddha and Jesus as his predecessors.

69062.q: Why was Manichaeism persecuted in the Persian Empire?
a: The Zoroastrian priests saw it as a rival
It called for war against Persia
69062.e: Under the great king Bahram I, Zoroastrian priests gained influence at court. Mani was arrested and died in prison around 276/277.
69062.m: Mani died in prison because his teaching was seen as a rival.

69063.q: Which later Church Father belonged to the Manichaeans as a ‘hearer’ for about nine years?
69063.e: Augustine describes this time in his ‘Confessions’. After his conversion he wrote several works against the Manichaeans.
69063.m: Augustine was a Manichaean for some years.

69064.q: Into which two groups was the Manichaean community divided?
69064.e: The Elect, in Latin electi, lived strictly ascetic lives. The Hearers, auditores, provided for them and lived less strictly.
69064.m: The Manichaeans were divided into the Elect and the Hearers.

69065.q: How far east did Manichaeism spread along the Silk Road?
a: Only to the border of Persia
69065.e: Merchants carried the teaching along the Silk Road as far as China. Among the Uyghurs it was even the state religion in the 8th century.
69065.m: Manichaeism reached as far as China via the Silk Road.

69066.q: On which island were the manuscripts of the Edda written in the Middle Ages?
69066.e: The Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda were written down in Iceland in the 13th century. They preserve the myths of the Norse gods.

69067.q: Who wrote the Prose Edda around 1220 as a textbook of poetry?
69067.e: Snorri Sturluson was an Icelandic scholar and politician. His Edda explains the old myths and poetic images to poets.
69067.m: Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda.

69068.q: What is the downfall of the gods and the world called in the Edda?
69068.e: In the Edda, a seeress tells of the end of the world, Ragnarök, in which gods and giants fight. Afterwards a new world arises.
69068.m: Ragnarök is the end of the world in Norse mythology.

69069.q: Which gods does the Edda tell of?
69069.e: The Edda is the most important source for the world of the Norse gods. It tells of Odin, his son Thor and the cunning Loki.
69069.m: The Edda tells of the Norse gods.

69070.q: What does the Old Norse term ‘Ragnarök’ literally mean?
69070.e: The common translation ‘Twilight of the Gods’ comes from the variant form ‘ragnarøkkr’. It refers to the downfall of the world of the gods.
69070.m: Ragnarök means fate of the gods.

69071.q: By whom is Odin swallowed at Ragnarök?
69071.e: The chained wolf Fenrir breaks free at the end of the world and kills Odin. Odin’s son Vidar then avenges him.
69071.m: At Ragnarök, the wolf Fenrir swallows Odin.

69072.q: What is the long winter called that comes before Ragnarök?
69072.e: The Fimbulwinter consists of three winters with no summers in between. It is regarded as a sign of the end of the world.

69073.q: According to the Völuspá, who sets the world on fire at the end of Ragnarök?
69073.e: Surtr comes from Muspelheim, the world of fire. Afterwards the earth sinks into the sea and later rises again, renewed.
69073.m: Surtr sets the world on fire.

69074.q: In which work does Gaius Julius Caesar describe the Gallic druids in detail?
69074.e: In the sixth book of his account of the Gallic War, Caesar describes the society of the Gauls. The druids take up a lot of space in it.
69074.m: Caesar describes the druids in De bello Gallico.

69075.q: According to Caesar, how long did the training to become a druid last for some students?
69075.e: The students had to learn a great number of verses by heart. According to Caesar, some therefore stayed in training for twenty years.
69075.m: According to Caesar, a druid’s training lasted up to 20 years.

69076.q: According to Caesar, why did the druids not write down their teaching?
a: So that it would not become widely known and memory stayed trained
Because the Romans burnt all books
69076.e: Caesar gives two reasons: the teaching was not to spread among ordinary people, and the students were to train their memory. For other purposes the Gauls used Greek letters.
69076.m: The druids passed on their teaching orally.

69077.q: Which teaching about the soul does Caesar attribute to the druids?
a: After death the soul passes into another
The soul perishes with the body
The soul stays living in the grave
69077.e: Caesar thinks this teaching took away the warriors’ fear of death. It is reminiscent of ideas about the transmigration of souls.
69077.m: According to Caesar, the druids taught that the soul lives on.

69078.q: Which people did the druids belong to?
69078.e: The druids were priests, judges and scholars among the Celts in Gaul and Britain. Celts also lived in what is now Switzerland.
69078.m: The druids were the priests of the Celts.

69079.q: According to Caesar, what was the harshest punishment the druids could impose?
69079.e: Anyone excluded from the sacrifices was regarded as godless and criminal. Everyone avoided him and he lost his rights.
69079.m: The harshest druid punishment was exclusion from the sacrifices.

69080.q: According to Caesar, which country did the teaching of the druids come from?
69080.e: Caesar reports that the teaching arose in Britain. Anyone who wanted to learn it thoroughly still travelled there in his day.
69080.m: According to Caesar, the druid teaching came from Britain.

69081.q: In which two present-day municipalities is the Roman town of Augusta Raurica?
69081.e: Augst is in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, Kaiseraugst in the canton of Aargau. The town lay right on the Rhine.
69081.m: Augusta Raurica lies in Augst and Kaiseraugst.

69082.q: Roughly when was the Roman town of Augusta Raurica founded?
69082.e: A funerary inscription of Lucius Munatius Plancus mentions a colony in the territory of the Rauraci in 44 BC. The town was permanently settled around 15 BC.
69082.m: Augusta Raurica was founded in the 1st century BC.

69083.q: Which gods did the people of Augusta Raurica worship?
a: Only Germanic gods such as Wotan
69083.e: In the temples of Augusta Raurica, Roman gods were often combined with Celtic ones, for example in the sanctuary at Grienmatt with its healing bath. The emperor was also worshipped.
69083.m: In Augusta Raurica, Roman and Celtic gods were worshipped.

69084.q: What is a Gallo-Roman ambulatory temple?
a: A temple with a square cella and a walkway around it
A round temple without a roof
A temple in a rock cave
A temple on a raft in the river
69084.e: This type of building combines Celtic tradition with Roman building methods. It appears several times in Augusta Raurica and Aventicum.
69084.m: An ambulatory temple has a cella with a walkway around it.
